Yumi Language Reference

This reference describes the whole Yumi language: every form a program can contain, what each one means, and the rules the compiler enforces. It is written to be complete rather than gentle. Read a chapter from the top to learn a feature, or jump to an entry to look one up.

Yumi programs are written in Brix, in .bx files. Each construct is stored as a form: an S-expression such as - name Type(param name Type). Brix is shown as rows, with indentation, dividers and operators, so the same parameter is shown as - name Type. This reference writes code as forms. The website shows the forms as rows, with a toggle to show the forms themselves. Each example is a whole program, and when it prints, its output follows it.

The core library's types, such as String, List and Map, are part of the language and are covered here. The rest of the standard library is surveyed in its own chapter.

Chapters

  1. Source text: files, rows, indentation, dividers, names and comments, and how rows and forms relate.
  2. Literals: numbers, text, characters, lists, maps and ranges.
  3. Modules: imports, exports, values that belong to a file, and the code a file runs.
  4. Functions: declarations, value bodies and step bodies, lazy bindings, parameters, results, calls, function values and generic functions.
  5. Types: classes, tuples, structs, properties, constructors, methods, generic types, inheritance, interfaces, delegation and extensions.
  6. Optionals: absence, null, fallbacks, chains and narrowing.
  7. Unions and enums: values that are one of several cases, and named values of one type.
  8. Conversions: what converts on its own, as, conversions a type declares, and joins.
  9. Operators: every operator, its precedence, and how a type defines its own.
  10. Control flow: locals and blocks, conditions, decision tables and loops.
  11. Patterns: match, every kind of pattern, and taking values apart.
  12. Text: strings, characters, building text from values, text bodies and atoms.
  13. Collections: lists, maps, arrays, views, tables, bitmaps and ranges as values.
  14. Streams: the stream family, generators, comprehensions, pipelines and targets.
  15. Stream patterns: grammars over text, bytes and other sequences.
  16. Errors: raising, propagation, catch, handlers, cleanup and panics.
  17. Concurrency: tasks, workers, channels and subscriptions.
  18. Reactivity: tracked reads, derived properties, rules, live statements and events.
  19. State machines: cases, transitions, payloads and lifetimes.
  20. Units: unit literals, unit families and conversions between them.
  21. Markup: elements, attributes, children, slots, and markup that follows state.
  22. Styles: styles, style sheets, rules, states, themes and motion.
  23. Probes: recording what a program does, and reading what it recorded.
  24. Native code and memory: C calls, C types, and memory outside the collector.
  25. Built-in types: the types every module can use without an import.

Two indexes close the reference, each pointing to the entry that explains what it lists:

  • Symbol index: operators, the marks that begin atoms and rows, names with a fixed meaning, and the functions core gives every module.
  • Form index: every Brix form, by its head, with its shape.

Source text

A Yumi program is text in files. A .bx file holds Brix forms, which are S-expressions. A .yumi file holds rows, which use indentation, dividers and operators. The two are views of one language: every form has a rows spelling, and every row a form. This chapter covers files, how forms are read, how rows are laid out, names, comments, and how the two views relate.

Files

  • Two kinds. The extension decides how a file is read: .bx as forms, and anything else as rows. Each file is read on its own, so one program can mix the two, and when x.bx and x.yumi sit side by side, an import of x reads x.bx. Modules covers how files find each other.
  • One kind in a file. A file holds forms or rows, never both.
  • UTF-8. Source text is UTF-8, with no byte-order mark. Write lines ending in LF; forms also accept CRLF.
  • Names. A file may have any name. The repository's files use lowercase words joined by hyphens. A dot in a file name marks a platform, as in input.macos.bx; see Platforms.
  • Empty files. An empty file is a module that declares nothing, and the last line needs no line ending.

Forms

/math

_ greeting String = "Hello"
-- greet("Ada")
-- hypotenuse(3.0, 4.0)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ greet String
    - name String

"$greeting, $name!"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ hypotenuse Float
    - a Float
    - b Float

sqrt(a * a + b * b)
(import /math)

(prop _ greeting String (= "Hello"))

(main
  (print (call greet "Ada"))
  (print (call hypotenuse 3.0 4.0))
)

(fn-expr + greet String
  (param name String)
  (str greeting ", " name "!")
)

(fn-expr + hypotenuse Float
  (param a Float)
  (param b Float)
  (call sqrt (+ (* a a) (* b b)))
)
Hello, Ada!
5

A file is a sequence of forms. A form is a list in parentheses, and its first item is its head, which says what the form is. The other items are its rows: atoms, texts and other forms.

  • Items. An item is an atom, such as greet, + or 3.0; a text in double quotes, which may span lines; or a list in parentheses.
  • Where an atom ends. An atom ends at whitespace, a parenthesis, a double quote or a ;. So (print(str"a""b")) is read like (print (str "a" "b")).
  • Heads. A head is a word from the language's vocabulary, such as fn-expr, let, if or print. A function is not a head: a call is written greet("Ada")(call greet "Ada").
  • Named arguments and operators. Two kinds of head are open. A head that starts with a colon names an argument, as in f • limit 3(call f (:limit 3)). A head between slashes is a named operator, as in 3 /max/ 4(/max/ 3 4).
  • One list with no head. The parameters of a function value are a plain list, as in :: a, b => a + b(=> (a b) (+ a b)).
  • The top level holds declarations, imports and (main …) forms, in any order. A function may come after the main that calls it.

Layout

-- area(2, 3)
-- "on one line"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ area Int
    - width Int
    - height Int

width * height

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

-- area(4, 5)
(main (print (call area 2 3)) (print "on one line"))
(fn-expr + area Int (param width Int) (param height Int) (* width height))
(main
  (print
    (call area
      4
      5
    )
  )
)
6
on one line
20
  • Whitespace separates items and means nothing else. Spaces, tabs and line breaks may go anywhere between items, and a form may sit on one line or spread over many.
  • The usual layout puts one row to a line, two spaces deeper than the form that holds it, and closes a form that spans lines on a line of its own. Functions, types and other declarations with bodies are set apart by a blank line. yumi lint --fix rewrites a file in this layout.
  • Hints. When a ) is missing or extra, the compiler uses the indentation to guess where it belongs.

Atoms

The first characters of an atom say what it is:

AtomRead as
A digit, or -, . or -. and a digitA number, as in -5, .5, 1'000, 0xff or 3km; see Literals.
'A'A character.
''TA type parameter.
.redA symbol or an enum case.
..nameAn anonymous case.
#nameA tracked read; see Reactivity.
&nameA reference.
$name, %nameA style read and a markup read.
C:nameA C name; see Native code and memory.
A capital letterA type name.
Anything elseA name.

Some atoms fill fixed places in a form:

  • Access. + is public, _ is private, and ^ shares a member with its file family, as in (fn-expr + greet String …).
  • The hole. _ in a type's place lets the compiler infer it, and in a pattern or a loop it stands for a value with no name.
  • Flags start with a colon, such as :get and :static, and annotations start with @, such as @inline. Both go in the header of a declaration, flags first.
  • Constants. true, false and null. nil, #t and #f are refused with a message that gives the Yumi spelling.

What is not an atom

  • No quoting. A ' starts a character or a type parameter and nothing else, and quote is not a form.
  • Generic types are forms. A list of integers is (of List Int), a map is (of Map String Int), and an optional is (? Int). List'Int is not a type name in forms.
  • Members are forms. A member read is (. corner x), and a method call is (call (. line split) ","). corner.x is not a name: the compiler says to write (. corner x).

What the reader refuses

(println "hello")
(main
  (println "hello")
)
Exception: `println` is not a form. Write `(print value)`.
<no file:3>
      (println "hello")
      ^
  • Unknown heads. A word that is not a form is refused. For a word some other language uses, such as lambda, defun, cond or try, the message names the Yumi form. Otherwise it shows how to call a function of that name.
  • A form in the wrong place. The message names the place and what it takes, as with (print …) cannot be a form at the top level of a file, which takes Top.
  • A form with too much. The message gives the form's shape, as with (let …) takes nothing more, and (list …) follows. Its shape is (let target:Binder/Pattern value:Expr/Block?).
  • Unbalanced parentheses and quotes are reported where the form or text began: Missing closing quote for the text opened at line 2, column 10.

Rows

The same program in rows:

/math

_ greeting String = "Hello"
-- greet("Ada")
-- hypotenuse(3.0, 4.0)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ greet String
    - name String

"$greeting, $name!"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ hypotenuse Float
    - a Float
    - b Float

sqrt(a * a + b * b)

Indentation

  • Four spaces make a level, and only spaces count. A row indented deeper than the row above belongs to it, as a body, a block or a parameter list.
  • Write whole levels. The level is the number of spaces divided by four, rounded down, and a tab counts for nothing. So a body indented with two spaces or a tab is not a body. A row may go one level deeper than the row above, not two.
  • Comment lines may be indented any way.
  • Blank lines do not end a block; only a row less indented does.

Dividers

A divider is a line of one glyph repeated at least three times, with nothing else on it, not even spaces. It begins a declaration that has a body, so the body can start at the left margin, and a method has the same shape as a function of the module.

DividerBegins
━━━━A declaration at the top level with a body: a function, a type with members, an extension or a style sheet.
────A function inside a type: a method, getter, setter, constructor or converter.
════A section of a value body.
  • Before the first divider come the file's imports, its module values, and the statements it runs.
  • After a divider comes the declaration's header, then its parameters, indented one level, then its body, flush with the header. A blank line between the header and the body is usual, but not required.
  • A body runs to the next divider. Anything below a body belongs to it, so the next declaration with a body needs its own divider: "+ g Int" is read as part of the body of "f", because no divider separates them; put a thick divider (━) on the line above it.
  • Back to the top level. A thick divider followed by a blank line ends the declaration above and returns to the top level, where module values and statements may follow.
  • Inside a type, a thick divider ends the type, and a thin divider begins a member function.

Row marks

A row begins with a mark that says what it is, followed by a space.

RowMeaningForm
+ name …, _ name …, ^ name …A public, private or shared declaration.(fn-expr + name …), (prop _ name …), (fn-do ^ name …)
- name TypeA parameter.- name Type(param name Type)
... name TypeThe rest parameter.(param ... name Type)
. name = valueA local.(let name value)
.. name = valueA lazy binding.(lazy name value)
= valueA return.= value(return value)
<= value, <<= values, <=? valueA yield of one item, of each item of a source, and of an item where it is not null.(yield value), (yield-all values), (yield? value)
-- valueA print.-- value(print value)
| patternA match arm, or a union case in a type.(case pattern …), (variant …)
|= value, |? condition, ??Arms taken on equality, on a condition, and otherwise.(case= …), (case? …), (default …)
|| pattern, ||= value, ||? conditionArms whose values keep their own types.(case-union …), (case-union= …), (case-union? …)
?! error if conditionA check.(throw error (if condition))
* value, ** valuesItems of a list built below it.(bullet value), (bullet* values)
?> condition, *> valuePipe stages, flush below a value.(pipe ?> condition), (pipe *> value)
• name valueA named argument.(:name value)
- value under a callOne argument.(arg value)
/path, ./pathAn import.(import /path)
// textA probe.(probe-log _ (text: "text"))
` textA comment.; text
A blank lineAn empty row.(blank)

Lines

  • Operators need spaces. A binary operator has a space on each side, because - can be part of a name: a-1 is one name, and a+b gives An operator needs a space on each side; write "a + b".
  • An expression ends at the end of its line. A line cannot end in an operator, a comma or an open bracket.
  • Longer constructs continue on indented rows.
    • A call with its arguments on - value rows below it.
    • A bullet at the end of a line takes the indented block below as its value, except on an if, else, while, match or for line, whose block is its body.
    • A list built from * rows below a builder.
    • Pipe stages, flush below the value they take.
    • A text continues on the next line after a \ at the end of a line.
  • One-line bodies. A colon puts a body of one step on the same line, as in if n > 9: -- "big" and for x in xs: -- x. In forms, such a step is wrapped in (inline …).
  • Braces. Blocks are written by indentation. if c { gives Blocks are written by indentation, not braces.

Names

. item-count = 3
. unit-price-2 = 20
. π = 3.5
-- item-count * unit-price-2
-- π * 2
. corner = Vec2(1, 2)
-- corner.x
-- List'Int(4, 5)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Vec2 is Tuple

+ x Int
+ y Int
(main
  (let item-count 3)
  (let unit-price-2 20)
  (let π 3.5)
  (print (* item-count unit-price-2))
  (print (* π 2))
  (let corner (call Vec2 1 2))
  (print (. corner x))
  (print (call (of List Int) 4 5))
)

(type + Vec2 (is Tuple)
  (prop + x Int)
  (prop + y Int)
)
60
7
1
4, 5
  • Values are named in lowercase words joined by hyphens, with digits allowed after the first letter: item-count, unit-price-2. A single Greek letter, such as π or Δ, is a name too, and so is °.
  • Types are named by a capital letter followed by letters and digits: Vec2, HttpRequest.
  • The first letter decides. A name that starts with a capital letter is read as a type, so a local cannot be capitalized and a type cannot start lowercase. A reader can tell a type from a value without finding its declaration.
  • Messages. A name in another case is refused with its kebab-case spelling: itemCount` is not a Yumi name. A name is lowercase words joined by hyphens: write `item-count`.
  • No ? or !. A name cannot hold ? or !. In rows, value! forces an optional and ?. chains one.
  • Reserved words. in, on, and, or, do, for, while, if and else cannot name a local or a parameter. Every other word can, including match, from, to, list and print.
  • C names are written C:name, in C's own spelling, as in C:getenv.
  • Generic names in rows. Rows write a type's arguments after an apostrophe, which needs no closing bracket and leaves < and > to comparison: List'Int is (of List Int), and Map'String'Int is (of Map String Int). The commonest types have shorter spellings: [Int] is (list Int), [String = Int] is (map String Int), <Int> is (stream Int) and Int? is (? Int).

Names with a meaning

  • This is the type being declared. A constructor is a function named This, and (call This count) makes another of the type.
  • this is the object a method was called on, as in this.count += 1(+= (. this count) 1). A property of the type can also be named bare inside the type.
  • each and it name the value in a pipe stage, a callback or a predicate arm.
  • _ is the hole (see Atoms), and at the start of a declaration it means private.

Shadowing

  • One name to a scope. Declaring a local twice in one scope is an error: "x" is already declared on line 1 in this scope.
  • Inner scopes may shadow. A local in a nested block, a loop item or a do body may reuse the name of an outer local, a parameter or an imported function. The inner one is used until its block ends.

Comments

` A comment runs from a semicolon to the end of its line.
` It has a row to itself, like any other row.
-- "one"

-- "two"
; A comment runs from a semicolon to the end of its line.
(main
  ; It has a row to itself, like any other row.
  (print "one")
  (blank)
  (print "two")
)
one
two
  • In forms, a comment runs from ; to the end of the line. It may come between any two items, but the usual layout gives it a row of its own. A ; inside a text is part of the text.
  • In rows, a comment is a line whose first character, after any spaces, is a backtick, as in ` A comment. It has a line to itself; there is no comment after code on the same line.
  • Not comments. In rows, # is refused with Comments start with a backtick, and // starts a probe; see Probes.
  • Doc comments. By convention, comment rows right under a declaration's header describe it. The compiler gives them no meaning.
  • Blank rows. (blank) is an empty row, kept so that the rows view can show it. It does nothing.

How rows and forms relate

RowsForms
Function+ double Int, a parameter - n Int, and the body n * 2━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + double Int - n Int n * 2(fn-expr + double Int (param n Int) (* n 2))
Step function+ do total Int(fn-do + total Int …)
Module value+ limit Int = 3+ limit Int = 3(prop + limit Int (= 3))
Local. shapes = [Square(2), Square(3)]. shapes = [Square(2), Square(3)](let shapes (list (call Square 2) (call Square 3)))
Calldescribe(2)describe(2)(call describe 2)
Membershape.areashape.area(. shape area)
Text with values"$a and $b""$a and $b"(str a " and " b)
Choiceif flag then "yes" else nullif flag then "yes" else null(if-expr flag "yes" null)
Named operator3 /max/ 43 /max/ 4(/max/ 3 4)
Function value:: x Int => x * 2:: x Int => x * 2(=> ((: x Int)) (* x 2))
  • Statements become (main …). The statements at a file's top level, before the first divider or after a thick divider and a blank line, are a (main …) form. Each run of them is one form, in file order.
  • Nesting. Forms nest by parentheses. Rows use operator precedence, and add parentheses where the forms need them: (+ (* a a) (* b b)) is a * a + b * b, and (* (+ a b) 2) is (a + b) * 2.
  • Layout is not carried over. Number spellings such as 1'000 and 0xff survive a trip from one view to the other and back. Several blank rows become one, several (main …) forms in a row become one, and a comment written after code moves to a row of its own.
  • Converting. yumi brix file.yumi writes file.bx beside the rows file, replacing any that is there.

Literals

A literal is a value written out in a program: a number, a text, a character, a truth, null, a list, a map, a tuple or a range. This chapter shows how each is written and what type it gets. Text, Collections and Units cover what can be done with them.

The rows view writes some literals differently from the forms. Where it does, this chapter shows both, as in [1, 2, 3](list 1 2 3) and [1, 2, 3].

Integers

-- 1'000'000
-- -17
-- 0xff
-- 300u8
-- 128i8
-- type-of 42
-- type-of 0x1'0000
-- type-of 9223372036854775808
(main
  (print 1'000'000)
  (print -17)
  (print 0xff)
  (print 300u8)
  (print 128i8)
  (print (type-of 42))
  (print (type-of 0x1'0000))
  (print (type-of 9223372036854775808))
)
1000000
-17
255
44
-128
[TypeInfo I64]
[TypeInfo U32]
[TypeInfo U64]
  • Decimal. An integer is written in decimal digits. A leading zero is not allowed in rows.
  • Separators. A ' between digits groups them and means nothing, as in 1'000'000. Each ' must have a digit on both sides.
  • Signs. A minus sign written against the digits is part of the literal, as in -17. There is no leading +.
  • Hexadecimal. 0x begins a hex literal, with digits in either case, as in 0xff or 0xFF. It prints in decimal.
  • No other bases. There are no binary or octal literals. 0b101 is read as 0 with the unit b101, and is an error: Unit "b101" not found.
  • Type. An integer with no suffix is an Int, which is an I64. One of 2^63 or more is a U64, and the largest is 18446744073709551615. One more is an error: Integer literal 18446744073709551616 does not fit U64.
  • A hex literal's type comes from how many digits it has, counting leading zeros: one or two make a U8, three or four a U16, five to eight a U32, and more a U64. So 0xff + 1(+ 0xff 1) is a U8 sum, and wraps to 0.

Suffixes

A suffix written straight after the number gives it a type:

TypeSuffixes
I8, I16, I32, I64i8, i16, i32, and i64, l or i
U8, U16, U32, U64u8, u16, u32, and u64, ul or u
F32, F64f32, and f64 or f
Boolb
I1i1
Charc
  • f is F64. 2f and 1.5f are F64s. Only f32 makes an F32.
  • Wrapping. A suffixed literal keeps the low bits that fit its type, so 300u8 is 44 and 128i8 is -128. Only one past the largest U64 is an error.
  • Whole numbers. An integer suffix takes no fraction or exponent: U8 holds whole numbers, so 1.5u8 cannot be written; write a whole number.
  • Units. Other suffixes are units, such as 16ms and 25%, which the modules that declare them must be imported for; see Units.

Floats

-- 2.5
-- .5
-- 2.5e-3
-- 1'000.25
-- 2.0
-- 1e21
-- 1.0 / 3.0
-- 1.0f32 / 3.0f32
-- 1.0 / 0.0
(main
  (print 2.5)
  (print .5)
  (print 2.5e-3)
  (print 1'000.25)
  (print 2.0)
  (print 1e21)
  (print (/ 1.0 3.0))
  (print (/ 1.0f32 3.0f32))
  (print (/ 1.0 0.0))
)
2.5
0.5
0.0025
1000.25
2
1e+21
0.3333333333333333
0.33333334
inf
  • Writing one. A number with a point or an exponent is a float: 2.5, .5, 5., 1e3, 2.5e-3, 4.2E+20. Separators work as in integers. There are no hex floats.
  • Type. A float with no suffix is a Float, which is an F64. f32 makes an F32.
  • No nan or inf. These have no literal. They come from arithmetic, as 1.0 / 0.0(/ 1.0 0.0) does, and print as nan, inf and -inf. A literal too large for its type is inf.
  • Printing. A float prints with the fewest digits that read back as the same number, so a whole float prints with no point, as 2 above. From 1e15 up and below 1e-4 it prints with an exponent, as 1e+21 and 1e-05.

The type a literal takes

A literal with no suffix takes the type of the place that holds it, or of a value beside it.

. small U8 = 200
. ratio Float = 2
. half F32 = 0.5
-- small + 100
-- small + 300
-- type-of ratio
-- type-of (half * 0.5)
-- [0, 4, 10.5]
-- twice(21)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ twice
    - n I32

n * 2
(main
  (let small U8 200)
  (let ratio Float 2)
  (let half F32 0.5)
  (print (+ small 100))
  (print (+ small 300))
  (print (type-of ratio))
  (print (type-of (* half 0.5)))
  (print (list 0 4 10.5))
  (print (call twice 21))
)

(fn-expr + twice _
  (param n I32)
  (* n 2)
)
44
500
[TypeInfo F64]
[TypeInfo F32]
0, 4, 10.5
42
  • Places. A declared local or property, a parameter, a list's declared item type and a result type each give a literal their type, as small, ratio and twice do above.
  • Neighbours. An operand beside a value of another number type takes that type: small + 100(+ small 100) is a U8 sum, which wraps to 44. A literal that does not fit stays an Int, and the sum is an Int, as small + 300(+ small 300) is.
  • Floats. An integer beside a float, or in a float's place, becomes a float, as the 0 and 4 in the list do. A float never becomes an integer this way: Expected I64 here, but this is F64, which becomes I64 only when asked; write "as I64".
  • Not other types. An integer never becomes a Bool or a Char by its place.
  • A hex literal keeps the type of its digit count, and converts only to a wider type.

A literal that does not fit its place is an error:

. small U8 = 200
. large U8 = 300
-- small + large
(main
  (let small U8 200)

  • Quotes. A text is written in double quotes, and "" is the empty text. Its type is String. Any character can be written as itself, including non-ASCII ones.
  • Escapes. A backslash begins an escape: \", \\, \$, \n, \t, \r, \xHH for a byte and \uHHHH for a character. Text lists them all.
  • Dollar signs. A $ must be escaped as \$. In rows, $name and ${…} insert values, and the forms write them with str: "Hi, $name" is "Hi, $name"(str "Hi, " name). See Text.
  • Line breaks. A line break inside the quotes is part of the text. The rows view writes it as \n.

Characters

-- 'A'
-- "[${' '}]"
-- '\n' as Int
-- 66c
-- type-of 'a'
-- 'a' + 1
(main
  (print 'A')
  (print (str "[" (char " ") "]"))
  (print (as (char "\n") Int))
  (print 66c)
  (print (type-of 'a'))
  (print (+ 'a' 1))

  • Single quotes. 'A' is a character. The forms write a visible ASCII character this way, except ", ', (, ), ; and \.
  • char. ' '(char " ") makes a character from a text of exactly one character, which may hold an escape. It is how the forms write a space, a quote, a non-ASCII character or a control character. The rows view writes all of them in single quotes, as ' ' and '\n'.
  • By code. The suffix c makes a character from its code point: 65c is A.
  • Type. A character is a Char, one Unicode code point, held in four bytes. It prints as the character, and arithmetic on it gives a U32, as 'a' + 1(+ 'a' 1) does. See Text.

  • Writing one. [2, 3, 5](list 2 3 5) is a list, written [2, 3, 5] in rows.
  • Item type. The items' common type is the item type, so [1, 2.5](list 1 2.5) holds F64s. Items with no common type are an error: This list mixes I64 and String, which have no common type; convert the items to one type. A declared item type is given to each literal item, as for ratios above.
  • Empty lists. [Int](list Int) as a local's type with no value declares an empty list, and List'Int()(call (of List Int)) makes one. A list literal with no items is an error, even where the type is declared: Incompatible types in list.
  • Printing joins the items with , . See Collections.

Maps

There is no map literal. A map is made by calling Map with its entries:

. sizes = Map • small 1 • large 3
. names = Map

    • (2) "two"

-- names[2]
-- names[5]

  (let sizes (call Map (:small 1) (:large 3)))

    (call Map
      (block

        (entry 2 "two")
      )
    )

  (print ([] names 2))

unknown
  • Entries. A named argument, as in • small 1(:small 1), is an entry whose key is its name, as text. • (key) value(entry key value) is an entry with any key, and •? (key) value(entry? key value) leaves the entry out when the value is null. In rows, Map • small 1 • large 3(call Map (:small 1) (:large 3)) is Map • small 1 • large 3.
  • Types. The keys' and the values' types come from the entries. The map type is written [String = Int](map String Int), and [String = Int] in rows.
  • Empty maps. [String = Int](map String Int) as a local's type with no value declares an empty map, and Map'String'Int()(call (of Map String Int)) makes one.
  • Repeated keys. The same name given twice is an error, while a later entry with the same key replaces the earlier one.
  • Reading a key gives an optional, null when the key is missing. See Collections.

Tuples

1, "a"(tuple 1 "a") is a tuple, written (1, "a") in rows. It prints as (1, a).

  • One item. A tuple of one item is that item, so a tuple form with only 1 in it is the Int 1.
  • Types. A declared tuple type gives each literal item its type, as in . point (Float, Float) = (1, 2)(let point (tuple Float Float) (tuple 1 2)).
  • Fields are read by a literal position, as in pair[0]([] pair 0). A position that is not a literal is an error: Value has no constant form. Named tuple types name their fields; see Types.

Other values written in place

  • Arrays. Int[4]([] Int 4) makes an array of four zeros. There is no array literal of items; Array'Int([2, 3, 5])(call (of Array Int) (list 2 3 5)) copies a list. See Collections.
  • Units. 16ms, 1.5s and 25% are numbers with units, once their modules are imported. See Units.
  • Cases. .name names a case of a union or an enum where its type is known, as in color == .red(== color .red). See Unions.
  • _ is not a value. It stands for a type to infer, a pattern that fits anything, or an open end of a range.

Constants

A module value whose value is a literal, such as + limit = 5(prop + limit _ (= 5)), is a constant: it is part of the compiled program and can be read before its module's code runs. An integer, a float, a text, a character, true or false makes a constant, and so does a minus sign on one of them. A list, a tuple, a call or any other expression is worked out when the module starts; see Modules.

Modules

A program is made of modules, and each module is one file. A file imports the modules whose names it uses, declares the values that belong to it, and may run code of its own when the program starts. This chapter covers how a file names another, what an import makes visible, exports, visibility, the values a file holds, the order in which files start, and how a program ends.

What a module is

  • One file. A module is a .bx file, in Brix, or a .yumi file, in rows. The two kinds import each other freely. A path names the file without its extension, so ./lib.bx(import ./lib.bx) is a missing module. When both.bx and both.yumi sit side by side, ./both is both.bx.
  • Folder modules. A folder is not a module, but it can hold one: a file with the folder's own name. /tui is the file tui/tui.yumi under the standard library. When a folder has such a file and a file of the same name sits beside the folder, the one inside the folder is the module. A folder with neither is a missing module, so /os(import /os) fails, while /os/path(import /os/path) finds os/path.yumi.
  • Platform modules. A file named with a platform after a dot, as in input.macos.bx, is part of that platform's builds only. Importing it for another platform imports nothing. Any other suffix is an error, except in a file family. Platforms lists the platforms and the families of them.
  • File families. A file named after another beside it, then a dot and more name, as box.scroll.bx is beside box.bx, belongs to the file family of that file, its base. .bx and .yumi files count alike.
    • The name after the base's may have several parts, and may end with a platform, as box.touch.ios.bx does, which makes the file part of that platform's builds only.
    • Only the family imports them. The base and the family's other files may import a family's files. Elsewhere it is an error: Module "./lib/box.scroll" belongs to the file family of box.yumi, so only that family can import it. Code outside imports the base, which imports the files of its family.
    • Ordinary modules. A family's files may declare anything a module may. A class's facets are declared in its family; see Types.
    • No base. A dotted name with no file of its first part beside it, such as host.macos.bx beside no host.bx, is no family's, and any module may import it.
  • Names. Stack traces, object text and some messages name a module.
    • The entry file, the one given to yumi, is always __source__, whatever the file is called.
    • A library module is named by its path without the leading /, as in os/path.
    • A program's other files are named by their path from the entry file's folder, as in models/account or ../shared/thing.

Imports

/math

-- sqrt(16.0)
-- abs(-2.5)
-- floor(2.7)
(import /math)

(main
  (print (call sqrt 16.0))
  (print (call abs -2.5))
  (print (call floor 2.7))
)
4
2.5
2
FormRowsFinds
/os/path(import /os/path)/os/pathos/path in the search paths.
./convert(import ./convert)./convertconvert beside the importing file.
./lib/shapes(import ./lib/shapes)./lib/shapesshapes in the folder lib beside it.
../shared/thing(import ../shared/thing)../shared/thingshared/thing from the importing file's parent folder.
+ ./circle(export ./circle)+ ./circleThe same as an import, and the names pass on; see Exports.
  • Every public name, unqualified. An import makes every public name of the module usable as if it were declared here: functions, types, module values, getters and setters, units, and the members of public extensions. There is no selective import, no renaming and no qualified access, so a module's own name is not a value.
  • One path each. An import takes one path, written bare and not in quotes. A file imports as many modules as it needs, one form each.
  • Where. An import stands at the top level of the file. Inside main it is an error.
  • Not passed on. An import gives its names to the file that writes it and to no other. When a imports b, a file that imports a must still import b to use b's names, unless a exports b.
  • Once. Each module is loaded once, however many files import it and however many times one file does.
  • Loaded even if unused. An import that nothing uses still loads its module, whose values are set and whose main runs. The compiler does not report it.
  • Private files. ./helper also finds _helper.bx beside the importing file when there is no helper file. Rooted paths name such files in full, as in /core/_bytes. A module whose name starts with _ belongs to the modules around it, by convention; the compiler does not stop others importing it.

Search paths

A rooted path, one that starts with /, is looked up in each search path in turn, and the first folder that holds it wins.

  • The default is the toolchain's standard library and nothing else.
  • YUMIPATH, when it is set, replaces the default with its colon-separated folders. List the standard library among them, because without it no program builds: Module "core" not found.
  • A program's own files are reached by relative paths, ./ and ../, from the file that imports them. There is no project file or manifest, and a project's root folder plays no part.

A name that is not imported

-- sqrt(16.0)
(main
  (print (call sqrt 16.0))
)
Exception: Function "sqrt" not found; it is declared in /math, which this module does not import. Add the import /math
<no file:3>
      (print (call sqrt 16.0))
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  • The suggestion. When a name is not found, the compiler looks for it in the modules the program loads and in the search paths, and names up to three modules that declare it.
  • A missing module is an error at the import: Module "no/such" not found for /no/such(import /no/such), and Module "./nothing" not found for ./nothing(import ./nothing).
  • The compiler's status. The compiler exits with status 2 when it reports errors.

Core

  • Always imported. Every module imports the core modules without writing them: core, core/error, core/number, core/string, core/type, core/backing, core/array, core/function, core/collection, core/list, core/map, core/range, core/stream, core/channel, core/event, core/tracker, core/parsing and core/task. That is where true, false, null, String, List, print and request-process-termination come from. Importing one of them by name changes nothing.
  • Imported on use. A module that writes stream patterns, markup or styles imports the core modules that support them without writing them.
  • The rest by name. Other modules under core, such as /core/table, are imported like any library. The Standard library lists them.

Overloads and clashes

  • Overloads across modules. Functions of one name overload one another across modules: a module's own describe taking a Float and two imported ones taking an Int and a String are one set, and each call reaches the one its arguments fit.
  • A module's own names first. A module value or type declared in the module hides an imported one of the same name.
  • Clashes between imports. The compiler does not report two imports that declare the same name; which one a use reaches depends on the order of the imports. The linter reports such clashes, as names/import-conflicts and names/local-shadows-import. Rename one of them.

Import cycles

Two modules may import each other, directly or through others, and the compiler does not report it. Each can call the other's functions. A cycle matters only to the values the modules set as they start: the module reached second starts first, so its values cannot read the other's eager values. Such a read panics, Global 'a-value' is read before it is initialized. A lazy value or a literal value breaks the dependency; see Order of initialization.

Exports

+ ./circle(export ./circle), in rows + ./circle, imports the module for this file and also passes its public names on to every file that imports this one.

  • The exporter uses them too. The exported module's names are usable in the file that exports it, as with an import.
  • Exports chain. When a exports b and b exports c, a file that imports a gets the names of all three.
  • Whole modules. An export takes one module path. There is no way to pass on one name.
  • Libraries. A library made of several files gathers them in its folder module. /tui is tui/tui.yumi, which exports the modules of the terminal library, so one import gives all of them. /units exports ./distance, so importing /units gives the distance units too, while importing /units/distance gives only those.

Visibility

Every declaration states its access: + is public and _ is private. That holds for module values, functions, types, members, extensions, events and units. A member may also be written with ^, shared with its file family.

  • Private means the file. A private name is usable anywhere in its own file: in functions, methods, setters and the rows of main. Two files in one folder cannot see each other's private names.
  • From another module, a private name is refused:
    • a private function or method: Function "helper" is private, declared with _, so only its own module can call it;
    • a private property, setter or computed property: Property "hidden" is private;
    • a private constructor: the message lists the constructors and says which are private to their module;
    • a private event: Event "poked" is private;
    • a private module value or type is not found, as if it were not declared: Name "secret" not found and Type "Hidden" not found.
  • Shared means the file family. A member declared with ^ is usable in every file of its module's file family, as a public one is, and refused elsewhere, as a private one is:
    • a shared method: Method "keep-end" of Box is shared, declared with ^, so only its own file family can call it;
    • a shared property: Property "width" is shared, declared with ^, so only its own file family can use it;
    • a shared constructor: the message lists the constructors and says which are shared with their file family.

    Only a member is shared, and ^ on anything else is an error: Only a member can be shared with its file family; declare this + or _. A shared event does not bubble, as a private one does not.

  • Facets. A file that declares a facet of a class reaches the private declarations of the file that declares the class, but that file does not reach the facet's. See Types.
  • Extensions. The members a public extension adds are visible in its own module and in the modules that import it or receive it through an export. A private extension's members are visible in its own module only. An extension must state its access, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + extend String ──────────────────── + shouted String self.uppercased(extend + String (fn-expr + shouted String (. self uppercased))).
  • Always public. Converters and unit equalities cannot be private: Converters must be public and Equalities must be public.

A prop at the top level of a file declares a module value. There is one of it for the whole program, shared by every task.

  • Defaults. A value with a type and no value takes the type's default: 0 for a number, "" for a String, null for an optional, an empty list for a list, and for a class, an object made by its constructor with no arguments.
  • Assigning. A module value can be assigned in its own file, and a public one in any file that imports it, with =, += and the other updates. A value computed at every read cannot be assigned: Setter not found.
  • Lazy values. A lazy value is computed at its first read, and never if nothing reads it. Assigning it before then skips its value. An error that leaves its value is reported at the read that started it.
  • What a value may read. A value's initializer reads other module values, functions and imports. It cannot read the locals of main, and neither can a function.
  • Not tracked. Module values cannot be tracked; see Reactivity.

  • Getters. A function marked :get is called wherever its name is read, in its module and in the modules that import it. A getter with no setter is a read-only module value.
  • Setters. A function marked :set is called wherever its name is assigned. An update such as += reads through the getter and stores through the setter.

Constants

A module value whose value is a literal number or text, with no decoration, is a constant. The program lays it down before any module starts, so any value or module may read it, even one that starts first. It can still be assigned.

A program starts in this order:

  1. Constants, in every module.
  2. Each module in turn, in initialization order:
    • its eager values, in the order the file declares them, whether anything reads them or not;
    • then its main.
  3. The entry file last.

The initialization order puts each module after the modules it imports, in the order its imports are written, and visits each module once. So when the entry file imports report and then tally, and report imports tally too, tally starts first, then report, then the entry file. In an import cycle, the module reached second starts first.

A file's eager values all come before its main, even those declared after it. Lazy values come when they are first read.

A value read before it is set

A value's initializer may read a value declared after it only if that value is a constant. Read directly, a later value is a compile error:
