  (param a Float)
  (param b Float)
  (call sqrt (+ (* a a) (* b b)))
)

(main
  (print (call hypotenuse ([] sides 0) ([] sides 1)))
)
first block
5
  • Every file's main runs. main holds the code that runs when its file starts, and every module's main runs once, after the module's values are set. A library's main runs before the files that import it.
  • Why. A program starts with what it does, with no entry function to declare. The cost falls on libraries: importing one sets its values and runs its main, which may read files or fail, so keep a library's main small.
  • Several main forms in one file are one body that runs in file order. A local of the first is visible in the next.
  • No main. A file without one only declares. Its values are still set as the program starts.
  • What main cannot hold. An import, a value standing alone, or a return: The top level of a module cannot return a value with "return"; remove the "return", or print the value with "print".
  • In rows, the statements of a file are its rows before the first divider. Another block of statements after the declarations follows a thick divider and a blank row, and becomes another (main …).

How a program ends

When the entry file's main finishes, the program waits for the tasks it started, then ends.

  • when-main-ends. The actions given to when-main-ends(action)(call when-main-ends action) run when main finishes, before its cleanups.
  • Errors. A recoverable error that leaves a main, the entry file's or another module's, ends the program with a report on stderr; see Errors.
  • Arguments and the environment come from libraries, not from core. /os/cli gives cmdline-args, a list of texts whose first item is the program's path, and cmdline, the arguments taken apart into a command, flags and options. /os/env gives env("HOME")(call env "HOME"), an optional text, and set-env("HOME", "/tmp")(call set-env "HOME" "/tmp").
-- "checking"
request-process-termination(3)
-- "main still ends its rows"
(main
  (print "checking")
  (call request-process-termination 3)
  (print "main still ends its rows")
)
checking
main still ends its rows
  • Requesting the end. request-process-termination(3)(call request-process-termination 3) asks the program to end with that status; with no argument the status is 130. The task goes on until it next waits, and the wait ends it. Tasks still running are not waited for.
StatusMeans
0The program ended normally.
1A recoverable error left a main or a task's body.
134A panic was not handled.
138The stack overflowed.
128 + the signalThe program was stopped by SIGHUP or SIGTERM.
Any otherThe program requested it.

Building and running

  • Checking. yumi app.bx checks the program: every declaration of the entry file, whether anything reaches it or not, and what it uses of other files.
  • Running. yumi app.bx -o build/app builds the executable at build/app and runs it, and exits with the program's status. Arguments for the program follow the source path; those that start with - follow --, as in yumi app.bx -o build/app -- --loud.
  • Building only. yumi app.bx --compile -o build/app builds without running.
  • Reached code. A build checks only the code the program reaches, so a broken function that nothing calls is reported by a check and not by a build.
  • A program in several files. Put the files in one folder, or in folders below it, import them with ./ and ../, and give yumi the entry file. yumi app.bx --list-sources lists every file the program loads.

Functions

A function is declared at the top level of a file or inside a type. Its header names it and states what it takes and gives. Its body is one of two kinds: a value body, whose rows describe the value the function gives, or a step body, whose rows run in order and return with = value(return value).

This chapter covers declarations, the two kinds of body, lazy bindings, results, parameters, calls, function values, generic functions, overloading and annotations. Methods, constructors and properties are functions inside a type; what is particular to them is in Types. Conversions a type declares are in Conversions, and operators a type defines are in Operators.

Declaring a function

-- describe(3)
-- area(2.0, 3.5)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - count Int

"$count ${noun(count)}"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
_ noun
    - count Int

if count == 1 then "item" else "items"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ area Float @inline
    - width Float
    - height Float

width * height
(main
  (print (call describe 3))
  (print (call area 2.0 3.5))
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param count Int)
  (str count " " (call noun count))
)

(fn-expr _ noun _
  (param count Int)
  (if-expr (== count 1) "item" "items")
)

(fn-expr + area Float @inline
  (param width Float)
  (param height Float)
  (* width height)
)
3 items
7

A declaration is a header, a parameter for each value the function takes, and then the body. In rows, the parameters are rows indented below the header row, and the body is flush with the left margin after a blank row. A thick divider (━) comes before a function at the top level of a file, and a thin divider (─) before a function inside a type.

A function with a value body is declared with fn-expr, and one with a step body with fn-do, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + do name Type body(fn-do + name Type body). The header then holds, in order:

  • Access. + makes the function public: other modules that import this one can call it. _ makes it private to its module. Private functions can be called anywhere in the module that declares them.
  • The name, in lowercase words joined by hyphens.
  • The result type, when it is written. Without one, _ in its place, the compiler infers it from the body.
  • Error types, each after ?!, naming the errors the function can raise, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + ratio Float ?! Error body(fn-expr + ratio Float (?! Error) body). See Errors.
  • Annotations, each starting with @.

Value bodies

A function declared with fn-expr, an expression function, has a value body. The body describes one value, and that value is what the function gives. A value body is the usual way to write a function, not a shorthand for small ones.

-- ratio(6.0, 4.0)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ratio Float ?! Error
    - width Float
    - height Float

?! Error("height is zero")
    if height == 0
-- "dividing $width by $height"

width / height
(main
  (print (call ratio 6.0 4.0))
)

(fn-expr + ratio Float (?! Error)
  (param width Float)
  (param height Float)
  (before
    (throw (call Error "height is zero") (if (== height 0)))
    (print (str "dividing " width " by " height))
  )
  (/ width height)
)
dividing 6 by 4
1.5

The value can be any expression. It can also be one of these forms, which give a value without being a single expression:

  • A decision table: |? condition value(case? condition value) arms, each with a condition and the value it gives, and a ?? value(default value) arm for every other case. A match is a table over one subject. See Control flow.
  • Bullets: rows such as * item(bullet item), each adding items to the list the function gives. See Streams.
  • A pipeline: a value followed by stage rows such as ?> condition(pipe ?> condition) and *> value(pipe *> value), each working on the result of the row above. See Streams.
  • A text body: the text the function gives, written as the text itself, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + ¶ greeting Hello.(fn-expr + greeting _ (paragraph "Hello.")). See Text.
  • Sections: a (header value) row, then value rows, each passed to the with method of what came before: the first to the header's value, and each later one to what the previous with gave. The function gives the last answer. In rows a section starts with a ════ divider.
-- size-label(2)
-- ", ".join(steps(true))
-- ", ".join(doubled-evens([1, 2, 3, 4]))

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ size-label String
    - count Int

|? count < 3
    "few"
|? count < 20
    "some"
??
    "many"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ steps [String]
    - verbose Bool

* "start"
*? "trace" if verbose
* "stop"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ doubled-evens [Int]
    - values [Int]

values
?> each % 2 == 0
*> each * 2
(main
  (print (call size-label 2))
  (print (call (. ", " join) (call steps true)))
  (print (call (. ", " join) (call doubled-evens (list 1 2 3 4))))
)

(fn-expr + size-label String
  (param count Int)
  (case? (< count 3)
    "few"
  )
  (case? (< count 20)
    "some"
  )
  (default
    "many"
  )
)

(fn-expr + steps (list String)
  (param verbose Bool)
  (bullet "start")
  (bullet? (only-if "trace" (if verbose)))
  (bullet "stop")
)

(fn-expr + doubled-evens (list Int)
  (param values (list Int))
  values
  (pipe ?> (== (% each 2) 0))
  (pipe *> (* each 2))
)
few
start, trace, stop
4, 8

The value cannot be Void. A value body that gives nothing, or a function declared Void with fn-expr, is an error: a function that only does work is a step body.

Rows before the value

A value body may run steps before its value, in its before section, in the order they are written:

  • Checks: ?! error if condition(throw error (if condition)) raises the error when the condition holds. See Errors.
  • Prints: -- value(print value).
  • Probes. See Probes.
  • do blocks: do body(do body), whose steps may assign to parameters and call functions.
  • finally: do finally body(finally body), steps that run when the function ends, however it ends.

Anything else that is a step is an error before the value: a return, a local declared with . name = value(let name value), an assignment or a call outside a do block, an if statement, a loop, a yield, and a lazy binding. Put the step in a do block, move the lazy after the value, or declare the function with fn-do.

These rules are checked where a function is declared, whether or not anything calls it. Function values written with => follow the same rules; see Function values.

Lazy bindings

A lazy binding names a value that is worked out when it is first read. It is written .. name = value(lazy name value). In a value body, lazy bindings come after the value, in its where section, so a function can give its answer first and define the parts it is built from below it, where a reader looks for them next.

-- describe(true)
-- describe(false)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - detailed Bool

if detailed then "total $total, still $total" else "no total"

.. total = computed-total()

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ computed-total Int

-- "computing"

42
(main
  (print (call describe true))
  (print (call describe false))
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param detailed Bool)
  (if-expr detailed (str "total " total ", still " total) "no total")
  (where
    (lazy total (call computed-total))
  )
)

(fn-expr + computed-total Int
  (before
    (print "computing")
  )
  42
)
computing
total 42, still 42
no total

describe(true)(call describe true) reads total twice, and computed-total runs once. describe(false)(call describe false) never reads it, and computed-total does not run.

  • When it runs. The value is worked out at the first read of the name, and not at all if nothing reads it. A lazy binding's value may read other lazy bindings, and they run in the order the reads reach them.
  • How often. At most once in each lifetime of the binding. Later reads give the same value. When the value raises a recoverable error, the error is kept too, and each later read raises it again without running the value a second time.
  • Lifetime. A binding has a new lifetime in each call of its function. A binding declared in the body of a loop has a new lifetime in each turn of the loop. A function value created in a call shares the binding with that call, and whichever reads it first runs it.
  • What it reads. The value reads names as they are when it runs, not as they were where the binding is written. A step that changes a name the value reads, run before the first read, changes the value.
  • No updates. Once worked out, the value stays, though the names it read change later. A value that follows them is a matter for Reactivity.
  • Assigning. A lazy binding can be assigned like a local. Assigning before the first read means its value never runs. += and other updates read the binding first, which runs its value.
  • A type. .. name Type = value(lazy name Type value) converts the value to the type. .. name Type(lazy name Type), with no value, is the type's default.
  • A pattern. .. first, second = pair()(lazy (tuple first second) (call pair)) takes a value apart into several names. The value runs once, at the first read of any of them. See Patterns.
  • Under one value. (scope value rows) gives a value with the lazy bindings it reads written under it, as in -- width * height .. width = 3 .. height = 4(print (scope (* width height) (lazy width 3) (lazy height 4))). In rows the bindings are indented below the value's row. A call takes such rows in its block.
reprice()

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do reprice

. price = 3
.. total = price * 2
price = 4
-- total
price = 10
-- total
(main
  (call reprice)
)

(fn-do + reprice _
  (let price 3)
  (lazy total (* price 2))
  (= price 4)
  (print total)
  (= price 10)
  (print total)
)
8
8

total reads price after it changes to 4, and keeps its value after it changes to 10.

A lazy binding that reads itself, directly or through the bindings it reads, is an error. So is a second binding of the same name in one body.

In a step body, a lazy binding can stand anywhere among the statements, including after the last return.

Because a lazy binding's value runs at its first read rather than where it is written, the order in which effects happen follows the order of reads. A value with an effect, such as reading from a channel or changing state, runs where it is first needed, and not at all on a path that never needs it.

Step bodies

A function declared with fn-do has a step body: rows that run in order. A step body can declare locals with . name = value(let name value), assign, branch, loop and yield, and it gives its result with a return.

-- first-negative([4, -2, 7, -9])
-- first-negative([1, 2])

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do first-negative Int?
    - values [Int]

for value in values
    =? value if value < 0
= null
(main
  (print (call first-negative (list 4 -2 7 -9)))
  (print (call first-negative (list 1 2)))
)

(fn-do + first-negative (? Int)
  (param values (list Int))
  (for (in value values)
    (return-if value (if (< value 0)))
  )
  (return null)
)
-2
unknown

The second call finds no negative value and returns null, which prints as unknown.

Returns

ReturnMeaning
= value(return value)Return the value.
=(return)Return from a function that gives nothing.
=? value if condition(return-if value (if condition))Return the value when the condition holds. Otherwise go on.
=? if condition(return-if (if condition))Return nothing when the condition holds.
=? value(return? value)Return the value when it is not null. Otherwise go on.

A returned value is converted to the function's result type, as an assignment would convert it. A function that gives nothing may return a call that gives nothing, as in = note(text)(return (call note text)).

-- grade(95)
-- grade(40)
log("ready")
log("")
-- cached-or-default(null)
-- cached-or-default(7)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do grade String
    - score Int

=? "excellent" if score >= 90
. passed = score >= 50
= if passed then "passed" else "failed"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do log
    - message String

=? if message == ""
-- "log: $message"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do cached-or-default Int
    - cached Int?

=? cached
= 0
(main
  (print (call grade 95))
  (print (call grade 40))
  (call log "ready")
  (call log "")
  (print (call cached-or-default null))
  (print (call cached-or-default 7))
)

(fn-do + grade String
  (param score Int)
  (return-if "excellent" (if (>= score 90)))
  (let passed (>= score 50))
  (return (if-expr passed "passed" "failed"))
)

(fn-do + log _
  (param message String)
  (return-if (if (== message "")))
  (print (str "log: " message))
)

(fn-do + cached-or-default Int
  (param cached (? Int))
  (return? cached)
  (return 0)
)
excellent
failed
log: ready
0
7

The end of the body

When the rows run out without a return, the function ends. What it gives then depends on its result type:

  • A function that gives nothing returns.
  • A Bool function gives false.
  • An optional function gives null.
  • Any other result type is an error, reported where the function is declared: the function can fall through without returning a value of its type.

The end is out of reach, and needs no return, after a return, a raise that always happens, a loop on the constant true with no break that leaves it, an if and else that both return or raise, and a match run as steps that must match and returns in every arm, as in do match subject | pattern = value(do (inline (match subject (case pattern (return value))))). A condition that is the constant false stands for its else.

A value standing alone as the last row is an error, not a return. In a function that gives a value, the compiler asks for = value(return value); in one that gives nothing, it asks to use the value or remove it. An assignment as the last row is a step, not a value, so the function falls through as usual.

Rows after a return, a continue or a raise that always happens are never reached, and the compiler does not check the names in them.

Result types

The result type follows the name in the header. When it is left out, _ in its place, the compiler infers it from the body.

  • A value body gives the type of its value. The arms of a decision table join into one type.
  • A step body gives the type its returns join into: returns of Int and Float join into Float, and returns of two classes join into a class both derive from. A body whose end can be reached after a return that may not happen gives an optional, as half below does. Returns with no common type are an error, which asks for one type or a declared result.
  • A step body with no returns of a value, or none at all, gives nothing. Void can also be written as the result type.
-- half(10)
-- half(7)
-- countdown(3)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do half
    - value Int

=? value / 2 if value % 2 == 0

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ countdown String
    - value Int

if value == 0 then "liftoff" else "$value ${countdown(value - 1)}"
(main
  (print (call half 10))
  (print (call half 7))
  (print (call countdown 3))
)

(fn-do + half _
  (param value Int)
  (return-if (/ value 2) (if (== (% value 2) 0)))
)

(fn-expr + countdown String
  (param value Int)
  (if-expr (== value 0) "liftoff" (str value " " (call countdown (- value 1))))
)
5
unknown
3 2 1 liftoff

A function that calls itself, directly or through other functions, must declare its result type, as countdown does. Otherwise the compiler reaches the call before it knows the type, and reports an error that asks for the declaration.

Parameters

Each parameter follows the header, with its name and its type: - name Type(param name Type).

-- greet("Ada")
-- greet("Ada", "Hi")
-- greet("Grace") • punctuation "?"
-- total(1, 2, 3)
-- total()
-- repeat("ab", 2.7)
-- plus(1)
-- plus(1.5)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ greet String
    - name String
    - greeting String = "Hello"
    - punctuation String = "!"

"$greeting, $name$punctuation"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do total Int
    ... values [Int] = []

. sum = 0
for value in values
    sum += value
= sum

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ repeat String
    - text String
    - count Int~

"".join(text in 0 .. < count)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ plus
    - value

value + 1
(main
  (print (call greet "Ada"))
  (print (call greet "Ada" "Hi"))
  (print (call greet "Grace" (:punctuation "?")))
  (print (call total 1 2 3))
  (print (call total))
  (print (call repeat "ab" 2.7))
  (print (call plus 1))
  (print (call plus 1.5))
)

(fn-expr + greet String
  (param name String)
  (param greeting String (= "Hello"))
  (param punctuation String (= "!"))
  (str greeting ", " name punctuation)
)

(fn-do + total Int
  (param ... values (list Int) (= (list)))
  (let sum 0)
  (for (in value values)
    (+= sum value)
  )
  (return sum)
)

(fn-expr + repeat String
  (param text String)
  (param count (similar Int))
  (call (. "" join) (in text (..< 0 count)))
)

(fn-expr + plus _
  (param value _)
  (+ value 1)
)
Hello, Ada!
Hi, Ada!
Hello, Grace?
6
0
abab
2
2.5
  • Defaults. - greeting String = "Hello"(param greeting String (= "Hello")) gives the parameter a default, which a call can leave out. The default is worked out by each call that leaves the argument out, when that call is made, so it can call functions and reads values as they are then. It is converted to the parameter's type. A default cannot read the members of the object a method is called on.
  • Order. A parameter without a default cannot follow one with a default.
  • Optional parameters. A parameter can be left out of a call only when it has a default. A parameter of an optional type, such as - nickname String?(param nickname (? String)), still has to be given, though it can be given null; - nickname String? = null(param nickname (? String) (= null)) can be left out. An optional argument that holds nothing, given for a parameter with a default, takes the default.
  • Rest parameters. A parameter marked ... takes every remaining positional argument as a list, as values does in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + sum Int ... values [Int] body(fn-expr + sum Int (param ... values (list Int)) body). It must be the last parameter. A call must give it at least one argument unless it has a default, as total does.
  • Converting parameters. - count Int~(param count (similar Int)) takes any value that as converts to Int, and converts it, so repeat("ab", 2.7)(call repeat "ab" 2.7) repeats twice. - count Int!(param count (exact Int)) takes exactly an Int, which matters when it is overloaded.
  • Untyped parameters. A parameter with no type, - value(param value _), takes a type from each call: the compiler makes a separate function for each type the parameter is called with, as for plus.
  • Function types. A parameter's type can be a function type written in place, with the function's own parameters inside it, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + name - func () Int - value Int body(fn-expr + name _ (param func (fn-type Int (param value Int))) body).
  • Type parameters. A row can also name a type parameter of a generic function, to give it a default or a constraint. See Generic functions.
  • Names. A parameter can be named by any word except in, on, and, or, do, for, while, if and else. Prepositions such as from, to, at, before and after make a call by name read as a phrase, distance • from origin • to corner(call distance (:from origin) (:to corner)), and are called prepositional arguments. They help most where two parameters share a type and swapping them would still compile.

A parameter is a local of the function. Assigning to it changes the function's local, not what the caller passed.

Calls

A call names a function and gives its arguments, as in name(a, b)(call name a b).

/stream/aggregate

. scores = [12, 40, 7, 33]
-- label("Ada")
-- label("Ada") • greeting "Hi"
-- label
    • name "Grace"
    • greeting "Hey"
-- clamp
    - 150
    - 0
    - 100
-- some(scores) • where each > 30
-- 5 |> clamp(0, 3)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ label String
    - name String
    - greeting String = "Hello"

"$greeting, $name"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ clamp Int
    - value Int
    - low Int
    - high Int

if value < low then low else if value > high then high else value
(import /stream/aggregate)

(main
  (let scores (list 12 40 7 33))
  (print (call label "Ada"))
  (print (call label "Ada" (:greeting "Hi")))
  (print
    (call label
      (block
        (:name "Grace")
        (:greeting "Hey")
      )
    )
  )
  (print
    (call clamp
      (block
        (arg 150)
        (arg 0)
        (arg 100)
      )
    )
  )
  (print (call some scores (:where (> each 30))))
  (print (|> 5 (call clamp 0 3)))
)

(fn-expr + label String
  (param name String)
  (param greeting String (= "Hello"))
  (str greeting ", " name)
)

(fn-expr + clamp Int
  (param value Int)
  (param low Int)
  (param high Int)
  (if-expr (< value low) low (if-expr (> value high) high value))
)
Hello, Ada
Hi, Ada
Hey, Grace
100
true
3
  • Arguments by name. • greeting "Hi"(:greeting "Hi") gives the parameter named greeting. Arguments by name follow the positional ones, in the call or one to a row in its block, and can give any parameter, with or without a default.
  • One argument to a row. A call can give its arguments as rows in a block, each - value(arg value), as the call of clamp does.
  • A block as an argument. An argument by name can take a block as its value, as in • name step value(:name (block step value)): steps, then the value as the last row.
  • Bullets as the argument. A call whose block holds bullets gives the list they build as its argument, as in ", ".join * "a" * "b"(call (. ", " join) (block (bullet "a") (bullet "b"))).
  • Callbacks that read each. An argument by name for a parameter of a function type can be an expression that reads each, as in some(scores) • where each > 30(call some scores (:where (> each 30))). The expression becomes the body of a function whose parameter is each. A callback given by position is written as a function value that names its parameters.
  • The rest of the row. name: value(call name (inline value)) gives the value as the last argument, written in rows as the rest of the row after a colon.
  • Pipes. value |> f(more)(|> value (call f more)) calls f(more, value)(call f more value): the piped value comes after the written arguments. See Streams.
  • Named operators. a /name/ b(/name/ a b) calls name(a, b)(call name a b). See Operators.

Arguments are worked out in the order they are written, arguments by name included. A piped value is worked out before the written arguments. Each argument is converted to its parameter's type as an assignment converts it, and a number written with no suffix takes the parameter's type.

A method is called through its object, as in text.trim()(call (. text trim)). The object is worked out before the arguments. object?.method(argument)(call (?. object method) argument) gives null, without working out the arguments, when the object is null. Methods are covered in Types.

A call that no function of its name can take is an error that names the argument types and the functions it could have called.

Function values

A function is a value. A name declared as a function can be passed, stored and called like any other value, and a function value can be written in place with =>.

. add = :: a, b => a + b
. greeting = => "hello"
. log = :: text String => do
    -- "log: $text"

-- add(2, 3)
-- greeting()
log("ready")
-- apply(4, double)
-- apply(4, :: n => "n is $n")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ double Int
    - value Int

value * 2

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ apply'Result
    - value Int
    - func () Result
        - value Int

func(value)
(main
  (let add (=> (a b) (+ a b)))
  (let greeting (=> () "hello"))
  (let log
    (=> ((: text String)) :do
      (block
        (print (str "log: " text))
      )
    )
  )
  (blank)
  (print (call add 2 3))
  (print (call greeting))
  (call log "ready")
  (print (call apply 4 double))
  (print (call apply 4 (=> (n) (str "n is " n))))
)

(fn-expr + double Int
  (param value Int)
  (* value 2)
)

(fn-expr + (of apply Result) _
  (param value Int)
  (param func (fn-type Result (param value Int)))
  (call func value)
)
5
hello
log: ready
8
n is 4
  • Parameters. :: a, b => value(=> (a b) value) names the parameters a and b. A function value with none is => value(=> () value). A parameter may have a type, as in :: text String => value(=> ((: text String)) value), and the last may take the rest of the arguments, as in :: ... keys [Int] => value(=> ((: ...keys (list Int))) value).
  • Untyped parameters. Where a function type is expected, as for the func parameter of apply, the parameters take their types from it. Elsewhere an untyped parameter is generic: each type it is called with makes a separate function.
  • Bodies. => value(=> () value) has a value body and follows the rules of value bodies: checks, prints and do blocks may run before the value, and lazy bindings may follow it. With :do after the parameter list, as in => do body(=> () :do body), it has a step body and returns with = value(return value).
  • Named functions. The name of a declared function, without a call, is a function value, as double is above.
  • Methods. A method read from an object without a call, as in counter.bump(. counter bump), is a function value bound to that object. Calling it calls the method on that object. Inside a method, the bare name of another method of the same type is bound to the same object.

A function value prints as its type, such as [Function Mapper'I64'I64].

Capture

A function value can read and assign the locals of the body that creates it. It does not copy them: the body and every function value created in it share each local, and an assignment by one is seen by all.

. total = 0
. add = :: amount Int => do
    total += amount

add(3)
add(4)
-- total

. readers = List'(Getter'Int)()
for item in [1, 2, 3]
    readers += => item * 10
for reader in readers
    -- reader()
(main
  (let total 0)
  (let add
    (=> ((: amount Int)) :do
      (block
        (+= total amount)
      )
    )
  )
  (blank)
  (call add 3)
  (call add 4)
  (print total)
  (blank)
  (let readers (call (of List (of Getter Int))))
  (for (in item (list 1 2 3))
    (+= readers (=> () (* item 10)))
  )
  (for (in reader readers)
    (print (call reader))
  )
)
7
10
20
30
  • Each call has its own locals. A function value created in one call of a function shares the locals of that call only, and keeps them after the call returns.
  • Each turn of a loop has its own locals. A loop's item, and each local declared in the loop's body, is new in every turn, so a function value created in a turn reads that turn's values. Locals declared before the loop are shared by every turn.
  • Reads happen at the call. A function value reads a local when it runs, so it sees the local's value at that moment, not the value it had when the function value was created.
  • Lazy bindings are shared the same way, and run at the first read by the body or by any function value created in it.
  • Locals declared later. A function value may name a local declared after it in the same body.

A task started with do new body(do-new body) is different: it copies the locals of the body that starts it. See Concurrency.

Function types

A function type is written with fn-type: the result type, then the parameters, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Step is () Int - amount Int(type + Step (is (fn-type Int (param amount Int)))). A function type whose result is Void gives nothing, and error types follow the result, as in - parse () Int ?! ParseError(param parse (fn-type Int (?! ParseError))). A function type can be declared with a name, or written directly where a type is wanted, as the type of a parameter or a property.

. steps = List'Step()
steps += double
steps += :: amount => amount + 1
for step in steps
    -- step(5)

. scale Scale = :: value, factor => value * factor
-- scale(3, 4)
-- scale(5) • factor 2

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Step is () Int
    - amount Int

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Scale is () Int
    - value Int
    - factor Int

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ double Int
    - value Int

value * 2
(main
  (let steps (call (of List Step)))
  (+= steps double)
  (+= steps (=> (amount) (+ amount 1)))
  (for (in step steps)
    (print (call step 5))
  )
  (blank)
  (let scale Scale (=> (value factor) (* value factor)))
  (print (call scale 3 4))
  (print (call scale 5 (:factor 2)))
)

(type + Step (is (fn-type Int (param amount Int))))

(type + Scale (is (fn-type Int (param value Int) (param factor Int))))

(fn-expr + double Int
  (param value Int)
  (* value 2)
)
10
6
12
10

The core library declares common function types, which every module can use:

TypeFunction
DoerTakes nothing, does something and may raise an Error.
Getter'Result(of Getter Result)Takes nothing and gives a result.
Mapper'Item'Result(of Mapper Item Result)Takes an item and gives a result.
Predicate'Item(of Predicate Item)Takes an item and gives a Bool.
Comparer'Item(of Comparer Item)Takes two items and compares them.

A value of a function type is called like a function. Its parameters' names can be used for arguments by name, as factor is above, and the arguments are worked out in the order written. An optional function value must be unwrapped before it is called, as in hook!(value)(call (!! hook) value) or inside if hook hook(value)(if hook (call hook value)).

Conversion. A function or function value converts to a function type on its own when a call through the type would convert each argument to what the function takes, and the function's result to what the type gives, on their own. So a function that takes a Float converts to a type whose parameter is an Int; a function that takes a base class converts to a type whose parameter is a class derived from it; any function converts to a type that gives Void; and a function that raises fewer errors converts to a type that allows more. Any other conversion between function types is written with as, and then each argument and the result convert as as converts them. A function that raises an error the type does not allow is an error at the conversion; a function with a different number of parameters cannot be converted at all.

Equality. Two function values are equal when they run the same code with the same captured locals. A declared function is equal to itself; two function values created by one call that capture nothing are equal; two created by separate calls that capture locals are not.

Partial application

A call that ends with ... in place of its remaining arguments, as in add(10, ...)(call add 10 ...), does not call the function. It gives a function value that takes the missing arguments and then makes the call. Arguments by name can follow the ..., and a call of a generic function can leave its type arguments to the later call too.

. add-ten = add(10, ...)
-- add-ten(5)
-- add-ten(32)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ add Int
    - a Int
    - b Int

a + b
(main
  (let add-ten (call add 10 ...))
  (print (call add-ten 5))
  (print (call add-ten 32))
)

(fn-expr + add Int
  (param a Int)
  (param b Int)
  (+ a b)
)
15
42

Generic functions

A function can have type parameters, written after its name: both'Item(of both Item) has one type parameter, Item, which its parameters and result can use.

-- both(4)
-- both("ab")
-- both'Float(2)
-- kind(3)
-- kind(2.5)
-- kind("three")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ both'Item
    - value Item

value, value

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ kind'Item
    - value Item
    - Item is Number

"a number"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ kind'Item
    - value Item

"something else"
(main
  (print (call both 4))
  (print (call both "ab"))
  (print (call (of both Float) 2))
  (print (call kind 3))
  (print (call kind 2.5))
  (print (call kind "three"))
)

(fn-expr + (of both Item) _
  (param value Item)
  (tuple value value)
)

(fn-expr + (of kind Item) _
  (param value Item)
  (constraint is Item Number)
  "a number"
)

(fn-expr + (of kind Item) _
  (param value Item)
  "something else"
)
(4, 4)
(ab, ab)
(2, 2)
a number
a number
something else
  • Inference. A call usually leaves the type arguments out, and the compiler infers them from the arguments, including from the result of a function value passed as an argument.
  • Explicit type arguments. A call can give them after the name, as in both'Float(2)(call (of both Float) 2). It can give the first ones and leave the rest to inference.
  • Each type makes a function. The compiler makes a separate function for each set of type arguments a program uses. A parameter with no type works the same way: it is a type parameter of its own.
  • Types as values. Inside the function, a type parameter is a value of its own, the type it stands for, and can be printed or passed.
  • Defaults. A type parameter can have a default type, which a call uses when it gives no type argument and none can be inferred. It is written as a parameter row, as String is for Item in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + both'Item - Item = String body(fn-expr + (of both Item) _ (constraint = Item String) body).

Constraints

A constraint is a parameter row that states a rule a type parameter must meet:

DeclarationRule
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + name'Item - Item is Type value(fn-expr + (of name Item) _ (constraint is Item Type) value)Item is Type, derives from it, or implements it.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + name'Item - Item is! Type value(fn-expr + (of name Item) _ (constraint is! Item Type) value)Item is exactly Type.

When several functions of one name could take a call, a function whose constraints the call meets is chosen over one without constraints, as kind shows. A static method called on a type parameter must be declared by one of its constraints.

Overloading

Several functions can share a name when their parameters differ in type or number. A call chooses among them by the types of its arguments, when the program is compiled.

-- describe(3)
-- describe(2.5)
-- describe("three")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - value Int

"the integer $value"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - value Float

"the float $value"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - value String

"the text $value"
(main
  (print (call describe 3))
  (print (call describe 2.5))
  (print (call describe "three"))
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param value Int)
  (str "the integer " value)
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param value Float)
  (str "the float " value)
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param value String)
  (str "the text " value)
)
the integer 3
the float 2.5
the text three

When more than one function could take a call, the one that needs the least conversion is chosen:

  • An argument that matches a parameter's type exactly is preferred to one that must be converted.
  • A parameter of a derived class is preferred to a parameter of its base class.
  • An integer parameter is preferred to a pointer parameter for an integer argument.
  • A function whose constraints the call meets is preferred to one without constraints.
  • A generic function and one that is not are compared after the generic one's type arguments are inferred.
  • A function value as the argument chooses a parameter of a function type over a parameter of a bare type parameter.
  • A call that gives type arguments considers only functions that have type parameters.

The choice uses the types the arguments are declared with. An argument whose declared type is an interface or a base class does not choose a function for a class that implements or derives from it, even when the object is one. Choosing by the object's class at run time happens only for the object a method is called on; see Types.

Two functions of one name with the same parameter types are an error. A call that no function of its name can take is an error that lists the functions it could have called. Functions of one name from different imported modules join into one set, whatever the order of the imports, and private functions of other modules are not part of it.

Annotations

An annotation is a word starting with @, written after a function's result and error types. Fields and stream pattern rules take annotations of their own, described with them.

AnnotationMeaning
@inlinePut the function's body in place of each call to it.
@liveKeep state across the runs of the live value that calls the function. See Reactivity.
@rollbackOn a stream pattern rule or action: undo the changes it made through the match's helper when the match goes back past it. See Stream patterns.
@no-heapThe function may not allocate memory the collector manages.
@no-suspendThe function may not suspend its task.
@no-safepointsThe function holds no point where the collector may stop it.
@no-probe-safepointsThe function holds no point where probes may stop it.
@no-gcAll of @no-heap, @no-safepoints and @no-suspend.
@gc-leaf, @gc-pollingHow the collector treats a native function. See Native code and memory.

A function that calls itself, directly or through other functions, cannot be inlined. The compiler calls it as usual and, with --warnings, reports each call it could not inline.

An annotation the compiler does not know is an error, and so are two that contradict each other.

Without and with

After its annotations, a function's header can take a (without …) part and (with …) parts:

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do step @inline without heap, suspend with depth = 2, scope = "step"

tick()
(fn-do + step _ @inline (without heap suspend) (with depth 2) (with scope "step")
  (call tick)
)
  • Without. (without heap) is @no-heap, and so for suspend, safepoints, probe-safepoints and gc. On a C function in a header module, (without gc) is @gc-leaf and (without blocking) is @gc-polling. A name that is none of these, or one named twice, is an error.
  • With. Each (with name value) sets a @stack property for the whole body, as a do-with around it would, the first outermost, so a later value can read an earlier one. It needs a fn-do.
  • Blocks. A (do …) takes the same parts after its annotations, as in do without gc with depth = 3 …(do (without gc) (with depth 3) …). There (without cancel) is also accepted, and changes nothing yet. A (do …) kept from anything but gc runs in place: the functions it calls are kept from the same, and its loops poll only as far as that allows.

Types

A type declaration names a kind of value and declares its members: the properties each value holds, the functions that work on it, and the constructors that make it. What the type is built on decides what kind of type it is.

This chapter covers classes, tuples, structs and interfaces, and what they share: properties, constructors, methods, static functions, type parameters, inheritance, delegation, extensions and facets. Unions are in Unions and enums, function types in Functions, and number types with units in Units. Conversions a type declares are in Conversions, operators it defines in Operators, and events and rules in Reactivity.

Declaring a type

. counter = Counter("clicks")
counter.add(3)
counter.add()
-- counter.summary
-- Counter.named("taps").summary

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Counter

+ label String
+ count Int
+ summary String => "$label: $count"
────────────────────
+ This
    - label String



────────────────────
+ do add
    - amount Int = 1

count += amount

────────────────────
+ static named Counter
    - label String

Counter(label)
(main
  (let counter (call Counter "clicks"))
  (call (. counter add) 3)
  (call (. counter add))
  (print (. counter summary))
  (print (. (call (. Counter named) "taps") summary))
)

(type + Counter
  (prop + label String)
  (prop + count Int)
  (prop + summary String (=> (str label ": " count)))
  (fn-do + This _
    (param label String)
  )
  (fn-do + add _
    (param amount Int (= 1))
    (+= count amount)
  )
  (fn-expr + named Counter :static
    (param label String)
    (call Counter label)
  )
)
clicks: 4
taps: 0

A type is declared at the top level of a file. Its header holds the access, + or _, the name, and what the type is built on, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Dog is Animal(type + Dog (is Animal)). After the header, the type names each interface it implements, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Square is Shape(type + Square (implements Shape)), and each rule its type parameters must meet, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Box'Item - Item is Titled(type + (of Box Item) (constraint is Item Titled)). The members follow in order: properties first, then functions. A type with no members is its header alone, and may be written with type-line in place of type.

In rows, a type follows a thick divider, ━, and each of its functions a thin divider, ─. A type with no members needs no divider.

The name is a capitalized word, such as Counter or HttpRequest. A type that takes type parameters names them after the name, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Box'Item(type + (of Box Item)); see Generic types. Other names for the type follow its name: ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Point (Spot)(type + Point (alias Spot)) lets Spot stand for Point. A lowercase name among them is a unit suffix, and only a number type can have one; see Units.

Kinds of type

DeclarationKindValues
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Name(type + Name), or ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Name is Base(type + Name (is Base)) with a class as baseA classObjects, shared by reference.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Name is Tuple(type + Name (is Tuple)), or ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Name is (x Int, y Int)(type + Name (is (tuple (: x Int) (: y Int))))A named tupleFixed groups of values, copied, never changed in place.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Name is Struct(type + Name (is Struct))A structFixed groups of values, copied, changed in place.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Name is Interface(type + Name (is Interface))An interfaceAny value of a type that implements it.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Name is Union(type + Name (is Union))A union; see Unions and enumsOne of several cases.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Name is Int || String(type + Name (is Int String))A type of alternativesA value of any one of the types, which keeps its own type.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Name is Int(type + Name (is Int)), or another number typeA number type; see UnitsNumbers of their own type.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Name is () Int(type + Name (is (fn-type Int)))A function type; see FunctionsFunctions.

Optional, Function, CFunction and Bool cannot be a base: a type built on one is an error, Type has illegal base class.

A tuple suits data that is nothing more than its values, compared and copied whole. A class suits a thing with an identity and a lifetime, which everyone who holds it shares. A struct suits values changed in place by their one holder. Inheritance suits a family that shares an identity and behavior worth sharing, at the cost that each subclass depends on choices its base makes. An interface suits a boundary where callers need only a small capability, and a union a fixed set of cases each caller should consider.

Members

DeclarationMember
+ name Type = value(prop + name Type (= value))A stored property.
+ name Type := value(prop + name Type (:= value))A lazy property.
+ name Type => value(prop + name Type (=> value))A computed property.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + This - name Type body(fn-do + This _ (param name Type) body)A constructor.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + name Type body(fn-expr + name Type body)A method.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + get name Type body(fn-expr + name Type :get body)A getter.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + do name = value Type body(fn-do + name _ :set (param value Type) body)A setter.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + static name Type body(fn-expr + name Type :static body)A static function.

A method, getter, setter or static function declared with fn-do has a step body, and one declared with fn-expr has a value body, as a function does; see Functions.

Access

A member written with + is public: any module that can see the type can use it. A member written with _ is private to the module that declares it, and code in other modules cannot read it, call it, or see it from a class derived from the type. The type's own access works the same way: a type declared with _ can be used only in its own module.

A member written with ^ is shared with the file family of its module, as (fn-do ^ keep-end _ …) or ^ do keep-end: code in the family's files uses it as a public member, and code elsewhere is refused as it is for a private one: Method "keep-end" of Box is shared, declared with ^, so only its own file family can call it. File families are in Modules. Only a member is shared: ^ on a type, or on a function or value of a module, is an error, Only a member can be shared with its file family; declare this + or _.

A type declares each name once. Declaring two members with one name, such as a property and a getter, is an error: Counter declares "count" twice (first on line 8); remove one of them, or rename it. Methods are the exception: several may share a name when their parameters differ, as functions do.

Inside a type

Inside a member, the type's other members are named alone, as count and label are in summary, or through this, the value the member was called on: this.count(. this count). This names the type that declares the code, so This(value)(call This value) inside a method makes another value of that type.

line.end.x = 9
-- line.end.x
-- line.length-squared()

-- measure()
-- Point.origin().y

  • Reading. line.end(. line end) reads a property or a getter. Several names read a member of each member in turn, so line.end.x(. line end x) is (. (. line end) x). In rows it is line.end.x.
  • Assigning. line.end.x = 9(= (. line end x) 9) assigns the last member named. A field of a struct is changed where the struct is held; see Structs.
  • Calling. line.length-squared()(call (. line length-squared)) calls a method. Named without a call, a method is a function value that remembers its object; see Methods.
  • Static functions are read on the type, as in Point.origin()(call (. Point origin)); see Static functions.
  • Optionals. value?.name(?. value name) reads a member of a value that may be null; see Optionals.

Classes and objects

A type declared with no is, or with a class after is, is a class. Its values are objects. Calling the class, as in Account("ana")(call Account "ana"), makes a new object, and a value of a class refers to an object: assigning the value or passing it shares the object rather than copying it.

. first = Account("ana")
. same = first
same.balance += 10
-- first.balance
-- first == same
-- first == Account("ana")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Account

+ owner String
+ balance Int
────────────────────
+ This
    - owner String
(main
  (let first (call Account "ana"))
  (let same first)
  (+= (. same balance) 10)
  (print (. first balance))
  (print (== first same))
  (print (== first (call Account "ana")))
)

(type + Account
  (prop + owner String)
  (prop + balance Int)
  (fn-do + This _
    (param owner String)
  )
)

true
false
  • Equality. Two objects are equal when they are the same object. A class can declare its own ==; see Operators.
  • Text. An object becomes text as [Object module:Class], such as [Object app/main:Account]. A class that declares a conversion to String becomes that text instead; see Conversions.
  • Null. A value of a class always holds an object. A value that may hold none has an optional type, such as Account?(? Account); see Optionals.
  • Lifetime. An object lives as long as something can reach it, and the collector reclaims it after that.

Properties

A property is a value each value of the type holds, or computes when it is read. Stored, lazy and computed properties are declared on one row each. Getters and setters are functions.

-- order.quantity
-- order.price
-- order.note
-- order.tags.length
-- order.total
order.quantity = 3
-- order.total

A stored property is written with its type, its value, or both:

  • + quantity Int = 1(prop + quantity Int (= 1)) has both. The value is converted to the type, so + price Float = 4(prop + price Float (= 4)) holds a Float.
  • + price = 2.5(prop + price _ (= 2.5)), with _ in the place of the type, takes its type from its value.
  • + item String(prop + item String) has no value, and starts with the empty value of its type.

A property with neither is an error: Property 'note' of 'Order' needs either a type or a value.

A property with no value starts with:

TypeValue
A number0
Boolfalse
String""
A list or a mapAn empty one.
An optionalnull
A class, tuple or structA new value, made by calling the type with no arguments.

Properties with no value whose types hold each other in a cycle would never finish being made, and are an error: Default of part never finishes: Part.owner builds Owner, and Owner.part builds Part again. Give one of these fields a value, make it lazy with :=, or make it optional.

Initialization

The values of stored properties are computed when a value of the type is made, in the order the properties are declared, a base class's before its subclass's, and before the constructor's body runs.

. box = Box()
-- box.area

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Box

+ area = width * height
+ width = 3
+ height = width + 1
(main
  (let box (call Box))
  (print (. box area))
)

(type + Box
  (prop + area _ (= (* width height)))
  (prop + width _ (= 3))
  (prop + height _ (= (+ width 1)))
)
12
  • Reading another property. A value may read the type's other properties, even ones declared after it. A property read before its turn gets its value at that read, once.
  • Cycles. A value that reads itself, directly or through other values, is an error.
  • Values given another way. A property that a constructor's parameter or lazy binding fills does not compute its own value. See Constructors.
  • What a value may read. The value of a stored property may read other stored and lazy properties, and call functions of the module. It may not read a getter or a computed property, Illegal to reference getters in eager properties, and may not name this: Illegal to reference 'this' in eager properties or properties referenced by them.

+ first = second + 1
+ second = first + 1

  (let pair (call Pair))
)

  (prop + second _ (= (+ first 1)))
)

Lazy properties

A property written with := computes its value the first time it is read, and keeps it.

. report = Report()
-- "made"
-- report.summary
-- report.summary
. other = Report()
other.summary = "written"
-- other.summary

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Report

+ summary String := summarize()
────────────────────
+ summarize String

-- "summarizing"

"3 rows"
(main
  (let report (call Report))
  (print "made")
  (print (. report summary))
  (print (. report summary))
  (let other (call Report))
  (= (. other summary) "written")
  (print (. other summary))
)

(type + Report
  (prop + summary String (:= (call summarize)))
  (fn-expr + summarize String
    (before
      (print "summarizing")
    )
    "3 rows"
  )
)
made
summarizing
3 rows
3 rows
written
  • Once. The value is computed at the first read, and later reads give the same value. A lazy property that is never read is never computed.
  • Assignment. Assigning the property before it is read replaces its value, and the value is then never computed. So does a constructor's parameter or lazy binding that fills it.
  • Assigning operators. An assigning operator such as += reads the property first, computing it if it has not been read.
  • What it may read. Unlike a stored property's value, a lazy value may name this, read getters and computed properties, and call methods, because it runs after the object is made.
  • No updates. A lazy property keeps its value when the properties it read later change. For a value that follows them, use a computed property, or a tracked one; see Reactivity.
  • Tasks. A task that reads a lazy property while another task is computing it waits for that value.

A lazy property is the property form of a lazy binding, .. name = value(lazy name value); see Functions.

Computed properties

A property written with => computes its value each time it is read, as total does in Stored properties. It holds nothing, and assigning it is an error: Setter not found. It is a getter written on one row.

To compute the value with steps, write :do and a block that returns it: + summary String => do . rounded = celsius as Int = "$rounded C"(prop + summary String (=> :do (block (let rounded (as celsius Int)) (return (str rounded " C"))))).

Getters and setters

A getter is a function that is read as a property. A setter is a function that runs when a property is assigned.

. t = Temperature()
-- t.fahrenheit
t.fahrenheit = 212
-- t.celsius
t.fahrenheit += 18
-- t.celsius

+ Temperature

+ celsius Float = 20
────────────────────
+ get fahrenheit Float

celsius * 9 / 5 + 32

────────────────────
+ do fahrenheit = value Float

celsius = (value - 32) * 5 / 9
(main
  (let t (call Temperature))
  (print (. t fahrenheit))
  (= (. t fahrenheit) 212)
  (print (. t celsius))
  (+= (. t fahrenheit) 18)
  (print (. t celsius))
)

(type + Temperature
  (prop + celsius Float (= 20))
  (fn-expr + fahrenheit Float :get
    (+ (/ (* celsius 9) 5) 32)
  )
  (fn-do + fahrenheit _ :set (param value Float)
    (= celsius (/ (* (- value 32) 5) 9))
  )
)
68
100
110
  • Getters. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + get fahrenheit Float body(fn-expr + fahrenheit Float :get body) declares a getter, or fn-do in place of fn-expr for a step body. It takes no parameters, and its body runs at each read. A read looks like reading a stored property, so a getter should cost and do no more than a reader would expect of one.
  • Setters. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + do fahrenheit = value Float body(fn-do + fahrenheit _ :set (param value Float) body) declares a setter. The assigned value is its one parameter, value here. A setter has a step body, and gives nothing, so its result type is _.
  • Together. A getter and a setter of one name make one property. An assigning operator, such as +=, reads with the getter and stores with the setter.
  • A setter alone. A property with a setter and no getter can be assigned but not read. A read is an error: Temperature has no property "fahrenheit".

Constructors

A constructor makes a value of its type. Calling the type, as in Span(2, 8)(call Span 2 8), calls the constructor whose parameters fit the arguments.

. a = Span(3)
-- "${a.low} ${a.high} ${a.span}"
. b = Span(2, 8)
-- "${b.low} ${b.high} ${b.span}"
. c = Span()
-- "${c.low} ${c.high} ${c.span}"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Span

+ low Int
+ high Int = 10
+ span Int
────────────────────
+ This
    - high

.. span = high - low

────────────────────
+ This
    - low
    - high

.. span = high - low
-- "made $low to $high"
(main
  (let a (call Span 3))
  (print (str (. a low) " " (. a high) " " (. a span)))
  (let b (call Span 2 8))
  (print (str (. b low) " " (. b high) " " (. b span)))
  (let c (call Span))
  (print (str (. c low) " " (. c high) " " (. c span)))
)

(type + Span
  (prop + low Int)
  (prop + high Int (= 10))
  (prop + span Int)
  (fn-do + This _
    (param high _)
    (lazy span (- high low))
  )
  (fn-do + This _
    (param low _)
    (param high _)
    (lazy span (- high low))
    (print (str "made " low " to " high))
  )
)

made 2 to 8
2 8 6
0 10 0

A constructor is declared with fn-do, with This as its name, _ as its result type, and its parameters as its first rows: ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + This - high Int(fn-do + This _ (param high Int)).

  • No arguments. A class can always be made with no arguments, as Span()(call Span) is above. Each property then takes its own value, and no constructor's body runs, unless the class declares a constructor with no parameters. Calling a class with arguments that no constructor takes is an error, No constructor of Span accepts (String), followed by the constructors it declares. A tuple or a struct that declares no constructor is made from its fields; see Tuples.
  • Parameters that fill properties. A parameter with the name of a property, the type's own or a base class's, fills that property, and the property does not compute its own value. The parameter's type may be left out, and is then the property's type. The argument is converted to the property's type.
  • Lazy bindings. A lazy binding such as .. span = high - low(lazy span (- high low)) in a constructor gives a property its value in place of the property's own. One whose name is not a property's binds a local the constructor can read. Lazy bindings run before the body, wherever they are written, in the order of the properties they fill.
  • The body. The constructor's other rows are steps. They run after every property has its value, and may assign properties and call methods. A constructor returns early as a step body does, with =? if condition(return-if (if condition)), and the value is then made. A constructor may instead give another value of its type, as in = This(item)(return (call This item)), which another constructor makes.
  • Several constructors. A type may declare several constructors, each with different parameters, as functions may be overloaded; see Functions.
  • Calling with another type's value. Calling a type with one value of another type converts the value, as as does, through a conversion the type declares; see Conversions.

A lazy binding runs before the object exists, so it cannot call the type's methods: A ".." initializer runs before the object exists, so it cannot call "measure", a method of Span; compute the value from the constructor's parameters, or assign it in the constructor's body. It runs before the body, too, so it cannot read a property the body assigns:

. log = Log("build")
-- log.size

+ size Int
────────────────────
+ This
    - name String

title = name
.. size = title.length

  (let log (call Log "build"))
  (print (. log size))
)

(type + Log
  (prop + title String)
  (prop + size Int)
  (fn-do + This _
    (param name String)
    (= title name)
    (lazy size (. title length))
  )
)

Reading the parameter, .. size = name.length(lazy size (. name length)), gives 5.

A constructor may take type parameters of its own, written after This, and choose the type's parameters from them, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + This'Storage - Backing = Storage.Backing'Item(fn-do + (of This Storage) _ (constraint = Backing (. Storage (of Backing Item)))). See Generic types.

Methods

A method is a function declared inside a type. It is called on a value of the type, as in route.child("bin")(call (. route child) "bin"), and that value is this in its body.

. route = Route(["usr", "local"])
-- route.text()
. deeper = route.child("bin")
-- deeper.text()
-- route.text()
-- route.text("\\")
-- Route.parse("a/b/c").text()

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Route

+ parts [String]
────────────────────
+ This
    - parts [String]



────────────────────
+ text String

this.text("/")

────────────────────
+ text String
    - separator String

separator ++ separator.join(parts)

────────────────────
+ child Route
    - name String

This(parts ++ [name])

────────────────────
+ static parse Route
    - text String

Route(List(text.split("/")))
(main
  (let route (call Route (list "usr" "local")))
  (print (call (. route text)))
  (let deeper (call (. route child) "bin"))
  (print (call (. deeper text)))
  (print (call (. route text)))
  (print (call (. route text) "\\"))
  (print (call (. (call (. Route parse) "a/b/c") text)))
)

(type + Route
  (prop + parts (list String))
  (fn-do + This _
    (param parts (list String))
  )
  (fn-expr + text String
    (call (. this text) "/")
  )
  (fn-expr + text String
    (param separator String)
    (++ separator (call (. separator join) parts))
  )
  (fn-expr + child Route
    (param name String)
    (call This (++ parts (list name)))
  )
  (fn-expr + parse Route :static
    (param text String)
    (call Route (call List (call (. text split) "/")))
  )

/usr/local/bin
/usr/local
\usr\local
/a/b/c

A method follows every rule of a function in Functions: value and step bodies, parameters, results, type parameters of its own and overloading. What is particular to methods:

  • Members by name. Inside a method, the type's properties and methods are named alone, as parts is in child, or through this, as in this.text("/")(call (. this text) "/").
  • Methods before functions. Inside a type, a call by name alone calls the type's method of that name. A function of the module with the same name is called only when no method's parameters fit the arguments.
  • This. This names the type that declares the method, so This(value)(call This value) makes another value of that type. In a method a subclass inherits, This is still the declaring class.
  • Unknown methods. Calling a method a type does not have is an error: Route has no method "length".
  • Bound methods. A method named without a call, as in route.text(. route text), is a function value bound to the value; see Functions.

Static functions

A function declared as ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + static name Type body(fn-expr + name Type :static body) belongs to the type rather than to its values. It is called through the type, as in Route.parse("a/b/c")(call (. Route parse) "a/b/c").

  • No this. A static function has no value to work on, so reading a property in it is an error: Required self not defined.
  • Its own names. A static function and a method may share a name: called on a value, the name calls the method, and called through the type, the static function.
  • Through a type parameter. A static function an interface requires can be called through a type parameter constrained to that interface, as in Item.kind()(call (. Item kind)); see Constraints.

A type holds no values of its own. A value shared by all values of a type is a value of the module; see Modules.

Generic types

A type can take type parameters, written after its name, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Box'Item(type + (of Box Item)). Inside the type, each parameter names a type, and each choice of types for the parameters makes a separate type.

. box = Box(5)
-- box.item
-- type-of box
. names = Box'String("x")
-- names.item
. doubled = box.map(:: each => "#$each")
-- doubled.item
-- type-of doubled
. pair = Box'(Int, Int)((1, 2))
-- pair.item

+ item Item
────────────────────

────────────────────

        - value Item

  (print (type-of box))

  (print (. names item))
  (let doubled (call (. box map) (=> (each) (str "#" each))))
  (print (. doubled item))
  (print (type-of doubled))
  (let pair (call (of Box (tuple Int Int)) (tuple 1 2)))

  • Declaring. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Box'Item(type + (of Box Item)) declares a type with one parameter, and ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Pair'First'Second(type + (of Pair First Second)) one with two.
  • Choosing the types. Box'String(of Box String) is the type with String for Item. In rows, a type argument that is itself generic, a tuple or an optional is written in parentheses: Box'(Int, Int), Box'(Box'Int), Box'(Int?). A list type needs none: Box'[Int].
  • Inference. Calling a generic type without type arguments infers them from the constructor's arguments: Box(5)(call Box 5) is a Box'Int(of Box Int).
  • Default types. A rule with = under the header gives a parameter a type it takes when none is chosen, as ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Box'Item'Backing - Backing = GCBacking(type + (of Box Item Backing) (constraint = Backing GCBacking)) does for Backing. List'Item'Backing(of List Item Backing) declares one, so [Int](list Int) is List'Int'GCBacking(of List Int GCBacking).
  • Constraints. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Box'Item - Item is Titled(type + (of Box Item) (constraint is Item Titled)) requires every type chosen for Item to implement Titled, and lets the type's members use what Titled declares; see Constraints.
  • Methods with parameters of their own. A method can take its own type parameters, as map'Out(of map Out) does, as functions can; see Functions.
  • Sharing a name. A type and a generic type, or two generic types with different numbers of parameters, may share a name. Each use picks the one whose number of type arguments matches.

Tuples

A tuple is a fixed group of values, its fields. Tuples are values, not objects: a tuple is copied where it is assigned or passed, two tuples are equal when their fields are, and a tuple is never changed in place.

. pair = (3, "three")
-- pair
-- pair[1]
-- pair.length
. corner (x Int, y Int) = (4, 5)
-- corner.x + corner.y
. p = Point(1, 2)
. moved = p.x = 10
-- p
-- moved
-- p == Point(1, 2)
-- p == (1, 2)
. q Point = (7, 8)
-- q.y

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Point is (x Int, y Int)
(main
  (let pair (tuple 3 "three"))
  (print pair)
  (print ([] pair 1))
  (print (. pair length))
  (let corner (tuple (: x Int) (: y Int)) (tuple 4 5))
  (print (+ (. corner x) (. corner y)))
  (let p (call Point 1 2))
  (let moved (= (. p x) 10))
  (print p)
  (print moved)
  (print (== p (call Point 1 2)))
  (print (== p (tuple 1 2)))
  (let q Point (tuple 7 8))

three
2
9

  • Writing a tuple. 3, "three"(tuple 3 "three") makes a tuple of two values. In rows, values separated by commas make a tuple, with or without parentheses: 3, "three" and (3, "three") are the same tuple. Tuples nest.
  • Tuple types. In . pair (Int, String) = value(let pair (tuple Int String) value), pair has the type of a tuple of an Int and a String. In . corner (x Int, y Int) = value(let corner (tuple (: x Int) (: y Int)) value), the tuple's fields have names.
  • Fields. A field is read by its position, as in pair[1]([] pair 1), or by its name, as in corner.x(. corner x). The position must be a constant. length is the number of fields.
  • Text. A tuple becomes text as its fields in parentheses: (3, three).
  • Assigning a field. p.x = 10(= (. p x) 10) does not change p. It gives a new tuple, with x changed and the other fields copied. To keep it, assign it back: p = p.x = 10(= p (= (. p x) 10)). An assignment whose new tuple is not kept is an error: Assigning x creates a new Point tuple that is discarded; write p = p.x = value.
  • Taking a tuple apart. . x, y = q(let (tuple x y) q) binds each field to a local; see Patterns.

Named tuple types

A type built on a tuple type, as Point is above, or on Tuple with properties as its fields, is a named tuple type.

-- TextStyle()
-- TextStyle("serif", 14)
-- TextStyle • size 20 • bold true
-- HeadingStyle("sans", 18, true, 2)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ TextStyle is Tuple

+ font String = "sans"
+ size Int = 12
+ bold Bool

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ HeadingStyle is TextStyle

+ level Int = 1
(main
  (print (call TextStyle))
  (print (call TextStyle "serif" 14))
  (print (call TextStyle (:size 20) (:bold true)))
  (print (call HeadingStyle "sans" 18 true 2))
)

(type + TextStyle (is Tuple)
  (prop + font String (= "sans"))
  (prop + size Int (= 12))
  (prop + bold Bool)
)

(type + HeadingStyle (is TextStyle)
  (prop + level Int (= 1))
)
(sans, 12, false)
(serif, 14, false)
(sans, 20, true)
(sans, 18, true, 2)
  • Fields. Each stored property is a field, in the order declared. Getters and computed properties are not fields. Lazy properties are not allowed.
  • Making one. Without a constructor of its own, a named tuple takes its fields as arguments, in order or by name, and a field left out takes its value, or the empty value of its type.
  • Methods. A named tuple type may declare constructors, methods, getters, conversions and operators, as a class does.
  • Deriving. A tuple type built on another, as HeadingStyle is on TextStyle, has the other's fields first, then its own.
  • Equality. Two tuples of one named type are equal when each of their fields is, using each field's ==. A named tuple is never equal to a tuple of another type, even one with the same fields, so Point(1, 2) == (1, 2)(== (call Point 1 2) (tuple 1 2)) is false.
  • Conversion. A tuple converts to a named tuple type whose fields its fields convert to, field by field in order, as 7, 8(tuple 7 8) does to Point above. The fields' names are not compared.

Structs

A type built on Struct is a struct: a named tuple type whose fields can be changed in place.

. a = Dimensions(1, 2)
. b = a
b.width = 10
-- a
-- b
grow(a)
-- a
a.height += 5
-- a

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Dimensions is Struct

+ width Int
+ height Int

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do grow
    - size Dimensions

size.width += 1
-- "grown to $size"
(main
  (let a (call Dimensions 1 2))
  (let b a)
  (= (. b width) 10)
  (print a)
  (print b)
  (call grow a)
  (print a)
  (+= (. a height) 5)
  (print a)
)

(type + Dimensions (is Struct)
  (prop + width Int)
  (prop + height Int)
)

(fn-do + grow _
  (param size Dimensions)
  (+= (. size width) 1)
  (print (str "grown to " size))
)
(1, 2)
(10, 2)
grown to (2, 2)
(1, 2)
(1, 7)
  • Changed in place. a.height += 5(+= (. a height) 5) changes a. The value of a field assignment is the value assigned.
  • Copied. Like a tuple, a struct is copied where it is assigned or passed, and when a method is called on it: a function that changes its parameter changes its own copy, and so does a method that changes a field of this. A method that changes a struct gives the changed struct back, as in size = size.widened(1)(= size (call (. size widened) 1)).
  • Stored inline. A struct held by another struct, or by a class, is stored inside it, so line.start.x = 7(= (. line start x) 7) changes line.
  • Fixed layout. A struct's fields cannot be added or removed. Lazy properties are not allowed: Property not supported.
  • A struct nothing holds. A field of a struct that no local, parameter or property holds, such as one as gives or a call returns, cannot be assigned, since the change would be lost: (size as Dimensions).width = 9(= (. (as size Dimensions) width) 9) is an error, Assigning width changes a Dimensions struct that nothing holds, so the change is lost; assign width where the struct is held.

Otherwise a struct is declared, made, compared and converted as a named tuple is.

Inheritance

A class declared is another class is derived from it. The derived class has every member of its base, and may declare more, and may replace the base's methods with its own.

. pets [Animal] = [Dog("Rex", "terrier"), Cat("Tom")]
for pet in pets
    -- pet.describe()
. first = pets[0]
-- first is Dog
-- first is Cat
-- (first as Dog).breed

+ Animal

+ name String

+ This

────────────────────
+ sound String

"..."

────────────────────
+ describe String

"$name says ${sound()}"

+ Dog is Animal

+ breed String
────────────────────
+ This
    - name String
    - breed String

super(name)

────────────────────
+ sound String

"woof"

────────────────────
+ describe String

"${super.describe()}, a $breed"


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Cat is Animal


────────────────────
+ sound String

"meow"

  (let pets (list Animal) (list (call Dog "Rex" "terrier") (call Cat "Tom")))
  (for (in pet pets)
    (print (call (. pet describe)))
  )
  (let first ([] pets 0))
  (print (is first Dog))
  (print (is first Cat))
  (print (. (as first Dog) breed))
)

    (param name String)
    (print (str "new " name))

  (fn-expr + sound String
    "..."

    (str name " says " (call sound))

  (prop + breed String)

    (param name String)
    (param breed String)
    (call super name)
  )
  (fn-expr + sound String
    "woof"
  )
  (fn-expr + describe String
    (str (call (. super describe)) ", a " breed)
  )

(type + Cat (is Animal)
  (fn-expr + sound String
    "meow"
  )
)

new Tom
Rex says woof, a terrier

false
terrier
  • What is inherited. Properties, methods, getters, setters, conversions and constructors. A derived class that declares no constructor is made with its base's, as Cat("Tom")(call Cat "Tom") is.
  • Overriding. A method, getter, setter or operator declared again in a derived class replaces the base's. A call is made to the method of the object's own class, even through a value whose type is the base, as describe and sound are above.
  • What an override may change. Its result may be a type the base's result converts to, such as a derived class. An override that may raise an error the base's method does not declare is an error: "sound" can fail with Error, but the method it overrides cannot; add "?! Error" to that method, or catch the error inside "sound".
  • The base's method. super.describe()(call (. super describe)) calls the base's method, and super.label(. super label) reads the base's getter, even from an override of it. super alone is not a value: Bare super is not a value.
  • The base's constructor. super(name)(call super name) calls a constructor of the base, and must be the constructor's first row: super constructor call must be first.
  • Properties. A derived class may give an inherited stored property a new value, as in + legs = 4(prop + legs _ (= 4)), and its value is converted to the type the base gave the property. It may not give the property another type, "name" is inherited from Animal, so it keeps the type it has there and cannot state its own; remove "Int", nor declare it another way: a property declared with = in the base is declared with = in the derived class too.
  • One base. A class has at most one base class. It may implement any number of interfaces.
  • Generic classes. A generic class may derive from a generic class, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Child'Item is Base'Item(type + (of Child Item) (is (of Base Item))), or from one choice of its types, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Numbers is Holder'Int(type + Numbers (is (of Holder Int))).

Values of a base class

A value of a derived class can be used where its base class is wanted: it can be assigned to a local of the base type, passed for a parameter of it, or added to a list of it. The reverse needs a test or a conversion:

  • is. pet is Dog(is pet Dog) is true when the object is a Dog, or of a class derived from Dog. pet is! Dog(is! pet Dog) is true only when the object's class is Dog itself. pet is not Dog(is-not pet Dog) and pet is! not Dog(is!-not pet Dog) are their opposites.
  • as. pet as Dog(as pet Dog) gives the object as a Dog. When it is not one, the program panics: Invalid cast to [Object app/main:Dog].
  • Patterns. A match arm | dog Dog value(case (: dog Dog) value) is taken when the object is a Dog, and binds it as one; see Patterns.

An if that tests pet is Dog(is pet Dog) does not yet change the type of pet inside it.

Interfaces

An interface declares members without being a kind of value of its own. A type implements the interface by having those members, and then its values can be used where the interface is wanted.

Declaring an interface

An interface is a type built on Interface. Its members are functions, getters, setters, static functions and associated types:

  • Required members. A member with no body that gives a value, such as area, must be declared by every type that implements the interface.
  • Hooks. A member with no body and no result may be left out; see Hooks.
  • Members with bodies. A member with a body, such as describe, is given to every type that implements the interface, which may declare its own instead. Its body may use the interface's other members, and calls them on the value it was called for.
  • Static functions. A static function with no body is required of each implementing type as a static function; see Constraints.
  • Deriving. An interface may be built on other interfaces, as ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Solid is Interface is Shape(type + Solid (is Interface) (implements Shape)) is on Shape. A type that implements it implements each of them too.
  • Type parameters. An interface can take type parameters, as Iterable'Item(of Iterable Item) does.
  • No storage. An interface holds no values, so a stored property in one is an error: Shape is an interface, so it cannot store "name"; declare a getter for the types that are Shape to answer, as in "+ get name String".
  • No values of its own. Calling an interface is an error, Shape is an interface, so it has no constructor; construct a class that is Shape, and so is declaring a local of an interface type with no value.

Hooks

A member with no body and no result, such as reset here, is a hook. A type that implements the interface may declare it or leave it out, and calling it on a value whose type leaves it out does nothing:

for shape in shapes
    shape.reset()
