A member that gives a value has no such default, so leaving one out is an error.

Implementing an interface

A type implements an interface by naming it after its header, as Square and Circle do: ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Square is Shape(type + Square (implements Shape)). Classes, named tuples, structs and number types can implement interfaces.

  • What must match. Each required member must be declared, with a result its own converts to. The parameter names need not match. A method may take more parameters than the interface's, when each of them has a default.
  • Properties for getters. A stored property satisfies a required getter of its name, as name does for Square, and a public one satisfies a getter and setter together.
  • Errors. A method may raise fewer errors than the interface declares, but not more.
  • A missing member is an error wherever a value of the type is made a value of the interface, reported at the type's declaration: Blob does not implement "area", which Shape declares without a body; declare "area" in Blob.
  • Only interfaces. A type implements only interfaces. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Box is Base(type + Box (implements Base)), with Base a class, is an error: Box cannot implement Base, which is not an interface; a type is built on one type, written in its header, as in "+ Box is Base".
  • Derived classes. A class implements every interface its base class does.

Values of an interface

A value of a type that implements an interface can be used where the interface is wanted, and converts to it on its own. A call on a value of an interface calls the member of the type the value holds.

  • is and as. held is Square(is held Square) tests what the value holds, and held as Square(as held Square) gives it, panicking when it holds something else. A match arm | square Square value(case (: square Square) value) does both; see Patterns.
  • Copies. A tuple or a struct held as an interface is a copy, and as gives another copy.
  • Equality. Two values of an interface holding objects are equal when they hold the same object. Two holding tuples or numbers are equal when the held values are, by their type's ==.
  • Narrower interfaces. A value of an interface does not convert to an interface derived from it: Shape cannot be cast to Solid; there is no conversion between them.

Constraints

A constraint among a generic function's parameters, or under a generic type's header, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Shelf'Item - Item is Titled(type + (of Shelf Item) (constraint is Item Titled)), requires the type chosen for Item to implement Titled. Code that knows only that Item is Titled can then use the members Titled declares, and call its static functions through the type parameter.

  • Static functions are called through the type parameter, as in Item.kind()(call (. Item kind)). Calling one through the interface itself is an error: Static methods cannot be called on an interface type. Calling one through a type parameter with no constraint that declares it is an error too: Static method kind is not declared by constraints on Item.
  • is!. The constraint in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Shelf'Item - Item is! Book(type + (of Shelf Item) (constraint is! Item Book)) requires exactly Book. See Functions for constraints on functions.

Associated types

An interface may declare a type that each implementing type chooses, by a member that names only a type, such as + Context(prop + _ Context), or a type with parameters, such as + Backing'Item(prop + _ (of Backing Item)). An implementing type binds it with + Context = I32(prop + _ Context (= I32)). Code constrained to the interface names the chosen type through the type parameter, as Storage.Context(. Storage Context), and can make a value of it with Storage.Context()(call (. Storage Context)). A type that implements the interface without binding one of its associated types is an error: Must implement associated type Context in Arena.

Types of alternatives

A type built on several types stands for any one of them. In rows it is written with ||, as + Choice is Int || String.

-- twice("ab")
-- kind(3)
-- kind("x")
. held Choice = 4
-- type-of held
-- type-of Choice("y")
-- Choice(2.5)

    - value Choice

  (print (call twice 3))
  (print (call twice "ab"))
  (print (call kind 3))
  (print (call kind "x"))
  (let held Choice 4)
  (print (type-of held))
  (print (type-of (call Choice "y")))
  (print (call Choice 2.5))

[TypeInfo I64]
[TypeInfo String]
2
  • Not a union. A type of alternatives has no values of its own. A value of it is a value of one of its types, and keeps that type, as held keeps Int. A union holds a case, and can tell which at run time; see Unions and enums.
  • A function for each type. A parameter of a type of alternatives makes a function generic: the compiler makes one function for each of the types the program passes, as for a type parameter; see Functions. In each, the parameter has that one type, so is is decided as the function is made.
  • Other types. A value of none of the types is an error: No function "twice" accepts (F64); it is declared as "twice(value Choice)".
  • Matches. A match over such a parameter is checked in each function made from it, so an arm for one type is an error in the others: Pattern has no possible matches. Test with is instead, or declare an overload for each type.
  • Calling the type with a value converts it as as does, to the first type as can convert it to: Choice(2.5)(call Choice 2.5) is the Int 2. With no value it is an error: Choice stands for any one of Int and String, so it has no constructor; give it a value of one of them, as in Choice(value).
  • Collections. A list or other collection of a type of alternatives cannot be built yet.
  • The stream family. <Int>(stream Int) is the best-known type of alternatives: Stream'Item stands for any one of the stream interfaces; see Streams.

Use a union for a value that can be in one of several states, an interface for behavior many types share, and a type of alternatives for a parameter that takes several types and handles each of them as it is compiled.

Delegation

A class can implement an interface by passing it to one of its properties. A delegation before a property, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Logger as Sink for + console Console(type + Logger (delegate Sink) (prop + console Console)), makes the class implement Sink, and each member of Sink the class does not declare itself is called on the property's value.

. logger = Logger()
logger.write("ready")
logger.flush()
. sink Sink = logger
sink.write("go")
-- logger.count

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Sink is Interface


────────────────────
+ do write
    - text String



────────────────────
+ do flush




━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Console
    is Sink


────────────────────
+ do write
    - text String

-- "> $text"

────────────────────
+ do flush

-- "flushed"


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Logger

as Sink for
+ console Console
+ count Int
────────────────────
+ do write
    - text String

count += 1
console.write("$count: $text")
(main
  (let logger (call Logger))
  (call (. logger write) "ready")
  (call (. logger flush))
  (let sink Sink logger)
  (call (. sink write) "go")
  (print (. logger count))
)

(type + Sink (is Interface)
  (fn-do + write _
    (param text String)
  )
  (fn-do + flush _)
)

(type + Console
  (implements Sink)
  (fn-do + write _
    (param text String)
    (print (str "> " text))
  )
  (fn-do + flush _
    (print "flushed")
  )
)

(type + Logger
  (delegate Sink)
  (prop + console Console)
  (prop + count Int)
  (fn-do + write _
    (param text String)
    (+= count 1)
    (call (. console write) (str count ": " text))
  )
)
> 1: ready
flushed
> 2: go
2
  • The class's own members win. Logger declares write, so its own runs. It does not declare flush, so flush is called on console.
  • Read at each call. The property is read each time a member is called, so assigning it another value sends later calls there. A getter can be the delegate, and runs at each call.
  • The delegate's type need not declare that it implements the interface: it needs only the members.
  • Several interfaces. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Logger as Sink, Source for + console Console(type + Logger (delegate Sink Source) (prop + console Console)) delegates two interfaces to one property, and a class may delegate different interfaces to different properties.
  • Identity. The class's values are the class: logger is Logger(is logger Logger) is true, and logger is Console(is logger Console) is false.
  • Derived classes inherit the delegation, and may declare members of the interface themselves.

Extensions

An extension adds members to a type declared elsewhere, including the core library's types.

. five = 5
-- five.doubled
-- "abc".shout()
-- [10, 20, 30].second

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ extend Int

+ doubled Int => this * 2

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ extend String


────────────────────
+ shout String

this.uppercased ++ "!"


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ extend List''Item''Backing

+ second Item => this[1]
(main
  (let five 5)
  (print (. five doubled))
  (print (call (. "abc" shout)))
  (print (. (list 10 20 30) second))
)

(extend + Int
  (prop + doubled Int (=> (* this 2)))
)

(extend + String
  (fn-expr + shout String
    (++ (. this uppercased) "!")
  )
)

(extend + (of List ''Item ''Backing)
  (prop + second Item (=> ([] this 1)))
)
10
ABC!
20

An extension is declared with extend, and has members as a type has them, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + extend Type + name Type => value(extend + Type (prop + name Type (=> value))).

  • What it can add. Methods, getters and setters, computed properties, conversions, operators and constructors. A stored property is an error: Stored properties are not allowed in extensions.
  • this is the value the member is called on, of the extended type.
  • Where it applies. An extension's members can be used in its own module and in modules that import it. Elsewhere the type does not have them.
  • Derived classes. An extension of a class reaches classes derived from it, and its members call the overrides of the object's class.
  • Generic types. In ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + extend List''Item''Backing(extend + (of List ''Item ''Backing)), each name after '' is a type parameter of the extension, so it extends every List. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + extend Box'Int(extend + (of Box Int)) extends only that choice. A where clause, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + extend Box''Item where Item is Titled(extend + (of Box ''Item) (where (constraint is Item Titled))), extends only the choices that meet it.
  • Conflicts. An extension may add an overload of a method the type declares, but not a member with the same name and parameters: Extension member conflicts with existing member. When two extensions add the same member, a call to it is an error: More than one extension declares "shout" for String, so the call is ambiguous; remove or rename all but one of them.

An as clause, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + extend Thing as Shape(extend + Thing (as Shape)), is reserved for making a type implement an interface from outside it. The compiler does not build it yet: Not yet implemented. Such an extension has no body, and is written (extend-line + Thing (as Shape)), in rows + extend Thing as Shape.

Facets

A facet is a part of a class declared apart from the class's body, usually in a file of its own. It adds stored properties and methods to the class, its owner, and they live in the owner's objects: an object and its facets are one object, with one identity.

. box = Box()
box.scroll-by(30)
box.scroll-by(30)
-- box.offset
-- box.describe()

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Box

_ height Int = 50
────────────────────
+ describe String

"height $height, scrolled $offset"


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ BoxScroll is facet of Box

+ offset Int = 0
────────────────────
+ do scroll-by
    - amount Int

offset += amount
if offset > height
    offset = height
(main
  (let box (call Box))
  (call (. box scroll-by) 30)
  (call (. box scroll-by) 30)
  (print (. box offset))
  (print (call (. box describe)))
)

(type + Box
  (prop _ height Int (= 50))
  (fn-expr + describe String
    (str "height " height ", scrolled " offset)
  )
)

(type + BoxScroll (facet-of Box)
  (prop + offset Int (= 0))
  (fn-do + scroll-by _
    (param amount Int)
    (+= offset amount)
    (if (> offset height)
      (= offset height)
    )
  )
)
50
height 50, scrolled 50

A facet is declared with facet-of, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + BoxScroll is facet of Box(type + BoxScroll (facet-of Box)), in rows + BoxScroll is facet of Box.

  • The owner. facet-of names a class, or another facet of one, and the chain ends at a class, the facet's owner. A facet of a facet reaches its parent's members. A class that takes type parameters has no facets: BoxScroll can't be part of Box, since a class that takes type arguments has no facets.
  • Where. A facet is declared in its owner's file or in a file of its family, named after it, as box.scroll.bx is beside box.bx; see Modules. Anywhere else it is an error: Extra is a facet of Box, so it is declared in the file family of box.yumi, in a module named after it.
  • One object. A facet's stored properties are stored in the owner's objects, after the owner's own. Each constructor of the owner, and of the classes derived from it, gives them their first values: the owner's first, then each facet's, in the order of the names of the files that declare them, and in the order they are declared within a file. A constructor's argument named after a facet's property gives it that value instead, as one named after the owner's own property does. A facet's private property takes no argument's value: outside the facet's file the argument is only an argument, and in it the argument is an error, since two facets may keep one name: hidden is private to facet BoxScroll, so a constructor's argument can't give it a value.
  • No constructors. A facet has no constructors and no static functions. Each of its stored properties needs a value or an optional type: offset needs a value or an optional type, since BoxScroll is a facet and no constructor gives it one.
  • What it may declare. Methods, getters and setters, stored, lazy and computed properties, operators, conversions, events, using, interfaces, sections, when and whenever rules and dependencies.
  • Interfaces. An interface a facet names, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + BoxScroll is facet of Box is Scrollable(type + BoxScroll (facet-of Box) (implements Scrollable)), in rows is Scrollable under the facet's line, is its owner's: the owner and the classes below it implement it, through the facet's members, which a class below may override. A facet names only interfaces: BoxScroll cannot implement Base, which is not an interface; a facet is part of its class and is built on no type. A member the facet leaves out is reported as the owner's, and names the facet: Box does not implement "position", which Scrollable declares without a body; declare "position" in BoxScroll. The other way, an interface the owner names is answered by its facets' public members as by its own, so a class hands an interface to a facet by naming it and leaving the members to the facet.
  • No markup. A class's content section, which gives its objects their children, is the class's alone, written in its body: BoxMarkup is a facet, so it writes no markup; a content section is its owner's alone.
  • Sections and rules. A facet's sections, when and whenever rules and dependencies are its owner's: each object of the owner runs them, after the owner's own and before those of a class below, and a facet's section subscribes to any event the facet reaches, its owner's or its own.
  • Styles. A facet's using gives its owner the style or style sheet, after the owner's own and in the order of the facets, as if the owner named it: the owner's objects have the style's properties wherever the owner is, markup writes them on its elements, and any code reads them, the facet's as $name. BoxFocus uses GUIBoxFocus, so the focus code and its style move together.
  • Events. A facet's events are its owner's objects' events. The facet, the owner's file and the facets that see it publish one by its name alone, other code subscribes to it on an object of the owner's type as to any event, and a public one bubbles as the owner's own do. Closing an object ends what subscribes to its facets' events too. An event's name is its owner's alone, private or not: Facets BoxFocus and BoxScroll of Box both declare shaken; an event's name is its class's alone, private or not.
  • this is the object the member is called on, of the owner's type.
  • Uses. Wherever the owner's type is visible, its objects have the public members of all its facets, as they have the owner's own, whatever the code using them imports, and in the owner's file family they have the members the facets share with ^ as well. Only the code of the facets' other files reaches fewer; see below. The owner's own members use them by name, as describe uses offset.

Facet values

A facet's name is a type, which goes wherever a class's does: a parameter, a property, a local, the items of a list, an optional. Its value is an object of the owner seen through the facet.

  • Narrowing is unasked. A value of the owner, or of a class below it, becomes a value of any of its facets, and a facet's value becomes a value of the facets it is part of. The object is the same object.
  • What it has. A facet's value has the members of its facet and of the facets it is part of, and no others: BoxScroll has no property "width"; a facet's value has only its facet's members and those of the facets it is part of. Write "as Box" to reach the rest of Box. A class below that overrides one of them answers for it, as on the owner's value. In a facet's file, a value of a sibling facet has its members only where the facet sees the sibling. A facet's events are not reached through its value yet, and its value becomes an interface only as its owner: write value as Box(as value Box) for either.
  • Widening is asked. value as Box(as value Box), in rows value as Box, gives the owner's value back, checked when the program is built: Expected Box here, but this is BoxScroll, which becomes Box only when asked; write "as Box". A cast to a class below the owner tests the object, as one from the owner does, and so do is and an arm of a match that name such a class.
  • No test for a facet. Every object of the owner has every facet, so is and an arm don't name one: BoxScroll is a facet, which every Box has, so no value is tested for it. (type-of value) of a facet's value is its owner's TypeInfo.
  • No constructor. BoxScroll is a facet of Box, so it has no constructor; a Box is a BoxScroll. A stored property of a facet's type needs a value or an optional type: held is a BoxScroll, a facet of Box, which has no constructor to give it its first value; give it a value, or make it optional.
  • Names outside the family. Code outside the owner's family can't import a facet's file, so importing the owner's module brings its facets' names, and nothing else of their files: Type "BoxScroll" not found; BoxScroll is a facet of Box, whose name comes with Box's module. Import that module to name it.

What a facet reaches

Code in a file of the family, other than the owner's own, that declares a facet reaches:

  • the facet's own members, and those of the facets it is part of;
  • every member the owner declares, private ones included, and the private functions, values and types of the owner's file;
  • the public and shared members of the sibling facets it names with sees.

In ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + BoxScroll is facet of Box sees BoxFocus(type + BoxScroll (facet-of Box) (sees BoxFocus)), sees names another facet of the same owner; in rows, sees BoxFocus goes on the line under the facet's. The grant is one way and is not passed on. A sibling's member that the facet does not see is an error: Name "focused" not found; facet BoxFocus declares it, and only the facets a facet sees are in reach. Write "sees BoxFocus" under the facet that uses it. A file that declares several facets of one owner reaches what they reach together. Other objects of the owner's type, such as a parent or a child, reach the same there and no more. The owner's own file reaches every facet, also when it declares one.

  • Private members of a facet are private to its file. Two facets may each declare a private member of one name, and the code of each file reaches its own.
  • Shared members, declared with ^, are for the owner's file family: the owner's file, the facets that see the facet, and the family's other files reach them, on any object of the owner's type. A facet shares what only the owner's family calls, such as a step the owner's layout runs, and keeps it from code outside.
  • Public and shared members are the owner's. A facet can't declare a member the owner has, its own or one a facet of a class above declares: offset is already a member of Box, so facet BoxScroll can't declare it. Two facets of one owner can't both declare a member of one name unless both are private.
  • Derived classes have the owner's facets and their storage. A derived class overrides a facet's method, getter or setter as it would one its base declares, with a member of the same name and kind. On the derived class's objects, every call of the facet's member runs the override, the facet's own calls included, and the override reaches the facet's through super. It gives a facet's stored or lazy property a new value by declaring the property with one, as it would its base's: its objects start with that value, and the facet's own code reads it. It can't declare any other member a facet declares: Panel can't declare offset, since facet BoxScroll of Box declares it.

Type information

A type's name used as a value is a TypeInfo, which describes the type. type-of value(type-of value) gives the TypeInfo of a value's type.

. pet Animal = Dog()
. info = type-of pet
-- info
-- info.name
-- info.concrete-name
-- Dog.base
-- (type-of 5).name
-- (type-of (1, 2)).size
-- type-of pet == Animal

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Animal



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Dog is Animal
(main
  (let pet Animal (call Dog))
  (let info (type-of pet))
  (print info)
  (print (. info name))
  (print (. info concrete-name))
  (print (. Dog base))
  (print (. (type-of 5) name))
  (print (. (type-of (tuple 1 2)) size))
  (print (== (type-of pet) Animal))
)

(type + Animal)

(type + Dog (is Animal))
[TypeInfo Animal]
Animal
Dog
[TypeInfo Animal]
I64
16
true
  • type-of gives the type the value is declared with, and evaluates its operand once.
  • name is the type's name, and concrete-name the name of the class the object was made as, or the type an interface value holds.
  • base is the type it is built on, and properties describes its stored properties.
  • size is the number of bytes a value of the type takes where it is stored. An object takes the size of a reference to it.
  • Equality. == compares two TypeInfo values.

Built-in types covers TypeInfo in full.

Optionals

A value that may be absent has an optional type. Int?(? Int) holds an Int or nothing, and null is the nothing. A value of an ordinary type always holds a value, so a program says where absence is possible by writing ?, and the compiler checks that absence is dealt with before the value is used.

Absence can then pass through an expression without a stand-in such as an empty text or -1. Absence is not failure: a lookup may well find nothing, and is an optional, while a request that could not get an answer raises an error; see Errors.

This chapter covers optional types, how values become optional, the ways to use one, optionals as conditions, narrowing, and the steps that skip a null. Optionals in patterns are in Patterns, and errors as values in Errors.

Optional types

. names = ["ana", "bo"]
. found = find(names, "bo")
. missing = find(names, "cy")
-- found
-- missing
-- missing ?? -1
-- found!
if found
    -- "found at $found"
if !missing
    -- "cy is missing"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do find Int?
    - items [String]
    - target String

. index = 0
for item in items
    =? index if item == target
    index += 1
= null
(main
  (let names (list "ana" "bo"))
  (let found (call find names "bo"))
  (let missing (call find names "cy"))
  (print found)
  (print missing)
  (print (?? missing -1))
  (print (!! found))
  (if found
    (print (str "found at " found))
  )
  (if (not missing)
    (print "cy is missing")
  )
)

(fn-do + find (? Int)
  (param items (list String))
  (param target String)
  (let index 0)
  (for (in item items)
    (return-if index (if (== item target)))
    (+= index 1)
  )
  (return null)
)
1
unknown
-1
1
found at 1
cy is missing

T?(? T) is the optional type of T. Any type can be made optional: numbers, Bool, text, classes, interfaces, tuples, structs, unions, enums, lists, function types and type parameters. An optional of an optional, T??, cannot be written.

  • null is the absent value. It converts to every optional type.
  • Text. An absent value becomes the text unknown, alone, in interpolation, and as a field of a tuple.
  • No value. A local, property or global of an optional type declared without a value starts as null.
  • Its type. type-of an optional Int gives [TypeInfo Optional'I64]. Optional'Int(4)(call (of Optional Int) 4) makes one that holds 4, and Optional'Int()(call (of Optional Int)) one that holds nothing.

Making an optional

A value converts on its own where an optional of its type is wanted: in a declaration, as an argument, as a returned value, or as an item of a list. T and T?(? T) share their values, so nothing is copied or boxed.

. size = 4
-- size if size > 3
-- size if size > 9
. picked = if size > 3 then "big" else null
-- picked
-- type-of picked
(main
  (let size 4)
  (print (only-if size (if (> size 3))))
  (print (only-if size (if (> size 9))))
  (let picked (if-expr (> size 3) "big" null))
  (print picked)
  (print (type-of picked))
)
4
unknown
big
[TypeInfo Optional'String]
  • With a condition. value if condition(only-if value (if condition)) gives the value when the condition holds, and null when it does not.
  • Joins. An if with null on one branch and a value on the other, such as if size > 3 then "big" else null(if-expr (> size 3) "big" null), gives an optional of the value's type. So does a match with an arm that gives null, and an if with an optional on either branch.
  • Results. A function whose result type is inferred, and which returns a value on some paths and null or nothing on others, gives an optional. A function declared with an optional result type that ends without returning gives null. match?, catch? and a decision table with no ?? value(default value) arm give optionals too.

Optional parameters

-- greet()
-- greet("bo")
. nobody String? = null
-- welcome(nobody)
-- welcome("cy")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ greet String
    - name String? = null

"hi ${name ?? "you"}"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ welcome String
    - name String = "friend"

"welcome, $name"
(main
  (print (call greet))
  (print (call greet "bo"))
  (let nobody (? String) null)
  (print (call welcome nobody))
  (print (call welcome "cy"))
)

(fn-expr + greet String
  (param name (? String) (= null))
  (str "hi " (?? name "you"))
)

(fn-expr + welcome String
  (param name String (= "friend"))
  (str "welcome, " name)
)
hi you
hi bo
welcome, friend
welcome, cy
  • Optional is not left out. A parameter declared - name String?(param name (? String)) may be given null, but must be given: No function "greet" accepts (); it is declared as "greet(name String?)"; "name" may be null but has no default, so a call must give it: pass null, or declare "name String? = null". Declared - name String? = null(param name (? String) (= null)), it may be left out.
  • Defaults. An optional given for a parameter that is not optional but has a default gives its value when it holds one, and the default when it holds nothing, as welcome(nobody)(call welcome nobody) does. For a parameter without a default, an optional is an error: No function "strict" accepts (I32?); it is declared as "strict(a I32)".

Using an optional

An optional cannot be used as its value until the compiler knows it holds one. These forms get the value out, or carry the absence along.

CodeValue
value!(!! value)The value. The program panics when it is null.
value ?? fallback(?? value fallback)The value, or the fallback when it is null.
object?.name(?. object name)The member, or null when the object is null.
list?[index](?[] list index)The item, or null when the collection is null.
value as Type(as value Type)The value, converted to the type. The program panics when it is null.
. user User? = User("ana", null)
-- user?.name
-- user?.manager?.name
-- user?.tags.length
. nobody User? = null
-- nobody?.name
-- nobody?.name ?? "anonymous"
-- user?.tags?[0]
nobody?.name = "cy"
-- nobody?.greet() ?? "silent"
-- user?.greet()

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ User

+ name String
+ manager User?
+ tags [String] = ["admin"]
────────────────────
+ This
    - name String
    - manager User?



────────────────────
+ greet String

"hi $name"
(main
  (let user (? User) (call User "ana" null))
  (print (?. user name))
  (print (?. (?. user manager) name))
  (print (. (?. user tags) length))
  (let nobody (? User) null)
  (print (?. nobody name))
  (print (?? (?. nobody name) "anonymous"))
  (print (?[] (?. user tags) 0))
  (= (?. nobody name) "cy")
  (print (?? (call (?. nobody greet)) "silent"))
  (print (call (?. user greet)))
)

(type + User
  (prop + name String)
  (prop + manager (? User))
  (prop + tags (list String) (= (list "admin")))
  (fn-do + This _
    (param name String)
    (param manager (? User))
  )
  (fn-expr + greet String
    (str "hi " name)
  )

Forcing

value!(!! value) gives the value of an optional, and panics when it holds nothing: Optional'core/number:I64 is null. The panic is not an error a function raises; see Errors. It works within a chain, as in holder.find(5)!.next!.value(. (!! (. (!! (call (. holder find) 5)) next)) value). Forcing a value the compiler knows is not null is an error: "count" is I64, which is never null here, so it needs no "!".

Forcing suits a value that some rule of the program keeps present, and makes the writer answer for that rule. Where absence is ordinary, a fallback, a branch or match? says more.

Fallbacks

value ?? fallback(?? value fallback) gives the value when it is not null, and the fallback otherwise.

  • Only when needed. The fallback is evaluated only when the value is null.
  • Chains. a ?? b ?? c(?? a b c) gives the first that is not null.
  • Type. When the fallback is not optional, the result is not optional either. When it is, the result is optional.
  • Values that are not optional. On a value that is not optional, ?? gives the fallback when the value is false as a condition: zero, empty text, an empty collection or false. So count ?? 1(?? count 1) gives 1 when count is 0. See Control flow for what is false as a condition.
  • After if. value if condition ?? other(?? (only-if value (if condition)) other) is an error, because it reads as one value or another: write if condition then value else other(if-expr condition value other).

So an empty text in an optional is present, and an empty text that is not optional is not:

. nickname String? = ""
-- "[${nickname ?? "Anonymous"}]"
. plain = ""
-- "[${plain ?? "Anonymous"}]"
. missing String?
-- "[${missing ?? "Anonymous"}]"
(main
  (let nickname (? String) "")
  (print (str "[" (?? nickname "Anonymous") "]"))
  (let plain "")
  (print (str "[" (?? plain "Anonymous") "]"))
  (let missing (? String))
  (print (str "[" (?? missing "Anonymous") "]"))
)
[]
[Anonymous]
[Anonymous]

Chains

object?.name(?. object name) reads a member of an object that may be null. When the object is null, the rest of the chain is skipped and the whole chain gives null, so user?.tags.length(. (?. user tags) length) gives null when user is null, and reads user.tags.length(. user tags length) otherwise.

  • Type. The result is an optional of the last member's type.
  • Once. The object is evaluated once, and the arguments of a call in the chain only when the object is not null.
  • Calls. object?.method()(call (?. object method)) calls the method when the object is not null. A method that gives nothing can be called this way as a step.
  • Assignment. object?.name = value(= (?. object name) value) assigns when the object is not null, and does nothing otherwise. Assigning operators such as += work the same way. The value on the right is evaluated either way.
  • Events. object?.event <- value(<- (?. object event) value) publishes to the event when the object is not null, and does nothing otherwise. Unlike an assignment, the value is not evaluated when the object is null.
  • A further optional. A member that is itself optional needs its own ?., as in user?.manager?.name(?. (?. user manager) name). Reading through it with . is an error: Property "name" is read from User?, which may be null; unwrap it first with ! or ?..
  • Values that are never null. object?.name(?. object name) and list?[index](?[] list index) are an error when the object or the list cannot be null: "user" is User, which is never null, so it needs no "?"; write "user.name".

Optionals as conditions

Where a Bool is wanted, an optional is true when it holds a value, so if found body(if found body) asks whether found holds one, and !missing(not missing) whether it does not. An optional holding 0, or a Bool?(? Bool) holding false, holds a value, and is true. To test the value of a Bool?(? Bool), compare it, as in flag == true(== flag true).

. flag Bool? = false
-- (if flag then "present" else "absent")
-- flag == true
. a Int? = 3
. b Int? = null
-- a == 3
-- b == null
-- a == b
(main
  (let flag (? Bool) false)
  (print (if-expr flag "present" "absent"))
  (print (== flag true))
  (let a (? Int) 3)
  (let b (? Int) null)
  (print (== a 3))
  (print (== b null))
  (print (== a b))
)
present
false
true
true
false
  • Equality. Two optionals are equal when both are null, or both hold equal values. An optional and a value are equal when the optional holds an equal value. value == null(== value null) and value != null(!= value null) test for absence.
  • Ordering. An optional cannot be compared with < and the other ordering operators: Operator "<" is not defined for I64 and I64?.

Narrowing

After a test that shows an optional holds a value, the compiler treats it as its value: it can be used where the value's type is wanted, and its members read with ..

. count Int? = 3
if count
    -- count + 1
-- double(count)
-- double(null)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do double Int
    - value Int?

=? 0 if !value
= value * 2
(main
  (let count (? Int) 3)
  (if count
    (print (+ count 1))
  )
  (print (call double count))
  (print (call double null))
)

(fn-do + double Int
  (param value (? Int))
  (return-if 0 (if (not value)))
  (return (* value 2))
)
4
6
0

Using an optional as its value without a test is an error. For an operator it is Operator "+" is not defined for I64? and I64, and where a value of the type is wanted, Expected I64 here, but this is I64?, which may hold nothing; write "!" after it to unwrap it, or "?? fallback" to give a value for nothing.

. count Int? = 3
-- count + 1
(main
  (let count (? Int) 3)
  (print (+ count 1))
)
Exception: Operator "+" is not defined for I64? and I64
<no file:4>
      (print (+ count 1))
             ^^^^^^^^^^^

What narrows

  • Conditions. if value body(if value body) and if value != null body(if (!= value null) body) narrow value in the body, and if !value body else other(if (not value) body (else other)) in the else. A while condition narrows its body, a when clause on a loop narrows the item, and the arms of a decision table see what the arms above them ruled out.
  • Early returns. A branch that leaves the function, such as =? 0 if !value(return-if 0 (if (not value))), narrows the rest of the body. So does a check that panics, as in ?! Panic("missing") if !value(throw (call Panic "missing") (if (not value))).
  • Joined conditions. In value && value > 3(and value (> value 3)), the right side sees value narrowed, and in !value || value > 3(or (not value) (> value 3)) too.
  • Values. In if value then value + 1 else 0(if-expr value (+ value 1) 0) and value + 1 if value(only-if (+ value 1) (if value)), the value is narrowed.
  • Assignment. Assigning a value that is not null narrows a local until it is assigned again. A local declared with no value and assigned on every path before a use is narrowed at the use. A declaration with a value, as in . count Int? = 3(let count (? Int) 3), does not narrow.
  • Paths. A test of a path such as box.child(. box child), where box is a local, narrows the path.

What ends narrowing

  • Assigning null, on any path, ends it after the paths meet.
  • Loops. A narrowed local stays narrowed in a loop only when every path back to the loop's start keeps it: Narrowing of 'value' is used in the loop but does not hold when the loop repeats.
  • A function value that assigns the local. Calling one ends it. Other calls do not.
  • Properties. A property read by name, or through this, is narrowed by the same tests, but any call, print or loop ends it, since it could change the property. So do assigning it and reading a lazy property. A getter is never narrowed.
. box = Box()
box.show()

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Box

+ label String?
────────────────────
+ do show

if label
    touch()
    -- label.length

────────────────────
+ do touch
(main
  (let box (call Box))
  (call (. box show))
)

(type + Box
  (prop + label (? String))
  (fn-do + show _
    (if label
      (call touch)
      (print (. label length))
    )
  )
  (fn-do + touch _)
)
Exception: Property "length" is read from String?, which may be null; unwrap it first with ! or ?.
<no file:12>
          (print (. label length))
                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Test again after the call, or copy the property to a local before testing it.

Narrowing also applies to unions and to the classes a value may hold; see Unions and enums, and Types. An if that tests value is Dog(is value Dog) on a value of a base class does not yet narrow it.

Steps that skip null

Several steps take an optional and do nothing when it holds nothing:

CodeStep
--? value(print? value)Print the value, unless it is null.
target =? value(=? target value)Assign the value, unless it is null.
target +=? value(+=? target value)Add the value, unless it is null. -=?, *=?, /=?, %=?, %%=? and ++=? do the same for the other updates.
=? value(return? value)Return the value, unless it is null.
<=? value(yield? value)Give the value to the stream, unless it is null.
use? resource(use? resource)Use the resource, unless it is null.
*? value(bullet? value)Give the item, unless it is null.
**? items(bullet*? items)Give every item of a collection, unless it is null.
. total = 10
. none Int? = null
. some Int? = 5
total +=? none
total +=? some
-- total
--? none
--? some
. label = "start"
label =? null as String?
-- label
(main
  (let total 10)
  (let none (? Int) null)
  (let some (? Int) 5)
  (+=? total none)
  (+=? total some)
  (print total)
  (print? none)
  (print? some)
  (let label "start")
  (=? label (as null (? String)))
  (print label)
)
15
5
start
  • The target is not optional. The value is what may be null. With an optional target the update is refused, as with Operator "*=" is not defined for I64? and I64.
  • As values. (=? target value) and (+=? target value) may be used as values, and give what the target then holds. The other updates are steps only.

Unions and enums

A union is a value that is one of several cases. Each case has a name, a type, or both, and may carry a value of its own, its payload. An enum is a type whose values are a fixed set of named values of one representation, such as numbers or tuples.

This chapter covers declaring unions, making and reading their values, unions of types, members, exhaustiveness, anonymous cases and enums. Matching in general is in Patterns, and optionals in Optionals.

Declaring a union

. downloads [Download] = [Download.waiting, Download.progress(300, 1200), Download.complete("report.pdf")]
for download in downloads
    -- describe(download)
. done = Download.complete("notes.txt")
-- done is .complete
-- done is .waiting
-- done
-- Download.waiting
-- done == Download.complete("notes.txt")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Download is Union

| waiting
| progress(received Int, total Int)
| complete String

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - download Download

match download
    | .waiting
        "waiting"
    | .progress(received, total)
        "$received of $total bytes"
    | .complete(path)
        "saved to $path"
(main
  (let downloads
    (list Download)
    (list
      (. Download waiting)
      (call (. Download progress) 300 1200)
      (call (. Download complete) "report.pdf")
    )
  )
  (for (in download downloads)
    (print (call describe download))
  )
  (let done (call (. Download complete) "notes.txt"))
  (print (is done .complete))
  (print (is done .waiting))
  (print done)
  (print (. Download waiting))
  (print (== done (call (. Download complete) "notes.txt")))
)

(type + Download (is Union)
  (variant waiting)
  (variant progress (tuple (: received Int) (: total Int)))
  (variant complete String)
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param download Download)
  (match download
    (case .waiting
      "waiting"
    )
    (case (call .progress received total)
      (str received " of " total " bytes")
    )
    (case (call .complete path)
      (str "saved to " path)
    )
  )
)
waiting
300 of 1200 bytes
saved to report.pdf
true
false
notes.txt
waiting
true

A union is a type built on Union that lists its cases. A case has a name or a type, and may have a payload or a fixed value:

DeclarationCase
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Download is Union | waiting(type + Download (is Union) (variant waiting))A name and no payload.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Download is Union | complete String(type + Download (is Union) (variant complete String))A name and a payload of one type.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Download is Union | progress(received Int, total Int)(type + Download (is Union) (variant progress (tuple (: received Int) (: total Int))))A name and a payload of several fields.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Value is Union | Int(type + Value (is Union) (variant Int))A type, with no name; see Unions of types.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Status is Union | failed = 1(type + Status (is Union) (variant failed (= 1)))A name and a fixed value.

The kinds of case can be mixed in one union. A union may take type parameters, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Maybe'Item is Union | some(Item) | none(type + (of Maybe Item) (is Union) (variant some (tuple Item)) (variant none)), and may hold itself through a list or an object, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Tree is Union | branch [Tree](type + Tree (is Union) (variant branch (list Tree))).

Making a union value

  • By case. Download.complete("report.pdf")(call (. Download complete) "report.pdf") makes the complete case with its payload. A case whose payload has several fields takes the fields as arguments, as Download.progress(300, 1200)(call (. Download progress) 300 1200) does. A case with no payload is named without a call: Download.waiting(. Download waiting).
  • By the case's name alone. Where the union's type is known, as for a parameter, a declared local, a returned value, an argument of == or the other items of a list, .waiting names the case without the type. When more than one visible type has a case of that name and the type is not known, the name is an error: Case '.waiting' is ambiguous between 'Download', 'Upload'.
  • By conversion. A value of a case's type converts to the union on its own: a local declared Value can be given 3 when Value has an Int case. A value that converts to a case's type only with as must be written with as.
  • By calling the union. Value(3)(call Value 3) makes the case whose type the value has.

Reading a union

. a = Status.failed("disk")
-- a.name
-- a.case
-- a == Status.failed("disk")
-- a == .done
-- label(.pending)
-- label(a)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Status is Union

| pending
| done
| failed String

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ label String?
    - status Status

match? status
    | .pending
        "pending"
    | .done
        "done"
(main
  (let a (call (. Status failed) "disk"))
  (print (. a name))
  (print (. a case))
  (print (== a (call (. Status failed) "disk")))
  (print (== a .done))
  (print (call label .pending))
  (print (call label a))
)

(type + Status (is Union)
  (variant pending)
  (variant done)
  (variant failed String)
)

(fn-expr + label (? String)
  (param status Status)
  (match? status
    (case .pending "pending")
    (case .done "done")
  )
)
failed
2
true
false
pending
unknown
  • match. An arm | .complete(path) value(case (call .complete path) value) is taken when the union holds that case, and binds its payload. A payload of several fields binds each, as in | .progress(received, total) value(case (call .progress received total) value). An arm for a case with no payload is | .waiting value(case .waiting value). See Patterns for every arm a match can have.
  • is. done is .complete(is done .complete) is true when the union holds that case. After the test, the compiler treats the value as that case; see Narrowing.
  • case and name. value.case(. value case) is the number of the case the union holds, counting from 0 in the order the cases are declared. value.name(. value name) is the case's name, and is empty for a case that is a type. A union may not declare members with these names, or type: Union property 'name' conflicts with reserved union property.
  • as. value as String(as value String) gives the payload as that type when the union holds a case that converts to it, and raises an error otherwise, which becomes the text Invalid union cast.
  • Equality. Two values of a union are equal when they hold the same case and equal payloads. A value compared with a union converts to the union first.
  • Text. A union becomes the text of its payload, or its case's name when it has none, as done and Download.waiting(. Download waiting) print above. A union that declares a conversion to String becomes that text instead.

Narrowing

A test that settles which case a union holds lets the code it guards read that case's payload.

. event = Event.click(10, 20)
if event is .click
    -- "click at ${event.x}, ${event.y}"
for fill in [.inherit, .none, Fill.color("blue")]
    -- describe(fill)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Event is Union

| click(x Int, y Int)
| key String

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Fill is Union

| inherit
| none
| color String

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - fill Fill

|? fill == .inherit
    "inherited"
|? fill == .none
    "no paint"
??
    "paint ${fill.uppercased}"
(main
  (let event (call (. Event click) 10 20))
  (if (is event .click)
    (print (str "click at " (. event x) ", " (. event y)))
  )
  (for (in fill (list .inherit .none (call (. Fill color) "blue")))
    (print (call describe fill))
  )
)

(type + Event (is Union)
  (variant click (tuple (: x Int) (: y Int)))
  (variant key String)
)

(type + Fill (is Union)
  (variant inherit)
  (variant none)
  (variant color String)
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param fill Fill)
  (case? (== fill .inherit)
    "inherited"
  )
  (case? (== fill .none)
    "no paint"
  )
  (default
    (str "paint " (. fill uppercased))
  )
)
click at 10, 20
inherited
no paint
paint BLUE
  • is narrows to the case it names, so event.x(. event x) reads the click's field.
  • == and != against a case with no payload narrow as is does, in if and else-if chains, guards and decision tables, and so does is-not.
  • Ruling cases out. Where every case but one has been ruled out, the value is narrowed to the last: the default row of describe reads the color case's text.
  • Payloads do not narrow. A comparison with a case that holds a value, as fill == Fill.color("blue")(== fill (call (. Fill color) "blue")), is an ordinary comparison and narrows nothing.

Unions of types

A case may be a type alone, with no name. A value of that type converts to the union on its own, and an arm that names the type matches it. A list written where a list of the union is wanted, as values is below, converts each item.

. values [Value] = [3, "three", 4.5, null]
for value in values
    -- "${describe(value)}, case ${value.case}"
. held Value = 7
-- held is Int
-- held as String
-- held.type

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Value is Union

| Null
| Int
| String
| Float

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - value Value

match value
    | n Int
        "number $n"
    | s String
        "text $s"
    | f Float
        "float $f"
    | Null
        "nothing"
(main
  (let values (list Value) (list 3 "three" 4.5 null))
  (for (in value values)
    (print (str (call describe value) ", case " (. value case)))
  )
  (let held Value 7)
  (print (is held Int))
  (print (as held String))
  (print (. held type))
)

(type + Value (is Union)
  (variant Null)
  (variant Int)
  (variant String)
  (variant Float)
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param value Value)
  (match value
    (case (: n Int)
      (str "number " n)
    )
    (case (: s String)
      (str "text " s)
    )
    (case (: f Float)
      (str "float " f)
    )
    (case Null
      "nothing"
    )
  )
)
number 3, case 1
text three, case 2
float 4.5, case 3
nothing, case 0
true
7
Class:core/number:I64
  • Which case. A value goes into the case whose type it has. When it has none of them, it goes into the first case it converts to on its own, before one it converts to only with as.
  • Null. A Null case holds null, and an optional converts to a union with a Null case: an absent value to Null, and a present one to its case. A local of a union whose first case is Null starts as null when it is declared with no value.
  • type. value.type(. value type) describes the type of the value the union holds.
  • Arms. An arm | n Int value(case (: n Int) value) is taken when the union holds an Int, and binds it. value is Int(is value Int) tests for it.

Named cases and type cases can be mixed. Named cases tell apart payloads of one type, such as two cases that each hold a String; type cases need no names when the types differ:

for move in [Move.vertical(12), Move.horizontal(5)]
    -- describe(move)
-- Move.vertical(12) == Move.horizontal(12)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Move is Union

| horizontal Int
| vertical Int

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - move Move

match move
    | .horizontal(distance)
        "across $distance"
    | Move.vertical(distance)
        "down $distance"
(main
  (for (in move (list (call (. Move vertical) 12) (call (. Move horizontal) 5)))
    (print (call describe move))
  )
  (print (== (call (. Move vertical) 12) (call (. Move horizontal) 12)))
)

(type + Move (is Union)
  (variant horizontal Int)
  (variant vertical Int)
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param move Move)
  (match move
    (case (call .horizontal distance)
      (str "across " distance)
    )
    (case (call (. Move vertical) distance)
      (str "down " distance)
    )
  )
)
down 12
across 5
false

Members of a union

A union can declare methods, getters, conversions and operators, and this is the union. A member the union does not declare is passed on to the value its case holds, when every case holds a value that has it.

. shapes [Shape] = [Circle(1), Square(2)]
for shape in shapes
    -- "${shape.label}: ${shape.area()}"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Shape is Union

| Circle
| Square
────────────────────
+ get label String

match this
    | Circle
        "circle"
    | Square
        "square"


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Circle is (radius Float)


────────────────────
+ area Float

3.0 * radius * radius


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Square is (side Float)


────────────────────
+ area Float

side * side
(main
  (let shapes (list Shape) (list (call Circle 1) (call Square 2)))
  (for (in shape shapes)
    (print (str (. shape label) ": " (call (. shape area))))
  )
)

(type + Shape (is Union)
  (variant Circle)
  (variant Square)
  (fn-expr + label String :get
    (match this
      (case Circle "circle")
      (case Square "square")
    )
  )
)

(type + Circle (is (tuple (: radius Float)))
  (fn-expr + area Float
    (* 3.0 radius radius)
  )
)

(type + Square (is (tuple (: side Float)))
  (fn-expr + area Float
    (* side side)
  )
)
circle: 3
square: 4
  • The union's own members win over the cases'.
  • Every case must have it. A member some case lacks is an error, such as Union case 'empty' has no payload for method 'area', or Union case 'right' has no complete dispatch for method 'area'.
  • Results. When the cases' members give different types, the result is a union of them.
  • No stored properties. A union declares no stored properties of its own.

Covering every case

A match over a union must have an arm for each case, or end with ?? value(default value) for the rest. A missing case is an error:

-- label(.pending)

| pending
| done
| failed String

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ label String
    - status Status

match status
    | .pending
        "pending"
    | .done
        "done"
(main
  (print (call label .pending))
)

(type + Status (is Union)
  (variant pending)
  (variant done)
  (variant failed String)
)

(fn-expr + label String
  (param status Status)
  (match status
    (case .pending "pending")
    (case .done "done")
  )
)

        (case .pending "pending")
        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

List every case when a new case should send each match back to be reconsidered, and end with a default arm when the cases left over share one answer on purpose: a default also takes any case added later, without a word.

With several missing, the message names each: This match on Result does not handle Config, FileNotFound and PermissionDenied; add a case for each, or "??" for the rest. match? need not cover every case, and gives null when no arm is taken, as label does in Reading a union. An arm for a type covers its derived classes.

Anonymous cases

A function can give one of several cases without a declared union. A value written ..accepted or ..accepted(name)(call ..accepted name) is a case of a union the compiler makes from every .. case that can be the result.

-- describe(check("Yumi"))
-- describe(check(""))
. result = check("x")
-- result is .accepted
-- result.name

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ check
    - name String

|? name.length > 0
    ..accepted(name)
??
    ..empty

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - result

match result
    | .accepted(name)
        "Hello, $name"
    | .empty
        "Enter a name"
(main
  (print (call describe (call check "Yumi")))
  (print (call describe (call check "")))
  (let result (call check "x"))
  (print (is result .accepted))
  (print (. result name))
)

(fn-expr + check _
  (param name String)
  (case? (> (. name length) 0)
    (call ..accepted name)
  )
  (default
    ..empty
  )
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param result _)
  (match result
    (case (call .accepted name)
      (str "Hello, " name)
    )
    (case .empty
      "Enter a name"
    )
  )
)
Hello, Yumi
Enter a name
true
accepted
  • Owners. The cases belong to the value they are given to: a function's result, a local, or a generator's items. A .. case where the result has no such owner is an error, Anonymous match case '..ok' needs a stable result owner.
  • Payloads. Each use of a case must give it the same number of values, or it is an error: Anonymous case '..value' has conflicting arity. The types of the values join, so ..value(1)(call ..value 1) and ..value(1.5)(call ..value 1.5) make a payload of Float.
  • Reading. Anonymous cases are read as named ones are: by match arms, is, value.name(. value name) and value.case(. value case). Once the union exists, .ok names one of its cases.

Enums

A type whose body lists cases, but which is built on a number, a tuple or a class rather than on Union, is an enum. Each case is one value of the type, with a name.

EnumUnion
A case isOne value, declared with the typeA kind of value, made by a call
Its data comes fromThe declaration: every case has the same fieldsThe call: each case has its own payload
Use it forNamed values of one shape: priorities, protocol codes, daysAlternatives that need different data, or one type in different roles
. level Level = .medium
-- level
-- describe(level)
-- describe(3 as Level)
-- Level.urgent as Int
-- Planet.earth
-- Planet.mars.weight
-- level == .medium

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Level is U8

| low
| medium
| high
| urgent = 10

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Planet is (name String, gravity Float)

| mercury = "Mercury", 0.5
| earth = "Earth", 1.0
| mars = "Mars", 0.25
────────────────────
+ get weight Float

80 * gravity

────────────────────
+ to String

name


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - level Level

match level
    |= .low
        "fine"
    |= .medium
        "watch"
    ??
        "act"
(main
  (let level Level .medium)
  (print level)
  (print (call describe level))
  (print (call describe (as 3 Level)))
  (print (as (. Level urgent) Int))
  (print (. Planet earth))
  (print (. Planet mars weight))
  (print (== level .medium))
)

(type + Level (is U8)
  (variant low)
  (variant medium)
  (variant high)
  (variant urgent (= 10))
)

(type + Planet (is (tuple (: name String) (: gravity Float)))
  (variant mercury (= (tuple "Mercury" 0.5)))
  (variant earth (= (tuple "Earth" 1.0)))
  (variant mars (= (tuple "Mars" 0.25)))
  (fn-expr + weight Float :get
    (* 80 gravity)
  )
  (fn-to-expr + String
    name
  )
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param level Level)
  (match level
    (case= .low
      "fine"
    )
    (case= .medium
      "watch"
    )
    (default
      "act"
    )
  )
)
1
watch
act
10
Earth
20
true
  • Number enums. In an enum built on a number type, each case is a number. A case without a value is its place among the cases, counting from 0, and a case can be given its own value, as urgent is in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Level is U8 | urgent = 10(type + Level (is U8) (variant urgent (= 10))). A number enum becomes text as its number.
  • Tuple and class enums. In an enum built on a tuple type, each case's value fills the tuple's fields in order. In one built on a class, each case is one object of the class, made from its value by the class's constructor. Their cases are values of the type, with its members, and become text by its conversion to String.
  • Naming a case. Level.medium(. Level medium), or .medium where the type is known, as for a union.
  • Numbers. 3 as Level(as 3 Level) gives the value of a number enum that is that number. For a tuple or class enum, a number gives the case at that place, counting from 0, and a number past the last case gives a new value made with no arguments. A number becomes an enum only with as: Expected Level here, but this is I64, which becomes Level only when asked; write "as Level".
  • Comparing. == and != compare enum values. The cases of a class enum are single objects, so a case equals itself.

Matching enum values

An enum's cases are values, not union cases, so an arm matches one by equality, written |= .low value(case= .low value). An arm | .low value(case .low value) on a number enum is an error, Level.low is an enum value, not a union case; match it with '|= .low', and an arm that is a name alone binds the name: Arm '| low' binds a new name, not the value Level.low; match the value with '|= Level.low'.

A match over a number enum must cover every case, or end with ?? value(default value): This match on Level does not handle Level.high; add "|= Level.high", or "??" for the rest. A match over a class enum is not checked for coverage, and fails when the program runs if no arm is taken.

Enums of Union

A union whose cases have no payloads, such as ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Color is Union | red | green | blue(type + Color (is Union) (variant red) (variant green) (variant blue)), serves as an enum whose values print as their names. Its arms are written | .red value(case .red value), as for any union.

Conversions

A value of one type becomes a value of another in two ways: on its own, where a place wants the other type, or when asked, with as. The rule that divides them is that a conversion happens on its own only where it keeps the value's meaning: where every value of one type has a value of the other that means the same. Every other conversion is written.

This chapter covers both, calling a type to convert, the conversions a type declares, parameters that take any value that converts, and the type an expression gets when its parts have different types.

Conversions on their own

. small I32 = 5
. wide Int = small
. real Float = small
-- "$wide $real"
. ints [I32] = [1, 2, 3]
. floats [Float] = ints
-- floats
. pair (I32, I32) = (1, 2)
. joined (Int, Float) = pair
-- joined
. maybe Int? = wide
-- maybe
(main
  (let small I32 5)
  (let wide Int small)
  (let real Float small)
  (print (str wide " " real))
  (let ints (list I32) (list 1 2 3))
  (let floats (list Float) ints)
  (print floats)
  (let pair (tuple I32 I32) (tuple 1 2))
  (let joined (tuple Int Float) pair)
  (print joined)
  (let maybe (? Int) wide)
  (print maybe)
)
5 5
1, 2, 3
(1, 2)
5

A value converts on its own where it is assigned, declared with a type, passed as an argument, returned, or added to a collection, when one of these holds:

  • Numbers. A number becomes a number type that holds every value of its own: I32 becomes Int and Float, U8 becomes Int and F32, and F32 becomes Float. A number that may not fit, or not exactly, needs as: Int becomes Float or I32 only when asked. Size and Index are the same width as Int, and convert both ways, and so does a number type declared on another, such as ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + Id is Int(type + Id (is Int)), with its base. Int is I64, Float is F64 and Byte is U8, and messages name them so.
  • Classes. An object becomes its base class, or an interface its class implements; see Types.
  • Functions. A function becomes a function type where calling it through the type would convert each argument and its result on their own; see Functions.
  • Optionals and unions. A value becomes an optional of its type, or a union with a case it converts to on its own. An optional becomes a union with a Null case and a case its value converts to. See Optionals, and Unions and enums.
  • Collections and tuples. A list, map or other collection becomes one of another item type when each item would convert on its own, so [I32](list I32) becomes [Float](list Float). A tuple becomes another tuple type, or a named tuple type, field by field.
  • Declared conversions. A value becomes a type that declares a conversion from its type, or that its type declares a conversion to; see Declared conversions.

Where none of these holds, a conversion the compiler knows of is an error that says to write it:

. wide Int = 5
. small I32 = wide
(main
  (let wide Int 5)
  (let small I32 wide)
)
Exception: Expected I32 here, but this is I64, which becomes I32 only when asked; write "as I32"
<no file:4>
      (let small I32 wide)
                 ^^^

Where the compiler knows no conversion, the error says so: Expected Point here, but this is String, and there is no conversion between them.

Literals

A number written in the source takes the type the place wants, when it fits: . byte U8 = 200(let byte U8 200) makes a U8. One that does not fit is an error: Integer literal 300 does not fit U8. The place can be a declaration, a parameter, a list's other items, or the other operand of an operator, so in [0, 4, 10.5](list 0 4 10.5) every item is a Float. Without a place to decide, a whole number is an Int and one with a point a Float. A suffix gives a literal its own type, as in 200u8; see Literals.

Text

A value becomes text on its own only inside a text, as in "$count items"(str count " items"), and where it is printed. Elsewhere it is converted with value as String(as value String): Expected String here, but this is I64, which becomes text only inside a text or a print, or when asked; write "as String", or write it inside a text, as in "$name".

as

value as Type(as value Type) converts a value to a type, by any conversion the compiler knows.

-- 2.7 as Int
-- -2.7 as Int
-- 300 as U8
-- -1 as U8
-- 65 as Char
-- 'B' as Int
-- true as Int
-- 0 as Bool
-- "42" as Int
-- "4.5" as Float
-- 4.5 as String
-- (3 as Float) + 0.5
(main
  (print (as 2.7 Int))
  (print (as -2.7 Int))
  (print (as 300 U8))
  (print (as -1 U8))
  (print (as 65 Char))
  (print (as 'B' Int))
  (print (as true Int))
  (print (as 0 Bool))
  (print (as "42" Int))
  (print (as "4.5" Float))
  (print (as 4.5 String))
  (print (+ (as 3 Float) 0.5))
)
2
-2
44
255
A
66
1
false
42
4.5
4.5
3.5

Beyond the conversions that happen on their own, as converts:

  • Floats to integers, dropping the fraction, so 2.7 and -2.7 become 2 and -2.
  • Integers to narrower integers, keeping the low bits, so 300 as U8(as 300 U8) is 44 and -1 as U8(as -1 U8) is 255. A signed integer converted to a wider unsigned type is sign-extended, so -128i8 as U16(as -128i8 U16) is 65408. Integers to floats, to the nearest float.
  • Numbers, Bool and Char to one another. A Char is its code point. true is 1, and a number is true when it is not zero.
  • Text to numbers, reading the whole text, white space aside, as a number. Text that is not one panics: "42x" is not a whole number, or for a float type, "1.5x" is not a number. A whole number too large for the type gives its largest value, so "300" as U8(as "300" U8) is 255. Anything to text, by its conversion to String.
  • Enums and numbers, both ways; see Unions and enums.
  • Down a class hierarchy, from a base class or an interface to a class the object is, panicking when it is not; see Types. Out of a union, to the type of the case it holds.
  • Optionals, to the type of their value, panicking when they hold nothing; see Optionals.
  • Pointers; see Native code and memory.

A conversion the compiler cannot make at all is an error, even with as: Color cannot be cast to I64; there is no conversion between them. A value of a declared type that can never hold such a value says so: "n" is declared Int, but its value is String, which can never be Int; convert the value, or declare "n" without a type.

In rows, as binds more loosely than arithmetic and named operators such as /and/, so a + b as U32 converts the sum, and a + (b as U32) converts one operand. It binds more tightly than == and assignment, and chains from left to right: value as Far as U32.

Calling a type

Calling a type with one value of another type converts it as as does: Int(2.5)(call Int 2.5) is 2, and Char(66)(call Char 66) is B.

-- Int(2.5)
-- Char(66)
-- Float(3)
-- String(42)
(main
  (print (call Int 2.5))
  (print (call Char 66))
  (print (call Float 3))
  (print (call String 42))
)
2
B
3
42

A tuple of one field is the exception: called with a value of its field's type, it is made from the value rather than converted. Calling a class with arguments its constructors take calls a constructor; see Types.

Declared conversions

A type can declare how its values become another type, with ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + to Type body(fn-to-expr + Type body), and how values of another type become its own, with ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + from name Type body(fn-from-expr + (: name Type) body), which names the value it converts. Each has a value body, or a step body when declared with fn-to-do or fn-from-do.

. m = Meters(3)
. f Float = m
-- f
-- half(m)
. c = Centimeters(m)
-- c.amount
. cms [Centimeters] = [m, Meters(0.5)]
-- cms[1].amount
-- "it is $m"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

────────────────────

amount

"$amount m"

────────────────────

Centimeters(m.amount * 100)


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

value / 2

  (let f Float m)
  (print f)
  (print (call half m))
  (let c (call Centimeters m))
  (print (. c amount))
  (let cms (list Centimeters) (list m (call Meters 0.5)))
  (print (. ([] cms 1) amount))

  (fn-to-expr + Float
    amount
  )

  • On their own. A declared conversion is used on its own, wherever a value of one type is given where the other is wanted, as m is for half and for the list of Centimeters. as and calling the type use it too. A conversion to String is the exception; see below.
  • One step. Conversions do not chain, even with as: a value converts by one declared conversion, not by one and then another. A type that converts to Centi, which converts to Kilo, does not convert to Kilo, and one that converts to I32 does not convert to Int.
  • from before to. When one type declares a conversion from a second, and the second a conversion to the first, the from is used.
  • Derived classes and interfaces. A class uses its base class's conversions, and declares its own to replace them, which are used even when the object is held as its base. An interface can declare conversions with bodies for the types that implement it.
  • Text. A conversion to String is how the type becomes text: where it is printed, inside a text, and with value as String(as value String), and nowhere else on its own. A type without one becomes text in its own way: see Types.
  • Step bodies. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + do to Iterable'Item body(fn-to-do + (of Iterable Item) body) can give a stream, yielding its items; see Streams.
  • Errors. A from that can raise an error raises it wherever it converts: in a declaration, an argument, an assignment, a return, as or a call of the type.
  • Public. A conversion cannot be private: Converters must be public.
  • Extensions. An extension can declare conversions for a type declared elsewhere; see Types.
. c Celsius = Fahrenheit(212.0)
-- c.degrees
-- (Fahrenheit(50.0) as Celsius).degrees

= Celsius(above * 5 / 9)
(main
  (let c Celsius (call Fahrenheit 212.0))
  (print (. c degrees))
  (print (. (as (call Fahrenheit 50.0) Celsius) degrees))
)

fn-from-do is a conversion from another type with a step body, which returns with = value(return value). In rows it is + do from f Fahrenheit, under a thin divider.

Parameters that take what converts

A parameter whose type is Float~(similar Float), as in - value Float~(param value (similar Float)), takes any value that converts to Float with as, and converts it. Text is the exception: as reads a number from text, but similar does not take text for a number. is~ tests the same: 3 is~ Float(is~ 3 Float) is true, and "4" is~ Float(is~ "4" Float) false, and value is~ not Type(is~-not value Type) is the opposite. A pattern such as amount Float~(: amount (similar Float)) takes what converts too; see Patterns.

-- describe(3)
-- describe(2 as U8)
-- 3 is~ Float
-- "x" is~ Float

"value $value"

  (param value (similar Float))

Joins

An expression whose parts may have different types, such as an if with a value on each branch, a list literal, ??, or a function with several returns, has a type that every part converts to on its own:

  • Numbers join to the one that holds the other: an I32 and an Int join to Int. A number literal takes the type of the other parts, so if exact then small else 7(if-expr exact small 7), with small an I32, is an I32.
  • Classes join to their nearest common base class, and a class and an interface it implements join to the interface.
  • null and a value join to the value's optional.
  • Tuples join field by field, so [(2.5, 1), (1, 2.5)](list (tuple 2.5 1) (tuple 1 2.5)) has the type [(Float, Float)](list (tuple Float Float)).
  • No common type is an error: This list mixes I64 and String, which have no common type; convert the items to one type. For the sides of an if it is The two sides of this "if" are I32 and F32, which have no common type; convert them to one type, and for returns Function "measure" returns Box here and F64 elsewhere, which have no common type; return one type, or declare the return type.

A declared type decides instead, where there is one: . ratio Float = if exact then 1 else 0.5(let ratio Float (if-expr exact 1 0.5)).

Operators

An operator combines values, such as a + b(+ a b), or changes one, such as -a(- a). In rows, most operators are written between two values, with a space on either side. A type can define what most of them mean for its values.

This chapter covers every operator, the order in which operators bind in rows, what the built-in ones do, and how a type defines its own. Operators on optionals are in Optionals, as in Conversions, is in Types and Patterns, conditions in Control flow, and the stream operators in Streams.

Writing operators

-- 1 + 2 * 3
-- (1 + 2) * 3
-- 10 - 4 - 3
-- 7 / 2
-- -7 / 2
-- -7 % 3
-- 2 %% 10
-- 7.0 / 2
-- "ab" ++ "cd"
-- [1, 2] ++ [3]
-- 3 is in [1, 2, 3]
-- 1 < 2 < 3
-- 5 > 3 && 2 > 1
-- !(5 > 3)
(main
  (print (+ 1 (* 2 3)))
  (print (* (+ 1 2) 3))
  (print (- 10 4 3))
  (print (/ 7 2))
  (print (/ -7 2))
  (print (% -7 3))
  (print (%% 2 10))
  (print (/ 7.0 2))
  (print (++ "ab" "cd"))
  (print (++ (list 1 2) (list 3)))
  (print (is-in 3 (list 1 2 3)))
  (print (< 1 2 3))
  (print (and (> 5 3) (> 2 1)))
  (print (not (> 5 3)))
)
7
9
3
3
-3
-1
1024
3.5
abcd
1, 2, 3
true
true
true
false
  • Spaces. In rows, a binary operator has a space on each side. a+1 is an error: An operator needs a space on each side; write "a + 1". A prefix operator is written against its operand, as in -x and !x, and ! x is an error.
  • One row. An expression ends where its row ends, so a row cannot end with an operator: An expression ends at the end of its line, so nothing follows this "+"; write the whole expression on one line.
  • Forms. An operator's form has the operator as its head and the operands after it, as in a + b(+ a b). An operator repeated in a row has one form for all its operands, as in 10 - 4 - 3(- 10 4 3).
  • Parentheses group an expression as one operand in rows, as in (1 + 2) * 3. In forms, nesting does the same.

Precedence

Precedence belongs to rows. When operators are mixed in rows, the one that binds more tightly takes its operands first. In forms, nesting decides. From the loosest to the tightest:

OperatorsKind
a, b(tuple a b)A tuple; see Types.

a ?? b(?? a b)Fallback; see Optionals.
value if condition(only-if value (if condition))A value only where a condition holds; see Control flow.

a |> b(|> a b) a |=> b(|=> a b) a *> b(*> a b) a ?> b(?> a b) a ?*> b(?*> a b) a *|> b(*|> a b) a -> b(-> a b) a *-> b(*-> a b) a ~> \rule(~> a \rule)Pipelines and stages; see Streams, and Stream patterns for ~>.
a || b(or a b)Either is true.
a && b(and a b)Both are true.
a < b(< a b) a > b(> a b) a <= b(<= a b) a >= b(>= a b)Order.
a == b(== a b) a != b(!= a b)Equality.
a as Type(as a Type)Conversion; see Conversions.
a is Type(is a Type) a is not Type(is-not a Type) a is! Type(is! a Type) a is~ Type(is~ a Type) a is in b(is-in a b) a not in b(not-in a b) a has b(has a b) a has not b(has-not a b)Tests and membership.
