a .. b(.. a b) a .. < b(..< a b) a .. b by step(.. a b (by: step))Ranges; see Control flow.
a ///name/// b(///name/// a b)A named operator, loosest form.
a //name// b(//name// a b)A named operator, looser form.
a /name/ b(/name/ a b)A named operator.
a + b(+ a b) a - b(- a b) a ++ b(++ a b)Sums and joins.
a * b(* a b) a / b(/ a b) a % b(% a b) a %% b(%% a b)Products, quotients, remainders and powers.

Prefix operators bind more tightly than any of these: -a(- a), !a(not a), -= a(-= a) (removing an item; see Collections), <- a(<- a) (reading from a stream) and type-of a(type-of a). Tighter still are the suffixes that read a value: a(b)(call a b), a.name(. a name), a[index]([] a index), a?.name(?. a name), a?[index](?[] a index) and a!(!! a).

  • Left to right. Operators of one level group from the left: 10 - 4 - 3 is 3, and 2 %% 3 %% 2 is (2 %% 3) %% 2, which is 64. %% binds as tightly as *, so 1 + 2 * 3 %% 2 is 1 + ((2 * 3) %% 2), which is 37.
  • Equality binds more tightly than order, so a < b == c compares b == c first. Write (a < b) == c to compare the result of <.
  • Orders chain. a < b < c(< a b c) means a < b && b < c(and (< a b) (< b c)), with b evaluated once, and directions may mix: 1 < 3 > 2(> (< 1 3) 2) is true. The chain stops at the first order that fails. In forms, a chain in one direction is one form, and a chain that changes direction nests. Equality does not chain: a == b == c(== a b c) compares a == b(== a b) with c.
  • as cannot be followed by a tighter operator: x as I64 + 1 is an error, A cast cannot be followed by an operator; wrap it in parentheses, as in "(x as I64) + 1". It can be followed by == or a looser operator.
  • Named operators bind more loosely than arithmetic, so 1 + 6 /least/ 3 is (1 + 6) /least/ 3. The forms with more slashes bind more loosely still, so one named operator can take the result of another without parentheses: a //least// b /least/ c is a //least// (b /least/ c).

Arithmetic

OperationValue
a + b(+ a b)The sum.
a - b(- a b)The difference.
-a(- a)The negation.
a * b(* a b)The product.
a / b(/ a b)The quotient.
a % b(% a b)The remainder.
a %% b(%% a b)a raised to the power b.
. big I32 = 2147483647
-- big + 1
. small U8 = 250
-- small + 10
. tiny I8 = 127
tiny += 1
-- tiny
-- 0 - 1u32
. whole I32 = 5
. part F32 = 1.5
-- type-of (whole + part)
-- 'a' + 1
-- 2 %% 0.5
-- 7.0 / 0.0
-- -7.5 % 2
(main
  (let big I32 2147483647)
  (print (+ big 1))
  (let small U8 250)
  (print (+ small 10))
  (let tiny I8 127)
  (+= tiny 1)
  (print tiny)
  (print (- 0 1u32))
  (let whole I32 5)
  (let part F32 1.5)
  (print (type-of (+ whole part)))
  (print (+ 'a' 1))
  (print (%% 2 0.5))
  (print (/ 7.0 0.0))
  (print (% -7.5 2))
)
-2147483648
4
-128
4294967295
[TypeInfo F32]
98
1.4142135623730951
inf
-1.5
  • Integer division drops the fraction, rounding toward zero: 7 / 2(/ 7 2) is 3, and -7 / 2(/ -7 2) is -3.
  • Remainders take the sign of the number divided: -7 % 3(% -7 3) is -1, and 7 % -3(% 7 -3) is 1. On floats, % is the remainder of a division rounded toward zero: -7.5 % 2(% -7.5 2) is -1.5.
  • Dividing by zero is not checked. For integers, x / 0(/ x 0) is 0 and x % 0(% x 0) is x. For floats, it gives an infinity, or a value that is not a number.
  • Overflow. Integer arithmetic that goes past its type's range wraps around, so 127i8 + 1i8(+ 127i8 1i8) is -128i8. An assigning operator computes in the type of its two operands, then wraps the result into the type of what it assigns.
  • Mixed types. The operands are brought to one type before the operation:
    • A float wins: the result is Float when either operand is a Float, and F32 otherwise, so an I32 plus an F32 is an F32.
    • Two integers of one signedness give the wider type.
    • A signed and an unsigned integer give the unsigned type when it is at least as wide as the signed one, and the signed type otherwise.
    • A Char counts as a U32, so 'a' + 1(+ 'a' 1) is 98.
    • A literal takes the other operand's type, so 0 - 1u32(- 0 1u32) is 4294967295, and 7.0 / 2(/ 7.0 2) is 3.5.

    This is not the join of Conversions: arithmetic may give a type that one operand does not convert to on its own.

  • Powers. a %% b(%% a b) has the type of a. It is computed as a Float and converted back, so 2 %% 0.5(%% 2 0.5) is 1.4142135623730951, but with a an Int holding 2 it is 1. An integer power too large for the type gives its largest value.
  • Updates. +=, -=, *=, /=, %= and %%= apply their operator to what a local, property or item holds and store the result there, so with n holding 30, n /= 4(/= n 4) leaves 7. += and -= on a list add and remove items instead; see Collections.
  • Paths. A type can give / another meaning; Path from /os/path joins with it: Path("/tmp") / "notes.txt"(/ (call Path "/tmp") "notes.txt") is /tmp/notes.txt.

Comparison

-- 2 == 2.0
-- -1 < 4000000000u32
-- [1, 2] == [1, 2]
-- (1, "a") == (1, "a")
-- "apple" < "banana"
-- 'a' < 'b'
. maybe Int? = null
-- maybe == null
-- maybe != 3
(main
  (print (== 2 2.0))
  (print (< -1 4000000000u32))
  (print (== (list 1 2) (list 1 2)))
  (print (== (tuple 1 "a") (tuple 1 "a")))
  (print (< "apple" "banana"))
  (print (< 'a' 'b'))
  (let maybe (? Int) null)
  (print (== maybe null))
  (print (!= maybe 3))
)
true
true
true
true
true
true
true
true
  • Numbers are compared by value, in the type their operands are brought to, so 2 == 2.0(== 2 2.0) is true. A signed and an unsigned integer are compared by sign first, so -1 < 4000000000u32(< -1 4000000000u32) is true. A float that is not a number is equal to nothing, itself included, and every order with it is false.
  • Text is compared by its characters, and ordered by them. Characters are ordered by code point.
  • Lists and arrays are equal when they have equal items in the same order.
  • Tuples are equal when their fields are, field by field, and named tuples only when their fields have the same names.
  • Objects are equal when they are the same object, unless their class defines ==.
  • Optionals. x == null(== x null) tests that an optional holds nothing. One that holds nothing is not equal to a value, and two that hold nothing are equal. An order cannot take an optional: Operator "<" is not defined for I64 and I64?.
  • != is true where == is false.
  • Types that do not compare are an error: Operator "==" is not defined for I64 and Bool.

Logic

a && b(and a b) is true when both operands are, and a || b(or a b) when either is. !a(not a) is true when a is false. In a && b(and a b) and a || b(or a b), b is evaluated only when it decides the result. Each gives a Bool, and takes as operands anything a condition can be; see Control flow.

Joining and membership

  • ++ joins two texts, or two collections of one item type, into a new one. With text on its left, it makes its right operand text, so "x" ++ 5(++ "x" 5) is x5. ++= joins onto what a local or property holds.
  • + on a list makes a new list with one more item: [1, 2] + 3(+ (list 1 2) 3) is 1, 2, 3. += adds one item to the list in place, and ++= adds each item of a collection. See Collections, and Text for the operators of text.
  • has tests whether a collection holds a value, as in items has 3(has items 3), and items has not 3(has-not items 3) whether it does not. 3 is in items(is-in 3 items) and 3 not in items(not-in 3 items) ask the same with the value first. A type answers all four by defining has; see below.

Bits

The bitwise operations are named operators, and take integers:

OperationValue
a /and/ b(/and/ a b)The bits set in both.
a /or/ b(/or/ a b)The bits set in either.
a /xor/ b(/xor/ a b)The bits set in one but not the other.
0 /not/ b(/not/ 0 b)The bits of b, inverted. The left operand is not used.
a /lshift/ n(/lshift/ a n)The bits of a, moved n places toward the high end.
a /rshift/ n(/rshift/ a n)The bits of a, moved n places toward the low end, copying the sign bit.
a /zrshift/ n(/zrshift/ a n)The bits of a, moved n places toward the low end, filling with zeros.
  • Types. Operands of different widths are brought to one type, as for arithmetic. A shift keeps the type of a, so 1u8 /lshift/ 8(/lshift/ 1u8 8) is 0. A float is an error: Expected I64 here, but this is F32, which becomes I64 only when asked; write "as I64".
  • Narrow types. A number narrower than 32 bits is extended by its sign before a shift, so on those types /zrshift/ gives what /rshift/ does.
  • Shift counts are not checked.
  • A function declared with one of these names replaces the built-in operation.

Named operators

Any function of two parameters can be used as an operator, with its name between slashes: 7 /clamped-to/ 5(/clamped-to/ 7 5) calls clamped-to(7, 5)(call clamped-to 7 5). A named operator puts a function between its values without a new symbol, and the slashes keep the name from being read as a value. See Precedence for the forms with more slashes.

Reserved operators

<<, >> and <| are read as operators, but no built-in type defines them: Operator "<<" is not defined for I64 and I64. A type can define them as it defines any operator; see Operators a type defines. ?<< and ?>>, in rows a? << b and a? >> b, are reserved: Brix form “(?<< …)” is not supported yet.

Operators a type defines

A type defines an operator for its values with a function whose name is the operator written with this, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + this + other Vec body(fn-expr + (infix this + (param other Vec)) _ body). Define one only where it means what the symbol means for numbers, such as adding or combining; otherwise use a function whose name says what it does.

. a = Vec(1, 2)
. b = Vec(3, 4)
-- a + b
-- a * 3
-- 3 * a
-- -a
a += b
-- a
-- a == Vec(4, 6)
-- a != b
. grid = Grid()
grid[1] = 5
-- grid[1]
-- grid has 5
-- 7 not in grid
-- grid(10)
-- 7 /clamped-to/ 5

DeclarationDefines
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + this + other Vec body(fn-expr + (infix this + (param other Vec)) _ body)A binary operator.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + -this body(fn-expr + (prefix - this) _ body)A prefix operator.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + this[index Int] body(fn-expr + (index-get this (param index Int)) _ body)Reading value[index]([] value index).
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + do this[index Int] = value Int body(fn-do + (index-set this (param index Int) (param value Int)) _ body)Assigning value[index]([] value index).
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + do -= this[index Int] body(fn-do + (index-delete this (param index Int)) _ body)Removing with -= value[index](-= ([] value index)).
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + this - bonus Int body(fn-expr + this _ (param bonus Int) body)Calling the value, as in grid(10)(call grid 10).
  • What can be defined. The binary operators +, -, *, /, %, %%, ++, ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=, has and a has not b(has-not a b), the assigning operators such as += and ++=, <-, the prefix operators -a(- a), !a(not a) (see Control flow) and <- a(<- a) (see Streams), indexing, and calls.
  • Bodies and results. A fn-expr body is a value, and a fn-do body is steps that return with = value(return value). A result type, as Int in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + this Int + n Int body(fn-expr + (infix this + (param n Int)) Int body), is _ where it is left to the body.
  • Left operand. An operator is looked up on the type of its left operand, and never on the right one's. For a value of another type on the left, as for 3 * a(* 3 a) above, declare the operator in an extension of that type; see Types.
  • Derived operators. A type that defines == gets !=, and one that defines != gets ==. A type that defines > and == gets <, and an order no function answers is the negation of its opposite, so <= is answered by >. a has b(has a b) and a has not b(has-not a b) each give the other, and b is in a(is-in b a) and b not in a(not-in b a) call them with the operands swapped.
  • Comparisons give Bool. An equality, order or membership operator with another result type is an error: Operator must return Bool.
  • Assigning operators. a += b(+= a b) uses the type's += when it defines one, and stores a + b(+ a b) in a otherwise. A += declared with fn-expr gives a new value, which is stored where a is held.
  • Indexes. An index parameter can be a range, as in - range Range'Int(param range (of Range Int)), to read, assign or remove a slice. Only one index parameter is allowed.
  • Overloads. A type may define one operator several times, for operands of different types, as Vec could for * with - factor Int(param factor Int) and with - other Vec(param other Vec).
  • Inheritance and interfaces. A derived class may define an operator again, and its version is used even where its object is held as the base class. An interface may declare operators, with or without bodies, for its types to define.

Control flow

A step body runs its rows in order. This chapter covers locals and the blocks that hold them, and what changes the order of rows: conditions, if and else, values chosen by a condition, decision tables and loops. Returns are covered in Functions, match in Patterns, and raising errors in Errors.

Locals

. count = 0
. ratio Float = 1
. low I32, name String
-- "$count $ratio $low [$name]"
count = 5
ratio += 0.5
. first, second = ("a", "b")
-- "$count $ratio $first$second"
(main
  (let count 0)
  (let ratio Float 1)
  (let (tuple (: low I32) (: name String)))
  (print (str count " " ratio " " low " [" name "]"))
  (= count 5)
  (+= ratio 0.5)
  (let (tuple first second) (tuple "a" "b"))
  (print (str count " " ratio " " first second))
)
0 1 0 []
5 1.5 ab
DeclarationDeclares
. name = value(let name value)A local of the value's type.
. name Type = value(let name Type value)A local of the type, which the value converts to.
. name Type(let name Type)A local of the type, holding its zero.
. a, b = value(let (tuple a b) value)A local for each field of a tuple; see Patterns.
. a I32, b Float(let (tuple (: a I32) (: b Float)))Several locals, each holding its type's zero.
(let name _ value)A local of the value's type, for a value that is itself a type.
  • Zero. A local declared with no value holds its type's zero: 0, false, "", an empty collection, or null for an optional.
  • Assigning. name = value(= name value) gives a local a new value, converted to its type, as ratio += 0.5(+= ratio 0.5) does above. An argument is a local of its function, and can be assigned too. A name nothing declares cannot be assigned: total = 5(= total 5) is an error, Variable "total" is not declared; declare it with ". total = 5".
  • Types as values. . kind I32(let kind I32) declares a local of type I32, holding 0. To hold the type itself, write _ for the local's type: . kind = I32(let kind _ I32), which prints as [TypeInfo I32].
  • Lazy locals. .. name = value(lazy name value) declares a local whose value is computed where it is first read; see Functions.
  • Order. A local is known from its declaration on. Reading it before is an error: Name "total" not found.

Blocks and scopes

The body of an if, else, loop or do is a block. A local declared in a block is known from its declaration to the end of the block, and not after it.

. count = 5
. label = "outer"
if count > 1
    -- label
    . label = "inner"
    -- label
    count = 9
-- label
-- count
do
    . doubled = count * 2
    -- doubled
(main
  (let count 5)
  (let label "outer")
  (if (> count 1)
    (print label)
    (let label "inner")
    (print label)
    (= count 9)
  )
  (print label)
  (print count)
  (do
    (let doubled (* count 2))
    (print doubled)
  )
)
outer
inner
outer
9
18
  • do runs its body as a block, where it stands, so its locals end with it. In a value body, do blocks run steps before the value; see Functions.
  • Shadowing. A local declared in a block may have the name of one outside it, even with another type. Until the inner declaration, the name reads the outer local, and after the block it does again.
  • Assigning in a block. An assignment, name = value(= name value) rather than . name = value(let name value), changes the local it names, wherever that local was declared, so count above is 9 after the if.
  • Redeclaring. A name declared twice in one block is an error: "x" is already declared on line 1 in this scope; to change its value, assign it without the ".", as in "x = value", or choose another name.
  • After the block. Reading a block's local after it is an error: Name "doubled" not found.

Conditions

A condition is the value tested by an if and the branches after it, a while, a loop clause, a && b(and a b), a || b(or a b) or !a(not a). It need not be a Bool:

ValueTrue when
BoolIt is true.
A numberIt is not zero.
TextIt is not empty.
A list, map or arrayIt is not empty.
An optionalIt holds a value, even 0, "" or false.
A value of another typeThe type defines !value(not value), and it gives false.
. count = 0
. name = "Ada"
. items = List'Int()
. maybe Int? = 0
-- (if count then "count" else "no count")
-- (if name then "named" else "no name")
-- (if items then "items" else "no items")
-- (if maybe then "maybe holds a value" else "maybe holds nothing")
-- (if count == 0 && name then "both" else "not both")
-- "" || "x"
(main
  (let count 0)
  (let name "Ada")
  (let items (call (of List Int)))
  (let maybe (? Int) 0)
  (print (if-expr count "count" "no count"))
  (print (if-expr name "named" "no name"))
  (print (if-expr items "items" "no items"))
  (print (if-expr maybe "maybe holds a value" "maybe holds nothing"))
  (print (if-expr (and (== count 0) name) "both" "not both"))
  (print (or "" "x"))
)
no count
named
no items
maybe holds a value
both
true
  • Logic. a && b(and a b), a || b(or a b) and !a(not a) give a Bool, whatever their operands' types. In a && b(and a b) and a || b(or a b), b is evaluated only when it decides the result.
  • Optionals. An optional is tested for whether it holds a value, not for the value it holds. Test the value with a comparison, as in maybe == 0(== maybe 0). See Optionals.
  • Narrowing. A condition that tests an optional, or tests a value with is, narrows it in the code it guards; see Optionals and Patterns.
  • Function values. A function named without a call is not a condition. !box.is-empty(not (. box is-empty)) is an error: Operator "!" is not defined for function is-empty; it is a function, so call it first.

Types as conditions

A type makes its values conditions by defining ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + !this body(fn-expr + (prefix ! this) _ body), which gives true where a value counts as false. The core library's lists, maps, arrays, text and channels define it.

. box = Box()
if box
    -- "full"
else
    -- "empty"
box.count = 2
if box
    -- "full"
-- !box

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Box

+ count = 0
────────────────────
+ !this

count == 0
(main
  (let box (call Box))
  (if box
    (print "full")
    (else
      (print "empty")
    )
  )
  (= (. box count) 2)
  (if box
    (print "full")
  )
  (print (not box))
)

(type + Box
  (prop + count _ (= 0))

empty
full
false
  • Result. The operator must give a Bool. With another result type declared, it is an error: Operator must return Bool.
  • Without it. A value of a type that does not define it cannot be a condition: Thing cannot be tested as a condition, since operator "!" is not defined for it.

if and else

for score in [95, 72, 40]
    if score >= 90
        -- "$score: excellent"
    else if score >= 60
        -- "$score: pass"
    else
        -- "$score: fail"
(main
  (for (in score (list 95 72 40))
    (if (>= score 90)
      (print (str score ": excellent"))
      (else-if (>= score 60)
        (print (str score ": pass"))
      )
      (else
        (print (str score ": fail"))
      )
    )
  )
)
95: excellent
72: pass
40: fail
BranchRuns its body
if condition body(if condition body)When the condition holds.
if a x else if condition body(if a x (else-if condition body))When no branch before it ran, and its condition holds.
if a x else body(if a x (else body))When no branch before it ran.
  • Bodies. The body of each branch is a block of its own. The branches after the first follow the if's body, inside its form, as in if a x else if b y else z(if a x (else-if b y) (else z)). Branches with a condition may repeat, and else comes last.
  • Steps, not values. An if with branches is a step. Where a value is wanted, write if condition then a else b(if-expr condition a b) or a decision table, below.
  • Patterns. An if can test whether a value fits a pattern, and name its parts: if | (n, word) = pair body(if (= (| (tuple n word)) pair) body). See Patterns.

Values chosen by a condition

. count = 3
-- (if count == 1 then "item" else "items")
. size = if count < 2 then "small" else if count < 5 then "medium" else "large"
-- size
-- "many" if count > 2
-- "few" if count < 2
(main
  (let count 3)
  (print (if-expr (== count 1) "item" "items"))
  (let size (if-expr (< count 2) "small" (if-expr (< count 5) "medium" "large")))
  (print size)
  (print (only-if "many" (if (> count 2))))
  (print (only-if "few" (if (< count 2))))
)
items
medium
many
unknown
  • One of two values. if condition then a else b(if-expr condition a b) gives a when the condition holds and b otherwise. Only the side chosen is evaluated, and the condition narrows it, as in if value then value + 1 else 0(if-expr value (+ value 1) 0). Its type is the join of the two sides' types; see Conversions. It chains: if a then x else if b then y else z(if-expr a x (if-expr b y z)).
  • A value or null. value if condition(only-if value (if condition)) gives the value when the condition holds, and null otherwise, so its type is an optional. In rows, it binds more loosely than every operator but ??, so if a then x else y if b is if a then x else (y if b).
  • A value, not a step. An if after a value never skips a step: -- "few" if count < 2(print (only-if "few" (if (< count 2)))) prints unknown. Only guards skip on a condition: ?! error if condition(throw error (if condition)) and =? value if condition(return-if value (if condition)), and the steps that skip null; see Optionals and Errors.
  • Not with ??. value if condition ?? other(?? (only-if value (if condition)) other) is an error: `value if condition ?? other` is not a choice of two values. Write `if condition then value else other`.

Decision tables

A value can be chosen by a table of conditions, tried in order. Each row is |? condition value(case? condition value), and a last row ?? value(default value) gives the value when no condition holds.

-- grade(95)
-- grade(85)
-- grade(40)
. score = 72
. passed =
    |? score >= 60
        "yes"
    ??
        "no"
-- passed

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ grade String
    - score Int

|? score >= 90
    "A"
|? score >= 80
    "B"
??
    "C"
(main
  (print (call grade 95))
  (print (call grade 85))
  (print (call grade 40))
  (let score 72)
  (let passed
    (block
      (case? (>= score 60)
        "yes"
      )
      (default
        "no"
      )
    )
  )
  (print passed)
)

(fn-expr + grade String
  (param score Int)
  (case? (>= score 90)
    "A"
  )
  (case? (>= score 80)
    "B"
  )
  (default
    "C"
  )
)
A
B
C
yes
  • Where. A table can be a function's value body, as grade's is, or the value of a declaration, assignment or print, as a block: . passed = |? condition a ?? b(let passed (block (case? condition a) (default b))). In rows, ?? value can be written on one row.
  • Type. The table's type is the join of its values' types. A table with no default row gives null where no condition holds, so its type is an optional.
  • A row with no value gives what its condition tested: |? cached(case? cached) gives the value cached holds.
  • Narrowing. A row's condition narrows what it tests in that row's value, and a condition that failed narrows what it tested for the rows after it.
  • Rows that raise. A row ?! error if condition(throw error (if condition)) raises where no row before it held, and a last row ?! error(throw error) can stand in for the default row; see Errors.
  • As steps. In a step body, a table can stand as a step, with steps in its rows. When no row holds and there is no default row, the steps after the table run. A match run as steps is written (do (inline (match …))), and the error for a bare one says so; see Patterns.
  • A table is a match with no subject: its rows are arms, and the arms of Patterns can mix with them.

Loops

for

for item in source body(for (in item source) body) runs its body once for each item of the source, with item naming the item.

for word in ["red", "green"]
    -- word
for c in "hé"
    -- c
. ages = Map'String'Int()
ages["Ada"] = 36
for name, age in ages
    -- "$name is $age"
for in ["p", "q"]
    -- each
. total = 0
for n in 1 .. 4
    total += n
-- total
(main
  (for (in word (list "red" "green"))
    (print word)
  )
  (for (in c "hé")
    (print c)
  )
  (let ages (call (of Map String Int)))
  (= ([] ages "Ada") 36)
  (for (in (tuple name age) ages)
    (print (str name " is " age))
  )
  (for (in (list "p" "q"))
    (print each)
  )
  (let total 0)
  (for (in n (.. 1 4))
    (+= total n)
  )
  (print total)
)
red
green
h
é
Ada is 36
p
q
10
  • Sources. A loop reads lists, arrays, text, maps, ranges, streams and generators, and values of types that implement Iterable, CursorIterable or Indexable; see Collections and Streams. A number is not a source: A for loop cannot iterate over I64; to count, loop over a range, as in "0 .. < 42".
  • Text gives its characters, not its bytes. A map gives each key and its value as a tuple. The order of a map's entries is not defined.
  • Taking items apart. The item can be a pattern: for name, age in ages body(for (in (tuple name age) ages) body) names the fields of each tuple, and _ skips one. A pattern that can fail, such as for | n Int in values body(for (in (| (: n Int)) values) body), passes over the items it does not fit. See Patterns.
  • Unnamed items. for in source body(for (in source) body) names no item, and the body reads it as each, or it.
  • Typed items. for i U8 in 0 .. < 3 body(for (in (: i U8) (..< 0 3)) body) converts each item to the type, as a declaration would.
  • The item is a new local in each pass, known only in the body, and cannot be assigned: Illegal to update const variables. A function value made in the body keeps that pass's item; see Functions.
  • What the loop reads. The source is evaluated once, before the first pass. A list that grows during the loop is read only to the length it had then.

Ranges

for n in 0 .. < 3
    -- n
for n in 5 .. 3
    -- n
for n in 0 .. 10 by 5
    -- n
for f in 0.0 .. 1.0 by 0.5
    -- f
for c in 'a' .. 'c'
    -- c
(main
  (for (in n (..< 0 3))
    (print n)
  )
  (for (in n (.. 5 3))
    (print n)
  )
  (for (in n (.. 0 10 (by: 5)))
    (print n)
  )
  (for (in f (.. 0.0 1.0 (by: 0.5)))
    (print f)
  )
  (for (in c (.. 'a' 'c'))
    (print c)
  )
)

1
2
5
4
3

10
0
0.5

a
b
c
RangeGives
a .. b(.. a b)From a through b.
a .. < b(..< a b)From a up to, but not including, b.
a .. b by step(.. a b (by: step))Every step from a.

A range whose start is past its end counts down. A range steps toward its end by the size of its step, so the step's sign does not matter: 10 .. 0 by -5(.. 10 0 (by: -5)) gives 10, 5 and 0, as 10 .. 0 by 5(.. 10 0 (by: 5)) does. A range can hold integers, floats or characters. An integer range gives Ints unless its bounds have another type. A range is a value, with a length and a start; see Literals and Collections.

Clauses

A header can end with clauses that decide, for each item, whether the body runs:

. total = 0
for n in 1 .. 10 when n % 2 == 0
    total += n
-- total
for n in 1 .. 10 while n < 4
    -- "while $n"
for n in 1 .. 10 until n == 3
    -- "until $n"
(main
  (let total 0)
  (for (in n (.. 1 10) (when (== (% n 2) 0)))
    (+= total n)
  )
  (print total)
  (for (in n (.. 1 10) (while (< n 4)))
    (print (str "while " n))
  )
  (for (in n (.. 1 10) (until (== n 3)))
    (print (str "until " n))
  )
)
30
while 1
while 2
while 3
until 1
until 2
ClauseFor each item
when condition(when condition)Skips the item unless the condition holds.
while condition(while condition)Ends the loop at the first item where the condition fails.
until condition(until condition)Ends the loop at the first item where the condition holds.

A clause reads the item, and the names a pattern in the header gives it. Clauses follow the source, as in for item in source when condition body(for (in item source (when condition)) body), and are tested in the order written: the first that skips the item or ends the loop decides, and the clauses after it are not tested for that item.

Several headers

A loop can read several sources together, one item of each in each pass. Each header after the first follows the one before it, and the last holds the body, as in for item in source and other in others body(for (in item source) (and-for (in other others) body)). The loop ends when any of its sources ends. An (or-for …) header, for a source joined as an alternative, is read but not built yet: Not supported by emission: this statement.

for word in ["a", "b", "c"]
and index in 0 .. < 10
    -- "$index $word"
for n in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] when n % 2
and label in ["x", "y", "z"]
    -- "$n$label"
(main
  (for (in word (list "a" "b" "c"))
    (and-for (in index (..< 0 10))
      (print (str index " " word))
    )
  )
  (for (in n (list 1 2 3 4 5) (when (% n 2)))
    (and-for (in label (list "x" "y" "z"))
      (print (str n label))
    )
  )
)
0 a
1 b
2 c
1x
3y
5z
  • Clauses on a header apply to it alone. A when skips items of its own source, and the other sources wait: the second loop above pairs the odd numbers with x, y and z. A while or until on any header ends the whole loop.
  • each and it name the first header's item when the headers name no items.

while

while condition body(while condition body) runs its body for as long as the condition holds, testing it before each pass.

. i = 0
while i < 5
    i += 1
    if i == 2
        continue
    if i == 4
        break
    -- "i is $i"
. counter = Counter()
while | value Int = counter.next()
    -- "got $value"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Counter

+ count = 0
────────────────────
+ do next Int?

count += 1
=? count if count < 3
= null
(main
  (let i 0)
  (while (< i 5)
    (+= i 1)
    (if (== i 2)
      (continue)
    )
    (if (== i 4)
      (break)
    )
    (print (str "i is " i))
  )
  (let counter (call Counter))
  (while (= (| (: value Int)) (call (. counter next)))
    (print (str "got " value))
  )
)

(type + Counter
  (prop + count _ (= 0))
  (fn-do + next (? Int)
    (+= count 1)
    (return-if count (if (< count 3)))
    (return null)
  )
)
i is 1
i is 3
got 1
got 2
  • Endless loops. while true body(while true body) loops until a break, a return or a raise leaves it. A function whose end follows such a loop with no break needs no return after it; see Functions.
  • Patterns. while | pattern = value body(while (= (| pattern) value) body) evaluates the value before each pass, and runs the body while it fits the pattern, with the names the pattern gives. See Patterns.
  • There is no do … while: a loop that runs at least once is while true body(while true body) with a break at its end.

break and continue

break leaves the nearest loop, and continue ends the current pass and goes on to the next item.

  • Nearest loop. In nested loops they act on the innermost loop that holds them. Loops have no labels.
  • Rows. Each stands alone on its row, as the last row of the block that holds it; to break when a condition holds, put it in an if. Rows after it in its block are never reached.
  • Several headers. continue goes on to the next item of every header.
  • In match. An arm of a match in a loop can break or continue it; see Patterns.
  • Outside a loop, including in a function value written in a loop, each is an error: `break` outside a loop and `continue` outside a loop.
  • Cleanup. A do finally body(finally body) block in a loop's body runs at the end of every pass, including one left by break or continue; see Errors.

Returns

A step body returns with = value(return value), or with =? value if condition(return-if value (if condition)) where a condition holds. A return in a loop or a block leaves the whole function. See Functions for every form of return, and for which bodies must end with one.

Patterns

A pattern describes a shape a value can have: a value it equals, a type it has, a condition it meets, or parts it is made of. Matching a value against a pattern tells whether the value fits, and names the parts the pattern names.

This chapter covers match, every kind of pattern, the other places patterns are written, taking values apart into locals, and the rule that a match covers every case. Unions are covered in Unions and enums, and patterns over streams of text and bytes in Stream patterns.

match

for value in [0, -4, 7, 25, 12]
    -- size(value)
. count = 3
. word = match count
    |= 1
        "one"
    |? it < 5
        "a few"
    ?? "many"
-- word

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ size String
    - value Int

match value
    |= 0
        "zero"
    | { it < 0 }
        "negative"
    | 3 | 7
        "lucky"
    | n { it > 20 }
        "large $n"
    | n
        "small $n"
(main
  (for (in value (list 0 -4 7 25 12))
    (print (call size value))
  )
  (let count 3)
  (let word
    (match count
      (case= 1
        "one"
      )
      (case? (< it 5)
        "a few"
      )
      (default
        (inline "many")
      )
    )
  )
  (print word)
)

(fn-expr + size String
  (param value Int)
  (match value
    (case= 0
      "zero"
    )
    (case ({} (< it 0))
      "negative"
    )
    (case (| 3 7)
      "lucky"
    )
    (case (: n ({} (> it 20)))
      (str "large " n)
    )
    (case n
      (str "small " n)
    )
  )
)
zero
negative
lucky
large 25
small 12
a few

A match takes a subject, then arms, each with its value, as in match subject | pattern value(match subject (case pattern value)).

ArmTaken when
| pattern value(case pattern value)The subject fits the pattern.
|= value result(case= value result)The subject equals the value.
|? condition value(case? condition value)The condition holds.
?? value(default value)No arm before it was taken.
?! error(throw error)No arm before it was taken; it raises the error. See Errors.
  • Order. Arms are tried in the order written, and the first that is taken gives the match its value. Later arms are not tried.
  • it is the subject, in every arm's pattern, condition and value. In an arm whose pattern names a type, it has that type.
  • Values. An arm's value is its body. A default arm can hold its value inline, on one row: ?? value(default (inline value)). An arm with no value gives what its pattern passed on, as in | { it > 20 }(case ({} (> it 20))), which gives the subject.
  • Type. The match's type is the join of its arms' values; see Conversions. Arms whose types have no join give an anonymous union; see Unions and enums. Arms that raise add nothing to it. To keep each arm's type even where a join exists, see Arms that keep their type.
  • Value first. value | pattern(select value (| pattern)) is an arm written with its value before its pattern, and is taken as | pattern value(case pattern value) is.
  • Raising arms. ?! error(throw error) raises for every value no arm before it took. With a condition, as in ?! error if condition(throw error (if condition)), it raises only where the condition holds, and the arms after it are tried otherwise.
  • Lazy locals. An arm can declare lazy locals after its value, as a value body can; see Functions.
  • No arm taken. Where no arm fits a value, the program panics: Pattern match failed. For a subject of a type with a fixed set of values, the compiler requires an arm for each; see Covering every case.

Arms that keep their type

for sound in ["woof", "meow"]
    . pet = adopt(sound)
    . kept = adopt-kept(sound)
    -- "${type-of pet} / case ${kept.case}, a Dog: ${kept is Dog}"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Animal



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Dog is Animal



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Cat is Animal



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ adopt
    - sound String

match sound
    |= "woof"
        Dog()
    ??
        Cat()

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ adopt-kept
    - sound String

match sound
    ||= "woof"
        Dog()
    ??
        Cat()
(main
  (for (in sound (list "woof" "meow"))
    (let pet (call adopt sound))
    (let kept (call adopt-kept sound))
    (print (str (type-of pet) " / case " (. kept case) ", a Dog: " (is kept Dog)))
  )
)

(type + Animal)

(type + Dog (is Animal))

(type + Cat (is Animal))

(fn-expr + adopt _
  (param sound String)
  (match sound
    (case= "woof" (call Dog))
    (default (call Cat))
  )
)

(fn-expr + adopt-kept _
  (param sound String)
  (match sound
    (case-union= "woof" (call Dog))
    (default (call Cat))
  )
)
[TypeInfo Animal] / case 0, a Dog: true
[TypeInfo Animal] / case 1, a Dog: false

case-union, case-union= and case-union? are taken as case, case= and case? are, but their values are not joined. From the first such arm on, the match's type is a union with a case for each arm, so adopt gives an Animal and adopt-kept gives a Dog | Cat. In rows they are ||, ||= and ||?.

  • Later arms. Every arm after the first case-union arm adds its case to the union, whatever its kind, as the default arm does above.
  • Earlier arms are not in the union, so their values must convert to it: Expected I64 | F64 here, but this is String, and there is no conversion between them.
  • A declared type. Where the match's type is declared, as by a function's result, its values convert to that type and no union is made.

match?

match? subject | pattern value(match? subject (case pattern value)) gives null where no arm is taken, so its type is an optional, and it needs no arm for every value.

Matches as steps

In a step body, do match subject | pattern body(do (inline (match subject (case pattern body)))) runs the arm that is taken, as steps, and uses no value, so arms may give values of any type or none.

  • An arm can return from the function, raise, or break or continue an enclosing loop.
  • With match?, a match run as steps goes on to the next step where no arm is taken; with match, it panics there.
  • A match written as a step, with arms that give no value, is an error that names the fix: This arm gives no value, and a match gives the value of the arm it takes; to run its arms as steps, write "(do (inline (match …)))". In rows it says write "do match".
  • A function whose last step is a match run as steps, with an arm for every value, each of which returns or raises, needs no return after it.

Several subjects

match a, b | x, y value(match (tuple a b) (case (tuple x y) value)) matches the tuple of its subjects, so each arm is a tuple pattern, as in | name String, count { it > 20 } value(case (tuple (: name String) (: count ({} (> it 20)))) value). See Tuples.

Kinds of pattern

PatternFits
_Any value. It names nothing.
nameAny value, and names it.
42, "text", nullA value equal to it.
TypeA value of the type.
name Type(: name Type)A value of the type, and names it.
Type!(exact Type)A value of exactly the type, not one that converts to it.
Type~(similar Type)A value that converts to the type.
{ condition }({} condition)A value for which the condition holds.
a b(all a b)Both patterns, in turn.
a | b(| a b)Either pattern.
a, b(tuple a b)A tuple whose fields fit.
.case, .case(a, b)(call .case a b)A union value holding the case.
[a, b](list a b), | [a, ...rest] value(case (list a ...rest) value)A list whose items fit.
| ["key" = a] value(case (map "key" a) value)A map holding the key, with a value that fits.
"start" ...rest(all "start" ...rest)Text that begins and ends as written.
..nameA value with a property name, which it names.
  • Tree relations. (/ a b), (*/ a b), (\ a b), (*\ a b), (++ a b) and (-- a b) are reserved for patterns over trees: a child, a descendant, a parent, an ancestor, the next sibling and the previous sibling. The compiler reads them and refuses them: Not supported.

Values and conditions

  • Literals. A number, text, null or other literal fits an equal value. A number literal takes the subject's type, so the arm | 3 value(case 3 value) matches a U8. |= value result(case= value result) compares with any value, not only a literal, as |= limit result(case= limit result) does.
  • Conditions. { condition }({} condition) fits where the condition holds, with it naming the value being matched at that point of the pattern. A condition can read the names given before it in the pattern, as in n Int { n > 10 }(all (: n Int) ({} (> n 10))).
  • Alternatives. a | b(| a b) tries each pattern in turn, and fits where one does. All of them share the arm's value. A name the alternatives give is one local, which the alternative taken fills, so .a(n) | .b(n)(| (call .a n) (call .b n)) reads n from either case.
  • Sequences. The patterns of a b(all a b) must all fit, from left to right, and each takes what the one before passed on. A type pattern passes on the value as its type, Type~(similar Type) passes on the converted value, and a condition passes on what it tested, so in n Int~ { it > 7 }(all (: n (similar Int)) ({} (> it 7))) the condition tests the converted value.

Names

  • A name alone fits any value and names it, so no arm may follow it: Arm '| n' takes every value, so the arms after it are never reached. _ is the same, and names nothing.
  • A name before a pattern names what fits the pattern, as in n { it > 20 }(: n ({} (> it 20))) and n Int(: n Int).
  • Scope. A name a pattern gives is known in its arm's value, or the body the pattern guards, and not after it. Two arms may give the same name, but one pattern may not give a name twice: "a" is bound twice in this pattern; give each place a name of its own.
  • Case names. A name alone is a name even where the subject's union has a case of that name: Arm '| red' binds a new name, not the case Light.red; match the case with '| Light.red'.

(type + Cat (is Animal)
  (fn-expr + meow String
    "meow"
  )
)

(type + Value (is Union)
  (variant Int)
  (variant Float)
  (variant String)
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param pet Animal)
  (match pet
    (case (: dog Dog)
      (str "a dog: " (call (. dog bark)))
    )
    (case Cat
      (str "a cat: " (call (. it meow)))
    )
    (default
      (inline "an animal")
    )
  )
)

(fn-expr + presence String
  (param value (? Int))
  (match value
    (case= null
      "nothing"
    )
    (case (: n Int)
      (str "holds " n)
    )
  )
)

(fn-expr + measure String
  (param value Value)
  (match value
    (case (: n Int)
      (str "an Int: " n)
    )
    (case (: f Float)
      (str "a Float: " f)
    )
    (case (: s String)
      (str "text: " s)
    )
  )
)

(fn-expr + read String
  (param value Float)
  (match value
    (case (: n (similar Int))
      (str "converts to " n)
    )
    (default
      (inline "does not convert")
    )
  )
)
a dog: woof
a cat: meow
an animal
nothing
holds 4
an Int: 3
a Float: 2.5
text: seven
converts to 4
  • Classes. A class fits an object of the class or of a class derived from it. In the arm, the name, or it, has the class, so its members can be read.
  • Optionals. A type fits an optional only where it holds a value of the type, so n Int(: n Int) does not fit null. Match null with |= null value(case= null value).
  • Unions. A type fits a union value holding a case of that type, and names the case's value.
  • Generic classes. A generic class written bare, such as List, fits a value of the class with any type arguments.
  • Exact and converted types. Type!(exact Type) fits a value of exactly the type, without converting it, and an object only of exactly the class, not of a class derived from it. Type~(similar Type) fits a value that converts to the type, as as would convert it, and passes on the converted value, so 4.0 fits Int~(similar Int) as 4. Text does not convert to a number this way.

Union cases

.case fits a union value holding the case, and .case(a, b)(call .case a b) also matches the case's values against patterns. A case of another union can be named in full, as in Light.green(. Light green).

  • .case passes on the union value. .case(pattern)(call .case pattern) passes on what its pattern passed.
  • Anonymous cases, made with ..case(value)(call ..case value), are matched the same way.
  • See Unions and enums for unions, and for matching values of enums.

Tuples

a, b(tuple a b) fits a tuple whose fields fit the patterns, by position. In rows, it can be written in parentheses, as in (x, y). A field pattern can be any pattern: | name String, count { it > 20 } value(case (tuple (: name String) (: count ({} (> it 20)))) value), | x { it > 5 }, _ value(case (tuple (: x ({} (> it 5))) _) value), or a literal, as in | 1, name value(case (tuple 1 name) value).

Lists

for items in [[1, 2, 3], [4], List'Int(), [5, 6]]
    -- shape(items)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ shape String
    - items [Int]

match items
    | []
        "empty"
    | [only]
        "just $only"
    | [first, second]
        "two: $first and $second"
    | [first, ..., last]
        "from $first to $last"
(main
  (for (in items (list (list 1 2 3) (list 4) (call (of List Int)) (list 5 6)))
    (print (call shape items))
  )
)

(fn-expr + shape String
  (param items (list Int))
  (match items
    (case (list)
      "empty"
    )
    (case (list only)
      (str "just " only)
    )
    (case (list first second)
      (str "two: " first " and " second)
    )
    (case (list first ... last)
      (str "from " first " to " last)
    )
  )
)
from 1 to 3
just 4
empty
two: 5 and 6
  • Items. [a, b](list a b) fits a list of exactly as many items as it has patterns, each fitting its pattern. [](list) fits only an empty list.
  • Rest. ... stands for any number of items, none included: | [first, ...] value(case (list first ...) value), | [..., last] value(case (list ... last) value) and | [first, ..., last] value(case (list first ... last) value). ...name names them, as a slice of the list's own type, which shares the list's storage as any slice does; see Collections. A pattern holds at most one rest: Pattern may contain only one remainder.
  • Sources. A list pattern fits lists, arrays, and values of any type that implements Indexable. It reads the length first, then the items it tests. It never fits text, which has patterns of its own.
  • One item. In | [only Int] value(case (list (: only Int)) value), the pattern is a list of one item. In a type, [Int](list Int) is a list type.

Maps

["key" = pattern, "other" = pattern](list (= "key" pattern) (= "other" pattern)) fits a map that holds each key, with a value that fits its pattern. The map may hold other keys too. ...name names a map of the entries the pattern did not name.

. settings = Map'String'Int()
settings["width"] = 10
settings["height"] = 4
do match settings
    | ["width" = w, "depth" = d]
        -- "box $w by $d"
    | ["width" = w, ...others]
        -- "width $w, and ${others.length} more"
    ??
        -- "no width"
(main
  (let settings (call (of Map String Int)))
  (= ([] settings "width") 10)
  (= ([] settings "height") 4)
  (do
    (inline
      (match settings
        (case (list (= "width" w) (= "depth" d))
          (print (str "box " w " by " d))
        )
        (case (list (= "width" w) ...others)
          (print (str "width " w ", and " (. others length) " more"))
        )
        (default
          (print "no width")
        )
      )
    )
  )
)
width 10, and 1 more

A key can be text, a number, or the value of a local, written $name, as in | [$key = value] result(case (map $key value) result).

Text

"start" ...rest "end"(all "start" ...rest "end") fits text that begins and ends with the literals written, and names the text between them, which may be empty. The literals and one rest may come in any order, as in ...name ".txt"(all ...name ".txt"), and the pattern fits the whole text. A literal can be named too, as in f "foo"(: f "foo").

for file in ["notes.txt", "photo.png", "README"]
    -- kind(file)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ kind String
    - file String

match file
    | ...name ".txt"
        "text named $name"
    | "photo." ...format
        "a photo in $format"
    ?? "$file is something else"
(main
  (for (in file (list "notes.txt" "photo.png" "README"))
    (print (call kind file))
  )
)

(fn-expr + kind String
  (param file String)
  (match file
    (case (all ...name ".txt")
      (str "text named " name)
    )
    (case (all "photo." ...format)
      (str "a photo in " format)
    )
    (default
      (inline (str file " is something else"))
    )
  )
)
text named notes
a photo in png
README is something else

Text patterns that read pieces, repeat, or choose between alternatives are stream patterns; see Stream patterns.

Properties

..name fits a value with a property name, and names a local name holding the property's value. A test can follow it: ..length { it > 3 }(all ..length ({} (> it 3))). A property the type does not have is an error: Pattern has no possible matches.

  • . ..length = "hello"(let ..length "hello") declares length, holding 5.
  • . word ..length = "hello"(let (: word ..length) "hello") names the whole value word, and declares no length.
  • In a match, a property pattern can only be the only arm.

Patterns inside patterns

Each part of a list, map or tuple pattern is a pattern, so one pattern can reach through several layers of a value, such as decoded JSON, and test each layer on the way. With match?, a missing key, a list that is too short or a value of the wrong type all give null, so a caller can pick out the one part it needs without a test for each layer.

/data/json

. replies = ["{\"choices\": [{\"message\": \"hi\", \"index\": 0}]}", "{\"choices\": [{\"index\": 0}]}", "{\"choices\": []}", "{\"error\": \"busy\"}"]
for text in replies
    -- first-message(JSON(text)) ?? "no message"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ first-message String?
    - response JSON

match? response
    | ["choices" = [["message" = message String], ...]]
        message
(import /data/json)

(main
  (let replies
    (list
      "{\"choices\": [{\"message\": \"hi\", \"index\": 0}]}"
      "{\"choices\": [{\"index\": 0}]}"
      "{\"choices\": []}"
      "{\"error\": \"busy\"}"
    )
  )
  (for (in text replies)
    (print (?? (call first-message (call JSON text)) "no message"))
  )
)

(fn-expr + first-message (? String)
  (param response JSON)
  (match? response
    (case (list (= "choices" (list (list (= "message" (: message String))) ...)))
      message
    )
  )
)
hi
no message
no message
no message

Patterns outside match

. pair = (3, "three")
if | (n, word) = pair
    -- "$n is $word"
. maybe Int? = 42
if | (n Int { it > 40 }) = maybe
    -- "big $n"
-- [1, 2, 3] is [1, ...]
-- | (Int { it > 40 }) = maybe
-- | (Int { it > 50 }) = maybe
-- match? 7
    | { it > 50 }
        "huge"
for | n Int in [1, null, 3]
    -- "got $n"
(main
  (let pair (tuple 3 "three"))
  (if (= (| (tuple n word)) pair)
    (print (str n " is " word))
  )
  (let maybe (? Int) 42)
  (if (= (| (all (: n Int) ({} (> it 40)))) maybe)
    (print (str "big " n))
  )
  (print (is (list 1 2 3) (list 1 ...)))
  (print (case (= (all Int ({} (> it 40))) maybe)))
  (print (case (= (all Int ({} (> it 50))) maybe)))
  (print
    (match? 7
      (case ({} (> it 50))
        "huge"
      )
    )
  )
  (for (in (| (: n Int)) (list 1 null 3))
    (print (str "got " n))
  )
)
3 is three
big 42
true
42
unknown
unknown
got 1
got 3
CodeGives
if | pattern = value body(if (= (| pattern) value) body)Runs the body where the value fits, with the pattern's names.
if condition body else if | pattern = value body(if condition body (else-if (= (| pattern) value) body))The same, as a branch of an if.
while | pattern = value body(while (= (| pattern) value) body)Runs the body for as long as the value fits; see Control flow.
for | pattern in source body(for (in (| pattern) source) body)Runs the body for each item that fits.
value is pattern(is value pattern)true where the value fits.
| pattern = value(case (= pattern value))What the pattern passes on, or null where the value does not fit.
result | pattern = value(= (select result (| pattern)) value)result where the value fits, or null.
. pattern = value(let pattern value)Declares the pattern's names; see below.
  • Fit, not truth. if | n Int = count body(if (= (| (: n Int)) count) body) runs its body whenever count holds an Int, even 0. The test is whether the value fits.
  • is. The right side of is is a type, a tuple type, as in pair is (Int, String)(is pair (tuple Int String)), or a list, map or text pattern, or _. value is not pattern(is-not value pattern) is its opposite. See Types for is with types.
  • Never fits. A match none of whose arms can ever fit its subject, and an if, while or declaration whose pattern can never fit its value, is an error: Pattern has no possible matches.

Where a value does not fit

CodeWhere no pattern fits
matchPanics, Pattern match failed, or, on a type with a fixed set of values, is an error unless every value has an arm
match?Gives null
match? run as stepsGoes on to the next step
if, else-if with a patternRuns the else, if any
while with a patternEnds the loop
for with a patternSkips the item
isGives false
| pattern = value(case (= pattern value)) and selectGive null
A declaration with a patternPanics, Pattern match failed

Taking values apart

A declaration whose name is a pattern takes its value apart, which other languages call destructuring, declaring a local for each name the pattern gives. The pattern states what the value is sure to be. Where a value may not fit as a matter of course, use match? or an if with a pattern instead.

. pair = (3, "three")
. first, second = pair
-- "$first, $second"
. x, (y, z) = (1, (2, 3))
-- x + y + z
. _, label = pair
-- label
. [head, ...tail] = [10, 20, 30]
-- "$head then $tail"
. a = 1
. b = 2
(a, b) = (b, a)
-- "$a $b"
(main
  (let pair (tuple 3 "three"))
  (let (tuple first second) pair)
  (print (str first ", " second))
  (let (tuple x (tuple y z)) (tuple 1 (tuple 2 3)))
  (print (+ x y z))
  (let (tuple _ label) pair)
  (print label)
  (let (list head ...tail) (list 10 20 30))
  (print (str head " then " tail))
  (let a 1)
  (let b 2)
  (= (tuple a b) (tuple b a))
  (print (str a " " b))
)
3, three
6
three
10 then 20, 30
2 1
  • Tuples. . a, b = pair(let (tuple a b) pair) declares a local for each field, by position: names are matched to fields by place, not by the fields' names. Fields can be nested, . x, (y, z) = value(let (tuple x (tuple y z)) value), skipped with _, or given types, . a Int, b String = value(let (tuple (: a Int) (: b String)) value), which convert them. Fewer names than fields take the first fields. More names than fields is an error: Pattern has no possible matches.
  • Existing locals. (a, b) = pair(= (tuple a b) pair) assigns the fields to locals that exist, so (a, b) = (b, a)(= (tuple a b) (tuple b a)) swaps two locals. Only a tuple is assigned this way: [x, y] = items(= (list x y) items) is an error, Names in brackets can be declared from a list, as in ". [x, y] = items", but not assigned again; assign a tuple to them, as in "x, y = items[0], items[1]".
  • Optionals. A tuple taken apart from an optional takes apart the tuple it holds, and panics where it holds nothing: Optional'Pair is null.
  • Patterns that can fail. A declaration with a pattern that does not fit its value panics, at the pattern: Pattern match failed.
  • Lazy declarations. .. a, b = value(lazy (tuple a b) value) declares lazy locals; the value is computed once, where any of them is first read. See Functions.
  • Loops. A loop header takes each item apart the same way: for name, age in ages body(for (in (tuple name age) ages) body). See Control flow.

Covering every case

A match over a value whose type has a fixed set of values must have an arm for each of them, or a ?? value(default value) arm, unless it is a match?. The fixed sets are:

SubjectCovered by
Bool|= true value(case= true value) and |= false value(case= false value).
An optionalAn arm for null, such as |= null value(case= null value), and arms that cover the value.
A unionAn arm for each case: .case, a pattern of the case's type, or _.
An enum|= Type.value result(case= (. Type value) result) for each value.
-- describe(4)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - value Int?

match value
    | n Int
        "holds $n"
(main
  (print (call describe 4))
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param value (? Int))
  (match value
    (case (: n Int)
      (str "holds " n)
    )
  )
)
Exception: This match on I64? does not handle null; add "|= null", or "??" for the rest
<no file:9>
        (case (: n Int)
        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  • Arms that do not count. An arm with a condition, such as | n Int { it > 0 } value(case (all (: n Int) ({} (> it 0))) value) or |? ready value(case? ready value), does not cover what it tests.
  • Lists in cases. Arms over a union case that holds a list cover it together when one takes some count of items and a rest, and the others take each smaller count: | .many([]) value(case (call .many (list)) value) and | .many([first, ...rest]) value(case (call .many (list first ...rest)) value) cover .many, as | .many([...items]) value(case (call .many (list ...items)) value) does alone.
  • Other types. A match over numbers, text, lists or classes is not checked: where no arm fits a value, it panics at run time.
  • Messages. Each names what is missing and how to add it: This match on Bool does not handle false; add "|= false", or "??" for the rest, This match on Result does not handle .bad; add a case for it, or "??" for the rest, and This match on I64? handles only null; add a case for a present value, as in "| value I64", or "??" for the rest.

Text

Text is a String: a sequence of Unicode characters, stored as UTF-8. One character is a Char. This chapter covers writing text, building it from values, text bodies, the members and operators of String and Char, converting to and from text, and atoms, which are names that compare by identity.

Text patterns are in Patterns, and grammars over text in Stream patterns.

Strings

. word = "Aé漢😀"
-- word.length
-- word.size
-- word.display-width
-- word[1]
-- word[1 .. < 3]
for letter in "héy"
    -- letter as Int
-- List("abc")
-- !""
(main
  (let word "Aé漢😀")
  (print (. word length))
  (print (. word size))
  (print (. word display-width))
  (print ([] word 1))
  (print ([] word (..< 1 3)))
  (for (in letter "héy")
    (print (as letter Int))
  )
  (print (call List "abc"))
  (print (not ""))
)
4
10
6
é
é漢
104
233
121
a, b, c
true
  • Three sizes. length counts characters, which are Unicode code points. size counts the bytes of the UTF-8 encoding. display-width counts terminal columns: a wide character such as 漢 takes two, and a combining mark takes none. All three are Size, which is I64.
  • Characters are code points. An accented letter written as a letter and a combining mark is two characters, so "e\u0301" has a length of 2. Yumi does not count grapheme clusters.
  • Looping over a text gives each Char in turn. A text converts to a list of its characters, and to a stream of them; see Streams.
  • Empty text is false. A text used as a condition is true when it is not empty, so !""(not "") is true. See Control flow.
  • String()(call String) makes the empty text, "".
  • Values. A text never changes. Assigning to an item or a range of it stores a new text in the variable; see Indexing and slicing.

Writing text

A text is written in double quotes. Inside the quotes, a backslash begins an escape:

EscapeCharacter
\"A double quote.
\\A backslash.
\$A dollar sign.
\nA line feed.
\tA tab.
\rA carriage return.
\xHHThe character with the code given by two hex digits, such as \x00.
\uHHHHThe character with the code given by four hex digits, such as \u00e9.
-- "She said \"hi\"."
-- "C:\\temp"
-- "costs \$5"
-- "a\tb"
-- "café"
-- "a\0b".length
(main
  (print "She said \"hi\".")
  (print "C:\\temp")
  (print "costs \$5")
  (print "a\tb")
  (print "caf\u00e9")
  (print (. "a\x00b" length))
)
She said "hi".
C:\temp
costs $5
a	b
café
3
  • A dollar sign must be escaped. A bare $ is an error: Unescaped “$” in Brix text. Write “\$” for a dollar sign, or build the text from its parts with (str …).
  • Characters beyond \uFFFF, such as emoji, are written as themselves.
  • A NUL character is an ordinary character: it counts in length and size, and what follows it is kept.

In rows

The rows view writes the same text with the same escapes, and adds \0, \b, \f and \v for the control characters the forms write as \x00, \x08, \x0c and \x0b. A backslash at the end of a line continues the text on the next line, adding nothing.

Building text from values

A str form makes one text from its parts, as in "Hello, $name!"(str "Hello, " name "!"). A part that is not text is converted with its type's to String, the same conversion print and value as String(as value String) use.

. name = "Ada"
. count = 3
. nobody String? = null
-- "Hello, $name!"
-- "$count items, ${count * 2} halves"
-- "pi is about ${3.14}"
-- "items: ${[1, 2, 3]}"
-- "pair: ${1, "a"}"
-- "nobody: $nobody"
-- "\${${nobody ?? "?"}}"
(main
  (let name "Ada")
  (let count 3)
  (let nobody (? String) null)
  (print (str "Hello, " name "!"))
  (print (str count " items, " (* count 2) " halves"))
  (print (str "pi is about " 3.14))
  (print (str "items: " (list 1 2 3)))
  (print (str "pair: " (tuple 1 "a")))
  (print (str "nobody: " nobody))
  (print (str "\${" (?? nobody "?") "}"))
)
Hello, Ada!
3 items, 6 halves
pi is about 3.14
items: 1, 2, 3
pair: (1, a)
nobody: unknown
${?}
  • Order. The parts are evaluated and converted from left to right, each converted before the next is evaluated.
  • Null becomes unknown.
  • Conversion. A type's own to String decides how its values appear; see Conversions. A ++ the type declares is never used for a part.
  • Nesting. A part may be any expression, including another str form.

In rows

In rows, a text with parts is one quoted text. $ followed by a name inserts that value, as in "Hello, $name!", and ${…} inserts any expression, as in "${count * 2} halves".

  • $ starts a part only before a lowercase letter, a Greek letter, ° or {. Elsewhere it is an ordinary character, so "$5" is the text $5.
  • $name reads a whole name, hyphens included, and then a chain of .member and ?.member, but no call. "$n-1" reads the name n-1: Name "n-1" not found; in a string, "$n-1" reads the whole name "n-1". Write "${n}-1" to put "-1" after the value. Punctuation after the name, as in "$name." or "$name's", stays text.

Printing

-- value(print value) writes a value's text to stdout, followed by a line break. In rows it is a row that starts with --, as in -- value.

-- "plain"
-- [1, 2, 3]
-- (1, "a")
. nobody Int? = null
-- nobody
print(5)
print-all(["x", "y"])
-- Box()
if true
    --
-- 2.50

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Box
(main
  (print "plain")
  (print (list 1 2 3))
  (print (tuple 1 "a"))
  (let nobody (? Int) null)
  (print nobody)
  (call print 5)
  (call print-all (list "x" "y"))
  (print (call Box))
  (if true
    (print)
  )
  (print 2.50)
)

(type + Box)
plain
1, 2, 3
(1, a)
unknown
5
x
y
[Object __source__:Box]
2.5
  • The text is the one str makes from the value: its type's to String, unknown for null, and [Object module:Type] for an object of a class with none.
  • No value. --(print) prints nothing, not even a line break. It stands for an empty body, where a form needs a row and there is nothing to do.
  • As a function. print is also a function core gives, so print(5)(call print 5) prints, and print can be passed as a value. print-all prints each item of a stream on a line of its own.
  • Output, not inspection. A print is part of what the program does, and what its tests check. To look at a program without changing its output, use a probe; see Probes.

Text bodies

A function whose body is a paragraph form returns text written as lines, as a template does in other languages. Each line is a text or a str form, and a blank form is an empty line. The lines are joined with line feeds.

-- receipt("Apples", 3, 2)
-- Item("pear", 2)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ receipt
    - name String
    - quantity Int
    - price Int

Receipt
=======
Item: $name
Quantity: $quantity

Total: $total (${if quantity > 1 then "several" else "one"})
    with "quotes" and $ signs
════════════════════
.. total = quantity * price

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Item is (name String, count Int)


────────────────────
+ ¶ to String

$name × $count
(main
  (print (call receipt "Apples" 3 2))
  (print (call Item "pear" 2))
)

(fn-expr + receipt _
  (param name String)
  (param quantity Int)
  (param price Int)
  (paragraph
    "Receipt"
    "======="
    (str "Item: " name)
    (str "Quantity: " quantity)
    (blank)
    (str "Total: " total " (" (if-expr (> quantity 1) "several" "one") ")")
    "    with \"quotes\" and \$ signs"
  )
  (where
    (lazy total (* quantity price))
  )
)

(type + Item (is (tuple (: name String) (: count Int)))
  (fn-to-expr + String
    (paragraph
      (str name " × " count)
    )
  )
)
Receipt
=======
Item: Apples
Quantity: 3

Total: 6 (several)
    with "quotes" and $ signs
pear × 2
  • Result. The function's result type is written _, and it returns a String.
  • Lazy bindings go in a where form after the paragraph, and the lines read them. See Functions.
  • White space. Each line keeps its leading spaces. White space written at the very end of the body is trimmed, but white space an inserted value gives is kept, so a body can end in spaces or a line break on purpose.
  • Converters. A type's to String may have a paragraph body, as Item does here.
  • Only bodies. A paragraph is a function body, not a value: (paragraph …) cannot be the `value` of (let …), which takes Expr or Block. A line cannot be a bare call either; put it in a str form.

A quoted text or a str form suits a short message. A text body pays off once the text has several lines, indentation or repeated parts. A value that has several text forms can have a text body for each, named for what it gives, rather than one to String. A document that code will read or change is better built as markup (see Markup) or by a library for its format.

Text bodies inside text bodies

A line can insert the text another text body gives. The inserted text is not reindented: its first line follows the text before it, and its other lines start at the start of the line. A separator that join puts between items is part of the result.

-- shopping-list(["Apples", "Pears"])
-- "--"
-- nested()
-- "--"
-- "[${ending("  ")}]"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ shopping-list
    - items [String]

Shopping list
${"\n".join(items *> shopping-item(each))}

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ shopping-item
    - item String

- $item

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ nested

Groups:
    ${shopping-list(["Tea", "Milk"])}

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ ending
    - pad String

kept$pad
(main
  (print (call shopping-list (list "Apples" "Pears")))
  (print "--")
  (print (call nested))
  (print "--")
  (print (str "[" (call ending "  ") "]"))
)

(fn-expr + shopping-list _
  (param items (list String))
  (paragraph
    "Shopping list"
    (str (call (. "\n" join) (*> items (call shopping-item each))))
  )
)

(fn-expr + shopping-item _
  (param item String)
  (paragraph
    (str "- " item)
  )
)

(fn-expr + nested _
  (paragraph
    "Groups:"
    (str "    " (call shopping-list (list "Tea" "Milk")))
  )
)

(fn-expr + ending _
  (param pad String)
  (paragraph
    (str "kept" pad)
    "    "
    (blank)
  )
)
Shopping list
- Apples
- Pears
--
Groups:
    Shopping list
- Tea
- Milk
--
[kept  ]

No escaping

An inserted value is its text, unchanged. A text body does not know what format it writes, so it escapes nothing: text for HTML, JSON or source code needs each value converted as that format requires, as json-quote does for JSON.

/data/json

. title = "Tom & \"Jerry\" <b>"
-- page(title)
-- record(title)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ page
    - title String

<title>$title</title>

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ record
    - title String

{"title": ${json-quote(title)}}
(import /data/json)

(main
  (let title "Tom & \"Jerry\" <b>")
  (print (call page title))
  (print (call record title))
)

(fn-expr + page _
  (param title String)
  (paragraph
    (str "<title>" title "</title>")
  )
)

(fn-expr + record _
  (param title String)
  (paragraph
    (str "{\"title\": " (call json-quote title) "}")
  )
)
<title>Tom & "Jerry" <b></title>
{"title": "Tom & \"Jerry\" <b>"}

In rows

In rows, a text body is a function marked ¶, as in + ¶ receipt. After its parameters and a blank row, every row up to the next divider is text, written without quotes: quotes need no escapes, and $name and ${…} insert values. The escapes of a quoted text still apply, so \$ writes a dollar sign and \\ a backslash. A ════ divider ends the text and begins the lazy bindings.

Characters

A Char is one Unicode code point, held in four bytes.

. letter = 'a'
-- letter
-- letter as Int
-- 66 as Char
-- 67c
-- letter.uppercase
-- (letter + 1) as Char
-- 'a' < 'b'
-- "Hi" as Char
-- "[${' '}]"
-- '漢'.display-width
-- '́'.category == .mark-nonspacing
for c in 'a' .. 'e'
    -- c
(main
  (let letter 'a')
  (print letter)
  (print (as letter Int))
  (print (as 66 Char))
  (print 67c)
  (print (. letter uppercase))
  (print (as (+ letter 1) Char))
  (print (< 'a' 'b'))
  (print (as "Hi" Char))
  (print (str "[" (char " ") "]"))
  (print (. (char "漢") display-width))
  (print (== (. (char "\u0301") category) .mark-nonspacing))
  (for (in c (.. 'a' 'e'))
    (print c)
  )
)
a
97
B
C
A
b
true
H
[ ]
2
true
a
b
c
d
e
  • Literals. A visible ASCII character is written in single quotes, as in 'A', except for ", ', (, ), ; and \. Any character, including those, a space and a non-ASCII character, is written as a char form with a one-character text, as in 'é'(char "é"). A text of any other length is an error: (char …) takes a text of one character, as in (char "a"), but this one has 2. A number with the suffix c is the character with that code, as in 65c.
  • Numbers. A character converts to and from a number only when asked: 'A' as Int(as 'A' Int) is 65, and 65 as Char(as 65 Char) and Char(65)(call Char 65) are A. Without as, the error names the conversion: Expected Char here, but this is I64, which becomes Char only when asked; write "as Char".
  • Arithmetic treats characters as U32: 'a' + 1(+ 'a' 1) is the number 98, and 'b' - 'a'(- 'b' 'a') is 1. Convert the result back with as Char.
  • Text. A character becomes text inside a text, in a print, or with c as String(as c String). "Hi" as Char(as "Hi" Char) and Char("Hi")(call Char "Hi") give the first character, and on empty text they panic: Index out of bounds (0 / 0).
  • Comparison is by code point. A character never equals a text: Operator "==" is not defined for Char and String.
  • Ranges of characters loop through the codes between them; see Control flow.
MemberValue
c.uppercase(. c uppercase)The uppercase character, or c.
c.lowercase(. c lowercase)The lowercase character, or c.
c.display-width(. c display-width)The terminal columns it takes: 0, 1 or 2.
c.category(. c category)Its Unicode general category, a UTF8Category such as .letter-uppercase, .number-decimal or .separator-space.

Char8 is a C char, one byte, written with the suffix c8. Its uppercase and lowercase change ASCII letters only. See Native code and memory.

Indexing and slicing

text[index]([] text index) gives the character at that index, counting characters from 0. A range gives the text it covers.

. word = "foobar"
-- word[0]
-- word[.last]
-- word[0 .. < 3]
-- word[0 .. 3]
-- word[3 ...]
-- word[... 3]
-- word[4 .. 1]
. before = word
word[0] = "J"
word[1 .. 2] = "ee"
word[.last] = 'Z'
-- word
-- before
(main
  (let word "foobar")
  (print ([] word 0))
  (print ([] word .last))
  (print ([] word (..< 0 3)))
  (print ([] word (.. 0 3)))
  (print ([] word (... 3)))
  (print ([] word (... _ 3)))
  (print ([] word (.. 4 1)))
  (let before word)
  (= ([] word 0) "J")
  (= ([] word (.. 1 2)) "ee")
  (= ([] word .last) 'Z')
  (print word)
  (print before)
)
f
r
foo
foob
bar
foo
ooba
JeebaZ
foobar
  • Indexes may be any integer type, or a Position: .first, .middle (half the length), .last, .end (the length) and .index(n)(call .index n).
  • Out of range panics with the index and the length, when reading and when assigning: Index out of bounds (6 / 6). A negative index panics too.
  • Ranges. a .. b(.. a b) includes b, and a .. < b(..< a b) stops before it. text[a ...]([] text (... a)) runs from a to the end, and text[... b]([] text (... _ b)) from the start to before b. A range that counts down covers the same characters as the one that counts up. A range past either end panics: Range out of bounds (8 / 5). A range with a step other than 1 panics: Only increments of 1 are currently supported.
  • Assigning to an item or a range stores a new text in the variable, property or item that held the old one. A copy made before keeps the old text. The new part may be a text of any length, or a Char. The assignment's value is the new text.

Comparing text

. composed = "é"
. decomposed = "é"
-- composed == decomposed
-- composed == decomposed.normalized
-- "Z" < "a"
-- "apple" < "apricot"
-- "b" >= "a"
(main
  (let composed "\u00e9")
  (let decomposed "e\u0301")
  (print (== composed decomposed))
  (print (== composed (. decomposed normalized)))
  (print (< "Z" "a"))
  (print (< "apple" "apricot"))
  (print (>= "b" "a"))
)
false
true
true
true
true
  • Equality compares the bytes. Two texts that look the same can differ, as a precomposed é and an e with a combining accent do. normalized makes both the precomposed form.
  • Order is by code point, so every uppercase ASCII letter comes before every lowercase one. It is not a dictionary order for any language.

Operators on text

OperationValue
a + b(+ a b)a followed by b, where b is a text or a Char.
a ++ b(++ a b)a followed by b converted to text; a must be a text.
text += more(+= text more)Appends a text or a Char.
text ++= value(++= text value)Appends any value, converted to text.
text * count(* text count)The text repeated count times.
a == b(== a b), a < b(< a b) and the other comparisonsSee Comparing text.
!text(not text)true when the text is empty.
-- "ab" + "cd"
-- "ab" + 'c'
-- "count: " ++ 5
-- "on: " ++ true
-- "=" * 10
. line = "a"
line += "b"
line ++= 3
-- line
(main
  (print (+ "ab" "cd"))
  (print (+ "ab" 'c'))
  (print (++ "count: " 5))
  (print (++ "on: " true))
  (print (* "=" 10))
  (let line "a")
  (+= line "b")
  (++= line 3)
  (print line)
)

abc
count: 5
on: true
==========
ab3
  • + takes text only. "foo" + 3(+ "foo" 3) is an error, Operator "+" is not defined for String and I64; use ++ or a str form.
  • ++ needs text on its left. 5 ++ "x"(++ 5 "x") is an error: Operator "++" is not defined for I64 and String.
  • * needs a count on its right, of any integer type. A count of 0 gives "", and a negative count panics: Repeated String size overflow.
  • No subtraction or membership. -, has and is in are not defined for text. To look for a part, use find, starts-with or ends-with, or a text pattern; see Patterns.

MemberValue
s.length(. s length)The number of characters.
s.size(. s size)The number of bytes.
s.display-width(. s display-width)The number of terminal columns.
s.find(part)(call (. s find) part)The index of the first part at or after index 0, or null. It takes the start index as a second argument.
s.find-reverse(part)(call (. s find-reverse) part)The index of the last part, or null.
s.starts-with(part)(call (. s starts-with) part)Whether s begins with part.
s.ends-with(part)(call (. s ends-with) part)Whether s ends with part.
s.trim()(call (. s trim))s without spaces, tabs, carriage returns and line feeds at either end.
s.truncate(n)(call (. s truncate) n)The first n characters followed by ..., when s is longer than n; otherwise s.

s.lowercased(. s lowercased)s with each letter lowercase.
