12
bad item at column 3

Locations

location in an action is where the arm matched, a MatchLocation of its begin and end. Each is a TokenLocation of a line and a column, both counted from 0, and end is the last item matched. In a throw arm, location is the farthest point the match reached before failing. Lines end at "\n", "\r\n" or "\r", and a column counts characters.

Helpers

A with form as a match's first row, or after the pattern of ~>, gives the match an object that takes part in it. A helper implements one or more interfaces from /core/parsing, such as PatternRecordBoundary, whose begin-pattern-record runs before each record.

. counter = Counter()
"one\ntwo\nthree\n"
~> word [a-z]+ \nl
    with counter
    "$word spans $location"
|> show
-- "${counter.count} records"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do show'Item
    - items <Item>

for item in items
    -- item

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Counter
    is PatternRecordBoundary

+ count Size
────────────────────
+ do begin-pattern-record

count += 1
(main
  (let counter (call Counter))
  "one\ntwo\nthree\n"
  (pipe ~> (seq (: word (+ (chars "a-z"))) \nl)
    (with counter)
    (str word " spans " location)
  )
  (pipe |> show)
  (print (str (. counter count) " records"))
)

(fn-do + (of show Item) _
  (param items (stream Item))
  (for (in item items)
    (print item)
  )
)

(type + Counter
  (implements PatternRecordBoundary)
  (prop + count Size)
  (fn-do + begin-pattern-record _
    (+= count 1)
  )
)

two spans ((1, 0), (1, 3))
three spans ((2, 0), (2, 5))
3 records

Errors

An error is a value a function raises in place of its result. Yumi has two kinds:

  • Recoverable errors are part of a function's type. A function declares the errors it can raise, and a caller handles them or lets them pass on to its own caller.
  • Panics are for mistakes, such as an index out of range. They need no declaration, pass through every caller and every handler, and end the task they happen in. Where the task was started, its do-new form can handle the failure.

This chapter covers error values, declaring and raising errors, how they leave a call, handling them, cleanup, and panics. Errors in generators and pipelines are also in Streams, and errors in tasks in Concurrency.

Error values

An error is an object of the class Error or a class derived from it.

. plain = Error("disk full")
-- plain
-- plain.message
. missing = NotFound("ada")
-- missing
-- missing.name
-- missing is Error

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ NotFound is Error

+ name String
────────────────────
+ This
    - name

message = "no user named $name"
(main
  (let plain (call Error "disk full"))
  (print plain)
  (print (. plain message))
  (let missing (call NotFound "ada"))
  (print missing)
  (print (. missing name))
  (print (is missing Error))
)

(type + NotFound (is Error)
  (prop + name String)
  (fn-do + This _
    (param name _)
    (= message (str "no user named " name))

MemberValue
messageThe error's text, "" by default. Converting an error to text gives its message.
sourceWhere it was raised, an ErrorSource of file, line and column, or null before it is raised.

  • Making one. Error(message)(call Error message) makes an error, and so does a constructor of a derived class. Making an error does not raise it.
  • Declaring a kind of error. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + NotFound is Error(type + NotFound (is Error)) declares one. It may add properties, and a constructor may set message.

The core library declares these kinds of error:

ClassKindRaised for
PanicPanicA mistake in the program; the base of every panic.
OutOfBoundsErrorPanicAn index outside a list, an array or a text.
TaskCancelationErrorPanicA canceled task; see Concurrency.
TaskTerminationErrorPanicA task ended because the process is ending.
IOErrorRecoverableA failed read or write.
TimeoutErrorRecoverableAn IOError for an operation that took too long.
SizeLimitErrorRecoverableInput larger than a limit.
SyntaxErrorRecoverableText that does not parse.
TypeErrorRecoverableA value of the wrong type.
UnionErrorRecoverableA failed conversion of a union; see Unions.

Declaring errors

A function names the errors it can raise after its result type, each in a ?! form:

-- checked-ratio(6, 3)
-- catch checked-ratio(6, 0)
-- scaled(5, 1)
-- catch scaled(5, 0)

    - bottom Int

    if bottom == 0

top / bottom

    - top Int
    - bottom Int

. ratio = checked-ratio(top, bottom)
-- "ratio is $ratio"
= ratio * 10
(main
  (print (call checked-ratio 6 3))
  (print (catch (call checked-ratio 6 0)))
  (print (call scaled 5 1))
  (print (catch (call scaled 5 0)))
)

  • Where. ?! follows the result type of a function, a method, a constructor, a generator or a function type, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + do read Int ?! IOError ?! SyntaxError body(fn-do + read Int (?! IOError) (?! SyntaxError) body) and () Int ?! IOError(fn-type Int (?! IOError)). A function with no result writes _ in its place.
  • Only errors. Only Error and its derived classes may follow ?!: I64 is not a recoverable error type; only subclasses of Error may appear after ?!. A panic is not declared: Panic cannot be returned as a recoverable error; use ?! Panic(...) to end the task, or convert it explicitly.
  • Classes cover their derived classes. Declaring Error itself allows every recoverable error.
  • Inferred errors. A function that declares no errors, such as scaled above, can raise whatever its body raises, and its callers know which. Function values and getters always infer their errors. Declaring a public function's errors anyway states the contract to its callers, and a change to its body that would raise another error is then caught where it is made.
  • Recursion. A function that calls itself must declare its errors: IOError can leave "walk", which calls itself, so its errors cannot be inferred; declare them on it, as in "(fn-do + walk Bool (?! IOError) …)", or catch them here.
  • Overrides may raise fewer errors than the method they override, not more, and so may a method that implements an interface's method: "read" can fail with IOError, but the interface method it implements cannot; add "?! IOError" to that method, or catch the error inside "read". A function value converts to a function type only if the type declares every error the function can raise.

A function that declares its errors cannot let any other error out:

-- parse("7")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

    - text String

?! IOError("unreadable")
    if text == ""

text as Int
(main
  (print (call parse "7"))
)

(fn-expr + parse Int (?! SyntaxError)
  (param text String)
  (before
    (throw (call IOError "unreadable") (if (== text "")))
  )
  (as text Int)
)
Exception: IOError can leave "parse", which does not declare it; declare it, as in "(fn-expr + parse Int (?! SyntaxError) (?! IOError) …)"
<no file:9>
        (throw (call IOError "unreadable") (if (== text "")))
        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

One exception: an error of a class above a declared class, such as a plain Error leaving a function that declares NotFound, compiles. It is converted to the declared class as it leaves, and panics then if it is not one: Invalid cast to [Object __source__:NotFound].

Raising

?! error(throw error) raises an error, and ?! error if condition(throw error (if condition)) raises it only when the condition holds.

  • Step bodies may raise anywhere, including in loops, branches and cleanups.
  • Value bodies raise in their before rows, which run before the value; see Functions. A match arm may also be a throw, and so may the whole body.
  • Narrowing. With an optional error, ?! failure if failure(throw failure (if failure)) raises the error it holds.
  • Errors as values. An error that is made and not thrown is an ordinary value: it can be stored, passed and returned without being raised.
  • After a call. A throw in the block of a call row reads the call's result as it, as in step(1) ?! Error("failed") if it == -1(call step 1 (block (throw (call Error "failed") (if (== it -1))))).

How errors leave

An error raised in a function ends the function, and every call it passes through, until something handles it:

  • A call whose error is not handled ends its own function the same way. Its cleanups run as it leaves; see Cleanup.
  • Loops and blocks end with the function that holds them.
  • main may let any error leave. Its cleanups run, then the program prints a report on the error stream and exits with status 1.
  • A task's body may let any recoverable error leave too. The task's cleanups run, and the program prints the report, which names the task and the task that started it, and exits with status 1.
  • Nothing is undone. What a function changed before the error stays changed. A cleanup can undo it; see Cleanup.

A call that can fail looks like any other. Most callers can only pass an error on, so the language does that for them, and handling is written only where a caller does something with the error. So a call does not show that it can end its function early: the function's declared errors show it, and yumi app.bx --explain name lists each error a function can raise and the call it comes from.

read()
-- "never printed"

+ do read ?! IOError

?! IOError("bad disk")
(main
  (call read)
  (print "never printed")
)

(fn-do + read _ (?! IOError)
  (throw (call IOError "bad disk"))
)

Handling errors

catch and catch?

catch expr(catch expr) gives a result: the value of expr, or the error it raised. The result prints as either, is tests it, and match takes it apart. catch? expr(catch? expr) gives the value, or null for any error. catch? drops which error it was and why, so it suits a place where having no value is a fine answer; where failures need different treatment, use a handler or catch.

for name in ["ada", "bob", ""]
    -- describe(name)
-- catch? lookup("ada") ?? -1
-- catch? lookup("bob") ?? -1
. held = catch lookup("")
-- held is BadName
-- held is NotFound

    = 36

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - name String

match catch lookup(name)
    | age Int
        "$name is $age"
    | missing NotFound
        "missing: ${missing.name}"
    | bad BadName
        "bad: ${bad.message}"
(main
  (for (in name (list "ada" "bob" ""))
    (print (call describe name))
  )
  (print (?? (catch? (call lookup "ada")) -1))
  (print (?? (catch? (call lookup "bob")) -1))
  (let held (catch (call lookup "")))
  (print (is held BadName))
  (print (is held NotFound))
)

(type + NotFound (is Error)
  (prop + name String)
  (fn-do + This _
    (param name _)
    (= message (str "no user named " name))
  )
)

(type + BadName (is Error))

(fn-do + lookup Int (?! NotFound) (?! BadName)
  (param name String)
  (throw (call BadName "empty name") (if (== name "")))
  (if (== name "ada")
    (return 36)
  )
  (throw (call NotFound name))
)

(fn-expr + describe String
  (param name String)
  (match (catch (call lookup name))
    (case (: age Int)
      (str name " is " age)

    (case (: missing NotFound)

    )
    (case (: bad BadName)
      (str "bad: " (. bad message))
    )
  )
)

missing: bob

-1
true
false
  • Matching a result must cover the value and every error the call can raise: This match on Result does not handle IOError; add a case for it, or "??" for the rest. A | e Error body(case (: e Error) body) arm covers every error.
  • Only the call's own errors. catch holds the errors of the expression it wraps. An error raised by working out a call's arguments still leaves.
  • Panics pass through catch and catch?.

Handlers

A call can carry handlers in its block. Each on-error form names a class of error, and gives the call's value in place of an error of that class.

-- load(0)
-- load(1)
-- load(2)
-- catch load(3)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ FileMissing is Error



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ AccessDenied is Error



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Corrupt is Error



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do read-config String ?! FileMissing ?! AccessDenied ?! Corrupt
    - outcome Int

?! FileMissing("no file")
    if outcome == 1
?! AccessDenied("not yours")
    if outcome == 2
?! Corrupt("bad bytes")
    if outcome == 3
= "custom"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do load String
    - outcome Int

. settings = read-config(outcome)
    catch FileMissing
        "defaults"
    catch err AccessDenied
        do -- "denied: ${err.message}"
        "guest"
= "using $settings"
(main
  (print (call load 0))
  (print (call load 1))
  (print (call load 2))
  (print (catch (call load 3)))
)

(type + FileMissing (is Error))

(type + AccessDenied (is Error))

(type + Corrupt (is Error))

(fn-do + read-config String (?! FileMissing) (?! AccessDenied) (?! Corrupt)
  (param outcome Int)
  (throw (call FileMissing "no file") (if (== outcome 1)))
  (throw (call AccessDenied "not yours") (if (== outcome 2)))
  (throw (call Corrupt "bad bytes") (if (== outcome 3)))
  (return "custom")
)

(fn-do + load String
  (param outcome Int)
  (let settings
    (call read-config outcome
      (block
        (on-error FileMissing
          "defaults"
        )
        (on-error (: err AccessDenied)
          (do
            (inline (print (str "denied: " (. err message))))
          )
          "guest"
        )
      )
    )
  )
  (return (str "using " settings))
)
using custom
using defaults
denied: not yours
using guest
bad bytes
  • Naming the error. catch err AccessDenied body(on-error (: err AccessDenied) body) binds the error to err.
  • Order. Handlers are tried in the order written. An error that no handler takes leaves as it would without them.
  • Bodies. A handler's last row is its value, and a do form before it runs steps. A handler may also return from the function, break or continue a loop, or raise, including the same error again with ?! err(throw err).
  • Raising a new error. catch Missing ?! LoadFailed("could not load")(on-error Missing (throw (call LoadFailed "could not load"))) raises the new error. A handler whose value is an error, (on-error Missing (call LoadFailed "could not load")), raises nothing: the call's value is then a result that may hold the error, and the function goes on with it.
  • The value of a call with handlers is the join of its own value and the handlers' values.
  • Nothing to handle. A handler on a call that cannot fail is an error: "plain()" cannot fail, so the catch attached to it has nothing to handle; remove the catch, or attach it to a call that can fail.

Transforming errors

A throw with an on-error form and no body raises nothing where it is written. It replaces each error of the named class that later leaves the function with a new error, and the new error's previous is the original. So each layer can report a failure in its own terms and keep the cause.

. result = catch load-settings()
-- result
-- (result as SettingsError).previous

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ SettingsError is Error



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do read-file String ?! IOError

?! IOError("disk unavailable")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do load-settings String ?! SettingsError

?! SettingsError("could not load settings")
    catch err IOError
= read-file()
(main
  (let result (catch (call load-settings)))
  (print result)
  (print (. (as result SettingsError) previous))
)

(type + SettingsError (is Error))

(fn-do + read-file String (?! IOError)
  (throw (call IOError "disk unavailable"))
)

(fn-do + load-settings String (?! SettingsError)
  (throw (call SettingsError "could not load settings") (on-error (: err IOError)))
  (return (call read-file))
)
could not load settings
disk unavailable
  • Scope. A transformer applies to errors that leave after its row. The new error is made before the function's cleanups run.
  • Rules. The new error's expression may not call a function that raises, so that translating one error cannot raise another, and two transformers that could take the same error are an error.
-- catch load(0)
-- catch load(1)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ConfigError is Error



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

?! IOError("disk")

= n

= read(n)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

    - n Int

?! AppError("from ${io.message}")
    catch err ConfigError <- io IOError
?! AppError("only ${other.message}")
    catch other ConfigError
= parse(n)

  (print (catch (call load 0)))
  (print (catch (call load 1)))
)

(type + AppError (is Error))

(type + ConfigError (is Error))

(fn-do + read Int (?! IOError)
  (param n Int)

  (return n)
)

(fn-do + parse Int (?! ConfigError)

(fn-do + load Int (?! AppError)

from disk
only plain
  • Chains. (caught (: err ConfigError) (: io IOError)) takes a ConfigError whose previous is an IOError, and names both. In rows it is catch err ConfigError <- io IOError. A plain transformer for the same class after it takes the errors whose chain does not fit.

Errors with no caller

Some errors have no caller to go to, such as one raised by a subscriber of a channel. These go to unhandled-error, a function the program may replace; by default it prints the report and the program goes on. See Concurrency.

Cleanup

A finally form holds steps that run when the block it is written in ends, however it ends.

-- run(false)
-- catch run(true)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Failed is Error



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Resource

+ name String
────────────────────
+ This
    - name

-- "open $name"

────────────────────
+ begin-using

this

────────────────────
+ do end-using

-- "close $name"


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do run Int ?! Failed
    - fails Bool

do finally
    -- "first cleanup"
. a = use Resource("a")
do finally
    -- "second cleanup"
. b = use Resource("b")
?! Failed("work failed")
    if fails
-- "working with ${a.name} and ${b.name}"
= 1
(main
  (print (call run false))
  (print (catch (call run true)))
)

(type + Failed (is Error))

(type + Resource
  (prop + name String)
  (fn-do + This _
    (param name _)
    (print (str "open " name))
  )
  (fn-expr + begin-using _
    this
  )
  (fn-do + end-using _
    (print (str "close " name))
  )
)

(fn-do + run Int (?! Failed)
  (param fails Bool)
  (finally
    (print "first cleanup")
  )
  (let a (use (call Resource "a")))
  (finally
    (print "second cleanup")
  )
  (let b (use (call Resource "b")))
  (throw (call Failed "work failed") (if fails))
  (print (str "working with " (. a name) " and " (. b name)))
  (return 1)
)

open b
working with a and b
close b
second cleanup
close a
first cleanup
1
open a
open b
close b
second cleanup
close a
first cleanup
work failed
  • When. A cleanup runs when its block ends: at the end, at a return, break or continue, when an error leaves, or when a panic ends the task. A cleanup in a loop body runs on every pass.
  • Order. Cleanups and uses run newest first.
  • Names. A cleanup can read only the locals declared before it.
  • Return values are worked out before the cleanups run. A cleanup cannot return a value: Illegal deferred statement.
  • Errors in cleanups. An error raised by a cleanup replaces an error that was already leaving.
  • One row. do finally -- "done"(finally (inline (print "done"))) holds one step.

A cleanup is not a rollback: it runs however the block ends, and undoes only what it is written to undo. To undo partial work, set a local when the work is done, and have the cleanup undo it only when the local is not set:

. first = ["tea"]
-- catch add-all(first, ["milk", "", "bread"])
-- first
. second = ["tea"]
-- catch add-all-or-none(second, ["milk", "", "bread"])
-- second
add-all-or-none(second, ["milk", "bread"])
-- second

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ BadItem is Error



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do add-all ?! BadItem
    - cart [String]
    - items [String]

for item in items
    ?! BadItem("an empty item")
        if item == ""
    cart += item

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do add-all-or-none ?! BadItem
    - cart [String]
    - items [String]

. start = cart.length
. finished = false
do finally
    while !finished && cart.length > start
        cart.pop()
for item in items
    ?! BadItem("an empty item")
        if item == ""
    cart += item
finished = true
(main
  (let first (list "tea"))
  (print (catch (call add-all first (list "milk" "" "bread"))))
  (print first)
  (let second (list "tea"))
  (print (catch (call add-all-or-none second (list "milk" "" "bread"))))
  (print second)
  (call add-all-or-none second (list "milk" "bread"))
  (print second)
)

(type + BadItem (is Error))

(fn-do + add-all _ (?! BadItem)
  (param cart (list String))
  (param items (list String))
  (for (in item items)
    (throw (call BadItem "an empty item") (if (== item "")))
    (+= cart item)
  )
)

(fn-do + add-all-or-none _ (?! BadItem)
  (param cart (list String))
  (param items (list String))
  (let start (. cart length))
  (let finished false)
  (finally
    (while (and (not finished) (> (. cart length) start))
      (call (. cart pop))
    )
  )
  (for (in item items)
    (throw (call BadItem "an empty item") (if (== item "")))
    (+= cart item)
  )
  (= finished true)
)

tea, milk
an empty item
tea

use

use value(use value) uses a resource until the end of the block: it calls the value's begin-using, gives what that returns, and calls end-using when the block ends, in order with the block's cleanups.

  • Resources. A type is a resource when it declares begin-using and end-using, or when it implements Closable, whose close is then called at the end.
  • Forms. . file = use open(path)(let file (use (call open path))) binds the resource. A do-use form uses a resource for the rows of its own block.
  • Null. use? and do-use? skip a null resource.

Panics

A panic is an error of the class Panic or a class derived from it. It reports a mistake that the code where it happens cannot handle, such as an index out of range. ?! Panic(message)(throw (call Panic message)) raises one, and needs no declaration. The core library panics for mistakes such as these:

MistakePanic
An index out of rangeList index 5 out of range, Index out of bounds (7 / 3)
value!(!! value) on nullOptional'core/number:I64 is null
A failed conversion to a classInvalid cast to [Object __source__:Dog]

A panic ends the task it happens in. The cleanups of the blocks it leaves still run, newest first, and nothing else in the task does.

-- "before"
fail()
-- "after"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do fail

do finally
    -- "cleanup"
?! Panic("broken invariant")
(main
  (print "before")
  (call fail)
  (print "after")
)

(fn-do + fail _
  (finally
    (print "cleanup")
  )
  (throw (call Panic "broken invariant"))
)
before
cleanup
  • Nothing stops it. catch, catch? and handlers let a panic pass, and nothing between the panic and the start of its task can stop it.
  • In main. A panic in the main task ends the program; see Unhandled panics.
  • In a cleanup. A panic raised by a cleanup takes the place of the one that was leaving, and the cleanups of the blocks around it still run.
  • In a subscriber. An event delivers each value in the task that publishes it, so a panic in one of its subscribers ends the publishing task.

Panics, exceptions and recover

A panic looks like an exception or like Go's panic, but it ends differently. No code in the failing task can stop it, and that task's stack is never resumed.

Yumi panicExceptions in Java or PythonGo's panicRust's panic!
What stops itNothing; an on-failure arm where the task was started handles it after the task endsAn enclosing catchrecover() in a deferred functionAn enclosing catch_unwind
What runs as it leavesCleanupsfinally blocksDeferred functionsDestructors
Where work goes onIn the task that started the failed one, which was never interruptedAfter the catch, on the same stackIn the caller of the function that deferred recover(), on the same stackAfter catch_unwind on the same stack, or in the thread that joins the failed one
When nothing stops itThe program ends, whichever task failedThe thread ends; in the main thread, the programThe program ends, whichever goroutine failedThe thread ends; in the main thread, the program
  • Not an exception. Exceptions use one mechanism for failures a caller expects, such as a missing file, and for mistakes, such as reading past the end of a list. A catch written for the first also stops the second, and the program goes on from whatever state the mistake left. Yumi keeps the two apart. Expected failures are recoverable errors, which a function declares and catch and handlers take. Mistakes are panics, which pass every catch and handler, so a handler can never hide a bug.
  • Not Go's recover. In Go, any deferred function in the failing goroutine can call recover(). The panic then stops, and the function that deferred it returns normally to its caller, which goes on running on the stack where the mistake happened. In practice defer with recover() becomes try and catch. Yumi's cleanups run as Go's deferred functions do, and a cleanup can read the panic with Task().failure(. (call Task) failure), but it cannot stop it.
  • Handled where the work began. In Go, a goroutine cannot handle a panic in a goroutine it started; the started one must recover inside itself, or the program ends. In Yumi, the task that started the work handles its failure with on-failure arms. That is the place that knows what the failure means, such as a server that drops one connection and goes on serving the others.
  • The closest relatives are Rust's threads, whose panic reaches the thread that joins them, and Erlang's processes, which fail whole and are restarted by a supervisor. Unlike Rust, Yumi has nothing like catch_unwind, and a panic that no arm handles ends the program even when it happens in a task other than the main one.

Ending the whole task is the point of the design. Code that just made a mistake is the code whose assumptions no longer hold, so no row of it runs again. What survives is the code that started it, which never saw the mistake happen.

Handling a failed task

on-failure arms at the end of a do-new form handle a panic that ends the task, where the task was started. An arm binds the panic and runs its rows in the failed task, after the task's cleanups.

. worker = start(3)
worker.wait()
-- worker.end == .panicked
start(-1).wait()
start(2).wait()
-- "main goes on"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do start Task
    - count Int

. task = do new
    -- "sum ${add-up([1, 2], count)}"
catch failure OutOfBoundsError
    -- "out of bounds: $failure"
catch failure
    -- "failed: $failure"
= task

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do add-up Int
    - items [Int]
    - count Int

do finally
    -- "cleanup after $count"
?! Panic("negative count")
    if count < 0
. sum = 0
for index in 0 .. < count
    sum += items[index]
= sum
(main
  (let worker (call start 3))
  (call (. worker wait))
  (print (== (. worker end) .panicked))
  (call (. (call start -1) wait))
  (call (. (call start 2) wait))
  (print "main goes on")
)

(fn-do + start Task
  (param count Int)
  (let task
    (do-new
      (print (str "sum " (call add-up (list 1 2) count)))
      (on-failure (: failure OutOfBoundsError)
        (print (str "out of bounds: " failure))
      )
      (on-failure failure
        (print (str "failed: " failure))
      )
    )
  )
  (return task)
)

(fn-do + add-up Int
  (param items (list Int))
  (param count Int)
  (finally
    (print (str "cleanup after " count))
  )
  (throw (call Panic "negative count") (if (< count 0)))
  (let sum 0)
  (for (in index (..< 0 count))
    (+= sum ([] items index))
  )
  (return sum)
)
cleanup after 3
out of bounds: List index 2 out of range
true
cleanup after -1
failed: negative count
cleanup after 2
sum 3
main goes on
  • Kinds. An arm that names a class handles only that kind of panic, as in do new work() catch failure OutOfBoundsError -- failure(do-new (inline (call work)) (on-failure (: failure OutOfBoundsError) (print failure))). One that names only its binding, as failure does in start above, handles any. The arms are tried in the order written. An arm takes only panics: A task's handler takes a panic.
  • No arm fits. A panic that no arm takes is unhandled, as is one raised in an arm.
  • After a failure. The failed task's own state is gone, but what it shared with other tasks is as the panic left it. Start work that may fail in a task of its own at a point that can decide what a failure means, such as one connection of a server.
  • Cancelling a task runs its cleanups, but not its on-failure arms, since it is not a failure.
  • The handle. A do-new form gives the task it starts. worker.wait()(call (. worker wait)) waits for it to end, and its end is panicked once a panic has ended it, handled or not. See Concurrency.
  • Recoverable errors that leave a task's body are not handled by on-failure; see How errors leave.

The failure in a cleanup

While a task's cleanups run, Task().failure(. (call Task) failure) gives the panic that is ending the task. Otherwise it gives null.

-- "main: ${ending()}"
. worker = do new
    do finally
        -- "cleanup: ${ending()}"
    ?! Panic("ending")
catch failure
    -- "handler: ${failure.message}, now ${ending()}"
worker.wait()

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do ending String

. failure = Task().failure
= if failure != null then failure.message else "nothing"
(main
  (print (str "main: " (call ending)))
  (let worker
    (do-new
      (finally
        (print (str "cleanup: " (call ending)))
      )
      (throw (call Panic "ending"))
      (on-failure failure
        (print (str "handler: " (. failure message) ", now " (call ending)))
      )
    )
  )
  (call (. worker wait))
)

(fn-do + ending String
  (let failure (. (call Task) failure))
  (return (if-expr (!= failure null) (. failure message) "nothing"))
)
main: nothing
cleanup: ending
handler: ending, now nothing

A cleanup can read the failure to log it or to undo work, but cannot stop it.

Unhandled panics

A panic that no on-failure arm handles, in any task, ends the program. It prints Unhandled panic: and its text, then the same report as an error, and crashes: the process ends with SIGABRT, status 134.

  • Crash reports. On macOS the crash leaves a report in ~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports, and the message and the stack also go to the system log as a fault, where Console shows them for an app whose output goes nowhere.
  • Stack overflow. A call too deep for its task's stack prints Stack overflow and the stack, with recursive calls folded into one line, and ends the program, even in a task with on-failure arms. On macOS it dies of SIGBUS, status 138.
  • Recoverable errors that leave main or a task's body end the program with status 1 rather than a crash, since they are expected failures, such as a missing file.

Choosing between them

The situationUse
A caller can deal with the failure, such as a missing file or bad inputA recoverable error, declared with ?!
This caller can do nothing about itNothing: let it leave
The caller has a value to use in its placeAn on-error handler on the call
The caller wants success and failure as one value to look atcatch, and a match
Any failure just means there is no valuecatch?
A layer should report the failure in its own termsA transformer
Something must be released or undone however the block endsfinally or use
A mistake in the program, which no caller can repair, such as a broken invariantA panic
A failure that should end only part of the programA panic, in a task with on-failure arms

Choose by how callers should respond, not by how serious the failure sounds. A recoverable error is part of a function's type, so every caller sees it and decides. A panic is not, so it suits a failure that callers should never have to think about.

Concurrency

A program can run many tasks. Tasks on the main thread take turns, running one at a time until each waits. Tasks on other threads, in a worker or in the shared pool, run in parallel. Channels carry values from one task to another, and subscriptions run code for each value a channel publishes.

This chapter covers tasks, workers, channels and subscriptions. Tracked properties, events and change rules are in Reactivity.

Tasks

A do-new form starts a task that runs the rows it holds. It gives the task, which can be kept to wait for it or cancel it; see Task handles.

. numbers Int<>
do new
    for n in 1 .. 3
        -- "send $n"
        numbers <- n
    numbers.close()
    -- "closed"
for n in numbers
    -- "got $n"
-- "done"
(main
  (let numbers (channel Int))
  (do-new
    (for (in n (.. 1 3))
      (print (str "send " n))
      (<- numbers n)
    )
    (call (. numbers close))
    (print "closed")
  )
  (for (in n numbers)
    (print (str "got " n))
  )
  (print "done")
)
send 1
got 1
send 2
got 2
send 3
got 3
closed
done
  • Taking turns. A task started on the main thread runs only when the task that started it waits, as main does here when it reads the channel, or ends. Each task then runs until it waits again. On the main thread, only one task runs at a time.
  • One call. do new send-all(items)(do-new (inline (call send-all items))) starts a task that makes one call.
  • Priority. @priority after do-new puts the task ahead of tasks without it.
  • Stack. A task's stack is smaller than main's, and deep recursion that main survives can overflow it: Stack overflow. @large-stack after do-new or do-new-thread, or a worker, gives the task a stack as large as main's.
  • Results. A task's body cannot return a value, and its handle holds none. A task passes results back through a channel, as in the next example, or a caller waits for a function with await; see Waiting for a result.
  • Failures. A panic ends the task it happens in, after the task's cleanups run. on-failure rows at the end of the do-new handle it where the task was started; see Errors. A panic that none handle crashes the program, and a recoverable error that leaves a task's body ends the program with status 1. The report names the task and the task that started it.

Calls that wait

No call is marked as one that waits: a function that waits on a channel, a file or the network is declared and called like any other, with no async on it and no await where it is called. A helper can start or stop waiting, as when a value read locally comes from a server instead, without a change to its callers.

. replies String<>
. log [String]
do new
    log += "worker ran"
    replies <- "pong"
-- ask(replies, log)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do ask String
    - replies String<>
    - log [String]

. before = log.length
. reply = receive(replies)
= "$reply; log had $before entries before the call and ${log.length} after"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ receive String
    - replies String<>

(<- replies)!
(main
  (let replies (channel String))
  (let log (list String))
  (do-new
    (+= log "worker ran")
    (<- replies "pong")
  )
  (print (call ask replies log))
)

(fn-do + ask String
  (param replies (channel String))
  (param log (list String))
  (let before (. log length))
  (let reply (call receive replies))
  (return (str reply "; log had " before " entries before the call and " (. log length) " after"))
)

(fn-expr + receive String
  (param replies (channel String))
  (!! (<- replies))
)
pong; log had 0 entries before the call and 1 after

While a call waits anywhere below it, other tasks run, and they can change what the caller read before the call, as the task here changes log. Read shared state again after a call that may wait. await is an ordinary function that runs another function in the pool; see Waiting for a result.

Where a task runs

FormRuns the task
do new work()(do-new (inline (call work)))On the queue of the task that starts it: the main queue from main, or a worker's queue from a task on that worker.
do new thread work()(do-new-thread (inline (call work)))On the shared pool of threads, in parallel with other tasks.
do (w) new work()(do-new (worker: w) (inline (call work)))On the worker w; see Workers.

The main queue and a worker with one thread run their tasks in turn, in the order they were started. Tasks in the shared pool, or on a worker with several threads, run in parallel and in no set order, so a program that needs an order waits on channels.

What a task sees

  • Locals of the function that starts a task are copied into the task when it starts. The task's assignments to them stay in the task, and later changes outside do not reach it.
  • Objects and module values are shared. A list the task adds to is the list everyone sees.
  • No checks. The compiler does not stop two threads from changing the same object at once. Share objects between threads only through channels or a Mutex.

Task handles

A do-new form gives the handle of the task it starts, and Task()(call Task) the handle of the task that calls it. A handle has id, is-finished and is-canceled. One that do-new gave also has end, how the task ended: running, finished, raised, panicked or cancelled. While a task's cleanups run, Task().failure(. (call Task) failure) gives the panic ending it. These are the methods:

MethodEffect
waitWaits until the task ends. A task cannot wait for itself.
cancelCancels the task. It ends the next time it waits, running up to its first wait if it has not started: its cleanups run, and a wait in one of them ends that cleanup, but its on-failure rows do not run.
closeCancels the task if it still runs, then waits for it. A use of a handle closes it where its block ends, so a task started in the block ends there, however the block is left.
suspendMakes the task wait until it is resumed, and gives whether it was canceled.
resume-now, resume-laterResumes a suspended task.
when-finishedRuns a function in a new task when the task ends.

When a program ends

When main's rows end, the functions given to when-main-ends run, then main's cleanups, and then the tasks that are still waiting to run. The program exits when no task is left. A task that waits forever keeps the program from exiting; there is no deadlock detection.

Waiting for a result

await'Int(function)(call (of await Int) function) runs a function in the shared pool and waits for its value. The task that calls it waits, so other tasks on its queue can run.

. results Int<>
for n in [3, 4, 5]
    do new
        results <- square(n)
. total = 0
for _ in 0 .. < 3
    total += (<- results)!
-- "total $total"
-- "awaited ${await'Int(=> square(6))}"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ square Int
    - n Int

n * n
(main
  (let results (channel Int))
  (for (in n (list 3 4 5))
    (do-new
      (<- results (call square n))
    )
  )
  (let total 0)
  (for (in _ (..< 0 3))
    (+= total (!! (<- results)))
  )
  (print (str "total " total))
  (print (str "awaited " (call (of await Int) (=> () (call square 6)))))
)

(fn-expr + square Int
  (param n Int)
  (* n n)
)
total 50
awaited 36
  • await without a type waits for a function that gives nothing. An error the function raises goes to unhandled-error, and the caller goes on; see Errors.
  • Semaphore passes one value from a task that calls post to one that calls await. Each post waits until a task takes its value.
  • Completion holds a value that one task finishes with finish and others await.

Workers

A Worker is a queue of tasks with threads of its own. Worker(1)(call Worker 1) makes one with one thread, and a do-new form with a worker: option starts a task on it, as in do (w) new work()(do-new (worker: w) (inline (call work))).

. worker = Worker(1)
. results Int<>
for _ in 0 .. < 2
    do (worker) new
        calls += 1
        results <- calls
-- <- results
-- <- results
-- "main thread calls $calls"
worker.stop()
+ @thread calls = 0
(main
  (let worker (call Worker 1))
  (let results (channel Int))
  (for (in _ (..< 0 2))
    (do-new (worker: worker)
      (+= calls 1)
      (<- results calls)
    )
  )
  (print (<- results))
  (print (<- results))
  (print (str "main thread calls " calls))
  (call (. worker stop))
)

(prop + calls _ @thread (= 0))
1
2
main thread calls 0
  • Threads. Worker(4)(call Worker 4) makes a worker with four threads, whose tasks run in parallel. usable-core-count gives the number of cores the program can use.
  • Stopping. stop waits for the worker's threads to finish and stops it. Tasks started on it afterwards never run.
  • Tasks within tasks. A do-new form in a task on a worker starts the new task on the same worker.
  • Idle workers do not keep a program from exiting.

Task groups

A TaskGroup waits for tasks started together. add takes a handle, and wait waits for every task added and then raises the first panic the group kept. Each task's on-failure arm keeps its panic with keep, so that a crash in one fails the work that started them:

. pool = Worker(2)
. group = TaskGroup()
. squares = [0, 0, 0]
for index in 0 .. < 3
    . task = do (pool) new
        squares[index] = index * index
    catch failed
        group.keep(failed)
    group.add(task)
group.wait()
-- squares
pool.stop()
(main
  (let pool (call Worker 2))
  (let group (call TaskGroup))
  (let squares (list 0 0 0))
  (for (in index (..< 0 3))
    (let task
      (do-new (worker: pool)
        (= ([] squares index) (* index index))
        (on-failure failed
          (call (. group keep) failed)
        )
      )
    )
    (call (. group add) task)
  )
  (call (. group wait))
  (print squares)
  (call (. pool stop))
)
0, 1, 4
  • Settling. settle waits for every task as wait does and leaves the panic kept, for a later wait to raise once other work is done.
  • Cancelling. cancel cancels each task that still runs.

A module property can hold a value for each thread, each task or each stack of calls:

FormHolds
+ @thread calls = 0(prop + calls _ @thread (= 0))One value for each thread. Tasks on the same thread share it.
+ @task depth = 0(prop + depth _ @task (= 0))One value for each task. Each task starts with the initial value.
+ @stack scope = "none"(prop + scope _ @stack (= "none"))One value for each stack of calls, given for a block by a do-with form, or by a (with name value) part of a do or a fn-do. A task starts with the value it was started under.

A @stack property with no initial value must be given one wherever it is read, through every call, interface and class method that reaches the read; where it is not, compiling fails with the calls that reach it. A closure or a task keeps the value given where it is made, so it must be made where one is given. A function that reads such a property cannot become a function value; write a closure that calls it.

Locks

A Mutex lets one task at a time run a block: a do-use form with the mutex locks it for the rows the form holds, and other tasks that reach the lock wait. See Errors for use.

Channels

A channel carries values from tasks that write them to tasks that read them. Int<>(channel Int) is a channel of Int, the type SyncChannel'Int. A declaration with a channel type and no value makes the channel.

A Sync channel is read by asking it for the next value, and its reads and writes may wait. An Async channel publishes each value to its subscribers. A SyncChannel is a rendezvous: it keeps a writer in step with its reader. A buffered channel lets the writer run ahead, at the cost of the memory its queue takes.

TypeWritingReadingAfter close
SyncChannelWaits until a reader takes the value.Waits for a value.Readers get the values still being written, then null. Writing panics: Can't write to closed channel.
SyncBufferedChannelAdds the value to a queue with no limit, and never waits.Waits while the queue is empty.Readers empty the queue, then get null. Writes are dropped.
AsyncChannelPublishes the value to every subscriber, and never waits; a value with no subscribers is lost.Subscribes; see Subscriptions.Subscribers get what was published, then end. Writing panics: Can't write to closed broadcaster.
AsyncBufferedChannelAs AsyncChannel, but keeps values while there are no subscribers and gives them to the first.Subscribes, or reads its kept values.Writes are dropped. <- reads the kept values, then gives null. A new subscription or loop panics: Illegal to subscribe while closed.
. queue SyncBufferedChannel'String
queue <- "a" <- "b" <- "c"
-- "queued 3 with no reader"
queue.close()
do new
    for item in queue
        -- "took $item"
    -- "drained"
-- "main done"
(main
  (let queue (of SyncBufferedChannel String))
  (<- queue "a" "b" "c")
  (print "queued 3 with no reader")
  (call (. queue close))
  (do-new
    (for (in item queue)
      (print (str "took " item))
    )
    (print "drained")
  )
  (print "main done")
)
queued 3 with no reader
main done
took a
took b
took c
drained
FormEffect
channel <- value(<- channel value)Writes a value, and gives the channel. With several values, writes each in turn.
value -> channel(-> value channel), items *-> channel(*-> items channel), channel <-* items(<-* channel items)Writes a value, or each item of a stream; see Streams.
channel? <- value(?<- channel value)Writes the value when channel is not null.
<- channel(<- channel)Reads the next value, or null once the channel is closed and empty.
A for loop over the channelReads values until the channel is closed and empty.
channel.close()(call (. channel close))Closes the channel.
  • Several readers of one SyncChannel or SyncBufferedChannel each take different values.
  • Hand-offs. On the main queue, a write to a SyncChannel that a task is waiting to read lets the reader run first, and the writer goes on after it.
  • Streams. A channel is a stream, so a function that takes a stream takes a channel. A stream converts to Broadcastable, the type of AsyncChannel, by a task that publishes its items.

A reader that stops early does not stop the task that writes: that task waits on its next write to a SyncChannel forever, and the program never exits. A reader that stops before the end cancels the writer, or closes a channel the writer watches.

. numbers Int<>
. producer = do new
    do finally
        -- "producer cleanup"
    for n in 1 .. 5
        numbers <- n
        -- "sent $n"
    numbers.close()
for n in numbers
    -- "got $n"
    if n == 2
        break
producer.cancel()
producer.wait()
-- "producer cancelled"
(main
  (let numbers (channel Int))
  (let producer
    (do-new
      (finally
        (print "producer cleanup")
      )
      (for (in n (.. 1 5))
        (<- numbers n)
        (print (str "sent " n))
      )
      (call (. numbers close))
    )
  )
  (for (in n numbers)
    (print (str "got " n))
    (if (== n 2)
      (break)
    )
  )
  (call (. producer cancel))
  (call (. producer wait))
  (print "producer cancelled")
)
got 1
sent 1
got 2
sent 2
producer cleanup
producer cancelled

Subscriptions

A loop written with on in place of in subscribes to a broadcaster such as an AsyncChannel. It does not wait: the code after it runs at once, and the loop's body runs later, for each value published.

. temps AsyncChannel'Int
for t on temps when t > 20
    -- "warm $t"
for t on temps
    -- "seen $t"
    if t == 25
        break
-- "subscribed"
temps <-* [18, 25, 30]
temps.close()
-- "published"
(main
  (let temps (of AsyncChannel Int))
  (for (on t temps (when (> t 20)))
    (print (str "warm " t))
  )
  (for (on t temps)
    (print (str "seen " t))
    (if (== t 25)
      (break)
    )
  )
  (print "subscribed")
  (<-* temps (list 18 25 30))
  (call (. temps close))
  (print "published")
)
subscribed
published
warm 25
warm 30
seen 18
seen 25
  • Delivery. Each subscription gets the values in the order they were published, in a task of its own on the queue of the task that published them. The publisher does not wait for it.
  • Clauses. when, while and until work as in other loops; see Control flow.
  • Ending. break ends the subscription. Closing the channel ends every subscription after it gets the values already published. The body cannot return a value: The body of a loop on "temps" cannot return with "="; skip to the next value with "continue", or stop the loop with "break".
  • Errors a subscription's body raises go to unhandled-error, and later values are still delivered.
  • Reading once. <- temps(<- temps) on an AsyncChannel subscribes, waits for the next value published, and ends the subscription.
  • One source. A loop subscribes to one broadcaster. Two on headers in one loop are an error: A loop on a stream subscribes to one source, so it cannot be joined to another; write a loop for each source.

The events of a class are broadcasters too, and deliver to their subscribers at once, before the publisher goes on. A class can also subscribe in its own body. See Reactivity.

Reactivity

A value can follow state. A read written with #, as in #count, is tracked, and a value that makes tracked reads is worked out again when what it read changes. A property whose value reads tracked state stays up to date, a rule in a class runs when what it reads changes, and an assignment or a lazy that reads tracked state follows it too. Events are the other half: a class declares an event, and its subscribers run as soon as a value is published to it.

This chapter covers tracked reads, derived properties, rules, live statements, streams of a value, events, and the order in which all of these run. Tasks and channels are in Concurrency, and markup that follows state is in Markup.

Tracked reads

#name reads a property, a local or a parameter and tracks it, and object.#name(. object #name) does so for another object's property. A tracked read gives the same value as a plain one. Where it is written in a value that follows state, such as a property's value, a rule's test or a live statement, the value follows what it read. Anywhere else it is a plain read.

ReadTracked
A stored property of a class: #celsius, t.#celsius(. t #celsius)Yes.
A local or a parameter: #nYes.
A listYes, with the changes made to it in place, such as items += 4(+= items 4).
A module valueNo: Untrackable name.
A getter, or a property computed each time it is readNo: Tracked getters are not supported; track concrete state instead.
A property of a structNo: "#x" reads a field of Point, whose values are copied, so it cannot be tracked; track a property of a class.
A method call: c.#size()(call (. c #size))No: "size" is a method, so "#" before it tracks nothing; track the properties it reads instead.
  • Only reads written in the value. A tracked read inside a function the value calls is not followed. Pass the tracked read to the function as an argument instead, as in noted(source.#count)(call noted (. source #count)).
  • Chains. Each # in a chain is followed: v.#source.#count(. v #source #count) follows a change to count and a new source. A chain that starts at a local, a parameter or a property of the object itself, as source.#count(. source #count) does in a class, follows that name too.

What a store notifies

A store notifies what follows the property, unless the value stored is the one already there.

  • Numbers compare by their bits, so storing -0.0 over 0.0 notifies.
  • Tuples compare by value.
  • Objects, text and lists compare by identity: storing a new list with the same items notifies. A whenever-rule then compares its own value again with !=; see Rules.

Derived properties

A property whose value makes a tracked read is derived. It is worked out when the object is made, and again after what it reads changes.

. cart = Cart()
-- cart.total
cart.quantity = 3
-- cart.total
cart.total = 0
-- cart.total
cart.price = 4
-- cart.total

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Cart

+ quantity = 1
+ price = 5
+ total = #quantity * #price
(main
  (let cart (call Cart))
  (print (. cart total))
  (= (. cart quantity) 3)
  (print (. cart total))
  (= (. cart total) 0)
  (print (. cart total))
  (= (. cart price) 4)
  (print (. cart total))
)

(type + Cart
  (prop + quantity _ (= 1))
  (prop + price _ (= 5))
  (prop + total _ (= (* #quantity #price)))
)
5
15
0
12
  • When it is read. A derived property that nothing follows is worked out again only when it is read after a change, once, however many changes came before.
  • Never mixed. A rule that reads a derived property and what it derives from sees them agree.
  • Writing one stores a value that stays until what the property reads changes.
  • Errors that its value raises when it is worked out again go to unhandled-error, and the property keeps its value.
  • Cycles. Values that read each other are an error: "a" depends on its own value, directly or through the values it reads; break the cycle.
  • Computed once. A property computed the first time it is read, + p := value(prop + p _ (:= value)), cannot make tracked reads: A lazy property is worked out once, when it is first read, so it cannot follow "#a"; write "=" in place of ":=" to keep it live, or read "a" without "#".
  • Closing. Calling the object's close stops its derived properties, rules and subscriptions. The class must declare close, even with an empty body, as in ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + do close(fn-do + close _).

Rules

A rule is a section of a class that runs when what it reads changes.

. t = Thermostat()
-- "start ${t.fahrenheit} F"
t.celsius = 30
-- "stored 30"
t.celsius = 30
-- "stored 30 again"
t.celsius = 18
-- "stored 18, changes ${t.changes}"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Thermostat

+ celsius = 20.0
+ fahrenheit = #celsius * 9 / 5 + 32
+ changes = 0
. counted < celsius
────────────────────
when #celsius > 25

-- "hot at $celsius"

────────────────────
whenever #fahrenheit

-- "now $fahrenheit F"

────────────────────
+ do counted

changes += 1
(main
  (let t (call Thermostat))
  (print (str "start " (. t fahrenheit) " F"))
  (= (. t celsius) 30)
  (print "stored 30")
  (= (. t celsius) 30)
  (print "stored 30 again")
  (= (. t celsius) 18)
  (print (str "stored 18, changes " (. t changes)))
)

(type + Thermostat
  (prop + celsius _ (= 20.0))
  (prop + fahrenheit _ (= (+ (/ (* #celsius 9) 5) 32)))
  (prop + changes _ (= 0))
  (depends counted celsius)
  (when-rule (> #celsius 25)
    (print (str "hot at " celsius))
  )
  (whenever-rule #fahrenheit
    (print (str "now " fahrenheit " F"))
  )
  (fn-do + counted _
    (+= changes 1)
  )
)

now 86 F
hot at 30

stored 30 again
now 64.4 F
stored 18, changes 2
RuleRuns
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ when #celsius > 25(when-rule (> #celsius 25))As the object is made, if the test holds, and then each time something it reads changes while the test holds.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ whenever #fahrenheit(whenever-rule #fahrenheit)Each time the value changes, compared with !=. Not as the object is made.
. counted < celsius(depends counted celsius)Calls the method counted each time one of the named properties changes. Not as the object is made.
  • when and whenever. Storing 1, 2, 0, -1 and 3 in turn runs ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ when #a > 0(when-rule (> #a 0)) at 1, 2 and 3, while the test holds, and ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ whenever #a > 0(whenever-rule (> #a 0)) at 1, 0 and 3, each time the test's value changes.
  • After the constructor. Rules start once the constructor ends. A store in the constructor runs no rule, and a when-rule first sees the values the constructor set.
  • Tracked reads. A rule's test must read tracked state: when rules must read at least one tracked property, and whenever value triggers must read at least one tracked property (like #bar). It may read other objects, as ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ whenever meter.#level(whenever-rule (. meter #level)) does.
  • depends stands with the class's properties. The method it names takes no argument it requires: A dependency calls "counted" with nothing, but it takes "n"; give "n" a default, or name a method that takes nothing. The properties it names are stored ones: "twice" is a getter, which is never stored, so a dependency on it never runs; depend on the properties it reads.
  • Inherited. A subclass runs the rules of its base class.
  • Leaving early. =(return) ends one run of a rule. A rule gives no value: A rule gives no value, so its body cannot return one with "="; end it early with "= alone".
  • Only in a class. A rule written at the top level of a file is a syntax error.

Live statements

An assignment or a lazy whose value makes a tracked read is live: it runs again each time what it reads changes, in main or in any function.

. counter = Counter()
. label = Label()
label.text = "count ${counter.#count}"
.. doubled = counter.#count * 2
. values = <counter.#count * 10>
-- label.text
-- doubled
-- <- values
counter.count = 2
counter.count = 2
counter.count = 3
-- label.text
-- doubled
-- <- values
-- <- values
label.close()
values.close()
counter.count = 4
-- label.text
-- doubled

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Counter

+ count = 1

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

+ text = ""

  (let counter (call Counter))
  (let label (call Label))
  (= (. label text) (str "count " (. counter #count)))
  (lazy doubled (* (. counter #count) 2))
  (let values (stream (* (. counter #count) 10)))
  (print (. label text))
  (print doubled)
  (print (<- values))
  (= (. counter count) 2)
  (= (. counter count) 2)
  (= (. counter count) 3)
  (print (. label text))
  (print doubled)
  (print (<- values))
  (print (<- values))
  (call (. label close))
  (call (. values close))
  (= (. counter count) 4)
  (print (. label text))
  (print doubled)

  • Assignments. A live assignment stores again each time what it reads changes, until the object it stores to closes.
  • Lazies. A live lazy is worked out at its first read, and then kept up to date.
  • let is set once, even when its value makes tracked reads. A local that follows state is a lazy.
  • Content. The rows of a class's content, such as ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ echo = #shown(content (= echo #shown)), run as the object is made, and those that read tracked state are live.

Streams of a value

<counter.#count * 10>(stream (* (. counter #count) 10)) is a channel that sends the value now, and then the value each time it changes. Its type is AsyncBufferedChannel, so a reader that is not waiting gets the values in order later, and close ends it. Storing the same value sends nothing. The value must make a tracked read: A stream of a value follows the reads written with "#", and this one has none, so it would never change; write "#" before what it follows, as in "<c.#count>".

##readings(## readings) is the latest value a stream has sent, and a value that reads it follows the stream. Before the stream sends anything, it is the type's empty value, such as 0. Named with a lazy, as in .. latest = ##readings(lazy latest (## readings)), it is read tracked as #latest.

. readings = AsyncChannel'Int()
.. latest = ##readings
.. enabled = true
. board = Board()
board.text = "latest ${#latest}"
for r on readings whenever #enabled
    -- "logged $r"
-- board.text
readings <- 4
readings <- 7
-- "sent 4 and 7"
let-tasks-run()
-- board.text
enabled = false
readings <- 9
let-tasks-run()
-- board.text
readings.close()

    done.post()
done.wait()

  (call let-tasks-run)
  (print (. board text))
  (= enabled false)
  (<- readings 9)
  (call let-tasks-run)
  (print (. board text))
  (call (. readings close))
)

  • Delivery. A channel's values reach ## and subscriptions in tasks of their own, after the publisher waits, so a value that follows ## may skip values sent in between.
  • whenever clauses. for r on readings whenever #enabled body(for (on r readings (whenever #enabled)) body) subscribes while the clause holds, and values sent while it does not are dropped. The clause must read tracked state, and cannot read the loop's item: whenever clauses must read at least one tracked property (like #is-open).

The current state, as in showing a reading##, which may skip values.

Events

A class declares an event with the type of the value it carries, and publishes values to it with <-. Each subscriber runs at once, before the publisher goes on.

. door = Door()
for who on door.rang
    -- "outside: $who"
-- "before"
door.ring("ann")
-- "after"
door.rang <- "bob"

rang <- who
-- "ring returns"

  (for (on who (. door rang))
    (print (str "outside: " who))

  (print "before")
  (call (. door ring) "ann")
  (print "after")
  (<- (. door rang) "bob")
)

  (event + rang String)

  • Declaring. + event rang String(event + rang String) declares an event in a class or an interface. A struct or a tuple cannot declare one: Only a class can declare an event, which belongs to an object, and P is a struct, whose values are copied; declare P as a class. The type is required; an event with nothing to carry is declared with Bool: An event gives each subscriber a value, so it cannot carry Void; an event that only signals carries Bool, as in "+ event rang Bool". A private event, with _, can be published and subscribed only in its own module: Event "hidden" is private.
  • Publishing. rang <- who(<- rang who) publishes inside the class, and door.rang <- "bob"(<- (. door rang) "bob") outside it. When nothing subscribes, the value is not even worked out.
  • Not a value. An event cannot be stored or passed: "rang" is an event of Door; it cannot be used as a value. Nor can it be read once: "rang" is an event of Door, which gives each value to its subscribers and keeps none to read with "<-"; hear the next one with "for value on d.rang", and end the loop with "break". Declared with the type Broadcastable, as in . e Broadcastable'String = door.rang(let e (of Broadcastable String) (. door rang)), it can be, and its subscribe and unsubscribe methods take a function. It can subscribe but not publish: Operator "<-" is not defined for Broadcastable'String. So a type can hand out an event as a Broadcastable to let others listen, and keep publishing to itself.
SubscriptionWritten
From any codefor who on door.rang body(for (on who (. door rang)) body)
In the class's body━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ for who on rang(subscribe-for (on who rang)), followed by its rows
In the class's body, with the value as each━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ on rang(subscribe (on rang)), followed by its rows
In the constructorA for loop on the event, as in the example
In a class's body, to another object's event━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ for who on door.rang(subscribe-for (on who (. door rang)))
  • Order. For one publication, subscriptions made in the constructor run first, then those in the class's body, the base class's first, then those made outside, in the order they were made.
  • Nesting. A value published inside a subscriber is delivered before that subscriber goes on. A subscription made during a publication starts with the next one.
  • Clauses. when, while and until work as in other loops; see Control flow.
  • Errors a subscriber raises go to unhandled-error, and the subscribers after it still run. A panic in a subscriber ends the task that published; see Errors.
  • One source. A loop subscribes to one event: A loop on a stream subscribes to one source, so it cannot be joined to another; write a loop for each source.

Ending a subscription

. ticker = Ticker()
. log = Log(ticker)
for n on ticker.ticked
    -- "first $n"
    if n == 2
        break
for n on ticker.ticked until n == 3
    -- "second $n"
for n in 1 .. 4
    -- "tick $n"
    ticker.ticked <- n
    if n == 3
        log.close()
ticker.close()
ticker.ticked <- 5
-- "log saw ${log.seen}"

────────────────────

seen += 1

  (let ticker (call Ticker))
  (let log (call Log ticker))
  (for (on n (. ticker ticked))
    (print (str "first " n))
    (if (== n 2)
      (break)
    )
  )
  (for (on n (. ticker ticked) (until (== n 3)))
    (print (str "second " n))
  )
  (for (in n (.. 1 4))
    (print (str "tick " n))
    (<- (. ticker ticked) n)
    (if (== n 3)
      (call (. log close))
    )
  )
  (call (. ticker close))
  (<- (. ticker ticked) 5)
  (print (str "log saw " (. log seen)))
)

  • break ends the subscription, and so does a while or until clause. until is tested before the body runs.
  • Closing the event's owner ends every subscription to its events.
  • Closing the subscriber ends the subscriptions in its class's body.
  • close must be declared for either: Ticker has no method "close".

Keyed and routed events

  • Keyed. + event messages Int keyed by U64(event + messages Int U64) declares an event keyed by a U64. A value is published to one address, as in box.messages[7] <- 3(<- ([] (. box messages) 7) 3), and an address has one receiver: a second is a runtime error, Duplicate keyed event receiver for 7:0. A key is an integer, a Char, a Bool or an interned identity, or a tuple of an index and a generation. A subscription names its address: Keyed event "messages" must be addressed with [key].
  • Routed. A value that implements RoutedEvent passes from its target to the next owners in turn, until a subscriber cancels it. The public events of an EventNode class bubble to its ancestors, which subscribe to them by the class's name. Markup uses both.

  • Before the next statement. A store runs every rule, derived property and live statement that follows it before the statement that stored goes on.
  • In turn. What follows a property runs in the order it began to follow it. A store made while these run, as rule A's store to price is, queues what it notifies behind what is already waiting, so rule C runs after rule B. Each runs once for each change.
  • Events nest; stores queue. A value published in a subscriber is delivered at once, inside it. A store made in a rule waits its turn.
  • Threads. Rules and live statements run in the task that stores, and subscribers in the task that publishes. Values sent to a channel reach its subscribers in tasks on the publisher's queue; see Concurrency.
  • Settling. Rules that keep changing what they read end the program after a million runs: Live actions kept changing what they read and never settled. A rule that stores to what it reads is fine when the stores stop.

Live functions

A function marked @live keeps state from one run of the live value that calls it to the next. It is for a value that changes over time on its own, as an animation does: GUI's animated is a live function, whose state is the motion that moves the value, and each frame of the motion runs the value again.

. meter = Meter()
-- meter.shown
meter.value = 3
-- meter.shown
meter.value = 4
-- meter.shown

  • State. live-state'Count()(call (of live-state Count)) finds the state of that type the function kept in the last run, or null, and keep-live-state(count)(call keep-live-state count) keeps one. A state is a Tracker: it is attached to the live value, and calling that value's action runs it again.
  • Several calls in one value keep a state each, in the order of the calls.
  • Only in live values. A live function called where nothing is read live is an error: The live function "counted" is called only where a value is read live. keep-live-state outside a live function panics: Only a live function keeps a live state.

State machines

A state machine is a value that is in one of several cases, and moves from case to case as values arrive from events, channels and other sources. A case can hold values, run rows when it is entered and left, and own locals, subscriptions and other machines that last while it is active. Rows in a machine are a description of what moves it; the machine runs on its own.

Use a machine when a value moves through phases, when which values matter depends on the phase, or when work should last only as long as a phase. Use a union for a value that only says which of several things it is, and a subscription for values each handled the same way whatever came before.

A first machine

  • Cases. ~> locked(state locked) declares a case. The machine starts in its first case that has no trigger.
  • Transitions. then unlocked on coins(then unlocked (trigger on coins)) in a case moves the machine to unlocked when a value arrives from coins while that case is active.
  • Ignored values. A value that no transition takes is ignored. There is no invalid transition: pushing a locked turnstile leaves it locked.
  • Reading. gate.phase is .unlocked(is (. gate phase) .unlocked) tests the case, a machine prints as its case, and name is the case's name as text.

Where a machine lives

DeclarationMachine
+ phase ~> ~> idle(prop + phase _ (machine (state idle))) in a classOne for each object, started when the constructor ends.
+ phase ~> ~> idle(prop + phase _ (machine (state idle))) in a moduleOne for the module, started when the module starts.
. flow ~> ~> idle(let flow (machine (state idle)))A local, started where it is declared. It keeps running after its function returns.
.. flow ~> ~> idle(lazy flow (machine (state idle)))A local started where it is first read.
~> idle(state idle) rows in main, or in a class's contentAn anonymous machine; see Anonymous machines.
~> ready + auth ~> ~> out(state ready (prop + auth _ (machine (state out))))A machine nested in a case, which runs while the case is active.
  • An initial case is required: State machine has no initial state. Only an anonymous machine may start with no case active.
  • Structs cannot hold one: State machine properties are not supported on structs. Nor can interfaces: Gate is an interface, so it cannot hold a state machine; declare the machine in the classes that are Gate.
  • The machine's type is a union of its cases that the program cannot name, so the property's type is written _.

Cases

A case is also called a state, as the state form and the compiler's messages call it.

  • Payloads. ~> placed(item, count)(state (call placed item count)) declares a case that holds two values; see Payloads.
  • Triggers. A case written with a trigger, as in ~> playing(track) for track on plays(state (call playing track) (trigger for track plays)), is entered each time the trigger fires, from any case.
  • Nested cases are active together with the case that holds them. Entering a case enters its first nested case that has no trigger, and a nested case with a trigger is entered only by it.
  • One name, one case. A case name written twice in one machine, at any depth, is an error: Redefinition of state case 'idle'.
  • Undeclared targets. A then that names a case no state declares declares it, at the place the then is written.

Transitions

TransitionMoves
then cooling on readings(then cooling (trigger on readings))On each value from readings.
then cooling on readings when each > 30(then cooling (trigger on readings (> each 30)))On each value that passes the guard. each is the value.
then cooling when each > 30 on readings(then cooling (trigger when-on (> each 30) readings))The same, with the guard written first.
then placed(item, count) for .place(item, count) on requests(then (call placed item count) (trigger for (call .place item count) requests))On each value that fits the pattern, which names its parts. A guard may follow the source.
then hunting if ready(then hunting (trigger if ready))When the case is entered, if the condition holds.
then valid(n) if | .valid(n) = login(then (call valid n) (trigger if-match (call .valid n) login))When the case is entered, if login fits the pattern.
then stopped(then stopped)When the case is entered, always.
?? checking(else-state checking)When no transition of the group before it moves; see Fallbacks.

  • When a transition listens. A then listens while its case is active. A trigger on a case at the top of the machine listens for the machine's whole life, and a trigger on a nested case while the case that holds it is active.
  • Groups. The transitions of one case on one source are a group, tried in the order written. The first whose pattern and guard pass moves the machine, and a value moves it once: a reading of 35 in heating goes to idle, not on to cooling.
  • Sources. A source is an event, a channel or another Broadcastable, or a list, a text, a generator or another stream, whose items arrive in turn as the case is entered. Anything else is an error: State trigger source is not broadcastable or iterable. The source is worked out each time its case is entered.
  • Only by transitions. Assigning a machine, or one of its cases, is an error: State machine "phase" moves only by its transitions, so it cannot be assigned; add a transition that enters the case.
  • Re-entry. A transition to the active case, or to a case that holds it, leaves that case and enters it again, running both its exit and entry rows. A move between branches leaves the cases up to the one both share, and enters down from it.
  • Decisions on entry. A transition with if, if-match or no trigger is decided when its case is entered, in the order written, and is not tried again when what it reads changes. Decisions that would enter a case again without a trigger are an error:

  • What it does. ?? checking(else-state checking) acts when a value arrives that no transition of the group before it takes. It leaves the named case and the cases active inside it, and enters nothing.
  • No active case. A fallback that leaves the machine's only active case leaves the machine with none: is is false for every case, and path is empty. Nothing starts it again.
  • Errors. A group has one fallback: Multiple fallbacks in one state transition group. A fallback needs a group before it: State fallback has no transition group.
