| place(String, Int)
| cancel

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Order

+ event requests Request
+ event payments F64
────────────────────
+ phase ~>

~> empty
    then placed(item, count) for .place(item, count) on requests
~> placed(item, count)
    then paid(item, count, each) on payments
~> paid(item, count, amount)

────────────────────
+ get summary String

match phase
    | .empty
        "empty"
    | .placed(item, count)
        "$count x $item"
    | .paid(item, count, amount)
        "$count x $item, paid $amount"
(main
  (let order (call Order))
  (print (. order summary))
  (<- (. order requests) .cancel)
  (print (. order summary))
  (<- (. order requests) (call .place "tea" 2))
  (print (. order summary))
  (<- (. order payments) 7.5)
  (print (. order summary))
  (print (. order phase))
)

(type + Request (is Union)
  (variant place (tuple String Int))
  (variant cancel)
)

(type + Order
  (event + requests Request)
  (event + payments F64)
  (prop + phase _
    (machine
      (state empty
        (then (call placed item count) (trigger for (call .place item count) requests))
      )
      (state (call placed item count)
        (then (call paid item count each) (trigger on payments))
      )
      (state (call paid item count amount))
    )
  )
  (fn-expr + summary String :get
    (match phase
      (case .empty
        "empty"
      )
      (case (call .placed item count)
        (str count " x " item)
      )
      (case (call .paid item count amount)
        (str count " x " item ", paid " amount)
      )
    )
  )
)
empty
empty
2 x tea
2 x tea, paid 7.5
(tea, 2, 7.5)
  • Giving values. The target of a transition gives the case its values: then paid(item, count, each) on payments(then (call paid item count each) (trigger on payments)) reads the payload of the case it leaves, and the value that arrived as each. A target may also read the names a pattern binds and the members of the object.
  • Names. The names in a case's own parentheses, such as amount, name its values in its rows and in match arms.
  • Types. A payload's types are those of the values its transitions give. A transition that gives values of other types is an error where it gives them, as an argument of the wrong type is.
  • Count. A transition gives a case as many values as it holds: Case "held" holds one value, and this transition gives none; give it one value.
  • Captures. A pattern on a case's trigger may bind names the case does not hold. They last for that activation: the case's entry rows, guards and targets read them, but they are not part of the machine's value.
  • Printing. A case with a payload prints as its payload, as a union's case does.

Reading a machine

. editor = Editor()
editor.report()
editor.focuses <- true
editor.report()
editor.saves <- "notes.txt"
editor.report()
-- editor.status

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Editor

+ event focuses Bool
+ event saves String
+ status = if #phase is .saved then "saved" else "unsaved"
────────────────────
+ phase ~>

~> editing
    ~> idle
    ~> focused on focuses
    then saved(name) for name on saves
~> saved(name)

────────────────────
+ do report

-- " > ".join(phase.path)
-- "editing ${phase is .editing}, focused ${phase is .focused}"
do match phase
    | .saved(name)
        -- "saved as $name"
    | .focused
        -- "match: focused"
    ??
        -- "match: ${phase.name}"
(main
  (let editor (call Editor))
  (call (. editor report))
  (<- (. editor focuses) true)
  (call (. editor report))
  (<- (. editor saves) "notes.txt")
  (call (. editor report))
  (print (. editor status))
)

(type + Editor
  (event + focuses Bool)
  (event + saves String)
  (prop + status _ (= (if-expr (is #phase .saved) "saved" "unsaved")))
  (prop + phase _
    (machine
      (state editing
        (state idle)
        (state focused (trigger on focuses))
        (then (call saved name) (trigger for name saves))
      )
      (state (call saved name))
    )
  )
  (fn-do + report _
    (print (call (. " > " join) (. phase path)))
    (print (str "editing " (is phase .editing) ", focused " (is phase .focused)))
    (do
      (inline
        (match phase
          (case (call .saved name)
            (print (str "saved as " name))
          )
          (case .focused
            (print "match: focused")
          )
          (default
            (print (str "match: " (. phase name)))
          )
        )
      )
    )
  )
)
editing > idle
editing true, focused false
match: idle
editing > focused
editing true, focused true
match: focused
saved
editing false, focused false
saved as notes.txt
saved
ReadGives
phase is .editing(is phase .editing)Whether the case is active, itself or through a case nested in it.
A match on the machineThe arm of the innermost active case. Arms bind the payload, and the match must cover every case.
phase.name(. phase name)The innermost active case's name.
phase.case(. phase case)Its position among the machine's cases, from 0.
phase.path(. phase path)The names of the active cases, outermost first, as a [String].
The machine in a print or a textThe innermost case's name, or its payload.
  • A copy. Reading a machine copies its case and payload. A local that holds the copy keeps them after the machine moves on, and is, match and path read the copy. == compares two copies. A case is tested with is, not ==: A state machine's case is tested with "is" or "is not", which count the cases nested in it; write "is .locked" in place of "== .locked".
  • Tracked reads. #phase is .saved(is #phase .saved) in a property's value or a rule's test follows the machine, as status does above; see Reactivity. Without #, the value is worked out once.
  • Cases are named with a dot, and a case the machine does not have is an error: Case ".nope" not found in state machine (.locked | .unlocked).
  • Nested machines are read only inside the cases of the case that holds them: from elsewhere, Name "auth" not found.

Anonymous machines

Cases written in main, or in a class's content, with no machine around them are an anonymous machine. Each case is a value of its own name: a Bool for a case with no payload, and an optional of its payload for one with a payload, present while the case is active.

+ messages AsyncChannel'String
+ counts AsyncChannel'Int
+ inbox ~>
    ~> empty
    ~> holding(count) for count on counts
~> waiting
~> received(value) for value on messages
-- "$waiting ${received ?? "none"} $inbox"
messages <- "hello"
counts <- 3
-- "$waiting ${received ?? "none"} $inbox"
do new
    -- "$waiting ${received ?? "none"} $inbox"
(prop + messages (of AsyncChannel String))
(prop + counts (of AsyncChannel Int))
(prop + inbox _
  (machine
    (state empty)
    (state (call holding count) (trigger for count counts))
  )
)

(main
  (state waiting)
  (state (call received value) (trigger for value messages))
  (print (str waiting " " (?? received "none") " " inbox))
  (<- messages "hello")
  (<- counts 3)
  (print (str waiting " " (?? received "none") " " inbox))
  (do-new
    (print (str waiting " " (?? received "none") " " inbox))
  )
)
true none empty
true none empty
false hello 3
  • Starting. An anonymous machine starts in its first case with no trigger. With none, it starts with no case active, and every case's value is false or absent.
  • Channels. Values written to an AsyncChannel move a machine in a task of their own, after the writer waits, so the machines here have moved only when the task do-new starts runs.

Entering and leaving

. player = Player()
-- "-- play"
player.plays <- "intro"
-- "-- play again"
player.plays <- "outro"
-- "-- stop"

+ event stops Bool
────────────────────

~> stopped

    do finally
        -- "exit playing $track"

  • Entry and exit. A case's do rows, as in do -- "enter"(do (print "enter")), run when it is entered, and its finally rows, as in do finally -- "exit"(finally (print "exit")), when it is left.
  • Order. A move leaves the active cases from the innermost out, runs the transition's own do rows, and then enters the target from the outermost in.
  • Again. playing has a trigger of its own, so a second track leaves it and enters it again.

Values that live in a case

/stream/timing

. kettle = Kettle()
kettle.ticks <- 0.5
kettle.switches <- 10.0
for i in 0 .. < 5
    kettle.ticks <- 0.5
    -- "${kettle.phase.name} ${kettle.heat}"
kettle.switches <- 20.0
kettle.ticks <- 0.5
kettle.switches <- 30.0
for i in 0 .. < 4
    kettle.ticks <- 0.5
-- "${kettle.phase.name} ${kettle.heat}"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Kettle

+ event switches F64
+ event ticks F64
+ heat F64 = 0
+ runs = 0
────────────────────
+ phase ~>

~> off
~> heating(rate) for rate on switches
    . run = next-run()
    do
        -- "run $run at $rate"
    for dt on ticks
        heat += dt * rate
    then whistling on delayed(ticks, 2)
~> whistling
    do
        -- "whistling"

────────────────────
_ do next-run Int

runs += 1
= runs

(main
  (let kettle (call Kettle))
  (<- (. kettle ticks) 0.5)
  (<- (. kettle switches) 10.0)
  (for (in i (..< 0 5))
    (<- (. kettle ticks) 0.5)
    (print (str (. kettle phase name) " " (. kettle heat)))
  )
  (<- (. kettle switches) 20.0)
  (<- (. kettle ticks) 0.5)
  (<- (. kettle switches) 30.0)
  (for (in i (..< 0 4))
    (<- (. kettle ticks) 0.5)
  )
  (print (str (. kettle phase name) " " (. kettle heat)))
)

(type + Kettle
  (event + switches F64)
  (event + ticks F64)
  (prop + heat F64 (= 0))
  (prop + runs _ (= 0))
  (prop + phase _
    (machine
      (state off)
      (state (call heating rate) (trigger for rate switches)
        (let run (call next-run))
        (do
          (print (str "run " run " at " rate))
        )
        (for (on dt ticks)
          (+= heat (* dt rate))
        )
        (then whistling (trigger on (call delayed ticks 2)))
      )
      (state whistling
        (do
          (print "whistling")
        )
      )
    )
  )
  (fn-do _ next-run Int
    (+= runs 1)
    (return runs)
  )
)
run 1 at 10
heating 5
heating 10
heating 15
whistling
whistling 20
whistling 20
run 2 at 20
run 3 at 30
whistling
whistling 90
  • Locals. A let or lazy in a case is made each time the case is entered. The case's entry rows and its transitions' sources read it.
  • Handlers. for dt on ticks heat += dt(for (on dt ticks) (+= heat dt)) in a case runs for each value while the case is active. It subscribes as the case is entered and ends as it is left. It takes one source and only a when clause: A state handler subscribes to a single source, A state handler accepts only a when clause. It gives no value: A state machine's handler gives no value, so it cannot return one with "="; end it early with "= alone".
  • Order. The handlers and transitions of a case take a value in the order they are written, so a transition written first may leave before a handler sees the value.
  • Timers. /stream/timing makes timers from a stream of F64 ticks, each the time since the last. delayed(ticks, 2)(call delayed ticks 2) passes ticks on once they add up to 2, totaled gives each tick with the total so far, and driven passes on the ticks a function accepts. A source is worked out each time its case is entered, so entering heating again starts its timer again. A timer belongs to the case whose transition or handler names it, so a timer on an enclosing case keeps counting while the cases nested in it change. Once delayed passes ticks on, its transition's guard is tested on each tick, so a guard that fails holds the move until a later tick passes it.
  • Nested machines start when the case that holds them is entered and stop when it is left; see Machines side by side.
  • Tasks that a case starts are not part of it, and go on after it is left.
  • Closing. Calling an object's close leaves every machine its properties hold, and the one its class's content writes, before the body of close runs, so their exit rows see the object as it was. The object's events and the live actions it owns close with them, and no transition moves them after.
  • Errors that a case's entry or exit rows raise go to unhandled-error.

Here the timer belongs to baking, so the move from top to bottom does not restart it. It reaches 4 at the fourth tick, while the door is open, and the move waits for the next tick:

/stream/timing

. oven = Oven()
for i in 1 .. < 7
    oven.door-open = i == 4
    if i == 2
        oven.flips <- true
    oven.ticks <- 1.0
    -- "tick $i: ${" > ".join(oven.phase.path)}"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Oven

+ event ticks F64
+ event flips Bool
+ door-open = false
────────────────────
+ phase ~>

~> baking
    ~> top
        then bottom on flips
    ~> bottom
    then done on delayed(ticks, 4) when !door-open
~> done
(import /stream/timing)

(main
  (let oven (call Oven))
  (for (in i (..< 1 7))
    (= (. oven door-open) (== i 4))
    (if (== i 2)
      (<- (. oven flips) true)
    )
    (<- (. oven ticks) 1.0)
    (print (str "tick " i ": " (call (. " > " join) (. oven phase path))))
  )
)

(type + Oven
  (event + ticks F64)
  (event + flips Bool)
  (prop + door-open _ (= false))
  (prop + phase _
    (machine
      (state baking
        (state top
          (then bottom (trigger on flips))
        )
        (state bottom)
        (then done (trigger on (call delayed ticks 4) (not door-open)))
      )
      (state done)
    )
  )
)
tick 1: baking > top
tick 2: baking > bottom
tick 3: baking > bottom
tick 4: baking > bottom
tick 5: done
tick 6: done

Machines side by side

A case can hold several machines. They move on their own, and all of them stop when the case is left. So two things that vary apart, such as who is signed in and whether the network is up, are two machines in one case, not a case for each combination.

. session = Session()
session.sign-ins <- true
session.connects <- true
session.drops <- true
session.quits <- true
-- session.phase

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Session

+ event sign-ins Bool
+ event connects Bool
+ event drops Bool
+ event quits Bool
────────────────────
+ phase ~>

~> running
    + who ~>
        ~> guest
            do
                -- "guest"
        ~> member on sign-ins
            do
                -- "member"
            do finally
                -- "member ends"
    + link ~>
        ~> offline
            do
                -- "offline, $who"
        ~> online on connects
            do
                -- "online, $who"
            do finally
                -- "online ends"
            then offline on drops
    then ended on quits
~> ended
(main
  (let session (call Session))
  (<- (. session sign-ins) true)
  (<- (. session connects) true)
  (<- (. session drops) true)
  (<- (. session quits) true)
  (print (. session phase))
)

(type + Session
  (event + sign-ins Bool)
  (event + connects Bool)
  (event + drops Bool)
  (event + quits Bool)
  (prop + phase _
    (machine
      (state running
        (prop + who _
          (machine
            (state guest
              (do
                (print "guest")
              )
            )
            (state member (trigger on sign-ins)
              (do
                (print "member")
              )
              (finally
                (print "member ends")
              )
            )
          )
        )
        (prop + link _
          (machine
            (state offline
              (do
                (print (str "offline, " who))
              )
            )
            (state online (trigger on connects)
              (do
                (print (str "online, " who))
              )
              (finally
                (print "online ends")
              )
              (then offline (trigger on drops))
            )
          )
        )
        (then ended (trigger on quits))
      )
      (state ended)
    )
  )
)
guest
offline, guest
member
online, member
online ends
offline, member
member ends
ended
  • Reading each other. The cases of a machine can read a machine declared before it in the same case, as link's cases read who. One declared after it is not found: Name "link" not found.

Timing

  • Events. A value published to an event moves the machine before the publish goes on. The event's other subscribers run first, then the machine's transitions.
  • One move at a time. A value published while a machine is moving waits until the move ends, and is delivered before the outermost publish goes on.
  • Channels. A value written to an AsyncChannel moves the machine in a task of its own, after the writer waits. A machine does not see what was written before it subscribed.

Refining a machine in a subclass

A subclass can declare a machine property of its base class again. Its cases name cases of the base machine, and add nested cases, entry and exit rows, handlers and transitions to them; the two make one machine.

  • A refinement adds no case at the top: Refinement cannot add top-level state case 'extra'.
  • A case is refined where the base declares it: State case 'inner' is declared elsewhere in the inherited machine.
  • A refined case keeps its trigger and payload: Refined state case 'busy' cannot change its trigger or payload.
  • Only a machine can be refined: Inherited property 'body' is not a state machine.
  • Transitions on one source at several levels are one group, the base's first.

Units

A unit is a name written straight after a number, as in 16ms, 90° or 25%. It makes the number a value of the unit's type: 16ms is a Milliseconds. Units of one family, such as the units of time, convert into one another by the ratios their declarations state, and arithmetic between them converts first.

A unit is declared as a number type with an alias. The standard library declares units for durations, angles, ratios, distances and more, and a program declares its own the same way.

Unit literals

/time/duration

. frame = 16ms
. pause = 1.5s
. back = -250ms
-- frame
-- frame as UnitString
-- pause as UnitString
-- back as UnitString
-- "frame lasts $frame"
-- "frame lasts ${frame as UnitString}"
-- 200u8 as UnitString
(import /time/duration)

(main
  (let frame 16ms)
  (let pause 1.5s)
  (let back -250ms)
  (print frame)
  (print (as frame UnitString))
  (print (as pause UnitString))
  (print (as back UnitString))
  (print (str "frame lasts " frame))
  (print (str "frame lasts " (as frame UnitString)))
  (print (as 200u8 UnitString))
)
16
16ms
1.5seconds
-250ms
frame lasts 16
frame lasts 16ms
200u8
  • Spelling. The unit follows the number with no space between them. Its name is lowercase letters and digits, as in ms and km; a currency symbol, such as $ or €; or %, µ or °, followed by more of these characters, as in %% and µs. In rows, 5 km is a syntax error.
  • Numbers. The number is an integer or a float, with a sign, an exponent or digit separators as numbers take them: -250ms, 2.5e3ms. An integer fills a unit stored as a float. A hex number takes no unit.
  • Fitting. A unit stored as an integer takes no fraction: M holds whole numbers, as I32 does, so 3.7m cannot be written; write a whole number. A literal of a unit the program declares must fit its storage: Integer literal 300 does not fit Tk.
  • Type. A literal is a value of the type whose alias its unit is. That type must be in scope: a unit declared in a module this file does not import is an error, Unit "ms" not found; it is declared in /time/duration, which this module does not import. Add the import /time/duration, and a unit nothing declares is Unit "zz" not found.
  • Number suffixes. The suffixes of the number types, such as u8, i32 and f, are units of the same kind: 200u8 is a U8. They keep the bits that fit, so 300u8 is 44 and 128i8 is -128.
  • Methods are called on a literal as on any value: (0.25s).wait()(call (. 0.25s wait)).
  • Constructors. When the unit's type declares a constructor, a literal is what the constructor gives. 3pm, from /time/datetime, is a Time. A type that is no number and has no such constructor takes no literals: Name is no number and declares no constructor that takes one, so no number can be written in its unit; declare Name as a number type.

Printing

A unit value prints as its number alone, in a print and inside a text. value as UnitString(as value UnitString) gives the number followed by its unit, as text. The unit printed is the type's last alias: Seconds has the aliases s and seconds, so 1.5s prints as 1.5seconds. A number with no unit of its own prints with its type's suffix, as 200u8 does. value.unit(. value unit) gives the unit alone: (3s).unit(. 3s unit) is seconds, and (4).unit(. 4 unit) is i.

Declaring units

A unit is a number type with an alias, and a unit of a family is declared from another unit of that family.

. price = 250cents
-- price as Dollars as UnitString
-- 3dollars as Cents as UnitString
-- (1dollars + 250cents) as UnitString
-- (250cents + 1dollars) as UnitString
-- (3dollars).label()

+ Cents (cents) is Money
+ Dollars (dollars) is 100cents

  (let price 250cents)
  (print (as price Dollars UnitString))
  (print (as 3dollars Cents UnitString))
  (print (as (+ 1dollars 250cents) UnitString))
  (print (as (+ 250cents 1dollars) UnitString))
  (print (call (. 3dollars label)))
)

(type + Money (is I64)

    (str this " " unit)
  )

(type-line + Dollars (alias dollars) (is 100cents))
2dollars
300cents
3dollars
350cents
3 dollars
DeclarationDeclares
+ Grams (g) is F64(type-line + Grams (alias g) (is F64))A unit stored as an F64.
+ Kilograms (kg) is 1000g(type-line + Kilograms (alias kg) (is 1000g))A unit equal to 1000 of another. It derives from that unit's type and joins its family.
+ Cents (cents) is Money(type-line + Cents (alias cents) (is Money))A unit of the family whose base type is Money.
+ 1inches = 25.4mm(unit + 1inches 25.4mm)An equality between two units, which joins their families.
  • Aliases. A unit's type may have several aliases, and each is a unit. The last is the one UnitString prints. A suffix names one unit, so a unit cannot take one that a number type, an imported unit or another unit of its module already has: "c" already names Char; give C a suffix of its own.
  • Storage. A unit is stored as the number type its chain of declarations starts from. A unit stored as an integer drops the fraction when it converts, toward zero: 250cents is 2dollars.
  • Family base. A unit declared from a number type of the program's own, as Cents is from Money, equals one of it. The methods of the base type belong to every unit of the family, and run on the value in its own unit, so (3dollars).label()(call (. 3dollars label)) reads 3. Inside them, unit is the receiver's unit, as text.
  • The base holds the first unit. A value of the base type is in the unit declared from it: Duration holds nanoseconds, so 1500ms stored as a Duration is 1500000000.
  • Ratios. The number in is is a literal with a unit, such as 100cents or 2.54cm. A negative or computed ratio is written as an equality. A sign in is is an error: A unit is declared from an amount of another unit with no sign, as in "+ Bar (bar) is 1foo"; to relate two units by a negative amount, declare Bar from a number type and write an equality, as in "+ 1bar = -1foo".
  • No type parameters. A unit's type takes none: Unit types must be numeric and unqualified.
  • Extending a family. A module adds units to a family another module declares, as in + Fortnights (fortnights) is 14days(type-line + Fortnights (alias fortnights) (is 14days)) in a module that imports /time/duration.

Equalities

An equality states that an amount of one unit equals an amount of another. It joins two families, so a program can relate units declared apart, or units from two modules.

-- 1inches as Mm as UnitString
-- 1inches as Cm as UnitString
-- (1m + 1ft) as UnitString
-- 1m > 3ft
+ Mm (mm) is F64
+ Cm (cm) is 10mm
+ M (m) is 100cm
+ Inches (inches) is F64
+ Ft (ft) is 12inches
+ 1inches = 25.4mm
(main
  (print (as 1inches Mm UnitString))
  (print (as 1inches Cm UnitString))
  (print (as (+ 1m 1ft) UnitString))
  (print (> 1m 3ft))
)

(type-line + Mm (alias mm) (is F64))
(type-line + Cm (alias cm) (is 10mm))
(type-line + M (alias m) (is 100cm))
(type-line + Inches (alias inches) (is F64))
(type-line + Ft (alias ft) (is 12inches))
(unit + 1inches 25.4mm)
25.4mm
2.54cm
1.3048m
true
  • Sides. Each side is a constant: a number with a unit, or numbers joined by arithmetic and bitwise operators, as in + 1third = 1 / 3whole(unit + 1third (/ 1 3whole)). Each side has one unit.
  • Errors. An equality must be public: Equalities must be public. A side with no unit is Ambiguous units, a side with two is Conflicting units, and a side that is not a constant is Invalid constant expression. A side's unit must be declared, Unit "zz" not found, and must not be a number type's suffix: An equality relates units a program declares, and F64 is a number type of the language; write each side in a unit the program declares. Neither side can be zero: A unit cannot be declared as zero of another, which no number of it would convert from; write a number other than zero.
  • Agreeing. Two equalities between the same two units must state the same ratio: Equalities between Bar and Foo disagree: one makes 1 Bar 2 Foo, another 3 Foo; keep one of them. Only equalities between the same pair are checked. One that disagrees with a path through other units is not reported, and is not used, so keep every path between two units in agreement.
  • Across modules. /time/flicks declares + 705600000flicks = 1seconds(unit + 705600000flicks 1seconds), so flicks convert to and from every duration.
  • Only ratios. An equality states a ratio. Units with an offset between them, such as degrees Celsius and Fahrenheit, cannot be declared as one family: An equality relates two units by a ratio alone, so a number with no unit cannot be added to or taken from one; write the ratio as one number in the unit.

Arithmetic

/time/duration

-- (8hours + 30minutes) as UnitString
-- (30minutes + 8hours) as UnitString
-- (2s - 250ms) as UnitString
-- (90s * 2) as UnitString
-- (2 * 90s) as UnitString
-- (90s + 30) as UnitString
-- (2hours / 30minutes) as UnitString
-- 500ms < 1s
-- 60s == 1minutes
(import /time/duration)

(main
  (print (as (+ 8hours 30minutes) UnitString))
  (print (as (+ 30minutes 8hours) UnitString))
  (print (as (- 2s 250ms) UnitString))
  (print (as (* 90s 2) UnitString))
  (print (as (* 2 90s) UnitString))
  (print (as (+ 90s 30) UnitString))
  (print (as (/ 2hours 30minutes) UnitString))
  (print (< 500ms 1s))
  (print (== 60s 1minutes))
)
8.5hours
510minutes
1.75seconds
180seconds
180seconds
120seconds
4hours
true
true
  • The left unit. For +, -, *, / and %, the right operand converts to the left operand's unit, and the result is in the left's unit.
  • No compound units. Multiplying or dividing two units does not make a new unit and does not cancel them: the right operand converts as for +, so 2hours / 30minutes(/ 2hours 30minutes) is 4hours. Units are not dimensional analysis. A quantity such as a speed is a unit of its own, made by a function that takes the two units, as in (fn-expr + per Speed (param distance Length) (param time Seconds) body).
  • Two families. +, -, *, / and % between units of two families that no equality joins give a plain number: with /units and /time/duration, (+ 100meters 20s) is 120. Only comparisons between them are errors.
  • Plain numbers. A plain number on the right is taken in the left's unit: 90s + 30(+ 90s 30) is 120seconds. A plain number on the left keeps the unit only for *; with the other operators the result is a plain number.
  • Comparisons convert the same way, so 500ms < 1s(< 500ms 1s) is true. Comparing units of two families that no equality joins is an error; see Conversions.
  • Assignment. total += 30s(+= total 30s) converts the value to the unit of total.
  • Units on their own. A unit that no declaration relates to another, such as px, is in no family. Arithmetic on it gives a plain number, which becomes the unit again when it is stored as one: . width Coord = 3px + 2px(let width Coord (+ 3px 2px)) is 5px.
  • Generic functions keep the unit of what they are given. A function that takes a plain number type, such as abs from /math, takes the value in its own unit and gives a plain number.

-- timeout as UnitString
-- describe(2minutes)

-- Milliseconds(2.5s) as UnitString
-- 2880minutes as Days as UnitString

-- 1500ms as Int

  (let timeout Seconds 1500ms)
  (print (as timeout UnitString))
  (print (call describe 2minutes))
  (print (call describe 45))
  (print (as (call Milliseconds 2.5s) UnitString))
  (print (as 2880minutes Days UnitString))

  (param wait Seconds)

1.5seconds
waits 120seconds
waits 45seconds
2500ms

1.5
1500
  • Within a family, a unit converts to another on its own wherever a value of the other is wanted: in a declaration, an argument, a return or an assignment. as and calling the type, as in Milliseconds(2.5s)(call Milliseconds 2.5s), convert the same way.
  • Ratios multiply along the declarations as exact fractions, so 2880minutes as Days(as 2880minutes Days) is exactly 2days. A ratio written as a decimal, such as 25.4mm, is a float like any other.
  • Integers. A unit stored as an integer drops the fraction, toward zero.
  • Plain numbers to units. A plain number given for a unit is taken in that unit: describe(45)(call describe 45) waits 45seconds. A number literal becomes any unit. A number that is not a literal converts as numbers do: a Float becomes a unit stored as an F64, but an Int becomes one only with as.
  • Units to plain numbers. A unit becomes a plain number by its value in its own unit, without converting: 1500ms as Int(as 1500ms Int) is 1500. It does so on its own where the number type holds every value of the unit's storage, and with as otherwise.
  • Other families. Units of two families that no equality joins do not convert:
/time/duration

-- 3dollars as Seconds
+ Cents (cents) is I64
+ Dollars (dollars) is 100cents
(import /time/duration)

(main
  (print (as 3dollars Seconds))
)

(type-line + Cents (alias cents) (is I64))
(type-line + Dollars (alias dollars) (is 100cents))

Units in the standard library

ModuleUnits
/time/durationns, µs, ms, s or seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months (31 days), years (365 days), decades, centuries and milleniums, on the base Duration.
/time/flicksflicks, joined to the durations.
/time/datetimesecond, minute and hour of a day, and am and pm, whose literals are a Time: 3pm.
/mathrad, and ° or deg. π is in radians.

/tui/primitivestx, a Coord stored as an I16, in no family.
/ui/virtualvcoord, in no family.
/media/synthhz and khz; st and oct.
  • Ratios. %% is a Ratio, in which 1%% is the whole, and % is a Percent, in which 100% is the whole: 25% as Ratio(as 25% Ratio) is 0.25%%. Write a fraction with its leading zero: 0.75%% is three quarters, and 75%% is seventy-five wholes.
  • Scales. A type that implements Scalable gives a range, a Scale, onto which a ratio converts: Hour gives 0 to 23, so 0.75%% as Hour(as 0.75%% Hour) is 18hour.
  • Durations have methods: (0.25s).wait()(call (. 0.25s wait)) waits, and interval makes a timer. Timeouts, waits and timers in the standard library take durations.
  • Styles use durations for motion, as in 200ms, and percentages for keyframe stops and sizes. See Styles.

Markup

Markup builds a tree of objects. An element names a class, makes an object of it, sets its properties, and hands it the elements written inside it as children. Nothing about it is text: the result is the objects. Any class can be an element, so markup is as much for data as for interfaces, and the GUI and terminal libraries build their views from it. Markup can also follow state: an element whose properties or children read tracked values is updated when they change.

This chapter covers elements, attributes, children, control flow inside markup, markup that follows state, components and their slots, and the links between elements. Style sheets, which markup elements use, are in Styles.

Elements

<Menu lunch "Lunch"
    <Dish "Soup"
        price = 4
    <Dish "Salad"
        price = 6
        vegetarian = true
    <Menu "Drinks"
        <Dish "Tea"
            price = 2
            vegetarian = true
lunch.show("")

(type + Dish (is Item)

(type + Menu (is Item)

  )
  (fn-do + show _
    (param indent String)
    (print (str indent name))
    (for (in item items)
      (if (= (| (: dish Dish)) item)
        (print (str indent "  " (. dish name) " " (. dish price) (if-expr (. dish vegetarian) " (v)" "")))

Lunch
  Soup 4
  Salad 6 (v)
  Drinks
    Tea 2 (v)

An element is (<> Type …), in rows <Type. After the type come, in this order, the element's name, the slot it fills, a parameter, its value, theme tags, style rules, and then its rows.

FormRowsGives the element
(id: lunch)<Menu lunchA name; see Names.
(slot: title)<Text (title)The slot of a component it fills; see Slots.
(param: who)<Text (row) - whoThe name of a value a repeated slot passes it.
(value: 3)<Count = 3Its constructor's first argument.
(text: "Lunch")<Menu "Lunch"The same, for a text.
(for: dark)A theme tag; see Styles.
(• loud)<Card • loudA style rule it uses; see Styles.
  • Making. An element calls a constructor of its class. Its value and its attributes fill the constructor's parameters by position and by name, and parameters with defaults may be left out.
  • Order. The constructor runs first. Then every attribute is set, wherever it is written among the rows. Then the rows run in order. A child is made and its own rows run before it is handed to its parent, so a parent receives each child complete.
  • What can be an element. A class, including a generic class with its type arguments written, as in (<> (of Box Int) (value: 3)). Core collections are classes too, so (<> (of List Int) 1 2 3) is a list. A struct, a tuple, a number or a String cannot be an element, and neither can an interface: Constructor not found.
  • No imports. Markup works in any program. A module that writes markup imports /core/markup without writing it.
  • Messages. The messages write an element as rows do, as in Markup element <Book gives no value for "title", which the constructor of Book requires.

Where elements go

An element is a value. It can be a row of a body, the value of a let, lazy, = or return, the body of a fn-expr, or an attribute's value. It cannot yet be written among a call's arguments, a list's items or the operands of an if-expr: Brix form “(<> …)” is not supported yet. Name it or bind it with let first.

Names

(id: lunch) names the element. The name is a local of the block the element is written in, and can be read after the element and by the element's own rows. A statement above the element that reads the name makes the element there, once. In a component's content, the name is a private property of the class; see Components.

Attributes

A row price = 4(= price 4) in an element's body is an attribute: it sets the element's property price, or fills a constructor parameter of that name.

  • Values may be any expression: a block of bullets, a tuple, a function value, or another element.
  • What the value can read. The value is worked out outside the element, so it reads the names around the element, not the element's own members. It cannot read the element by its name: Named markup element "t" is read before its markup constructs it.
  • Setters run as for any assignment.
  • Defaults. A property no attribute sets keeps its declared value.
  • Always an attribute. (= name value) in an element's body sets the element's property, even where a local of that name exists: Property "count" not found. To assign a local, write the assignment in a (do …) row.
  • Private properties can be set from markup in their own module only.
  • Messages. An unknown property gives Property "pages" not found, a value of the wrong type Expected I64 here, but this is String, and there is no conversion between them, and a required constructor parameter left out Markup element <Book gives no value for "title", which the constructor of Book requires.

Children

The rows of an element that give values are its content. Each is handed to the element's +=, as (+= menu dish) would, and a collection to its ++= when += does not take it. += may be overloaded, so an element can take texts, names and elements of different types in one body: "Hello, ", name and (<> Bold (value: "friend")) are all content.

  • Steps. Rows that give no value run as steps: print, let, lazy, do, and calls that return nothing. An element written inside a (do …) row is made but not added.
  • What a class needs. A class takes children when it declares += for their type. A line that no += takes gives Content not accepted.
  • More than children. Three classes in core give an element more:
ClassAdds
Any class with +=Children, attributes that follow state, and slots.
A class that implements (of MarkupParent Child)Children of class Child with no += written, kept in children, and the links between them.
A class that extends MarkupNodeChildren of any MarkupNode class, links, and loops and branches that follow state.
A class that extends MarkupRootThe same, with updates gathered into batches; see Batches.
  • MarkupNode gives children, and (call (of children-of Text)) gives the children of one class, looking through the rows of loops and branches.

Control flow in markup

. scores = [7, 2, 9]
. winner Player = Human("Ann")
<Report report
    for s in scores when s > 5
        <Line "score $s"
    if scores.length > 2
        <Line "a full game"
    else
        <Line "a short game"
    match winner
        | h Human
            <Line "won by ${h.name}"
        | b Bot
            <Line "won by a bot"
    .. rounds = scores.length
    <Line "$rounds rounds"
    do
        <Line "made, not added"
for line in report.lines
    -- line

| Human
| Bot

+ name String
────────────────────

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

+ Bot

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

────────────────────

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

────────────────────
+ do this += line Line

lines += line.text
(main
  (let scores (list 7 2 9))
  (let winner Player (call Human "Ann"))
  (<> Report (id: report)
    (for (in s scores (when (> s 5)))
      (<> Line (text: (str "score " s)))
    )
    (if (> (. scores length) 2)
      (<> Line (text: "a full game"))
      (else
        (<> Line (text: "a short game"))
      )
    )
    (match winner
      (case (: h Human)
        (<> Line (text: (str "won by " (. h name))))
      )
      (case (: b Bot)
        (<> Line (text: "won by a bot"))
      )
    )
    (lazy rounds (. scores length))
    (<> Line (text: (str rounds " rounds")))
    (do
      (<> Line (text: "made, not added"))
    )
  )
  (for (in line (. report lines))
    (print line)
  )
)

(type + Player (is Union)
  (variant Human)
  (variant Bot)
)

(type + Human

(type-line + Bot)

for, if, match, let, lazy and print work in an element's body as they do anywhere, and the elements their rows give are children of the element. A loop or an arm may give several elements, and an if may test a pattern. There is no fragment element: control flow is how one row gives several children.

Markup that follows state

. players = ["ann", "bo"]
<Board board
    <Text "players"
        note = "${#players.length} playing"
    for name in #players keyed by name
        <Text name
    if #players.length > 2
        <Text "table full"
    else
        <Text "seats free"
board.show()
players += "cy"
board.show()
players -= "ann"
board.show()
players = ["bo", "cy"]
board.show()

────────────────────

for child in children-of'Text()
    parts += if child.note == "" then child.text else "${child.text} (${child.note})"

  (let players (list "ann" "bo"))
  (<> Board (id: board)
    (<> Text (text: "players")

    )

  (call (. board show))

(type + Text (is MarkupNode)
  (prop + text String)
  (prop + note _ (= ""))
  (fn-do + This _
    (param text _)
    (print (str "  make " text))
  )
)

(type + Board (is MarkupNode)
  (fn-do + show _
    (let parts (list String))
    (for (in child (call (of children-of Text)))
      (+= parts (if-expr (== (. child note) "") (. child text) (str (. child text) " (" (. child note) ")")))
    )
    (print (call (. ", " join) parts))
  )
)
  make players
  make ann
  make bo
  make seats free
players (2 playing), ann, bo, seats free
  make cy
  make table full
players (3 playing), ann, bo, cy, table full
  make seats free
players (2 playing), bo, cy, seats free
players (2 playing), bo, cy, seats free

Markup that makes tracked reads, #players here, follows the values it reads; see Reactivity.

Where the read isWhen the value changes
An attributeThe attribute is set again. Nothing is made again.
(value: …) or (text: …)The property of the constructor parameter's name is set again. The parameter must name a property: Tracked markup constructor argument must match a property.
A content rowThe row is made again, and replaces the old child. A class that is not a MarkupNode must declare replace to take it.
The condition of an if or the subject of a matchThe branch is made again, only when the arm it takes changes.
The source of a forThe rows follow the collection.
  • Keys. (keyed-by name) keeps each row with its key. Moving items, or assigning a new list with the same keys, makes nothing, as the last assignment above shows. Only new keys make rows, and the rows of removed keys go. Without keys, rows follow positions, so removing the first item makes again every row after it.
  • Loops and branches that follow state need a MarkupNode parent: Dynamic markup loop parent must implement MarkupElement. Each row of such a loop is one element: A markup loop row must be one element; wrap its elements in one. It takes no when, while or until clauses.
  • When. Without a batch root, each change updates the markup before the statement that made it goes on, as above.
  • Lifetime. An element follows its reads until it is closed. A MarkupNode closes its children when it closes.
  • Errors raised while an attribute is set again go to unhandled-error, and the element keeps its old value.

Batches

<Outline doc
    <Heading "Intro"
    for title in #chapters
        <Heading title
-- doc.summary
doc.chapters += "Ending"
-- doc.summary
doc.settle()
-- doc.summary
for h in doc.headings
    -- "${h.text} in ${h.outline!.name}"

────────────────────

    - text

+ name = "doc"
+ chapters [String] = ["Middle"]
+ headings Descendants'Heading
+ summary = "${#headings.length} headings"
(main
  (<> Outline (id: doc)
    (<> Heading (text: "Intro"))
    (for (in title #chapters)
      (<> Heading (text: title))
    )
  )
  (print (. doc summary))
  (+= (. doc chapters) "Ending")
  (print (. doc summary))
  (call (. doc settle))
  (print (. doc summary))
  (for (in h (. doc headings))
    (print (str (. h text) " in " (. (!! (. h outline)) name)))
  )
)

(type + Heading (is MarkupNode)
  (prop + text String)
  (prop + outline (of Ancestor Outline))
  (fn-do + This _
    (param text _)
  )
)

(type + Outline (is MarkupRoot)
  (prop + name _ (= "doc"))
  (prop + chapters (list String) (= (list "Middle")))
  (prop + headings (of Descendants Heading))
  (prop + summary _ (= (str (. #headings length) " headings")))
)
2 headings
2 headings
3 headings
Intro in doc
Middle in doc
Ending in doc

Under a MarkupRoot, changes to the tree wait and are made together: when the program next waits, or at (call (. doc settle)). So summary still counts 2 headings after the third chapter is added, until the root settles.

  • Queries. A property of type (of Ancestor Outline) holds the nearest Outline above the element, and one of type (of Descendants Heading) the Headings below it. Both follow the tree as it changes, and both need a MarkupRoot above them; under a plain MarkupNode they hold nothing.

Components

A component is a class with a content section: rows that run each time an object of it is made, whether by markup or by a call. In rows, content is the section after a thin divider with no header. The elements it gives are the object's own children, and its rows read the class's members by name, tracked or not.

  • Named elements in content are private properties of the class, which its methods can read. A name the class already declares as a property receives the element.
  • (<> This …) as the only row of content sets the object's own properties, as defaults that a caller's attributes override.
  • Order. content runs as the object is made, after attributes for stored properties are set and before the caller's rows.
  • Messages. An empty content gives Empty content section not permitted, and two give Only one content section permitted.

Slots

<Card empty
-- outline(empty)
<Card note
    <Text (title) "Note"
    <Text "Buy milk."
-- outline(note)
<Card letter
    <Text "Dear Bo,"
    <Text "See you soon."
-- outline(letter)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do outline String
    - node MarkupNode

. parts [String]
for child in node.children
    if child is Text
        parts += (child as Text).text
    else
        parts += "[${outline(child)}]"
= " ".join(parts)

+ <Text title
    <Text "Untitled:"
+ <MarkupNode
    <Text "(empty)"
<Text "--"
(main
  (<> Card (id: empty))
  (print (call outline empty))
  (<> Card (id: note)
    (<> Text (slot: title) (text: "Note"))
    (<> Text (text: "Buy milk."))
  )
  (print (call outline note))
  (<> Card (id: letter)
    (<> Text (text: "Dear Bo,"))
    (<> Text (text: "See you soon."))
  )
  (print (call outline letter))
)

(fn-do + outline String
  (param node MarkupNode)
  (let parts (list String))
  (for (in child (. node children))
    (if (is child Text)
      (+= parts (. (as child Text) text))
      (else
        (+= parts (str "[" (call outline child) "]"))
      )
    )
  )
  (return (call (. " " join) parts))
)

(type + Text (is MarkupNode)
  (prop + text String)
  (fn-do + This _
    (param text _)
  )
)

(type + Card (is MarkupNode)
  (content
    (+<> Text (id: title)
      (<> Text (text: "Untitled:"))
    )
    (+<> MarkupNode
      (<> Text (text: "(empty)"))
    )
    (<> Text (text: "--"))
  )
)
Untitled: (empty) --
Note Buy milk. --
Untitled: [Dear Bo, See you soon.] --

A slot is a place in a component's content that a caller fills. (+<> Text (id: title) …), in rows + <Text title, declares the slot title, and a caller's element with (slot: title) fills it. (+<> MarkupNode …), with no name, is the default slot, which the caller's other rows fill.

  • Placement. What a caller gives goes where the slot stands, in the component's order, whatever order the caller writes it in.
  • Fallback. The elements in a slot's body are used when the caller gives none, and must be of the slot's type. Attributes in its body are set on what the caller gives instead.
  • One or several. One element given to the default slot fills it. Several are built into one element of the slot's type, as the letter's two texts are.
  • Subclasses. A subclass's content fills its base's default slot when the base has one, and follows the base's content otherwise. A caller's rows given to a component with no default slot follow its content.
  • Messages. Filling a slot twice gives Duplicate slot content, a slot the class lacks Unknown slot, and a slot filled from inside an if or a for Slot binding is only valid directly inside markup body.

  • Repeated slots. A slot inside a loop of the content is filled once for each item. (param: name String) passes the item to the caller's element, which names it with its own (param: who).
  • Passing a slot on. (<+ row), in rows <+ (row), gives the content a component's caller gave for row to the element it is written in. It declares the slot row for the component, as Page does, and an unfilled slot leaves the inner element its own fallback.

undo
  • Links. %parent, %first-child, %last-child, %previous-sibling and %next-sibling read an element's neighbors, as undo.%parent(. undo %parent), or %parent alone in a method. Each gives an optional. They work on classes that implement MarkupParent or extend MarkupNode: Markup link "%first-child" not found.
  • Types. On a MarkupNode, a link gives a MarkupNode?, so read a member of another class after as.
  • Handlers. A (for (on name pressed) …) row in an element's body subscribes to the element's own event, and reads the element's members by name. It ends when the element closes.
  • Events that rise. A class that implements EventNode and gives its parent as event-parent sends its events up the tree, where an ancestor subscribes to them by class, as Toolbar does to (. Button pressed). See Reactivity.
  • Function values given as attributes, such as (= on-hover (=> () :do …)), are ordinary attributes.

Styles

A style is a set of properties that describe how something looks or behaves, such as a font, a width or a color, kept apart from what the thing is. Elements of markup take style properties from the elements around them, from style sheets, and from their own markup. A style sheet holds style rules, which set style properties on the elements they select, and slots, values a whole tree of elements can share and a theme can change. The values an element ends up with are worked out together, by settling, and read with $.

Nothing here is tied to a screen. The GUI and terminal libraries build their looks from styles, and so can any program: every example in this chapter prints its results.

A style rule is not the rule of Reactivity, which runs code when tracked values change. This chapter says "style rule" where the two could be confused, and "rule" otherwise.

Styles and style properties

/core/style

<Page page
    <Para intro "Intro"
        font = "serif"
        size = 14
        <Para note "Note"
    <Para footer "Footer"
for para in [intro, note, footer]
    para.describe()
-- note.$font
. loose = Para("Loose")
loose.describe()

Note: serif 12
Footer: sans 12
serif
Loose: sans 12
  • A style is a class that extends Style. Its properties are style properties. A property's initial value is what an element reads when nothing sets it.
  • (using Lettering) gives a class the style's properties. In rows it is using Lettering in the class's header.
  • Setting a style property in markup is written as setting any property, (= font "serif").
  • Reading it is $font on this, or (. note $font) on another object. In rows it is $font and note.$font.
  • @inherited: an element that sets nothing takes its parent's value, so note is in serif. size is not inherited, so note has the initial 12. @inherited is the only annotation a style property can have.
  • The tree. Style properties set in markup take effect on elements under a root: a class that extends MarkupRoot. The elements in it extend MarkupNode. A root works out its elements' values when its markup is built, and again when the program next waits or the root is told to settle; see When values change.
  • Outside a tree, an element reads initial values, as loose does.
  • The import. A module that declares or extends a style sheet imports /core/style on its own. One that only declares a style or reads $ values imports it itself, as this one does.

The UI libraries' Box types are a MarkupNode and a MarkupRoot of this kind, with styles of their own.

(style FormSheet …) declares a style sheet, a class that extends StyleSheet. In rows it is • FormSheet. It holds:

  • using rows, naming the styles whose properties its rules set.
  • Style rules, (rule name …), which set style properties.
  • Slots, (prop + name Type (= value)), values its rules and markup can read; see Slots and themes.
  • Keyframes, slots that describe motion; see Motion.
  • Domains, (style-domains …); see Domains.

A class that uses the sheet, as Form does, makes its rules reach the elements beneath it.

Which rules apply

A rule is applied to an element of markup. These apply to an element, in this order, and the order they are written in the sheet does not matter:

  1. The rule named for the element's type, or for a type it extends: (rule Field …) applies to every Field and every subclass of Field. A generic type is matched by its name alone.
  2. The rule named for the element's id: (rule user …) applies to (<> Field (id: user)).
  3. The rules the element names with (• name), from left to right. In rows they follow the element's name: <Field email • wide.
  4. The element's own assignments, which come last, so code is 8 wide.

A later rule's value replaces an earlier one's. A name no visible rule has is ignored, so a misspelled (• wied) is never reported. So is a rule named for a type that does not exist.

Parameters

A rule takes at most one parameter: (rule rows (param count Int) (= height count)), applied as (• rows 4). In rows the rule is • rows:count Int and the element applies it as • rows:4 or • rows(4).

  • Several values go in one tuple parameter: (param size (tuple Int Int)), applied as (• sized (tuple 3 4)).
  • Overloads. Rules of one name can take parameters of different types; the argument picks one, an exact type before one it converts to.
  • The argument must fit: a missing, extra or wrongly typed argument is Type mismatch, and a parameter with no type is Argument type not found. A parameter's default value is not used.

Rules that apply rules

Rules named in a rule's header run before its body: (rule boxed (• wide) (= border "double")) sets the width first, then the border. A rule cannot reach itself through others: Recursive style rule application: loud -> quiet -> loud. A rule in a sheet names rules only in its header; its body holds declarations and generated content.

Conditions

(• name (if: #flag)) applies a rule while a tracked Bool property of the element is true, and follows it as it changes. In rows it is • name = #flag. The condition must be a tracked property of the element, written with #; (if: is-on) and (if: (not #is-on)) are refused: Style rule conditions must be a tracked boolean property reference (like #is-disabled). For a condition that is false, use a state; see States.

What a rule sets

A rule's rows are assignments, (= property value), nested rules, states and generated content. += and other steps are refused: (+= …) cannot be a `row` of (rule …), which takes Style.

  • Values are ordinary values of the property's type: text, numbers, Bool, characters, tuples, union cases such as (. Align right), null, units such as 50% or 250ms, colors and objects. A value that does not convert to the property's type is an error, as anywhere.
  • What a value can read. A sheet rule's value can read literals, names of the module, the rule's parameter, and the sheet's slots. It cannot read the element's properties or style values.
  • inherit: (= font inherit) makes an @inherited property take its parent's value, over a lower layer's. On a property that is not @inherited it is an error: Style property "pad" is not @inherited, so it cannot be assigned "inherit".
  • Properties a rule may set are those of the styles the element's class uses and those the visible sheets use. Setting any other name in a sheet rule is Not supported; in markup it is Property "colour" not found.

Which value wins

Every assignment to a style property is on a layer. A later layer wins over an earlier one, and in one layer the assignment made later wins.

LayerWritten as
Defaults(rule This …) in the element's class, and the root of its content
ContentAttributes of the elements a class's content declares
RulesRules by type, by id and by •, from the class or a sheet
Default stateswhen-style in (rule This …)
Stateswhen-style and style-set in other rules, and rules applied with (if: …)
InlineAssignments in the element's own markup
CodeAn assignment from code, as (= (. lamp tone) "code")
<Room room
    <Lamp "a"
    <Lamp "b" • warm
    <Lamp "c" • lit
        tone = "inline"
    <Lamp d "d" • warm
room.show("off")
for lamp in room.children-of'Lamp
    lamp.is-on = true
room.settle()
room.show("on")
d.tone = "code"
room.settle()
room.show("code")

off
  a default
  b warm
  c inline
  d warm
on
  a default-on
  b default-on
  c inline
  d default-on
code
  a default-on
  b default-on
  c inline
  d code
  • A rule beats the defaults, so b is warm.
  • A state beats a rule, even the class's default state: once b is on, its default-on beats warm.
  • Inline beats every rule, so c stays inline.
  • Code beats inline. An assignment from code lasts until code assigns again.

A state is a tracked Bool property of the element. (when-style #is-done …) holds what applies while it is true, and (when-style (not #is-done) …) while it is false. In rows they are when #is-done and when !#is-done. (style-set is-late note " (late)"), in rows is-late:note = " (late)", is a state with one assignment.

  • What a state holds: assignments of style properties, (• name) rows, nested rules, which then apply only while the state holds, and generated content. An assignment of a property that is not a style property is refused: Conditional style declarations may only set style properties, and "glow" is an object property.
  • The property is looked up on each class the rule is applied to. A class without it is an error at the rule: Style state "is-on" is not a property of Line. One that is not a Bool is too: Style state "count" must be a boolean property, but Lamp.count is I64.
  • Only in rules. A state cannot be written in markup: (when-style …) cannot be a `row` of (<> …), which takes Child.
  • Where states come from: any tracked Bool. The GUI library's Box has is-hovered, is-pressed, is-focused, is-entering and is-leaving, among others. The case of a state machine in a class's content is one too:

When values change

The values a state selects, like every style value, are worked out by settling. A root settles when its markup is built, so values are right as soon as the markup statement ends. After that, a change to anything style values follow, such as a state, an (if: …) condition, a theme tag or a tracked value in an assignment, shows at the next settle: when the program next waits, or when code calls the root's settle. Until then, reads give the old values, as the second block of the board's output shows. The same markup statement records its assignments once, however many elements it makes.

Slots

A slot is a property of a sheet: (prop + accent String (= "blue")). Rules read it by its bare name, as text-color above.

  • Where a slot is read: in a sheet rule's values, in an element's own assignments, alone as a rule's argument, and in other slots' values. In ordinary code a slot's name is not found.
  • Late. A value that reads a slot reads it from the sheet in force at the element, so a theme changes it without the markup running again: dusk turns white when late does.
  • One sheet's slots. A value reads slots of one sheet only. A slot whose name is also a local or a module's name is an error, not a choice: "bright" is ambiguous: it names both a StyleSheet slot of AppTheme and a lexical value.
  • No other values. A value that reads a slot can read no local, member, style value or tracked value: A style value that reads StyleSheet slots may read no local, member, style or tracked value; read a slot as "$name" to compute with one.
  • Alone as an argument. A slot passed to a rule is passed alone, as (• ink-of dim), not in an expression.

Themes

(style DarkPalette (is Palette) (for dark) …) derives a sheet from Palette, for the theme tag dark. In rows it is • DarkPalette is Palette for dark. The base and the sheets derived from it, at any depth, are a family.

  • What a derived sheet holds: new values of its base's slots, and rules. It cannot add slots: Derived StyleSheet "Dark" can only override slots of Base, which has no slot "extra". A rule it writes replaces its base's rule of that name; the two are not merged.
  • Tags are turned on for an element and everything under it with the attribute (for: dark), in rows for dark. (for: dark #late), in rows for dark = #late, follows a value; false turns a tag off beneath, and null takes the tag from above.
  • One sheet of a family is in force at each element: of the sheets whose tags, with their bases' tags, are all on, the one with the most tags, then the one derived furthest, then the first declared. Sheets of one family never mix, so two sibling sheets whose tags are both on do not combine: one of them applies. To combine looks, such as a shape and a color scheme, give each its own family.
  • A tag only names a sheet. (style Dark (for dark) …) without is is refused.

Extending a sheet

(style-extend Palette …), in rows • extend Palette, adds using rows and rules to a sheet declared elsewhere, in the same module or one that imports it. An extension in a module that nothing imports is not merged.

  • What an extension cannot add: slots, StyleSheet extensions may not declare slots, and a This rule.
  • Libraries spread one theme across modules this way: each terminal component module extends the terminal library's default theme with its own rules.

  • A nested rule reaches every matching element beneath the element its rule is applied to: the content its class declares, the content written in its body, slot content, content inside loops and branches, and generated content. (rule Part …) in framed reaches heading and body, not after, and not the card.
  • (own-rule …), in rows • own Part, reaches only the markup the element's own class and its bases declare, and the content its rules generate: heading and rule, not body.
  • Generated content. Markup in a rule adds elements next to the element or inside it, in the slot (slot: …) names: before, after, first-child or last-child. In rows it is <Part (first-child) "rule". Markup without a slot is refused, and so is any other slot name: Unknown style content slot "middle"; expected before, after, first-child, or last-child. Generated content can be inside a state, so it comes and goes with it. The content a rule generates does not take generated content from that rule again.

A class can declare rules of its own, and so can a class with no styles at all. Its rules apply to its instances made with markup, in the order of Which rules apply.

  • Ordinary properties. A class rule can set the class's ordinary properties. The assignment is made once, when the element is built, after its constructor. A later rule sees what earlier rules set, as primary and doubled do. An assignment that reads a tracked value with # follows it.
  • What a class rule can read: the class's properties, as in (++ text "!"), and $ values. A $ read in a class rule is made once, while the element is built and before it settles.
  • Shadowing. A class rule hides a sheet rule of the same name and parameter.
  • (rule This …) is the class's defaults: it applies to every instance, at the defaults layer. It takes no parameter, a sheet cannot declare one, and • cannot name it. Today it takes effect only in a program that loads /core/style, which a module that declares a style sheet does.
  • A class's content can set defaults too: assignments on its root (<> This …) are at the defaults layer.

Reading style values

  • $name reads the value of a style property that settling worked out, on this. (. node $name) reads it on another object, and (?. node $name) gives null for a null object.
  • Checked by type. A read is checked against the styles the object's type uses, including those an interface it implements declares. A property those styles lack is Style property "tone" not found, whatever rules set at run time. A bare $tone in main, which has no this, is that error too.
  • Reads never settle. Before a root first settles, an element reads initial values: in its constructor and in its mounted hook. After a change, reads give the old values until the next settle.
  • Out of the tree. An element outside a tree reads initial values, and one removed from its tree goes back to them. An assignment from code to an element never placed in a tree is read back at once.
  • Not tracked. A style value is not a tracked value: a derived property that reads $tone does not follow it, and #$tone is not a name.
  • Not assignable. (= $tone "red") is refused: Style values are computed by settling; "$tone" is not assignable. Assign the property itself, (= (. lamp tone) "red"), which is an assignment at the code layer. Reading it without $, (. lamp tone), is Not supported.

Motion

The language gives styles two things for motion: keyframes, which describe a change over time as a value, and a host that a library installs to play changes out over time. The GUI library builds its animations on both. Without a host, as in a program with no GUI, a change of style takes effect at once.

(keyframes fade animation 200ms …) declares a slot whose value is built by calling the function its kind names, here animation:

  1. animation(200ms, repeat: 2), from the duration and the settings, (= name value).
  2. Then one call per row, in order, on what the last call returned:
    • (range opacity 0.0 1.0) calls .range(property, from, to). _ for an end passes null.
    • (track offset (at 0% 0.0) …) calls .track(property) and then .at(property, at, value) for each stop.
    • A bare (at 50% 1.2) calls .at(at, value).
    • Options after a row, as (:easing (. Easing ease-out)), are named arguments of its call.
  3. Each property is passed as a StyleProperty, naming the style property the row moves.

Each row must name a style property the sheet uses, Style property "glow" not found, and give values of its type. A sheet that derives from this one can restate a keyframes slot, as a theme for reduced motion does.

A shape has one parameter: (keyframes shake (param distance Float) …). A rule gives it a value with (shape shake 4.0), in rows shake:4.0. Its argument must be a constant; a rule's parameter is refused.

A rule plays keyframes by assigning their slot, as (= clip fade). In rows a keyframes slot is:

• fade animation 200ms
    repeat = 2
    opacity = 0.0 .. 1.0

Rows know two kinds, animation, which the GUI library defines, and motion, which /math/motion defines. Its motion builds a Motion that can be sampled at a time:

/math/motion

300ms 1

Keyed properties and the motion host

  • Keyed properties. A style can declare a property whose name has a dot, (prop + motion.size Motion …). It is a property of its own, set by its whole name, in Brix (= (. motion size) …), in rows motion.size = …. Only a style can declare one: Only a Style may declare a keyed property such as "motion.size". A keyed property cannot be read with $.
  • The motion host. Settling reports each changed style value to a StyleMotionHost, if one is installed. A value the host presents is what $ reads until it takes the value away, which is how a change plays out over frames. Values that can be blended implement Animatable. The core library installs no host.
  • In the GUI library, Box installs a host and drives it from the frame clock. Its styles have motion, one Motion for every property that only repaints, and keyed motion.size, motion.position, motion.opacity and others for one property each, as well as animation, which plays keyframes. Motions come from /math/motion: spring, ease-out, linear, cubic-bezier, steps and instant. #is-entering and #is-leaving style arrival and departure. See the standard library.

How styles reach elements

  • Using. A class takes a style's properties with using. Without it, setting the property is Property "tone" not found and reading it Style property "tone" not found. using names a style or a sheet; anything else is Using target must be a Style or StyleSheet. An interface can name styles with using, and a class that implements it must use them: Chip must use TintStyle to implement Tinted.
  • Visible sheets. The sheets an element sees are those its own class uses and those the classes of the elements around it use, through bodies and component content. A rule from a sheet no element above uses does nothing, silently.
  • Two sheets, one name. Two visible sheets with a rule of one name, or a slot of one name, are an error where the name is used: Style rule "loud" is ambiguous between visible style sheets One and Two.
  • Two styles, one property. Two visible styles with a property of one name and different types are an error: Style property "tone" has conflicting types in visible styles TextStyle and OtherStyle.
  • A sheet's styles reach further. A sheet's using lets its rules set those properties on elements whose classes do not use the style, such as a root, and an @inherited value set there passes down.

Domains

A style can say what work a change to a property makes necessary:

/core/style

<Screen screen
    <Panel side
        <Panel rows
rows.ink = "red"
screen.settle()
screen.redraw(side, rows)
rows.width = 20
screen.settle()
screen.redraw(side, rows)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Look is Style

+ ink String = "black"
+ width Int = 10
. ink -> paint
. width -> layout, layout on parent

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Panel is MarkupNode
    using Look



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Screen is MarkupRoot


────────────────────
+ do markup-batch-did-flush
    - flush MarkupBatchFlush

-- "settled: paint ${flush.is-paint-invalid}, layout ${flush.is-layout-invalid}"

────────────────────
+ do redraw
    - side Panel
    - rows Panel

-- "  side: paint ${side.$is-paint-invalid}, layout ${side.$is-layout-invalid}"
-- "  rows: paint ${rows.$is-paint-invalid}, layout ${rows.$is-layout-invalid}"
for panel in [side, rows]
    panel.$is-paint-invalid = false
    panel.$is-layout-invalid = false
(import /core/style)

(main
  (<> Screen (id: screen)
    (<> Panel (id: side)
      (<> Panel (id: rows))
    )
  )
  (= (. rows ink) "red")
  (call (. screen settle))
  (call (. screen redraw) side rows)
  (= (. rows width) 20)
  (call (. screen settle))
  (call (. screen redraw) side rows)
)

(type + Look (is Style)
  (prop + ink String (= "black"))
  (prop + width Int (= 10))
  (style-domains ink (domain paint))
  (style-domains width (domain layout) (domain layout parent))
)

(type + Panel (is MarkupNode)
  (using Look)
)

(type + Screen (is MarkupRoot)
  (fn-do + markup-batch-did-flush _
    (param flush MarkupBatchFlush)
    (print (str "settled: paint " (. flush is-paint-invalid) ", layout " (. flush is-layout-invalid)))
  )
  (fn-do + redraw _
    (param side Panel)
    (param rows Panel)
    (print (str "  side: paint " (. side $is-paint-invalid) ", layout " (. side $is-layout-invalid)))
    (print (str "  rows: paint " (. rows $is-paint-invalid) ", layout " (. rows $is-layout-invalid)))
    (for (in panel (list side rows))
      (= (. panel $is-paint-invalid) false)
      (= (. panel $is-layout-invalid) false)
    )
  )
)
settled: paint false, layout false
settled: paint true, layout false
  side: paint false, layout false
  rows: paint true, layout false
settled: paint false, layout true
  side: paint false, layout true
  rows: paint false, layout true
  • (style-domains width (domain layout) (domain layout parent)), in rows . width -> layout, layout on parent, says a change to width needs layout of the element and of its parent. A target is self, the default, or parent. Names are free, and a program has at most 32.
  • Flags. Settling a change raises the domain on the element as $is-layout-invalid, and on each element above it as $is-layout-invalid-below. These are the only $ values code can assign: the code that does the work clears them.
  • The root is told after each settle that changed something, by markup-batch-did-flush, with a MarkupBatchFlush whose flags are the domains raised. A settle that changes nothing does not call it. The terminal library decides when to repaint this way.
