On an element's row, rules come before theme tags: <Line "dusk" • loud:4 for dark = #late.

Probes

A probe records what a program does while it runs: a line of text with values in it, a value that changed, a count, or how long a stretch of work took. Probes are written in the source, but they are not part of the program. A build leaves them out unless it is asked for them with --probes, and a build that has them writes what they record to a trace file, not to the program's output. yumi shows the records on stderr while the program runs, and yumi probes reads a trace afterward: it filters records, times groups, sums counters and compares runs.

This chapter covers the kinds of probe and what each records, the code a probe can hold, where probes can be written, how a build chooses its probes, the console and the trace, the commands that read a trace, and how probes differ from prints.

A first probe

. names = ["Ada", "Grace", "Edsger"]
for name in names
    // greeting $name
    -- "Hello, $name!"
//greet.done// greeted ${names.length} people
(main
  (let names (list "Ada" "Grace" "Edsger"))
  (for (in name names)
    (probe-log _ (text: "greeting " name))
    (print (str "Hello, " name "!"))
  )
  (probe-log greet.done (text: "greeted " (. names length) " people"))
)
Hello, Ada!
Hello, Grace!
Hello, Edsger!

The output is the same with probes or without them. Saved as greet.bx and run with yumi greet.bx --probes, the program prints those three lines to stdout, and yumi writes what the probes recorded to stderr:

·      0ns  greeting Ada  greet.bx:4
·   16.0µs  greeting Grace  greet.bx:4
·   20.0µs  greeting Edsger  greet.bx:4
·   23.0µs  [greet.done] greeted 3 people  greet.bx:7
── probes ── exit 0 · 246.7ms · 4 records
busiest: greeting … 3× greet.bx:4
records: 4 logs over 23.0µs
trace: …/.tmp/build/probes/greet-1794767186696.trace
query: yumi probes summary · log · agg --field F · durations · tree · timeline · outliers (yumi probes --help)

Each line is one record: the time since the run's first record, the text with its values written in, and the file and line of the probe. The first probe has no key, which _ stands for; the second has the key greet.done, shown in brackets. The lines below the rule are the footer, which sums up the run. Times differ from run to run, and so do the times in every console output in this chapter.

In rows, a probe is a row that starts with //. The two probes above are // greeting $name and //greet.done// greeted ${names.length} people. In rows, // never starts a comment; see Source text.

Kinds of probe

There are five probe forms. Each is a step, and each can be written where a step can, with the exceptions in Where a probe can be written.

FormRowsWhat it records
// paint $frame(probe-log _ (text: "paint " frame))// paint $frameA log: a line of text, with each value kept as a field.
//gui.paint// painted $n(probe-log gui.paint (text: "painted " n))//gui.paint// painted $nA log under a key.
//net.request -> url, status(probe-log net.request (items: url status))//net.request -> url, statusAn event: a key and values, with no text.
//tui.box.root(probe-log tui.box.root)//tui.box.rootAn event with no values.
//status = value(probe-assign status value)//status = valueA property set: an event whose fields are property and value.
//parse.tokens ++(probe-count parse.tokens)//parse.tokens ++A counter, plus one.
//parse.bytes += size(probe-count parse.bytes size)//parse.bytes += sizeA counter, plus an amount.
//+app.frame// frame $n(probe-group + app.frame (text: "frame " n))//+app.frame// frame $nThe start of a group, with text.
//-app.frame// done(probe-group - app.frame (text: "done"))//-app.frame// doneThe end of the group, with text.
//+ setup(probe-group + _ (text: "setup"))//+ setupThe start of a group with no key.
//+parse.pass(probe-group + parse.pass)//+parse.passThe start of a group with no text, kept for its time.
//+-tui.layout// layout $box(probe-group +- tui.layout (text: "layout " box))//+-tui.layout// layout $boxA group that ends where the block it is written in is left.
//!gui.frame.objects . start0 = 5(probe gui.frame.objects (let start0 5))//!gui.frame.objects . start0 = 5Nothing: a statement probe, a step that runs only in a build that has it.

A probe of an object writes (: object key) in place of the key; see Probes of an object.

Logs

A log is a line of text. Its text: part is strings and values, as in str. Each value is kept in the record as a field of its own, with its type, so the tools can filter and add up values, not only read the text. A log with a key shows the key in brackets before its text.

Events and property sets

. orders = [("apple", 3), ("pear", 1), ("apple", 5), ("fig", 2)]
. total = 0
for sku, quantity in orders
    //shop.order -> sku, quantity
    total += quantity
    //shop.total = total
-- total
(main
  (let orders (list (tuple "apple" 3) (tuple "pear" 1) (tuple "apple" 5) (tuple "fig" 2)))
  (let total 0)
  (for (in (tuple sku quantity) orders)
    (probe-log shop.order (items: sku quantity))
    (+= total quantity)
    (probe-assign shop.total total)
  )
  (print total)
)
11

An event has a key and values but no text. In rows it is //shop.order -> sku, quantity. A property set records that a value changed, as //shop.total = total; it is an event whose fields are property and value. With --probes, the console shows:

·      0ns  shop.order: apple, 3
·      0ns  shop.total = 3
·      0ns  shop.order: pear, 1
·      0ns  shop.total = 4
·    1.0µs  shop.order: apple, 5
·    1.0µs  shop.total = 9
·    1.0µs  shop.order: fig, 2
·    1.0µs  shop.total = 11
── probes ── exit 0 · 245.8ms · 8 records
busiest: shop.order 4× · shop.total 4×
records: 8 events over 1.0µs

The console shows no file and line for events; yumi probes log shows them. Events suit values that the tools should add up: yumi probes agg --field quantity sum,count,max --by sku sums the orders above by product. See Reading a trace.

Counters

. values = [72, 15, 98, 41, 63, 8, 55]
sort(values)
-- values

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do sort
    - values [Int]

for next in 1 .. < values.length
    . at = next
    while at > 0 && values[at - 1] > values[at]
        //sort.swaps ++
        . moved = values[at]
        values[at] = values[at - 1]
        values[at - 1] = moved
        at -= 1
    //sort.passes ++
(main
  (let values (list 72 15 98 41 63 8 55))
  (call sort values)
  (print values)
)

(fn-do + sort _
  (param values (list Int))
  (for (in next (..< 1 (. values length)))
    (let at next)
    (while (and (> at 0) (> ([] values (- at 1)) ([] values at)))
      (probe-count sort.swaps)
      (let moved ([] values at))
      (= ([] values at) ([] values (- at 1)))
      (= ([] values (- at 1)) moved)
      (-= at 1)
    )
    (probe-count sort.passes)
  )
)
8, 15, 41, 55, 63, 72, 98

A counter adds one, or the amount it is given, to a number kept for the whole run. It writes no record each time: counters are summed in memory and written once, when the program ends, so they appear only in the footer and in yumi probes counters. With --probes:

── probes ── exit 0 · 244.5ms · 0 records
counters: sort.passes 6 · sort.swaps 13
  • The amount is converted to U64 as as converts it, so 1.5 adds 1 and a negative amount wraps around. Text is refused.
  • One number per run. A counter is not a series. To see a value change over time, record it with an event or a property set.
  • A counter of an object is kept for each object: //this:parse.reads ++(probe-count (: this parse.reads)).

Groups

. words = ["pear", "fig", "plum"]
//+shop.load// loading ${words.length} items
for word in words
    //+-shop.item// item $word
    // weighing $word
//-shop.load// loaded
-- find(words, "fig")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do find Int
    - words [String]
    - wanted String

//+-shop.find// finding $wanted
for at in 0 .. < words.length
    =? at if words[at] == wanted
= -1
(main
  (let words (list "pear" "fig" "plum"))
  (probe-group + shop.load (text: "loading " (. words length) " items"))
  (for (in word words)
    (probe-group +- shop.item (text: "item " word))
    (probe-log _ (text: "weighing " word))
  )
  (probe-group - shop.load (text: "loaded"))
  (print (call find words "fig"))
)

(fn-do + find Int
  (param words (list String))
  (param wanted String)
  (probe-group +- shop.find (text: "finding " wanted))
  (for (in at (..< 0 (. words length)))
    (return-if at (if (== ([] words at) wanted)))
  )
  (return -1)
)
1

A group marks a stretch of work. + begins it, - ends it, and what is recorded in between nests inside it. With --probes:

·      0ns  + loading 3 items  shop.bx:3
·    1.0µs    + item pear  shop.bx:5
·    1.0µs      weighing pear  shop.bx:6
·    1.0µs    - item pear 0ns  shop.bx:5
·    2.0µs    + item fig  shop.bx:5
·    2.0µs      weighing fig  shop.bx:6
·    2.0µs    - item fig 0ns  shop.bx:5
·    2.0µs    + item plum  shop.bx:5
·    2.0µs      weighing plum  shop.bx:6
·    2.0µs    - item plum 0ns  shop.bx:5
·    3.0µs  - loaded 3.0µs  shop.bx:8
·    3.0µs  + finding fig  shop.bx:15
·    3.0µs  - finding fig 0ns  shop.bx:15
── probes ── exit 0 · 205.2ms · 14 records
groups: shop.load 3.0µs · shop.find 0ns · shop.item 3× 0ns (max 0ns)
busiest: weighing … 3× shop.bx:6
records: 14 logs over 3.0µs
  • The end line shows the end's text and how long the group took.
  • +- begins a group that ends where the block it is written in is left, by any way out: at the end of each turn of a loop, and at a return, as in find above. In a value body's before, a +- group also spans the value.
  • A group with no text shows its key, as + app.load. It is kept for its time, which is what yumi probes durations, tree and outliers read.
  • An end closes the innermost open group of its task, whatever its key. Keys on an end name it for the reader; they are not matched.
  • An end with no group open stops the program with a panic, in a build that has the probe.
  • Tasks. Each task has its own groups; see Tasks and threads.

Statement probes

. items = [3, 1, 2]
//!app.check if items.length != 3
    -- "wrong count"
//! -- "items: $items"
-- "ok"
(main
  (let items (list 3 1 2))
  (probe app.check
    (if (!= (. items length) 3)
      (print "wrong count")
    )
  )
  (probe _ (print (str "items: " items)))
  (print "ok")
)
items: 3, 1, 2
ok

probe holds one step, which runs only in a build that has the probe, and records nothing. It is for work that only looking needs, such as a check or a print while finding a fault. In rows it is //! followed by a key and the step. Run without --probes, the program above prints only ok.

Text and values

The text of a log is strings and values. In rows, values are written into the text with $:

RowsFormMeaning
$name, $a.b, $a?.bname, (. a b), (?. a b)A value, written as text.
${expr}the expressionAny expression.
$?name, $?{expr}(preview name)A preview: an object or array by its id, not as text.
$!name, $!{expr}(snapshot name)A snapshot: the object's contents, copied into the trace.
\$, $$"$"A dollar sign.

How a value is kept:

  • Numbers, Bool, Char and String are kept as they are, each a field of its own type.
  • In a log, any other value is written as its text, made as a print makes it: a list as 1, 2, 3, and an object of a class with no conversion to String as [Object module:Type].
  • In an event, an object of a class (a List is one), an Array, or an Inspectable tuple is written by its id, as List#1002. Other values are written as text.
  • A preview writes an object or array by its id even in a log. A preview of a value that has no id writes the name of its type in brackets, as [Tuple].
  • A snapshot of an Inspectable object runs its inspectable-snapshot and records what that writes; of an array, it copies its bytes; of any other object, it writes only the id. An event's values in rows take previews but not snapshots. yumi probes counts snapshots but does not show what they hold; an inspector attached to the running program does.
  • Ids come from a counter in the runtime and change when the program changes. Don't depend on them.

Each value is a field, and each field has a name, which the tools use, as in --where 'ms > 2' or agg --field quantity:

ValueField name
A nameThe name: frame.
A chain of membersIts path: values.length.
A callThe function's name: noisy.
A preview or snapshotThe name inside it.
Anything elsevalue and its place among the values: value1.
A property setproperty and value.

Names bound by a tuple pattern are names too, so (for (in (tuple sku quantity) orders) …) gives the fields sku and quantity.

Probes of an object

A probe of an object writes (: object key) in place of the key, as //items:status = "ready"(probe-assign (: items status) "ready"), in rows //items:status = "ready". Its record belongs to the object, and the console shows it with the object's id, as List#1002.status = ready. In a method, the object is this: //this:parse.reads ++(probe-count (: this parse.reads)).

  • The object must be an object of a class, an Array or an Inspectable value. Any other value is an error where the probe compiles: Not supported.
  • A +- group cannot be of an object.

Code under a probe

Rows indented under a probe belong to it. In Brix they are the probe form's last item, a (block …). They run only in a build that has the probe, before it records, so they can work out a value for the probe alone:

. scores = [12, 40, 7, 33]
//stats.best -> best
    .. best = highest(scores)
-- scores.length

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do highest Int
    - scores [Int]

-- "looking for the best score"
. best = 0
for score in scores
    if score > best
        best = score
= best
(main
  (let scores (list 12 40 7 33))
  (probe-log stats.best (items: best)
    (block
      (lazy best (call highest scores))
    )
  )
  (print (. scores length))
)

(fn-do + highest Int
  (param scores (list Int))
  (print "looking for the best score")
  (let best 0)
  (for (in score scores)
    (if (> score best)
      (= best score)
    )
  )
  (return best)
)
looking for the best score
4

In rows the probe is //stats.best -> best, with .. best = highest(scores) under it. The build above has the probe, so highest runs and prints. Without --probes the program prints only 4: none of a probe is compiled, neither its values nor the code under it.

. count = 0
//demo.calls ++
//demo.total += noisy()
//demo.value -> noisy()
//demo.state = noisy()
// said ${noisy()}
//demo.more
    count = 99
count += 1
-- count

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do noisy Int

-- "noisy"
= 1
(main
  (let count 0)
  (probe-count demo.calls)
  (probe-count demo.total (call noisy))
  (probe-log demo.value (items: (call noisy)))
  (probe-assign demo.state (call noisy))
  (probe-log _ (text: "said " (call noisy)))
  (probe-count demo.more
    (block
      (= count 99)
    )
  )
  (+= count 1)
  (print count)
)

(fn-do + noisy Int
  (print "noisy")
  (return 1)
)
1

Built with --probes, the same program prints noisy four times and then 100: each value is worked out, and the block under demo.more runs. So never put work the program needs in a probe. What the program needs belongs in ordinary code, where it runs in every build.

Where a probe can be written

Place
A step body: main, fn-do, a loop, an if, a match arm, a do blockYes
A constructor or method, including probes of thisYes
The before of a value bodyYes
The block of a function value, before its answerYes
An arm of a decision table, before the arm's resultYes
A value body without before, or after its valueNo
Between the bullets of a list bodyNo
A whereNo
The value of a let, or any other valueNo
The members of a typeNo
The top level of a fileNo

A value body has one value, so a probe goes in its before:

-- double(4)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ double Int
    - n Int

n * 2
// doubling $n
(main
  (print (call double 4))
)

(fn-expr + double Int
  (param n Int)
  (* n 2)
  (probe-log _ (text: "doubling " n))
)
Exception: A `fn-expr` body has one value, and (probe-log …) follows the value (* …). Put checks, prints, probes and `do` forms in `(before …)`, other steps in a `(do …)` there, and lazies in `(where …)`, or write `fn-do` and return with `(return value)`.
<no file:9>
      (probe-log _ (text: "doubling " n))
      ^

-- double(4)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ double Int
    - n Int

// doubling $n

n * 2
(main
  (print (call double 4))
)

(fn-expr + double Int
  (param n Int)
  (before
    (probe-log _ (text: "doubling " n))
  )
  (* n 2)
)
8

At the top of a file, a probe is refused like any other step:

// loading
-- "ok"
(probe-log _ (text: "loading"))

(main
  (print "ok")
)
Exception: (probe-log …) cannot be a form at the top level of a file, which takes Top. A file holds declarations at its top level. Code that runs goes inside `(main …)`.
<no file:2>
    (probe-log _ (text: "loading"))
    ^

Keys

A key is one or more names joined by dots, each a lowercase letter followed by letters, digits and hyphens, as in tui.box.root or net.request-2. _ stands for no key. A key does two things:

  • It names what the probe explains. Records, groups and counters are listed by key.
  • It selects. --probes chooses probes by key, and yumi probes filters by key. Give each probe a key under the part of the program it explains, such as parse.tokens in a parser, so a selector can take the part whole.

A probe with no key is for looking at one thing now. Remove such probes when the looking is done, and keep the ones that explain work someone will want to see again.

Choosing probes

Without --probes

A build without --probes leaves every probe out:

  • Nothing runs. No value of a probe is worked out and no code under it runs, as the noisy example above shows.
  • Nothing is built. The executable has no probe runtime and no catalog. A function that only a probe calls is not built.
  • Names are still checked. A probe that reads a name that does not exist is an error in every build:
// missing $nowhere
-- "ok"
(main
  (probe-log _ (text: "missing " nowhere))
  (print "ok")
)
Exception: Name "nowhere" not found
<no file:3>
      (probe-log _ (text: "missing " nowhere))
                                     ^^^^^^^

The other checks of a probe are made only where it compiles: a counter given text, or a probe of a value that is not an object, builds without --probes and is an error with it.

--probes and selectors

yumi app.bx --probes builds the program with probes, runs it, and records its trace. Without -o, the executable is built at .tmp/build/probes/bin/app; with -o PATH it is built there. --compile builds without running, and needs -o.

OptionMeaning
--probes [SELECTORS]Compile probes in, run, and record the trace.
--timeout DStop the program after D (500ms, 30s, 2m) and exit with 124.
--trace PATHWrite the trace at PATH.
--quiet-probesPrint only the footer, not each record.

--trace and --quiet-probes need --probes. --probes and --timeout need a target that runs on this machine.

Without selectors, --probes compiles every probe in the program's own file, and, in every other file, each log, group and statement probe with no key. Selectors choose instead. They are joined by commas or spaces in one argument:

SelectorChooses
key, key.*The probes with that key and the keys inside it.
log:Logs with no key.
log:keyLogs under a key.
logEvery log, with a key or not.
counter:*, counter:keyEvery counter, or the counters under a key.
event:key, data:key, statement:keyEvents, groups with no text, or statement probes under a key.
profile:keyCounters and groups with no text under a key, kept as metrics: no records, only totals.
gcThe collector's counters: gc.cycles, gc.pauses and gc.assist.nanos.
*, allEvery probe, the core library's too, and the collector's counters.
. words = ["one", "two", "three"]
//parse.words// parsing ${words.length} words
for word in words
    //parse.tokens ++
    // token $word
-- words.length
(main
  (let words (list "one" "two" "three"))
  (probe-log parse.words (text: "parsing " (. words length) " words"))
  (for (in word words)
    (probe-count parse.tokens)
    (probe-log _ (text: "token " word))
  )
  (print (. words length))
)
3

What each selection records, from the console, without its footer's last lines:

$ yumi words.bx --probes
·      0ns  [parse.words] parsing 3 words  words.bx:3
·    1.0µs  token one  words.bx:6
·    2.0µs  token two  words.bx:6
·    2.0µs  token three  words.bx:6
counters: parse.tokens 3
$ yumi words.bx --probes parse
·      0ns  [parse.words] parsing 3 words  words.bx:3
counters: parse.tokens 3
$ yumi words.bx --probes parse.tokens
counters: parse.tokens 3
$ yumi words.bx --probes log:
·      0ns  token one  words.bx:6
·    1.0µs  token two  words.bx:6
·    1.0µs  token three  words.bx:6
$ yumi words.bx --probes log:parse
·      0ns  [parse.words] parsing 3 words  words.bx:3
$ yumi words.bx --probes nothing
warning: --probes selector nothing matched no probe sites
  • No key. With selectors, a log with no key needs log: or log. A statement probe with no key compiles into every build with --probes, whatever the selectors.
  • No match. A selector that matches no probe is a warning, and the program still runs.
  • What a selector is. Selectors are letters, digits, spaces and . * : , - _. A word after --probes with other characters is not taken as selectors: it goes to the program as its first argument, and the build compiles the probes it would compile with no selectors.
  • Metrics. With profile:, the footer has a metrics: line in place of records, as metrics: lib.calls 1 · lib.pass 1× 333ns.

What probes cost

A probe left out costs nothing. A probe compiled in costs the time to record it, and a build with probes also checks, at a probe safepoint in each loop, whether the program should pass on what it has recorded, unless every selector is a profile: one. The annotation @no-probe-safepoints keeps a function free of safepoints; see Functions. Compare times only between runs built with the same probes.

The console

yumi runs the program, follows its trace as it grows, and prints each record to stderr. The program's stdout stays its own. The console reads the trace every few milliseconds, so where its lines fall among the program's own output means nothing.

  • A line is ·, the time since the run's first record, two spaces for each group the record is in, and the record. Logs and groups end with their file and line.
  • At most 400 lines are printed. The footer then says how many were not shown; the trace has them all.
  • The footer begins with a rule that gives the exit status, how long the program ran, and the number of records. Then come lines for what the run has: counters:, metrics:, groups: (each key's count, total time, and longest), busiest: (the sites that wrote two or more records), records: (by kind, and the time they span), trace: (the trace's path) and query: (the commands that read it). Each list shows eight entries and then +N more.
  • Warnings in the footer: a group that never ended, a selector that matched nothing, and a program that wrote no trace because no probes were compiled in.

The trace

Where it is kept

Traces are kept in .tmp/build/probes/ under the project's root, the nearest folder up that holds .git. Each run leaves three files, named after the program and a stamp:

FileHolds
name-stamp.traceThe records.
name-stamp.probes.jsonThe catalog: each probe's kind, key, text, field names, file and line.
name-stamp.run.jsonThe program, its arguments, its exit status and whether it timed out.

last.json names the latest run, which yumi probes reads by default. The 20 latest runs are kept. A build with -o build/app and --probes also writes the catalog beside the executable, as build/app.probes.json.

What a record holds

  • Its site: the probe that wrote it, and so its kind, key, text, file and line.
  • Its values, each with its type.
  • Its time: the clock time, in nanoseconds. Tools show it as the time since the run's first record.
  • Its owner: the object it is of, or else the innermost group open in its task. Owners are how records nest.

A record does not hold its task or thread. The trace describes itself: the program declares each probe at the start, so yumi probes can read a trace with no catalog. Without the catalog, fields are named value1, value2, and so on.

How a run ends

  • The exit status is the program's own. After --timeout, it is 124, and the footer's rule says timed out after 300.0ms in place of exit 124.
  • A panic keeps its status, and the trace keeps what was recorded before it.
  • Signals. A panic, an unhandled error, a request to end the process, --timeout, SIGTERM and SIGHUP all finish the trace. SIGKILL and Ctrl-C lose the counters and the last few milliseconds of records.

Running a probed program yourself

A program built with probes runs as any other program when it is run directly, and records nothing. Two environment variables turn recording on:

VariableMeaning
PROBES_PATHThe trace file. Without it, nothing is recorded.
PROBES_ENABLEDRecording starts when it is set and not empty. Its value is not read: which probes record is chosen when the program is built.
PROBES_CONTROL_PATHA channel through which an inspector asks the running program about live objects.

yumi app.bx --probes and yumi probes run set these themselves and clear any others starting with PROBES_. Others tune the buffers: PROBES_SEGMENT_SIZE, PROBES_SEGMENT_POOL, PROBES_SEGMENT_TABLE_CAPACITY, PROBES_TASK_BUFFER_SIZE, PROBES_FLUSH_THRESHOLD and PROBES_FLUSH_INTERVAL_MS.

Reading a trace

yumi probes COMMAND [TRACE] reads a trace. TRACE is last by default, or a .trace file, or a .run.json file.

CommandPrints
summaryRecords, groups by time, counters and the busiest sites.
sitesEach probe with its fields, location and number of records.
logRecords in order, filtered.
around INDEX|TIMERecords around a record's index (120) or a time (1.5s).
aggStatistics of a field, as agg --field ms p50,p95,max --by frame.
durationsGroups by key: count, total, mean, p50, p95 and longest.
treeNested groups as a tree, with total and own time.
countersCounters and metrics.
timelineRecords over time, as bars.
outliersThe slowest groups, or the largest values of a field, against the median.
diff A BChanges between two traces: records per site, group times and counters.
run COMMAND…Runs a program built with probes and records its trace.

Filters, for the commands that list records:

FilterKeeps
--key K[,K]…Records whose key matches a glob, as gui.* or *.frame. A plain key also takes the keys inside it.
--where EXPRRecords whose fields compare as asked, joined by &&: 'ms > 4 && frame < 10'. The operators are ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= and ~. duration, time, depth, index, key, label, text and location can be compared too.
--text SRecords whose text contains S.
--source F[:L]Records written at a file, or a file and line.
--since D, --until DRecords in a span of time from the first record: 250us, 100ms, 1.5s.
--kind K[,K]…log, event, group, begin, end, system, or open for groups that never ended.

--limit N and --offset N page through what a command prints; text is capped, and says how to see more. --format json prints one JSON value and --format jsonl one JSON object per line. --catalog PATH names the catalog when it is not beside the trace.

An example

The outputs below read the trace of this program, saved as frames.bx:

/time/duration

for frame in 0 .. < 6
    //+app.frame// frame $frame
    . ms = 1 + frame % 3
    // paint frame $frame took $ms
    //app.paints ++
    (ms as Milliseconds).wait()
    //-app.frame// frame $frame done
-- "done"
(import /time/duration)

(main
  (for (in frame (..< 0 6))
    (probe-group + app.frame (text: "frame " frame))
    (let ms (+ 1 (% frame 3)))
    (probe-log _ (text: "paint frame " frame " took " ms))
    (probe-count app.paints)
    (call (. (as ms Milliseconds) wait))
    (probe-group - app.frame (text: "frame " frame " done"))
  )
  (print "done")
)
done

Sites are matched by file and line, so in a renamed file every site is new.

Values the tools read

--format jsonl shows a record as the tools see it:

{"label": "shop.order", "depth": 0, "key": "shop.order", "text": "shop.order: apple, 3", "fields": {"quantity": 3, "sku": "apple"}, "location": "orders.bx:5", "time_ns": 0, "index": 0, "kind": "event"}

A record of an object adds its owner, as "owner": "List#1002". For the orders program in Events and property sets:

$ yumi probes agg --field quantity sum,count,max --by sku
sku    sum  count  max
apple    8      2    5
fig      2      1    2
pear     1      1    1
$ yumi probes log --where 'quantity > 2'
#0         0ns  shop.order: apple, 3  orders.bx:5
#4         0ns  shop.order: apple, 5  orders.bx:5

A program built once

yumi probes run runs a program that was built with probes, as yumi runs one with --probes:

$ yumi frames.bx -o build/frames --compile --probes
$ yumi probes run --quiet --trace build/frames.trace -- build/frames

--quiet prints only the footer and --trace names the trace. The catalog is found beside the executable. Run on a program built without probes, it warns that there is no catalog and that the program wrote no trace.

Probes and other features

Tasks and threads

Each task has its own groups, so a record nests inside the group open in its own task. The records of every task and thread go to one trace, in the order of their times. A record does not say which task wrote it.

/time/duration

. a = do new
    //+work.task// task a
    (2ms).wait()
    // a inside
    //-work.task// a done
. b = do new
    //+work.task// task b
    (1ms).wait()
    // b inside
    //-work.task// b done
a.wait()
b.wait()
-- "done"
(import /time/duration)

(main
  (let a
    (do-new
      (probe-group + work.task (text: "task a"))
      (call (. 2ms wait))
      (probe-log _ (text: "a inside"))
      (probe-group - work.task (text: "a done"))
    )
  )
  (let b
    (do-new
      (probe-group + work.task (text: "task b"))
      (call (. 1ms wait))
      (probe-log _ (text: "b inside"))
      (probe-group - work.task (text: "b done"))
    )
  )
  (call (. a wait))
  (call (. b wait))
  (print "done")
)
done

With --probes:

·      0ns  + task a  tasks.bx:6
·    8.0µs  + task b  tasks.bx:14
·    1.1ms    b inside  tasks.bx:16
·    1.1ms  - b done 1.1ms  tasks.bx:17
·    2.1ms    a inside  tasks.bx:8
·    2.1ms  - a done 2.1ms  tasks.bx:9
── probes ── exit 0 · 204.5ms · 8 records
groups: work.task 2× 3.2ms (max 2.1ms)
records: 8 logs over 2.1ms

Task b's group began while a's was open, but it is not inside it. To find where a program hangs, put groups around its waits and run it with --timeout: yumi probes log --kind open lists the groups that never ended.

Tests and benchmarks

  • A case checks prints. What a test compares is what the program prints, so a probe never changes a case's expected output, unless code under it prints. To see why a case fails, run its program with --probes.
  • %probes: selectors in a .test case compiles those probes into its program, and a bare %probes compiles what --probes compiles with no selectors. The case runs alone, and its trace is removed with the case's directory.
  • Test modules run by yumi test have no probes, and yumi test clears any PROBES_ variables for the programs it runs.
  • Benchmarks. A benchmark profile can name probes selectors to build with, and read counters as metrics.

Tools

  • yumi app.bx --list-probes prints one JSON line for each probe in every module the program loads, the core library's included, with its key, file, kind and line, for a tool that lets someone choose keys:
    {"key": "io.dispatch", "path": "…/stdlib/core/_io.yumi", "kind": "log", "line": 220}
  • An inspector can attach to a running program through PROBES_CONTROL_PATH, follow its trace and ask it about live objects, such as the contents of a snapshot.
  • The compiler's own probes. In the Yumi repository, bin/yumi --compiler-probes [SELECTORS] builds a copy of the compiler with those probes, runs it on the rest of the command line, and records its trace. Without selectors, it compiles the probes of the compiler's command line and every probe with no key. Its keys include compiler.phase, typing.phase and emit.walks.

Probes and prints

A print is part of the program. A probe looks at it.

PrintProbe
CompiledAlways.Only with --probes, when a selector chooses it.
RunsAlways.Only where it is compiled.
Writes tostdout.The trace, which yumi shows on stderr.
KeepsText.Each value with its type, the time, the file and line, its group or object.
Read byWhoever runs the program, and its tests.yumi probes, which filters, adds up, times and compares.
  • To see what a program does, write a probe, not a print, and run it with --probes.
  • Output the program owes its user is a print, and so is anything a test should check.
  • A probe and a print on one row. In rows, a probe cannot follow a print on the same row: -- // done is a syntax error.

Native code and memory

A Yumi program can call C directly. It imports a C header as it imports a module, calls the header's functions by their C names, and passes numbers, text, structs, pointers and callbacks across. This chapter covers C headers and calls, how C's types appear in Yumi, pointers, and memory that the collector does not manage: memory from C, arenas, constant data, and code that runs without the collector.

Importing C

/ctype.h
/errno.h
/limits.h
/stdlib.h
/string.h

. phrase = "native code"
-- C:strlen(phrase)
-- C:strstr(phrase, "code")
-- C:strerror(C:ENOENT)
-- C:atoi("42 apples")
-- C:toupper('y') as Char
-- C:INT_MAX
-- type-of C:strlen(phrase)
-- C:getenv("YUMI_REF_UNSET") ?? "unset"
(import /ctype.h)
(import /errno.h)
(import /limits.h)
(import /stdlib.h)
(import /string.h)

(main
  (let phrase "native code")
  (print (call C:strlen phrase))
  (print (call C:strstr phrase "code"))
  (print (call C:strerror C:ENOENT))
  (print (call C:atoi "42 apples"))
  (print (as (call C:toupper 'y') Char))
  (print C:INT_MAX)
  (print (type-of (call C:strlen phrase)))
  (print (?? (call C:getenv "YUMI_REF_UNSET") "unset"))
)
11
code
No such file or directory
42
Y
2147483647
[TypeInfo U64]
unset

/string.h(import /string.h) imports a C header, and C:strlen names a function it declares. In rows the import is /string.h and the call C:strlen(phrase).

  • Where headers come from. A path that names a header is looked up as a header before it is looked up as a module.
    • A path whose first folder is one of the toolchain's libraries, such as /sqlite/sqlite3.h or /YuCore/YuCore.h, names that library's header.
    • /c/unistd.h names a header of the C library explicitly.
    • Any other path is looked up among the target's C library headers, subfolders included, as /sys/stat.h and /arpa/inet.h are.
    • A header beside the program, a framework's header, or a missing header is a missing module: Module "./mylib.h" not found.
  • What becomes a C: name. Functions with C names whose parameter and result types all have a Yumi type, and integer constants: macros whose value is an integer, and the cases of enums. A header's own includes count too, so /string.h also gives the functions of /stdlib.h.
  • What does not. Functions that take a variable number of arguments, such as printf and open, are left out, and so are functions that take or return a union. Floating and text macros, macros with parameters, global variables and type names are not C: names either: C:M_PI gives Function "M_PI" not found.
  • Per module. A header's names are visible in the module that imports it, as a module's are. A module that uses them without the import gets C function "abs" is not declared by any header this module imports. + /stdlib.h(export /stdlib.h) passes them on, as an export of a module does.
  • Only headers declare C names. A program cannot declare one of its own: C symbol names belong to header modules.

Linking

A program is linked with the runtime, with each toolchain library whose header it imports, and with the target's system libraries: on macOS, libSystem (the C library, math and threads), libc++ and zlib. There is no way to link another library. A header of the SDK whose library is not linked, such as /curl/curl.h, passes the check, and the build fails at the link with Undefined symbols.

Calling C

  • Arguments convert as as would convert them to the parameter's type, as in C: a Float given for an int is truncated, and an Int keeps its low bits. A literal that does not fit is an error: Integer literal -1 does not fit U64. A number, a Bool or a Char never becomes a pointer, and null is the null pointer.
  • Mismatches name the declarations: No C function "strlen" accepts (I64); it is declared as "strlen(CPointer'Char8)".
  • Text to C. A String is given where C takes a char *, and C sees its UTF-8 bytes ending in a zero byte. Slices and joined texts arrive the same way. An optional String? holding nothing is a null pointer.
  • Text from C. A char * result is an (of CPointer Char8). It prints as the text it points at, converts to a String where one is wanted, and becomes text inside str. Each conversion copies the text, so the String does not change when C's memory does. A null char * becomes "", and pointer ?? "fallback"(?? pointer "fallback") gives the fallback text for a null pointer.
  • Results. An int is an I32, a size_t a U64, a double an F64, a pointer a CPointer, and a struct returned by value an anonymous struct; see C types.
  • C functions as values. A C function is a value of a function type, so . measure Measure = C:strlen(let measure Measure C:strlen) works where Measure is (fn-type U64 (param text String)), and a call with some arguments left out gives a binding.

Out parameters

/stdlib.h

. text = "12 34 56 left"
. cursor CPointer'Char8 = text
. next CPointer'Char8
. total = 0
while true
    . value = C:strtol(cursor, &next, 10)
    if next == cursor
        break
    total += value
    cursor = next
-- total
-- "rest: \"$cursor\""
(import /stdlib.h)

(main
  (let text "12 34 56 left")
  (let cursor (of CPointer Char8) text)
  (let next (of CPointer Char8))
  (let total 0)
  (while true
    (let value (call C:strtol cursor &next 10))
    (if (== next cursor)
      (break)
    )
    (+= total value)
    (= cursor next)
  )
  (print total)
  (print (str "rest: \"" cursor "\""))
)
102
rest: " left"

&next is a pointer to the local next, which C writes through. Only a name can follow &: a local, a parameter, or a struct local. A pointer local declared with no value starts as null.

  • The type. (c-fn-type Result (param name Type) …) declares the type of a C function. In rows it is (*C) I32 with its parameters below. Its pointer parameters may be more specific than the header's, as (of CPointer I32) is for const void * here.
  • The function is a function declared at the top level of a module, given with as. A method is refused: Illegal to cast this function to CFunction. A type that does not fit is refused at the call.
  • Context. To give a callback an object, pass (as tally Pointer) where C takes a void *, and turn it back with (call (of gc-object-from-pointer Tally) context), from /core/intrinsics. The object must stay referenced from Yumi while C holds it; see What the collector follows.
  • Panics in a callback end the task as anywhere else.

How a C call runs

  • Blocking. A C call may block, as usleep and read do, without stopping the collector: the task leaves the collector's view for the call, and the collector does not wait for it. The call does hold its thread, so the other tasks on that thread run only after it returns, where a wait in Yumi, such as (50ms).wait()(call (. 50ms wait)), lets them run. Make a long blocking call in a task on the pool, with do-new-thread.
  • Short calls. Functions that cannot reach the collector, such as strlen, strcmp and the math functions, are called directly. The annotations @gc-leaf, for such a function, and @gc-polling, for one called between two of the collector's checks, are given to C functions by the toolchain's own headers. A program cannot give them to a C function, and on a Yumi function they do nothing.
  • errno is not a C: name. (call C:yumiGetErrNo), from /YuCore/YuCore.h, reads it on every platform.
  • Output. print writes to C's stdout and flushes it, so output from puts and print comes out in the order it was written.

  • Layout. A struct type, (type + Tm (is Struct) …), has C's layout: its fields in order, each aligned to its size. So a struct declared with the fields of C's struct tm reads and writes one, through a pointer converted with as, or by & of a local as timegm takes it.
  • Anonymous structs. (c-struct (: bits U32)) is a struct type with no name, as a C function returns one. A named type can be one, as Address is below.
  • By value. Structs pass to and from C by value, and assigning one copies it. Reading an item through a pointer gives a copy, while assigning a field of ([] fields 0) writes C's memory.
  • No unions. C unions have no Yumi type, and a header's struct cannot be named in Yumi: declare a struct with the same fields.
  • Objects are not structs. An object of a class reaches C as a pointer to the object, whose layout is the runtime's. Give C a struct, not an object, when C reads the fields.

  • Types. (of CPointer T) points at values of type T. Pointer is a pointer to bytes, (of CPointer Byte).
  • Making one. &name points at a local, a parameter or a struct local. (. array data) points at an array's items. Pointer()(call Pointer) is the null pointer, and 4096 as Pointer(as 4096 Pointer) a pointer to an address.
  • Reading and writing. p[i]([] p i) reads the item i places on, and p[i] = value(= ([] p i) value) writes it. Nothing checks the index.
  • Moving. p + n(+ p n) moves a pointer by n items, back when n is negative. The difference of two pointers is refused; compare their addresses, (. p address), which are U64s.
  • Comparing. ==, !=, < and the others compare addresses, and a pointer compares with null. A pointer is a condition, true when it is not null.
  • Printing. A pointer to Char8 prints the text it points at. Any other prints its type, as [CPointer core/number:I32*].
  • Arrays over C memory. (call (of Array I32) pointer count) is an array over memory it does not own. Writes go through to the memory, and indexing is checked, as with Index out of bounds (4 / 4) for the fifth item of four.

Memory outside the collector

The collector is the default so that objects can refer to one another freely, through parent links, callbacks and several views of one model, with no rule about who frees what. Leave it only where a lifetime or a pause matters: an arena for many values that one piece of work makes and can drop together, memory from C for what a C API owns, and @no-gc for code that must never pause. The collector frees memory, not resources: close a file, a socket or a subscription with use or close, since its object may be reclaimed much later.

What the collector follows

The collector finds the objects a program can still reach and frees the rest. It does not move objects, so an object's address stays the same while it lives.

  • Pointers it follows. A pointer to values, such as a Pointer or an (of CPointer I32), in a local, a field or an array the collector owns, keeps the object it points into alive.
  • Pointers it does not. A pointer to pointers, and memory from C, such as malloc's, are not looked into. An object referenced only from there is freed. So an object given to C, as a callback's context, must also stay referenced from Yumi for as long as C may use it.
  • /gc can run the collector, (call collect-garbage), and run code when an object is freed, on-reclaim; see the Standard library.

Memory from C

(call C:malloc n), calloc, realloc and free give and take back memory the collector does not manage, as in the example in Pointers. Nothing tracks it: there is no report of memory never freed, and no check of memory used after free. An array over it gives checked indexing.

scratch[999] = 1
-- arena.active-bytes > 8000

-- arena.active-bytes < 8000

-- arena.owns(name as Pointer)

  (let scratch (call (of (. arena allocate) I64) 1000))
  (= ([] scratch 999) 1)
  (print (> (. arena active-bytes) 8000))
  (call (. arena rewind) mark)
  (print (< (. arena active-bytes) 8000))
  (let name (call (. arena copy-string) "kept in the arena"))
  (print name)

An Arena, from /core/arena, holds memory that is freed all at once.

  • Making one. (call Arena) makes one, and (call Arena bytes) gives it a starting size. (use (call Arena)) releases it when the block ends; otherwise call its release.
  • Allocating. (call (of (. arena allocate) I64) 4) gives a pointer to 4 zeroed I64s, and try-allocate gives null when there is no memory. allocate-raw takes a byte count and an alignment, and does not zero. copy-string copies a text into the arena.
  • Storage in an arena. Arrays, array builders, tables, bitmaps and Scratch stacks take an arena in place of the collector, as (call (of Array I64) arena 4) does; see Collections. A table in an arena cannot hold objects, except texts: Arena type Holder contains managed pointers through Holder.box.
  • Freeing. mark gives a point to come back to, and rewind frees what was allocated after it. reset frees everything and keeps the memory for reuse. release gives it all back.
  • Questions. owns says whether a pointer is in the arena, and active-bytes, reserved-bytes, peak-active-bytes and others report its use.
  • Mistakes that are checked. Rewinding to another arena's mark panics: Arena mark is stale or belongs to another Arena. So does mark after release, Arena is already released, and allocating after it. A view of an arena's array after a reset or rewind panics with Stale array view.
  • Mistakes that are not. Reading an arena's storage after release, reset or rewind is not checked, and reads whatever the memory holds. That includes a text the arena holds, and a text made from one by an operation that gives back what it was given, such as a slice of the whole text, an interpolation of it alone, or a join of it alone.
  • Keeping a text. text.copied(. text copied) gives a copy the collector owns, which outlives the arena.

(call (of ConstArray U8) 31 28 …) is data written into the program when it is built, as C's static const arrays are.

  • Items are constants, converted to the item type as the program is built. Anything else is refused: ConstArray item must be constant.
  • Reading. table[i]([] table i) reads an item, with no check of the index. A ConstArray has no length.
  • Read-only. Assigning an item is refused: ConstArray values are read-only.
  • To C, a ConstArray is a pointer to its items, as greeting is for strlen.

@no-gc, on a function or on a (do @no-gc …) block, makes code that never meets the collector: it allocates nothing the collector manages, never pauses for it, and never suspends its task. The core library's arrays, tables and arenas use it for their inner loops. Each restriction can also be written as a (without …) part after the annotations, as in do without gc …(do (without gc) …) or ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ + do mean F64 without heap, suspend …(fn-do + mean F64 (without heap suspend) …); see Functions.

AnnotationRefuses
@no-heapMaking objects, arrays, lists and text; closures, tasks and (do @no-gc …) blocks that capture locals; a struct or other value that is no object made a value of an interface; a view of an array's rows or fields; calling a generator; a method bound to its object made a function value; and reading a global written with (:= …).
@no-safepointPausing for the collector.
@no-suspendSuspending the task, calling function values, and reading a global written with (:= …).
@no-gcAll three.
  • Messages. Making an object gives allocation is not allowed in a GC-free zone (entered at …), storing an object anywhere but the zone's own locals gives storing a managed pointer is not allowed in a GC-free zone, and waiting gives cannot suspend inside a GC-free zone. Each is reported where it happens, with the calls that reach it from where the restriction is placed, as in mean (@no-gc) → helper → Box(). Code a restriction reaches is checked under it however it is called: directly, through an interface or a class's method, or through a conversion. Reading a global written with (:= …) gives cannot read lazy global 'name' inside …, since its first read runs its value, as that read may run any code and wait while another task runs it.
  • What may run. Numbers, structs, pointers, arrays made outside the code, method calls, C calls, and an arena's methods, which are themselves @no-gc. A C function marked @gc-polling may reach the collector, so under @no-heap or @no-suspend one counts as allocating and as suspending unless the compiler knows it does neither.

What is checked

  • When compiling: that a C: name is declared by an imported header; the number and types of a C call's arguments; pointer conversions; constants that do not fit; that a C callback is a module function; writes to ConstArray items; what an arena's table holds; and what code without the collector does.
  • When running: array indexes, including arrays over C memory; arena marks, rewinds and allocation after release; and stale views.
  • Not at all: pointer indexes, null pointers, memory used after free, an arena's storage used after it is freed, memory never freed, and objects referenced only from C memory. Reading through a null pointer ends the program with status 139, with no report.

Platforms

  • Headers differ. macOS and iOS builds read the SDK's headers, and Linux builds the sysroot's, so a function can have a different declaration on each. qsort_r takes its context first on macOS and last on Linux. Put calls that differ in platform modules; see Modules.
  • Libraries differ. macOS links libSystem, libc++, zlib and two system frameworks, iOS libc++ and zlib, and Linux glibc, libm and static libstdc++, without zlib.
  • Toolchain libraries differ. A header of a toolchain library that is not built for the target is refused, as … requires … , which the runtime build config does not build for linux. See Platforms.

Built-in types

Every module imports the core library's 18 always-imported modules without writing them; see Modules. Their public types are the built-in types. Most belong to a chapter of their own, and this one lists them all and says where each is covered. It covers fully the ones no other chapter does: the number types as a family, type information, function types, the interfaces the language itself uses, and a few others. It ends with the names that look like types but are not, and the functions core makes visible.

  • On the type. size is a type's size in bytes, min and max its least and greatest value, and bit-width an integer type's width in bits. is-integer, is-signed and is-number say what kind of number it is.
  • Other names. Int, Float, Byte and the others in the last column are the same type under another name: (== Int I64) is true, and the type prints as I64. Programs write Int, Float and Byte.
  • Size, Index and Increment are types of their own built on I64, and Hash on U32. They convert to and from their base on their own, arithmetic on them gives the base, and they keep their own names: (== Size I64) is false.
  • Number is the base of every number type, Bool and Char. As a constraint, (constraint is Item Number) admits all of them; as a parameter's type it takes nothing.
  • Text. (call (. n pad) 5) writes an integer with zeros in front, to 5 characters with the sign, or a float with exactly that many decimals. places writes a float with at most that many, dropping zeros at the end. as Hex, as Binary and as UnitString write an integer in hex, in bits, or followed by its unit, as 2.5f32 is. Text converts to a number with as, and a number that does not fit the type is clamped: (as "300" U8) is 255.
  • I1 holds 0 or 1, as a Bitmap'I1 does. Arithmetic on it gives an I32.
  • Endian names a byte order, .big or .little, for reading and writing numbers in a byte array; see Collections.

A type's name used as a value is a TypeInfo, and so is what type-of value(type-of value) gives. It prints as [TypeInfo Shape], and a generic type with its arguments joined by ', as [TypeInfo List'I64'GCBacking].

MemberGives
nameThe type's name as it prints: I64 for Int.
keyThe type's full key, with its module, as Class:core/number:I32.
concrete-name, concrete-keyFor an object, the class it was made as, read when the program runs.
sizeThe bytes a value takes where it is stored: 8 for any object.
min, max, bit-width, is-integer, is-signed, is-numberWhat a number type holds; see Numbers.
is-tuple, is-structWhether it is a tuple, or a struct.
read-onlyFalse for a class, a struct and a table column, whose values can be changed in place.
baseThe type it is built on. A type with none is an error: No base type.
propertiesIts stored properties, base class first, as a PropertyList.
compare(other)How a value of this type relates to other, as a TypeRelation.
compare-unified(other)How it relates to the type both have in common.
  • Equality. == and != compare types: type-of shape == Shape(== (type-of shape) Shape) is true for the declared type, and false for the class the object was made as.
  • type-of works out its operand once, and gives its declared type.
  • Properties. A PropertyList has a length, can be indexed and looped over, and finds one property with (call (. list named) "side"), giving null where there is none. Each PropertyInfo has a name, type-name, offset, size, and flags such as is-float and is-reference.
  • Relations. A TypeRelation prints its kind and the two types: UpCast to a base class, DownCast to a derived one, SideCast between numbers or into an optional, Converter through a declared conversion, Illegal where there is no conversion, and others. Its cast converts a value as the relation says.
  • In generic functions, a type parameter is a TypeInfo, so (. Item name) names the type a call was made with.

Function types

/stream/sort

. words = ["pear", "fig", "banana"]
-- sort(words) • using by-length

-- shout("hey")
. report Statement'String = :: word => do -- "saw $word"
report("fig")
. even OptionalMapper'Int'Int = :: n => n if n % 2 == 0
-- even(3)
-- even(4)
. answer Lazy'Int = => 42
. known Int = answer
-- known
-- type-of by-length
-- type-of shout

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ by-length Comparison

    - right String

|? a < b

|? a > b

??
    .equal

.. a = left.length
.. b = right.length
(import /stream/sort)

(main
  (let words (list "pear" "fig" "banana"))
  (print (call sort words (:using by-length)))
  (print (call by-length "fig" "kiwi"))
  (let shout (of Selector String String) (=> (word) (. word uppercased)))
  (print (call shout "hey"))
  (let report (of Statement String) (=> (word) :do (print (str "saw " word))))
  (call report "fig")
  (let even (of OptionalMapper Int Int) (=> (n) (only-if n (if (== (% n 2) 0)))))
  (print (call even 3))
  (print (call even 4))
  (let answer (of Lazy Int) (=> () 42))
  (let known Int answer)
  (print known)
  (print (type-of by-length))
  (print (type-of shout))
)

  (param left String)
  (param right String)

    .lesser
  )
  (case? (> a b)
    .greater
  )
  (default
    .equal
  )
  (where
    (lazy a (. left length))

  )

sink <- "end"

-- <- countdown
-- <- countdown
do use Door("front")
    -- "inside"
do use Session()
    -- "working"

Some interfaces give a type a place in the language itself, not only in libraries:

InterfaceWhat it givesWhat a type declares
Readable'MessageReading with (<- value).(prefix <- this), giving Message?.
Writable'MessageWriting with (<- value item).(infix this <- (param item Message)).
Closableuse and do-use call close at the end.close.
Usable'Useduse binds what begin-using gives, and calls end-using at the end.begin-using and end-using.
Iterable, CursorIterable, Indexable, BroadcastableLoops and the stream family; see Streams.Their members.
Collection'ItemTracked reads follow the changes it reports; see Reactivity.Its members, and the notifications.
HashableUse as a map key; see Collections.hash and ==.
RoutedEvent, EventNodeRouted and rising events; see Reactivity.Their members.
  • use goes by members. A type that declares close, or begin-using and end-using, can be used whether or not it names the interface. One with neither cannot: Plain cannot be used, as it has no "begin-using" and is not Closable.
  • Reading is not looping. A type that is only Readable is read with <-, not looped over: A for loop cannot iterate over Countdown.
  • Protocols that are not interfaces. A type becomes text through a conversion to String, and converts through its fn-to and fn-from declarations; see Conversions. It compares through the operators it defines; see Operators.

Display text

. plain = DisplayText("abc")
. wide = DisplayText("a漢b")
-- "${plain.display-width} ${plain.codepoint-count} ${plain.is-single-cell}"
-- "${wide.display-width} ${wide.codepoint-count} ${wide.is-single-cell}"
-- wide.width-at(1)
-- ", "(wide.widths)
. both = plain + wide
-- both.text
-- both.display-width
-- plain
(main
  (let plain (call DisplayText "abc"))
  (let wide (call DisplayText "a漢b"))
  (print (str (. plain display-width) " " (. plain codepoint-count) " " (. plain is-single-cell)))
  (print (str (. wide display-width) " " (. wide codepoint-count) " " (. wide is-single-cell)))
  (print (call (. wide width-at) 1))
  (print (call ", " (. wide widths)))
  (let both (+ plain wide))
  (print (. both text))
  (print (. both display-width))
  (print plain)
)
3 3 true
4 3 false
2
1, 2, 1
abca漢b
7
(abc, 3, 3, U8[0])

A DisplayText holds a text with how many columns of a terminal it takes, measured once when it is made. widths gives each character's width, and is empty when every character takes one column, as is-single-cell says. width-at gives one character's width, and + joins two. The terminal libraries keep their text this way.

More channels

. ticks = AsyncOnDemandChannel'Int(Ticker())
-- "no subscriber yet"
for t on ticks
    -- "tick $t"
    if t == 2
        break
ticks <- 1
ticks <- 2
. gate = OneShotChannel()
. waiter = do new
    <- gate
    -- "gate opened"
do new
    -- "waiter end ${waiter.end}"
    gate.done()
-- "main done"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Ticker
    is Usable'Void


────────────────────
+ do begin-using

-- "first subscriber: start"

────────────────────
+ do end-using

-- "last subscriber gone: stop"
(main
  (let ticks (call (of AsyncOnDemandChannel Int) (call Ticker)))
  (print "no subscriber yet")
  (for (on t ticks)
    (print (str "tick " t))
    (if (== t 2)
      (break)
    )
  )
  (<- ticks 1)
  (<- ticks 2)
  (let gate (call OneShotChannel))
  (let waiter
    (do-new
      (<- gate)
      (print "gate opened")
    )
  )
  (do-new
    (print (str "waiter end " (. waiter end)))
    (call (. gate done))
  )
  (print "main done")
)

(type + Ticker
  (implements (of Usable Void))
  (fn-do + begin-using _
    (print "first subscriber: start")
  )
  (fn-do + end-using _
    (print "last subscriber gone: stop")
  )
)
no subscriber yet
first subscriber: start
main done
tick 1
tick 2
last subscriber gone: stop
waiter end 0
gate opened
  • AsyncOnDemandChannel is a broadcaster made with a Usable. Its first subscription calls begin-using, and when the last one ends it calls end-using, so a source runs only while someone listens. Values written with no subscriber are dropped. Timers and signals in the standard library are made this way.
  • OneShotChannel is a gate. (<- gate) waits until some task calls (call (. gate done)), which lets every waiting task go on. A task that reads the gate after that waits for the next done.
  • TaskEnd prints as a number: 0 while the task runs, as above.

Watching a collection

. items = ["a", "b"]
. watcher CollectionObserver = :: change => do show(change)
observe-collection(items, watcher)
items += "c"
items.insert("x", 0)
items[1] = "A"
items.move(0, 2)
items.remove(0, 2)
unobserve-collection(items, watcher)
items += "unseen"
-- items

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do show
    - change CollectionMutation

-- "${change.kind} at ${change.index}, ${change.from-index} to ${change.to-index}, count ${change.count}"
(main
  (let items (list "a" "b"))
  (let watcher CollectionObserver (=> (change) :do (call show change)))
  (call observe-collection items watcher)
  (+= items "c")
  (call (. items insert) "x" 0)
  (= ([] items 1) "A")
  (call (. items move) 0 2)
  (call (. items remove) 0 2)
  (call unobserve-collection items watcher)
  (+= items "unseen")
  (print items)
)

(fn-do + show _
  (param change CollectionMutation)
  (print (str (. change kind) " at " (. change index) ", " (. change from-index) " to "
    (. change to-index) ", count " (. change count)))
)
append at 2, 0 to 0, count 1
insert at 0, 0 to 0, count 1
set at 1, 0 to 0, count 1
move at 0, 0 to 2, count 1
remove at 0, 0 to 0, count 2
b, c, unseen

(call observe-collection items watcher) calls the watcher with a CollectionMutation for each change to the collection, until unobserve-collection. A mutation's kind is append, insert, set, remove, replace, move or reset, and its index, from-index, to-index and count say where.

Other types

  • NTuple2'T to NTuple6'T are tuples of 2 to 6 values of one type, with fields a to f: (of NTuple2 Int) is (a Int, b Int). A list takes one as an index to assign several items: (= ([] xs (tuple 0 2)) 7) sets the items at 0 and 2.
  • Subscriber'Message is the function type a broadcaster delivers to: (item Message, broadcaster (of Broadcastable Message)) Void. (call (. ticks subscribe) printer) subscribes one without a loop, and unsubscribe with the same value ends it.
  • UnhandledErrorHandler is the type of unhandled-error, which takes an error and gives nothing. Assigning unhandled-error replaces what is done with errors that have no caller; see Errors.
  • Optional members. An optional's has-value says whether it holds a value. Read the value with !! or a pattern; see Optionals.
  • Type families. A type with several is types and no body, as + Plain is Int || String(type-line + Plain (is Int String)), is a family: as a parameter's type it takes any of them, and the function is made once for each. Stream is one.

Names that are not types to write

  • Backings in printed types. type-of shows a collection's backing, as in [TypeInfo List'I64'GCBacking]. A program writes (list Int) and names a backing only to choose another, such as an arena's.
  • Names only seen at run time. Closure, Binding, and Tuple and Union for anonymous tuples and unions, appear in type-of output, but are not types to declare values with.
  • Core's own. Function, Capture, Or, GCTypeMap, StorageBacking, the types of array views, the trackers, and the pattern runtime's types are public because the core and the code the compiler writes use them. A program does not name them.

There is no query that lists types or members. yumi app.bx --list-sources lists the modules a program loads, core's among them, and yumi app.bx --explain hash-for finds a function's declarations.

The Standard Library

The standard library comes with the compiler. Its source is in the stdlib folder of the toolchain, one folder for each library, and it is the reference for what each module declares: a declaration marked + is public.

Importing

A module's import path is its path under stdlib, without the file's extension: /os/path is the module in stdlib/os/path. An import, /os/path(import /os/path), makes the module's public names usable in the file that imports it. Modules covers imports in full.

A folder's module of the same name gathers its library: /tui is stdlib/tui/tui, which passes on the public names of the library's modules. Importing it imports the whole library; importing one module, such as /tui/table, imports only that module and what it passes on.

Some modules are imported into every module without being named:

  • Always: core and the core modules for errors, numbers, strings, types, backing storage, arrays, function types, collections, lists, maps, ranges, streams, channels, events, tracked values, parsing and tasks.
  • In a module that writes stream patterns: core/tokenstream and core/patterns.
  • In a module that writes markup: core/markup.
  • In a module that declares or extends a style sheet: core/style.
  • In a program's entry module, and in a module that writes probes, when probes are compiled in: core/probes.

Modules whose names start with _ are the libraries' own internals.

Language support

core

The types and runtime the language itself is built on. Most of it is imported into every module; see Importing. The Built-in types chapter covers what those modules declare: numbers, String, List, Map, Array, ranges, errors, streams, channels, tasks and function types.

These core modules must be imported by name:

ModuleHolds
/core/tableTable and ImmutableTable: rows of a struct type stored as columns. See Collections.
/core/bitmapBitmap and BitmapBuffer: bits read and set by index. See Collections.
/core/arenaArena: memory that is freed all at once, outside the collector. See Native code and memory.
/core/array-builderArrayBuilder: an array that grows as items are added. See Collections.
/core/scratchA stack of scratch memory in an arena.
/core/atom-poolInterning: one shared copy of each text.
/core/gcWeak: a reference that does not keep its object alive.
/core/animatableAnimatable: the interface of values that motion can move between.
/core/list-cursorListCursor: a position in a list that steps and wraps.
/core/domNode: a generic tree of content nodes.
/core/pattern-helpersHelpers for stream patterns that keep state while they match.
/core/intrinsicsLow-level operations, such as counting leading zero bits.

stream

Operations on streams. /stream gathers all but one of its modules.

ModuleHolds
/stream/aggregatereduce, scan, sum, count, first, last, all, some.
/stream/filtertake, skip, distinct, every.
/stream/combinezip, product, indexed, repeat, and or, which merges two streams as their items arrive.
/stream/coincidencebuffer, window, pairwise, partition.
/stream/inspectany, contains, reversed, forever.
/stream/sortsort and merge-sort.
/stream/routerRouter and EventDispatcher: sending each item to the handlers it matches.
/stream/timingStreams of numbers driven by time. Not part of /stream.

gc

Control over the garbage collector. /gc passes on Weak from /core/gc, and adds on-reclaim, which runs a cleanup after an object is collected, as well as collect-garbage and return-free-memory. Modules that hold native resources, such as open files, use it to release them. gc-memory reports the collector's memory: live bytes, the heap goal, committed bytes and how much of them spans hold, free committed bytes and how scattered they are, peak demand, the retention target, the free bytes not yet returned, footprint and the collection count. set-minimum-heap-goal sets the smallest heap goal, the size the heap may reach before a collection starts, which is 32 MB by default. A program that would rather spend memory than run more collections, such as the compiler, sets a larger one.

Values and data

time

Durations, dates, clocks and timers. /time gathers every module except /time/timer.

  • /time/duration: Duration, the units from ns to milleniums, wait and timeout.
  • /time/clock: ClockTime and measure.
  • /time/datetime: DateTime, Date, Time, Month, now and today.
  • /time/zone: TimeZone, utc and local.
  • /time/timestamp: reading and writing ISO 8601, RFC 2822 and RFC 3339 timestamps.
  • /time/deadline: Deadline.
  • /time/debounced: debounced and throttled streams.
  • /time/flicks: Flicks, a unit of 1/705,600,000 of a second, chosen so that a frame at common video and audio rates lasts a whole number of flicks.
  • /time/timer: Timer, TimerLoop and AnimationLoop.

math

  • /math: π, angles in radians and degrees (rad, deg, °), abs, round, floor, sqrt, trigonometry, random, min, max and clamp. Random is a generator of its own: (call Random 42u) gives the same numbers on every run, and split makes another from it.
  • /math/easing: Easing and CubicBezier.
  • /math/motion: motions that move a value over time: spring, ease-in-out, linear, steps, decay and keyframes.

units

/units declares Percent (%), Ratio and scaling, and passes on /units/distance, the lengths from nm to miles. Pixels are declared in /graphics/primitives and durations in /time/duration. Units explains how unit families are declared and converted.

data

Data formats. /data itself declares only the interfaces of readable and writable data; each format is its own module.

ModuleHolds
/data/jsonJSON, parse-json and to-json.
/data/jsonlJSON Lines.
/data/jsonrpcJSON-RPC requests and responses.
/data/csvA stream pattern for CSV files.
/data/markdownParsing Markdown into a tree of nodes.
/data/sexpS-expressions.
/data/source-tree, /data/source-sexpAn editable tree of source text.
/data/plistBinary property lists.
/data/protobufReading and writing protocol buffers.
/data/binaryByteReader and ByteWriter.
/data/streamDataStream.
/data/sqliteSQLite databases, statements and rows.
/data/diffLine diffs.
/data/fuzzyFuzzy matching and edit distance.

regex

/regex: Regex, which matches, finds, replaces and splits text, and RegexMatch.

crypto

/crypto gathers ChaCha20Poly1305 encryption, SHA-1 and SHA-512 digests, HMAC and HKDF, random-bytes, and an SRP client for password logins.

The system

os

Files, processes and the environment. There is no /os module; import each one.

  • Files and paths: /os/path (Path, with joining by /, file information, directory listings and change notifications), /os/file (File, standard input and output, and reading and writing whole files), /os/file-tree and /os/file-session (watched trees of files).
  • The environment: /os/env (environment variables and the working directory), /os/cli (command lines: CommandLine, subcommands, flags, options and arguments), /os/shell (the login shell's environment), /os/bundle and /os/app-support (an app's bundle and its application support folder).
  • Processes: /os/process (Process, and pipes to and from processes), /os/pty, /os/signal, /os/memory-pressure (memory-pressure, which sends a warning or critical level when macOS or iOS runs short of memory), /os/tty, /os/shared-memory, /os/message-channel, /os/outbox and /os/mach-port.
  • Terminals: /os/terminal gathers a terminal emulator, a shell session in a pseudo-terminal, and terminal paths.

net

Networking. There is no /net module; import each one.

ModuleHolds
/net/urlURL and query strings.
/net/dnsAddresses, ports and name resolution.
/net/socketTCP and TLS connections and listeners.
/net/httphttp-get, http-post, http-fetch, requests and responses.
/net/http-serverHTTPServer and its routes, which may answer WebSocket upgrades.
/net/sseServer-sent events.
/net/websocketWebSocket, either end of a WebSocket connection.
/net/dns-sdFinding services on the local network.

git

/git reads and changes Git repositories by running the git command: status, logs, diffs, commits, merges, fetching and pushing, worktrees, and watching a worktree for changes. It needs git to be installed.

Interfaces

ui

What graphical and terminal interfaces share. /ui gathers commands and their history, undo, key combinations and key maps, input, selection, modes, recent items and type-to-select. Import /ui/panes for pane layouts, /ui/virtual, /ui/virtual-layout and /ui/virtual-recycler for lists that create only the rows in view, and /ui/app-state for state saved between runs.

gui

Native desktop and mobile apps, written as markup and styled with style sheets. /gui gathers 78 modules and /ui:

  • Apps and layout: App, Window, Box, flex, flow and grid layouts, positions, themes and style shorthands.
  • Text and images: Text, Label, TextInput, images, vector images and icons.
  • Controls: buttons, check boxes, switches, toggles, sliders, number and color fields, color pickers, selects, combo boxes, segmented controls, progress bars and disclosures.
  • Collections: list boxes, tree boxes, column trees, thumbnail grids, virtual lists, tab bars, sidebars, toolbars and timelines.
  • Overlays: popups, popovers, menus, dialogs, tooltips, toasts and command palettes.
  • Motion and gestures: animation, keyframes, swiping, pinching, dragging, zooming and resizing.
  • The system: the clipboard, file dialogs and status items.

Other modules are imported by path: /gui/desktop (the trash and opening URLs), /gui/web-view, /gui/terminal-view, /gui/workbench, and views of UIs that another process renders. /gui/markdown, /gui/code-editor, /gui/file-browsing and /gui/chat each gather a larger component. Icons from the Lucide set are each a module of their own, such as /gui/icons/lucide/star.

tui

Terminal apps, written as markup with the same model as gui. /tui gathers apps, boxes, windows, layouts, canvases, borders, styles, themes, colors, events and shortcuts, text and a text editor, tables, buttons, dialogs, forms, panels, progress bars, spinners and status bars, as well as /ui/input, /ui/key-combo and /units. Import /tui/listbox, /tui/treebox, /tui/columntree, /tui/virtual and /tui/terminal separately. /tui/code-editor and /tui/file-browsing each gather a larger component.

code

The model behind code editors. /code gathers the text of a document, an editing session with selections and undo, a document backed by a file, folding and comment toggling. Import /code/syntax for syntax coloring, /code/code-find for find and replace, /code/file-names and /code/file-text for finding files by name and by content, and /code/structure for editing Brix source by its structure.

Graphics and media

graphics

Drawing, text, shaders and vector geometry. There is no /graphics module; import each one.

  • Values: /graphics/primitives (Coord in px, Rect, Dimensions, Insets and drawing settings), /graphics/point, /graphics/color (RGBA, HSVA and named colors), /graphics/matrix and /graphics/gradient.
  • Drawing: /graphics/canvas (Canvas, drawing to images, SVG and PNG), /graphics/image, /graphics/text (fonts and text layout), /graphics/outline, /graphics/surface and /graphics/movie.
  • Shaders: /graphics/shader and filters such as CRT, pixelate, wave, halftone and glitch.
  • Geometry: /graphics/path, /graphics/vector (path commands and shapes), SVG paths, curves and curve fitting, intersections, polygons, offsets, strokes and boolean operations, and vector networks.
  • Documents: a scene graph of graphic nodes, paint styles, and vector documents with their rendering.

media

Sound. There is no /media module. /media/synth declares sound patches in hz, /media/mixer mixes voices, /media/audio-output plays them, /media/spectrum analyzes them, and /media/wave-file writes WAV files.

AI

ai

Conversations with AI models. /ai gathers the model of a conversation (messages, tools and events), branching chats, chat sessions and their storage in SQLite, API keys and sign-ins, and image generation. Each provider is imported on its own: /ai/claude and /ai/codex drive those command-line tools, /ai/openai/completions, /ai/openai/responses and /ai/openai/images call the OpenAI API, and /ai/mcp serves tools over MCP. /ai/services connects the default setup.

Embedding

script

/script is a small expression language for formulas that a program's users write: reading, parsing, printing and evaluating them, rewriting them, and solving them for a value. Its values include numbers, points, colors and ranges.

Tools

These libraries serve the toolchain rather than programs.

  • lang is the Yumi compiler. Programs use one part of it: /lang/product/mac-app and /lang/product/ios-app declare the app bundle a program builds into, with its name, id, icon and document types.
  • probes reads the records that probes write, for yumi probes. Writing probes needs no import; see Probes.
  • test is the library test modules use: /test declares test cases and how they report. See yumi test --help.

Platforms

Yumi builds programs for macOS, iOS and Linux. Most of the standard library is written in Yumi and builds for all three. Some modules call native libraries that come with the toolchain, and those libraries are built only for some platforms. A program that imports such a module builds only for the platforms its native library is built for.

Native libraryUsed bymacOSiOSLinux
Drawing: CoreGraphics, CoreText, ImageIO, Metalgraphics, and gui and everything that drawsyesyesno
Apple UI: AppKit, UIKitguiyesyesno
Audio: CoreAudio, AudioToolboxmediayesyesno
OpenSSLnet/socket and the network modules above it, cryptoyesnoyes
SQLitedata/sqlite, and the chat history in aiyesyesyes
PCRE2regex, and find and replace in codeyesyesno
Tree-sittercode/syntaxyesnono
Terminal emulationos/terminal-emulatoryesnono
WebKitgui/web-view, gui/web-sign-inyesnono
AVFoundationgraphics/movieyesnono
  • Most graphics modules draw through the drawing library. /graphics/primitives, /graphics/point, /graphics/color and /graphics/matrix do not, and build everywhere.
  • ai uses graphics, so it builds where graphics does.
  • /os/mach-port uses Mach ports, which only Apple's systems have.

Form index

Every Brix form, by its head, with its shape, what it means, and the entry that explains it. The forms are grouped as the compiler's form catalog groups them, and a head with several shapes has a row for each.

A shape names each slot of the form with the kind of thing it takes, as name:Kind. A slot followed by ? may be left out, * repeats it any number of times, and + at least once. / joins the kinds a slot accepts, as in Expr/Block. A word in the shape that has no kind, such as This or :static, is written as it stands. Operators and other symbols, and how they are written in rows, are in the symbol index.

A form marked "Not built yet" is in the catalog, but the compiler does not build what it means yet: a program that uses it is refused or fails to build, except *., which reads only one member. A form marked "Not supported yet" is refused with a message. A form marked "Reserved" is read, and kept for a meaning to come.

is(is base:Type)The style sheet this one derives from. It inherits the base's slots and rules, and overrides a slot with (prop + name _ (= value)).Styles: Themes
for(for tag:Name+)The tags under which a derived style sheet applies, such as light or dark. It follows (is ...).Styles: Themes
style-extend(style-extend name:Type row:Style/Member*)Rules added to a style sheet declared elsewhere.Styles: Extending a sheet
rule(rule name:Name parameter:Param? use:Use* row:Style*)A named style rule.Styles: Style sheets
own-rule(own-rule name:Name parameter:Param? use:Use* row:Style*)A style rule written in another that reaches only the markup of the class of the element the other is applied to, not what is written in the element's body or given its slots.Styles: Nested rules, own rules and generated content
when-style(when-style state:Expr row:Style*)Rows that apply while the element is in a state.Styles: States
when-style(when-style state:Expr body:Inline)The same, with one row.Styles: States
style-set(style-set state:Name name:Name value:Expr)One style value that applies while the element is in the named state.Styles: States
keyframes(keyframes name:Name parameter:Param? kind:Atom duration:Expr row:Keyframe*)A keyframe animation or motion: a slot whose value calls the builder its kind names. A parameter makes it a shape, which (shape name value) binds.Styles: Keyframes
=(= name:Name value:Expr)A setting the builder takes, such as repeat.Styles: Keyframes
range(range property:Keyed from:Expr/Hole to:Expr/Hole option:Named*)A property that moves from one value to another. _ leaves an end out.Styles: Keyframes
track(track property:Keyed option:Named* stop:Stop*)A property that passes through its stops.Styles: Keyframes
at(at at:Expr value:Expr option:Named*)The value at a point of the animation.Styles: Keyframes
shape(shape shape:Expr value:Expr)A shape bound to a value, as shake:3 binds shake to 3.Styles: Keyframes

State machines

HeadShapeMeaningSee
state(state target:Expr trigger:Trigger? row:State/Step*)A state, what enters it, and what happens in it.State machines: Cases
then(then target:Expr trigger:Trigger? row:Any*)A move to another state.State machines: Transitions
else-state(else-state target:Expr)When no move before it applies, leave the named state. It does not enter it.State machines: Fallbacks
trigger(trigger kind:Atom part:Any+)What causes a move, or what a whenever-rule watches.State machines: Transitions

Probes

HeadShapeMeaningSee
probe(probe target:Any part:Any*)Run a step only when the probe is on.Probes: Statement probes
probe-count(probe-count target:Any amount:Expr? deps:Block?)Count an event. The block names what the count reads.Probes: Counters
probe-group(probe-group mark:Atom target:Any part:Any*)Open or close a group of probe output.Probes: Groups
probe-assign(probe-assign target:Any value:Expr deps:Block?)Record a value. The block holds rows that belong to the probe.Probes: Events and property sets
probe-log(probe-log target:Any part:Any*)Record a line of output.Probes: Logs
items:(items: value:Any+)The values a probe logs.Probes: Events and property sets
